Resident Evil 4 (2005)

The graphics are honestly the least of my concerns. For its time, they were probably great – but after 20+ years, that’s not really the issue.

What really bothers me is the control scheme. I’m playing with an Xbox 360 wireless controller on Windows 10, and aiming just feels frustrating. Resident Evil 1–3 were more about getting used to the controls, but here the game expects fast and precise aiming – and that’s exactly where it falls apart for me. The reticle constantly sways (probably for “realism”), but it just makes hitting smaller targets unnecessarily tedious. Shooting those hanging blue medallions feels like a chore – especially if you’re expected to hit around 15 of them for achievements.

The camera doesn’t help either. Enemies can get right up close and hit you without you ever seeing them coming, because you’re busy dealing with the ones in front of you. If that’s an intentional design choice, then it’s just not working for me.

Maybe this is just how Resident Evil 4 is supposed to feel – but then it’s probably just not for me. It also makes me wonder if Resident Evil 5 plays the same way.

Curious to hear what others think. Is it just something you get used to, or has it simply aged poorly?

The original Resident Evil 4 is and has always been one of the greatest entries in the series, contrary to what the LARPers and tourists who don't actually play the games will tell you ("I didn't get the Carlos DLC"). It goes without saying that it is possible to enjoy the 2023 Remake and the original simultaneously as both games are fun and do the story justice. Just had to add that bit in there because I have seen an uptick of people online who cry about the old games and "muh tank controls" and quiver at the thought of playing a game made before 2015.

All that aside, RE4 is an excellent game which did a lot for the survival horror genre and the franchise as a whole. The biggest standout from past RE games is the addition of an over the shoulder perspective, a trait which would become a staple in subsequent games. I remember playing this game for the first time as a kid and feeling that this was a groundbreaking improvement from the shooting mechanics of the earlier titles. As far as features go, this game has nothing but content. Mercenaries and the side stories like Assignment Ada and Separate Ways are obvious standouts here.

A lot has been said about this game since its initial release that I won't rehash here. There is quite literally over two decades of buzz about this game. I'll mainly just add my two cents here and say that this game (and the Remake) should definitely be on your radar if you like RE games and survival horror in general. The story is good, the characters are memorable, dialogue is just cheesy enough at times, and the experience is quite memorable even all these years later. This game will always hold a special place in my heart and will always be one of my most favorite games of all time. Give it a shot.

Even on the hardest difficulty, it's genuinely hard to put down because it just has so much fun content to offer from start to finish. Every weapon has a special use case that makes it super effective if applied properly, every enemy encounter is structured in a way that makes individual rooms a joy to mow down, and it never lets anything get in the way of the core gameplay loop. In an era of games that pad themselves with needless side content, mediocre subplots and fetch quests, Resident Evil 4 deserves utmost praise for its dedication to remaining a corny action/horror B-movie at all times. Even though the remake replicates a lot of the same attributes, I still believe that this is the superior game. Not only because it revolutionized third-person shooters, but because I wear an ear-to-ear grin throughout every subsequent playthrough.

Picked this up after playing remake since everyone was arguing which one was better. Really great game.

I'd argue it's a different type of game than remake, but this one is closer to the resident evil formula while the remakes tried to reinvent the originals into modern third person shooters. I still enjoy them and think they're well made, but they were absolutely made that way to be as inoffensive as possible to appeal to the modern gamer that never played anything before RE7.

Took maybe an hour to get used to what I thought was a worse aiming and movement system, but it really did becoming super satisfying to play once I figured it out as well as how to quickly change weapons in inventory. It's been said before but not being able to move while shooting or look behind yourself without turning Leon really makes situations more intense and forces you to make decisions. Each gun is good in certain situations and new situations arise as you go through the game more, allowing for each gun to be useful. They all feel satisfying to use, especially the handguns because you can always use them to stun an enemy if you land a headshot, which you can't do in remake for some reason. Durability not being a factor on the knife is appreciated and the kick is a great get out of ♥♥♥♥ button. This was also the game that made me appreciate the quick turn button, which is super useful and speeds up movement tremendously.

Exploration is great and there aren't really any points where backtracking gets annoying. The pacing of the game is much better than remake and it feels like every chapter ends when its supposed to; nothing gets dragged on too long. 

Atmosphere, graphics, and style are all great. The remake does look great graphically but it doesn't add anything that you didn't expect to be there, like checking off the "good graphics" box on the list of what needs to be included. I think most people will find themselves looking around and appreciating the "look" of og more than remake. A lot of people seem to like older games' graphics because they think the idea of older graphics are appealing, but in reality the reason why is because they just look good lol. RE4 og is appealing not because the graphics are old but because they look good. The audio levels are also balanced much better so voices aren't muted down like they are in remake. Ambient sound is also actually audible and it really adds to the atmosphere.

The talk about dialogue being changed between the two is a bit overblown but there is some merit. The calls with Hunnigan and the villains are way better in og mainly because the ui is boring in remake and for some reason they removed the villain calls. The reason for the removal seems to be Capcom's desire to make remake into a serious story with goofy elements contained to Leon's quips, which are only really said during combat or outside of cutscenes. The original seemed to be a story that took itself seriously (meaning it respected the universe it was in) and integrated goofiness within itself, which is what most people refer to when they talk about how resident evil has "never been a goofy game." Also Leon's quips in remake kind of sound like a pale imitation of what he's supposed to be in og, but its not that big of a problem.

Highly recommend, great game. Might take an hour or two to get used to the older aiming and movement system but I promise its really rewarding. Would have to replay remake to see what I like more but for right now they are tied for what I think is the best RE game.

I suspect by now everyone knows Resident Evil 4 is good. Its release changed the way we think about action games and even now it is still used as a benchmark against which all 3rd person over-the-shoulder shooters are measured. It changed the direction of the Resident Evil series and acted as the first plot cleansing of the series. Blah blah blah, no new information there. The question then is what reason does someone have to pick up the 2005 original now that the remake is out?

First and most obvious, value for money. The original is $20 USD at time of writing and frequently goes on sale for less than $5. Much cheaper than the remake which is $50 including the DLC. This is for a game that, as mentioned, still plays great even now 20 years on. It’s an easier game than the remake and feels a bit clunkier, but not in a detractive way. Furthermore since it’s an older game by now you can run it on everything. They’re also about the same length in terms of playtime too so it’s not like you’re getting less game if you’re the type that values hours per dollar.

The second and larger difference in the change in tone between the two games. The original is a lot goofier than the remake. Leon is a wisecracking dork whose attempts at being cool were so lame that they somehow wrapped back around to being cool. Ashley, Ada and Ingrid are all excellent foils for Leon's bravado. All the villains are far closer to cartoon characters than horror movie monsters and as a consequence the banter between the characters and situations they put each other in are a lot more ridiculous.  Personally I prefer this to the more serious writing, acting and set pieces of the remake, although I’ll grant you that is a personal preference. At the very least it makes it more unique amongst the series.

Put another way, the difference between the two would be that while the remake is slicker and technically more impressive, the original is the one you quote with your friends. I’m going to avoid the thing I’ve noticed a lot of reviewers do where they discuss this game and the remake in a sort of zero-sum way since I think it’s actually a bit more complicated than one just being “better” than the other. The remake is undeniably richer in gameplay, but I'm not convinced that the improvements made by that game are sufficient to wholly discard the original. 

If money is tight, hardware is limited or you're a fan of sillier writing get the original. Then if you like it, try the remake in a few years. Likewise if you got the remake and found it fun if a bit dry, boot up the original.

ENG:

Almost twenty years after its release, RE4 remains an experience that every fan of the genre absolutely must try at least once. Despite the recent remake (which I haven't finished yet, but from what I remember, it was solid), the 2005 original maintains a unique and incredibly satisfying feel. I’m not saying the remake isn’t up to par, that would obviously be a lie but the original has a soul and a pacing that, in my opinion, remains unbeaten.

I often see a lot of hate for Ashley online that I just don't get. In the 2005 version, she responds to "Wait" and "Follow" commands with surgical precision. If you tell her to stay put, she stays exactly where you told her. This allows for a more tactical approach, letting you leave her in a "safe" spot on the map while you move ahead to clear the area (though it's still better not to stray too far). Resident Evil 4 was my first real introduction to the Resident Evil (Biohazard) franchise. While I haven’t played every entry, I’ve followed the series closely ever since — and it all started here.

One of the first things that stands out is the tone. The dialogue is quirky, sometimes outright ridiculous, but the game never presents itself in a way that expects you to take it too seriously. Because of that, it mostly lands well — either as genuine charm or just good humor. It has a very distinct identity that sets it apart from more grounded horror experiences.

Gameplay is where the game really shines. It’s extremely fun and consistently satisfying. You’re not just shooting your way through enemies — you’re learning how to deal with different situations using the tools available to you. Whether it’s using the environment, managing positioning, or figuring out the best way to handle certain enemy types, there’s always a layer of strategy involved that keeps things engaging.

The inventory system is another standout feature. It’s limited by space rather than weight, and organizing it becomes a game in itself. It has a very “Tetris-like” feel to it, where you’re constantly rearranging items to maximize efficiency. It’s simple, but surprisingly addictive, and adds another layer of decision-making to the experience.

The game also has strong replay value. Once you understand the mechanics and flow, it becomes very rewarding to go back and optimize how you approach different encounters, or even complete a playthrough using a completely different toolset. With so many weapons available — and limited space to carry them — you’re naturally encouraged to experiment and approach the game in different ways each time.

If there’s one downside, it’s Ashley. Escorting her can sometimes make your mission feel unnecessarily difficult, and there are moments where protecting her becomes more frustrating than fun. That said, it’s also part of the experience — and by the end of the game, it adds to your overall sense of achievement… along with a healthy dose of resentment for the sections where you had to guard her.

Overall, Resident Evil 4 is a standout entry that blends action, strategy, and personality into something that still holds up extremely well. It’s easy to see why it became such an influential title, and why so many people consider it a classic.

When Resident Evil started making remakes, this was the game I was hoping they would revisit. So I was more than elated when they did — and while I consider the remake to be incredible, it also has a different identity to this game.

This game is extremely accessible hardware, piracy, and cost wise and the PC port doesn't suffer from any significant instability issues despite its age unlike other games such as GTA-4 and Fallout New Vegas. 
In regards to gameplay the games combat system takes center stage and to this day remains a unique, engaging, and rather intuitive system. Different weapons classes and individual weapons have different very exaggerated capabilities that should be exploited to conserve the resources your provided. Enemies react to shot placement in satisfying and consistent ways. Shoot an enemy in the head and they stop or stagger back to cover their eyes, shoot them the arm and they drop what they're holding and lurch to the side, shoot them in the leg while they're moving and they'll crouch down or even fall over completely allowing you to follow up with a knife to save ammo. Shotguns provide crowd control with wide and exaggerated shot patterns that knock down or simply kills attackers, Rifles let you pick off dangerous and tanky enemies that might not react to your other weapons as consistently, and finally the TMP provides much needed flexibility and volume to replace the handgun in emergencies or against weak or vulnerable targets. The combat system alone makes the modern remake look like a complete joke in comparison but there's others more involved in that who are probably better at explaining the issues anyways

Despite the small playtime on steam, I used to own the 2014 version on console and it more or less is just a port of that HD remaster but to PC, and it's as every bit as fun as I'd remembered it - moreso after starting a long standing franchise marathon of most all of the canon entries.

This game is probably one of my top three most favorite Resident Evils and it fights tooth and nail to keep that spot, not with post content or modernized game engine, not even a really relatable selection of cast members either. No this game stays high in my heart because of how good everything feels, the attention to certain details, cheesy dialogue at practically every turn that breaks away from the B-Movie hero dialogues from RE2 and RE3, gunplay that's incredibly smooth and intricate with certain weakpoints or interactions, and more.

Starting off with the story, it's honestly as silly and over the top as it gets before jumping the shark too hard; 6 years after the events of Resident Evil 2, Leon is working as an operative for the US Government to go rescue the president's daughter who had been abducted mysteriously and suddenly, heading into southern america as intel points that's her possible last known location, only to end up jumping headfirst into a new nightmare with the sole purpose to save the girl. 
Just from the spoiler-free synopsis it's easy to tell they've abandoned most of the up front horror for something far more action packed, setting that biological horror as more of an obstacle that Leon must overcome, and it only gets more insane the longer it goes in what I feel is the best ways the series could've gone.

Combat in general started getting more intricate with this one, shifting from the fixed camera perspectives for an over the shoulder (Sometimes Second Person, Sometimes Third Person) with a proper aim you can adjust and drag to whatever you want freely. But not just the mechanical improvements from the engine upgrades, but as well there's incentives to go for more than just headshots; shooting limbs will make enemies drop their weapons or even funnier yet blow up explosives in their hands, or make them stagger/kneel for prompt based melee attacks that do both incredibly high damage as well as crowd control stagger. Combine all of that with the merchant/store system unique to a handful of RE games, you can upgrade gear to absurd proportions that make it cathartic as a zombie shooter instead of a stressful survival horror.

Location designs I think is extremely good for what they chose, there's no shortage of interesting spots from the village in the introduction, to a [spoiler]run down castle filled with spanish themed decor and embossed pieces of valuable furnishings, trophies, and suits of medieval armor[/spoiler], and a few other spots worth making the playthrough for.

Characters themselves are almost all charming, fun, or interesting in their own regards; this was the start of Leon being the snarky one-liner machine who has a quip for literally every single thing that happens in his general vicinity, Ashley is kind of a brain off college campus kind of girl but she isn't standing around useless - even going out of her way in some cases to help Leon directly, Hunnigan is straightforwardly a bit of a no-nonsense handler for Leon to make sure the mission goes as smooth as possible, and the personalities go on. (I'll avoid spoiling the best lad's personality here, but there's a mention of Ballistics somewhere there.)


There's also some very real pain points though, like for starters; the age of the game and how clunky it can get without some simple qol mods for visual fidelity or control rebinding is a bit of an objective turn off for some, they didn't exactly record a massive number of soundfiles for enemy lines so you eventually hear them repeat the same 5 lines gratingly on loop several dozen to hundred times over the course of the game. I'll also say the soundtrack isn't as good as older games, it has positive moments for certain, but aside the Saferoom OST and generic "Combat" soundtrack there's really not a lot to write home about here.



I would strongly recommend this game even at full price, any sales is a huge steal for this game, between being fun to practice speedrunning with or just being a very replayable story based "Zombie" game, there's a lot of fun to be had either in the main story or the handful of extra modes that are included after the first clear of the main story.

One of the best and most influential games of all time. Do not be fooled by the existence of its remake. This game stands the test of time, it plays extremely well today still, and its design is actually better crafted than that of its remake (as great as the latter is).

The original actually has more content and set pieces than the remake. Despite that, it takes fewer hours to complete. Why? Because the pacing is faster, resulting in an experience that is not only more varied, but also more fun. 

The combat loop is another thing that I find more satisfactory in the original than in the remake. In the original, every precise shot guarantees that the enemy will be staggered, which means that you can consistently and reliably use the melee action. This is different in the remake, where there is a factor of randomness that determines whether the enemy will be staggered or not. In higher difficulties this factor is so low that it turns the melee action into a very unsafe and unreliable one, resulting in a simplified gameplay loop where you find yourself just shooting at enemies from a distance. This waters down and simplifies the gameplay that made the original so memorable and engaging.

The atmosphere is also superior in the original, in my estimation. The remake went for a darker and more serious atmosphere more typical of horror stories, whereas the original has that "horror in broad daylight" vibe that made it so unique. The castle in the remake feels generic, more like a bland dungeon than a castle. Meanwhile, the original's castle feels as majestic as it feels oppressive (and it had better music, too). 

If you play this with the HD Project mod, it feels almost like a game released today. The remake is great and very fun on its own merits, but do not make the mistake of thinking that it replaces the original. This game is still one of the best games ever made. It was so 20 years ago, and it is still so today.

Reviewing this game is redundant, you all know what RE4 (2005) is. It is to gaming what Skyrim is to modding, a game so innovative and influential that it will stand the test of time forevermore.

This game pioneered over-the-shoulder camera, it brought RE into the 3D era a lot smoother than Code: Veronica poorly attempted to.  A lot of people cry that the action RE's "killed the series" but OG2 and OG3 were very action-heavy and Shinji Mikami has always said RE4 was the type of RE game they wanted to make since the series' inception.  These games aren't scary, and when they drop that pretense and give you bombastic action against cults, zombies and the like, what you get is a timeless masterpiece that feels fantastic despite being twenty-one-years-old and rising. 

I do, overall, prefer the RE4 remake but it says a lot that I can still come back to this while playing it side by side with 4R and find things to love and appreciate in both.  RE4 didn't just birth the modern action formula of RE, it also birthed Dead Space, another superb series that deserves its flowers in the annals of gaming history.

There's things I prefer in this over the Remake like so:
*Although the knife has less utility and mechanical depth, it's a great ammo-saver even on New Game Professional which I played as my most recent playthrough, using the re4tweaks mod to give the game a more modern FOV.  You can down a Ganado and knife stunlock them and it's endlessly satisfying.
*The Silver Ghost pistol is just better in this than the remake, landing critical headshot explosions well before you even buy the Exclusive upgrade.
* Krauser's backstory and voice acting is better.
* More environmental interactivity.  I know the remake had the eyes you could shoot on the Novistadore nest, but the OG lets you down it with sheer firepower and gives you dozens of jewels as a prize. Very satisfying.

Things I hate about the OG:
* Separate Ways is lazy and sucks balls.
* Assignment Ada will always be mid.
* Crashes, especially on windows 11.
* "HD edition" needs a mod called HD project to actually look HD.
* Default binds for inventory management require tweaking an .ini file.
* Mandatory QTEs which don't have an auto-complete like the updated versions of 5 and 6. 
* Ashley's AI.
* Island section is worse than the remake which trims the fat massively.
* Less an issue with the game version, but Leon's pinstripe suit has never looked good to me and I wish I could have him in his default outfit while allowing Ashley to be in the Knight armor. Thankfully, 4R remedies that.

Anyway go play this, it's timeless and has barely aged a day.

I always played the first stage in RE4 and RE3 but I never got bothered to play them past that. Well now I played 1 to 4 (the original ones, I plan to play the remakes after I finish the whole mainline series). Take into consideration this review doesn't take into account the games that came after, only the mainline ones that came before it (1, 2 and 3). With that being said, Resident Evil 4 is one of the best games of all time but it's not even the best Resident Evil game. After playing the first three original games from the PS1 era it even feels like a spinoff after spending those first games all in raccoon city with S.T.A.R.S. and wesker (he shows up in this but for like 2 seconds and for a dlc) and the t and g virus and the tyrants (mr x, nemesis). I get that they couldn't use raccoon city anymore after the ending of 3 but still, it feels like they changed a lot more than that. They introduce a completely new area (Spain) and a completely new zombie disease (las plagas) with a main mission that feels like a sidequest (rescue the president's daughter) compared to what was at stake in the very first games it feels like an underwhelming task. The only actually scary part about this game is the very first time you encounter a regenerator which makes you feel extremely helpless and terrified and even then you later find a thermal scope to fight them off so it's not scary anymore. Everything before and after that is more leaning towards an action game. Still, the core game is incredible. Even if it feels like a spinoff it's like one of the best spinoffs ever made, the village feels like an actual village and everything is extremely detailed, if you shoot at fish they react, if you shoot at lightbulbs they break, the hens lay eggs in the farm if you stay for a long time and not scare them, the zombies react to the shots depending on where you shoot them, you shoot a pendant that's hanging on a ceiling and if you don't shoot at a wooden plank to close the well with dirty water below it you'll pick up the pendant but it's all muddy and won't be worth as much when you sell it compared to if you actually shot at the plank and let it fall on the well's lid so that it's actually clean, along many other super cool details. It's also the goriest game out of the first 4 games which is definitely what i expect from a resident evil game. All of this included with the graphics for 2005 was an insane technical feat, it really feels like the attention to detail only a multimillion dollar budget can give you and it shows. This definitely passes the test of time and it's only on some character model faces during cutscenes where you can see some aging in the technology, otherwise this game feels fresh and unique even 21 years later. This game deserves every bit of love it receives, my only complain is that I was expecting more development in the entire story that was being developed in the first three games, all of a sudden this game starts like "hey remember that one corporation we were trying so hard to dismantle during the first three games? Well it doesn't exist anymore because they went bankrupt lmao sorry". Which is super anticlimactic, like all that buildup they were amassing with Chris and Jill in RE1 and 3 and Leon's ending in his B scenario in RE2 led nowhere. Anyways, I still recommend this game to all gamers, this is a must play for everyone, this is definitely one of those games that you should play at least once in your life because it encapsules the spirit of what makes amazing games, amazing games. 9/10

[h1][u]A Brief Introduction[/u][/h1]
If you’re even seeing this review, it’s almost a guarantee you’ve heard of the Resident Evil franchise. The pioneer of survival horror. The front runner in zombie games. And if you know anything about Resident Evil, you know about Resident Evil 4.

For its time, RE4 was a shocking big step for the franchise. The first three games had been slow, tense survival games where you suffered from limited resources, complex puzzles, and the ever-dreaded fixed camera angles. RE4 was a wild new direction; a third person action shooter where you could suplex zombies and roundhouse kick their heads clean off. Normally this kind of drastic tone shift would be the death knell for a franchise desperate to find a new hook…. but almost all Resident Evil fans LOVE the fourth entry. Want to find out why? 

[h1][u]In-Depth Analysis[/u][/h1]
[h1]Gameplay[/h1]
As aforementioned, Resident Evil 4 was a turning point for the franchise… and not everyone liked where the series went after this. But this was the first time we got a real focus on gunplay from the franchise, with a third person controllable camera instead of the famous fixed camera angles of the original games. In older games you pointed whatever weapon still had ammo at the nearest shambling enemy and hoped you got lucky with a headshot or it eventually stopped moving. RE4 added (perhaps not pioneered, but certainly featured) mechanics such as locational damage, aiming down sights, and other first steps of modern gunplay. You can shoot an infected in the leg to cause them to collapse, in the arm to drop their weapons, or in the head to stagger them for a kick.

Still, while RE4 was the grandfather of third person shooters in the same way that Doom was the daddy of FPS, it has suffered somewhat in the aging department. The game made great strides in many ways that inspired innumerable TPS copycats, but as one of the first to do it, we also had remnants of the older, not so good ways.
https://steamcommunity.com/sharedfiles/filedetails/?id=3701678660
RE4 is very much a product of its time (2005, to be specific), for good and bad. The game can ONLY be played with tank controls, a layout in which the player cannot strafe, but instead can only move forward or backwards and turn. The inventory is a sorted grid, which must be sorted manually, and can be extremely tedious to deal with if you have a lot of random items bogging you down. The third person camera is a bit too far off to the side instead of actually over the shoulder, making the provided laser sights on every weapon legitimately mandatory for shooting any enemy further than a few feet in front of you.

Despite the fact I am accustomed to old, clunky games (Go try out Phantasy Star Online EP1&2 if you want TRUE clunky), I find that Resident Evil 4 is still remarkably playable, just awkward to handle. The tank controls and awkward camera angle make aiming half a fight against your own laser reticle as much as the enemy, but the game’s pacing ensures that you’re rarely pressured to hit your shots RIGHT NOW. Extremely fast enemies only appear later in the game, after you’ve been given time to adjust.
https://steamcommunity.com/sharedfiles/filedetails/?id=3701679066
Instead, Resident Evil 4 provides a different sort of tension than its older siblings, in the form of swarms. Enemies slowly close in from all angles, at all times, boxing you in, forcing you to stop and shoot. Ammo management is tight; if you’re a good shot, you’ll always have enough ammo to get the job done, but only just enough. If you’re settling for bodyshots and mag dumping into basic infected, you’ll find yourself surrounded with only a few bullets in no time.

At the end of the day, the gameplay is old, but it's still perfectly enjoyable, and a fascinating time capsule showing people what 2005 console gaming felt like. There were definitely times that I felt like a death was absolutely more of the game’s fault than my own, and I’m not the biggest fan of Ashley’s follower mechanics (especially not the fact she can die to friendly fire), but she spends most of the story kidnapped and not with Leon, so I never felt like she was an active detriment to my enjoyment.

I do want to give a special shoutout to Quick Time Events, a mechanic I am absolutely glad DIED over a decade ago. If there is one thing I must complain about, it is RE4’s fetish for QTE spam. They force QTEs wherever and whenever they can, and often many with extremely narrow windows. It’s not the same button either, as it can swap between several just to force you to stay alert for a button mashing jumpscare. Some of them are genuinely demanding too, requiring you to actually mash your keyboard or else suffer a scripted death. I hate these. Everyone hates these. It’s just how gaming used to be for a few years in the early 2000s before we all realized, “Wait…. These are terrible.” Glad they’re gone.

[h1]Story[/h1]
Every Resident Evil game is a mix between delightfully goofy and delightfully intelligent. Resident Evil 4 definitely leans more on the goofy side, and I can’t tell if it's intentional half the time. The president’s daughter, Ashley Graham, has been kidnapped, and Leon is the man to rescue her. Wacky cultist shenanigans ensue. 

There’s a good chance if you know anything about RE4 Leon, it’s that he is an absolute dork, and every villain is just as unserious as him. Ramon Salazar feels like a Saturday morning cartoon villain, cackling and busting out Scooby-Doo traps on his guests for the fun of the game. Saddler acts like a sassy old man indulging his kids in a game of pretend. It is profoundly difficult to take the game seriously…. So I don’t! Resident Evil 4 has got to be one of the funniest games I’ve ever played.
https://steamcommunity.com/sharedfiles/filedetails/?id=3701679768
However, more seriously, I’d say the side characters suffer a lot in the memorability department, as many are shallow or barely have any screen time. If you’re coming from RE4 Remake, be prepared to be vastly disappointed by how much of a useless, boring bum 2005 Luis is. The remake added a lot of depth to many characters that was completely absent in the original.

[h1]Visuals[/h1]
RE4 looks about as good as a two decade old game can look. It’s dated, but it does the best with what it has. Models do look awkward, and definitely unrealistic, but that was just how things were at the time. It definitely suffers from the “everything is beige and grey” problems that early 2000s gaming had, so don’t expect cheery or interesting environments. I think the walls of Salazar’s castle looked dirtier than the last public bathroom I was in. 

[h1]Audio[/h1]
The game sounds about as old as it is too. Sound effects are simple, and many are just grunts or stock sound effects. Shooting metal sounds like a noise from Looney Tunes. An amusing tidbit of knowledge is that despite taking place in Spain, the enemies speak in a South American accent. Most of the dialogue is enemies muttering random Spanish phrases, like “Behind you!” or “Death, death, death.” It's alright.

[h1]Technical[/h1]
I suffered a rather unique problem. The game runs well, at a stable framerate. However, what it does NOT do is render in widescreen or ultrawide well at all, chopping off the entire bottom of the window and stretching the rest of the screen. I had to download a program called “Flawless Widescreen” that thankfully you can easily find an RE4 specific fix to make it compatible.

There is also a notorious door transition crash in one of the last rooms of the game that forced me to redo nearly 30 minutes of a tedious, unfun section. Left a sour taste in my mouth.

[h1]Conclusion[/h1]
[h1][u]Clunky, but a classic nonetheless. Pick it up if you want to experience one of the best old console shooter classics.[/u][/h1]

Resident Evil 4.

I've had this game in my library for quite some years already, even made a couple of attempts to play it in the past, but never got further than the first village section. And it's kinda crazy, as I've always been a fan of the RE franchise. Of course, that came from what I'd read on magazines about the games, watch on gaming-related TV shows, or what little I'd play at my cousin's house, as he owned a PS1 while I didn't. I also enjoyed the first two RE movies back as a kid.

Anyway, onto the franchise itself. With all the hype surrounding Resident Evil Requiem, I decided it was finally time to give the games a go, and decided to go back and finish this one first, before doing a chronological order playthrough (I didn't want to go with a release order playthrough as the original trilogy wasn't here on Steam, only the remakes, but it seems Capcom actually rectified that). Before playing, though, I did download the Resident Evil 4 Tweaks mod (not sure if it's related to the HD project), as I remembered the game having issues otherwise. And thus, I started playing, and I became hooked with it.

Now, I'm aware that Resident Evil 4 changed the nature of the franchise, going from a fixed camera perspective to an over the shoulder third person shooter style. This also caused a shift in gameplay, towards something more action oriented. Of course, I'm talking without actual experience in the previous games, but in this case, I'd say the gameplay here is extremely solid and enjoyable, and while it's not full-on survival horror, sometimes I did feel the need to scavenge for supplies. Starting out the game can feel threatening, as you begin with only a handgun, limited inventory space, and the enemies can feel overwhelming. As you progress, though, and get access to more weapons and upgrades (as well as learn certain combat tricks), it becomes an amazing experience.

The story is entertaining; you play as Leon Kennedy as he's sent to rescue the President's daughter, who's been kidnapped and is currently held at a small village in Spain. This village, however, holds a dark secret, as it's been taken over by a cult possessed by parasitic creatures known as "Las Plagas". While there are a few points in the story that I feel might be a bit weak, overall I'd say it's very good, and I loved that the game doesn't take itself too seriously, with Leon cracking jokes from time to time.

The game offers a lot of replayability as well. Beating it for the first time unlocks Professional difficulty; basically hard mode, as well as the option to restart your cleared save file with new weapons unlocked. On top of that, you also unlock extra game modes, including the Separate Ways campaign, in which you play as Ada Wong, getting to see what she was up to during her encounters with Leon. Beyond the extra weapons, you can also unlock special costumes both for beating the main game and Separate Ways, and one of them becomes very useful for a Professional mode run, as, unlike the special weapons, costumes can be selected for any new game.

When it comes to graphics... Well, it's rather dated, and with some effects that, unless you use the mod I mentioned above, might bother you. I remember my first attempt trying to play the game gave me motion sickness, something that didn't happen this time around. Even then, it looks pretty decent, as I'm never really bothered by old graphics. The soundtrack is good, with a sort of dynamic system, as the music might change depending on whether enemies have detected you or not.

Something I was forgetting to mention was that the game has plenty of boss fights, as, besides the regular enemies you'll fight (which are kinda like traditional zombies), you also get to fight some really hideous monsters. And the creature design for the monsters is, for a 2005 game, some truly horrific stuff. Expect lots of body horror.

All in all, a solid game, and one I see myself replaying for a third time further down the line. I recommend it.

I remember playing the original versions of this many years ago and being hooked, but so long after the fact and after so many newer iterations with actual move and shoot mechanics I thought my opinion of this game would have cooled down by now. It did not.

The original 2005 RE4 was a hallmark title for action games and for good reason. It's not just about how good it felt control-wise to play, but how all of the game's encounters and setpieces are perfectly setup around it, You always manage to feel both overwhelmed AND in control. The action is at a rather break-neck pace where you have to constantly have environmental awareness of all the foes converging on you, some significantly more deadly than others (those f@#$ing chainsaw freaks!) Overall, this is indeed the best version I've played, with a few caveats:

Pros:
-This version actually works on modern PCs easily
-Controls (specifically KB&M) are significantly better than the 2007 PC port (customizable too.)
-30/60 mode toggle (trust me, you want that 30 as well, see below.) Playing it in 60fps feels like a new game at times, despite its bugs.
-Choice of the original GameCube version graphics (not the muddled PS2/OG PC port) or a fresh new set of textures which look crisp at 1080p+ (played at 1440p.) Pretty much all UI elements got a very clean facelift as well.
-Best of all worlds in content, both Ada side contents are here along with Mercenaries mode and other unlocks
-You have achievements from the 360/PS3 versions and Steam goodies
-Plays excellent on Steam Deck even at high resolutions and low TDP settings.

Cons:
-It's easy to miss but the 60fps mode is kind of bugged in several spots. The game was never designed with this in mind due to fps and game speed being tied like many games of the time. If some things feel harder, it's not just you. This difference causes oddities like harder timing in several of the damned QTEs and unusually larger hitboxes for Leon, Ashley & Ada. This is mostly fixable with community patches like re4_tweaks.
-Not EVERYthing got the HD-ified treatment. Some textures/objects can still look really low quality and you also see it in the cutscenes for Ada's campaigns which are pre-rendered and really low res (this is based on the content coming from PS2 version which was made differently.)
-The quick time events and just how many there are. I didn't like them then and I still don't like them now. (Psst there's ways to negate them.)

Overall yes, I know RE4's been remade by now and it's wonderful, but still. Don't discount this iteration of the 2005 original. As it was originally designed it remains a masterpiece of action gaming and when you get into the flow of it's combat encounters it remains incredible still even 20+ years later.

Leon S. Kennedy has been my hero for as long as I can remember. But what really makes this game special is how alive it feels. The pacing is perfect. The story pulls you in and never lets go. Every area feels memorable, every encounter feels intentional, and somehow, even after all these years, it still manages to keep me fully locked in. Replaying it now didn’t just feel like playing a game. It felt like revisiting one of the rare good pieces of my childhood. The sounds, the atmosphere, the moments, I remembered more than I expected, and at the same time, I felt like I was experiencing it all over again.

I could honestly talk about this game all day, but I’ll keep it simple:

I love it. I always will.

[h1] Lightning in a bottle [/h1]

Two of the most important elements of a good game are [b] Engaging Core Gameplay Mechanics [/b] and its [b] Replayability Value [/b] , RE4 exceeded these conditions in leagues above any other games.

During the period when the Resident Evil series was going through an identity crisis, longtime collaborator Hideki Kamiya was assigned to give resident evil a fresh new start but his vision strayed far away from the classic Resident Evil formula, ultimately Shinji Mikami (Creator of Resident Evil franchise) stepped in and made a game that revolutionised the third-person shooter genre forever. 

The combination of Tank controls with the new Over-The-Shoulder camera made for a refreshing take in the horror-action genre unlike anything that ever came before. Taking the freedom of movement away from the player is never a good move but in a horror game it works on the contrary. It adds another layer of tension and uncertainty for the player to keep in mind while trying to survive an already hostile environment. For someone who's accustomed to modern triple AAA shooters, this took some time to getting adjusted to, but with the laser-point accuracy of your shots and the super-responsive controls in accordance with your actions led to a very satisfying gun combat experience. 

The story has its usual Resident Evil charm to it - Memorable boss fights, Unique locations and Amazing Action Set-Pieces spaced out well enough to keep you engaged and also keeping the story well-paced complimented with Leon's unapologetic charisma and confidence with his one-Liners as a cherry-on-top over everything. 

Combine everything I said above together and you will have a game that will provide a unique challenge but will also the provide you the tools to overcome that said challenge, making you want to revisit everytime for some more. Truely a [b] Lightning in a Bottle [/b] experience.

[h3] FUN FACT [h3] : Resident evil 4 went through 4 iterations before settling down on the final product that we see today. The very first iteration under Hideki Kamiya was so far devoid of the Resident Evil formula that CapCom gave him the permission to turn it into his own game which eventually became the [b] "Devil May Cry" [/b]  series and the 2nd iteration was turned into its own game [b]  "Haunting Grounds" [/b] , a very underrated survival horror game.

It's "clunky" if you haven't played the original RE games, but I found it easy to get used to having not played them, and after going back and playing said games, it feels great. 
Combat feels good, really playing into a risk-reward style where you can unload your ammo at the zombies with the potential to eventually run out, or get up close and personal when shooting to try getting a free kick in at the risk of being attacked yourself. I found myself early on playing at a distance swapping between guns, but at harder difficulties and in bigger hordes you really want to conserve as much as possible, making for really hectic combat scenarios. This is where the controls can make or break it for you, but thankfully you have options with what you want to use in 99% of your fights.
RE4 is also a lot funnier than the entries before it and even after. Salazar is stupid funny, Leon feels almost absurd, and a good chunk of the jokes are cheesy, but in the right way. Story is nothing like the previous entries, which could be a negative to some, pushing aside the long built up villainous Umbrella for a newer mostly unrelated crisis, but it also makes it a great entry point that also serves as a way to freshen up the series with more potential villains and new types of enemies.
There's a reason this is often touted as the best or most approachable in the series, and while I might personally find later and earlier entries better, I still absolutely recommend this game to anyone even slightly curious about Resident Evil.

Resident Evil 4 blew my 11 year old mind back when I first played it on my PS2 when it originally came out. Since then I've played it on the Wii, PS3 and PS4 and now Steam. Only on PS3 I didn't 100% it. Even when everyone else is playing and loving Resident Evil Requiem I decided to play RE4 for almost 50 hours (Beat it 3 times and Separate Ways twice) in a 2 week stretch and 100% it on Steam. Heck I love the original RE4 so much I've been hesitate and haven't played the RE4 remake yet.
Why do I love this game so much? 

First off nostalgia but honestly it still holds up. It set the standard for third person action games for 20 years and is still one of the definitive action horror titles. No matter how good you get at this game one false move can be punishing which helps the combat encounters always feel engaging. You have to be efficient which can lead to you being up close and personal with chainsaw wielding freaks trying to knife them on the ground. The weapons have satisfying feedback to them with enemies reacting to every bullet which makes the combat have such a visceral weight to it. There's a reason the Mercenaries mode is a fan favorite. 

RE4 is the one of if not the best paced game I've ever played making it so easily replayable. The opening chapters in the village have such an amazing creepy atmosphere. The castle and island just keep ramping things up on the action side yet they still manage to throw in tense moments. During all this it maintains such a perfect tone of campy fun horror. Leon is a national treasure for a reason with endearing one-liners. 

RE4 rewards exploration with hidden treasures that fund upgrading your weapons which fuels the gameplay loop beautifully. New game plus is always a joy running through with upgraded or unlocked weapons that break the game in a fun "victory lap" playthrough. Once you beat the game you unlock the extra modes which just keeps the momentum going of wanting to keep playing (aforementioned Mercenaries mode and Separate Ways). 

It's always bittersweet for me when I 100% RE4 because it's such a fun time while it lasts. Even after 2 decades of playing hundreds of games it's still one of my favorites. I hope for all the new RE fans who might have missed out on this masterpiece give it a try.

Ah yes the classic original 2005 Resident Evil 4. It's a masterpiece, I think it's fair to just put that out there immediately. 

This game was revolutionary and it pretty much forever changed the Resident Evil series. The atmosphere, sound design, gameplay, characters, all of it are top notch in this game.

Well, I know there isn't anything for me to say that hasn't already been said about RE4; as we all know, the game is goated and one of the best of its time (even now dare I say), however I still wanted to make a nice review about one of my childhood games.

For starters, this is the game that brought the RE series more toward a third-person style, since it introduced the whole over-the-shoulder view; before, every other RE game had fixed cameras. Apart from that, one of the many reasons why RE4 is so unique for its time is because of the motion capture technology used to create more fluid character movements; it really gives that extra authenticity because they all act with human-like movements and facial expressions, especially during the cutscenes.

[h3]Gameplay[/h3]
Gameplay-wise, this was the game that introduced Leon to many of us, and oh boy did he learn a lot of new tricks since his RE2 newbie debut! Roundhousing, straight-kicking or straight up suplexing enemies is certainly one of the high points of this game; it's also convenient since it gives Leon temporary i-frames (as well as many other animations.. wish I'd caught up with this mechanic back in my PS2 era), and is also quite satisfying tbh. Really helps to keep the gameplay fresh and not boring, since otherwise we'd just be shooting the bad guys like every other game ever. The QTEs present in the game are nostalgic for me as well, I remember struggling so much, especially in the mashing parts before, but now it's just a nice little extra mechanic, it's pretty cool to see Leon dodging bosses by pressing the correct buttons in time! On the other hand, I also love seeing all the "death scenes" present in the game, in case you happen to fail the cutscene's QTEs; really shows how much care was put into RE4! And not only during the QTEs, since Leon can actually die in many gruesome ways in this game lol; one that I totally forgot existed, for example, can happen in the castle, where the game introduces us to those bug-like enemies that fly around and latch onto Leon, and his death in case he's not healthy enough is literally having half his face corroded, falling to the floor and revealing his skull; both for the time and even now, there are some very graphic deaths, and I find it awesome! (like not the "dying like that" part, just that it's in the game lol)

[h3]"Must have" mods[/h3]
Anyways, I could keep on rambling about how cool the other stuff in the game is, but at least for now, I'd like to recommend two mods to literally improve your experience with the game, while keeping it vanilla!
So, the first one is [url=https://www.nexusmods.com/residentevil4/mods/101]RE4_tweaks[/url]; it gives you control over many QoL options that improves the way both the game and gameplay feels, and also provides some nice graphical improvements. The most game changing options for me were being able to actually increase the camera's FOV and using my mouse to look to the sides, making Leon much faster compared to the usual "hold A/D to look around" and quick turning, I mean even the 180º quick turn looks slow compared to using the mouse, it's much more convenient!

The second one is more of a remaster, and it's none other than [url=https://re4hd.com]RE4 HD Project[/url]! The 2 people behind most of the mod literally remade every model present in the game from scratch, making them look the best way they possibly can in this game. It's a very competent remaster that keeps everything vanilla, just much, much prettier! It certainly brings new life to the game if you're already used to playing RE4, so you should definitely at least give it a try. Just one little thing, this mod already includes RE4_tweaks, so in case you're thinking about trying it, there's no need to download the one I suggested before. Fun fact: This mod apparently took 8 whole years to be made... that's a lot of time. Show it some love! Also, in the link I provided, there's an "Extras" option where there's even more mods created by them to enhance other things within the game, so definitely check that out as well.

An honorable mention regarding mods would be the randomizers, they can randomize enemies, key item spawns and even the doors! I'll leave it here in case you're interested as well: [url=https://www.patreon.com/dukemods]Best RE4 Randomizer imo[/url]
There's also another mod worth mentioning called "World S", that changes pretty much everything, enemies, locations, items.

[h3]Final Farewell[/h3]

Resident Evil 4 is the first game that actually made me enjoy playing a full story game from start to finish. Before this, I tried games like Assassin’s Creed II and Hitman, But Resident Evil 4 was completely different for me. From the beginning the game keeps you engaged with constant action, enemies, and tense situations. There is almost no moment where the game feels slow.

What I liked the most is the gameplay. Managing ammo, upgrading weapons, fighting different types of enemies, and facing boss fights makes every chapter exciting. The combat feels very satisfying, especially when you use the shotgun or perform knife attacks after stunning enemies. The atmosphere and horror elements also add a lot to the experience, making every new area feel dangerous and interesting.

I enjoyed the game so much that I finished it in just two days on Normal difficulty, which was surprising for me because I usually lose interest in games quickly. After finishing it, I immediately started playing again on Professional difficulty because I wanted to experience the challenge and improve my gameplay.

Overall, Resident Evil 4 is one of the most engaging and addictive games I have played. It perfectly balances action, horror, and progression. For me, it’s a game that never felt boring and always made me want to keep playing the next chapter.

[h1]One of the Best if Not THE Best Game of All Time[/h1]
There's a reason this horror game released on the humble little GameCube two decades ago has been ported about as many times as Doom and Skyrim have been re-released. This game is why you have multiple console generations of third person action games. This is why AAA horror games never went back to tank controls. It's why entire franchises like Dead Space and Last of Us exist. Resident Evil 4 is a badass shot to the system that redefined both horror games and action games ever since, and is required reading for anyone who wants to know what a good video game looks like.

Resident Evil 4 follows Leon Kennedy diving into rural Spain to fight off cultists in order to save the US president's daughter. The story and premise is insane and divorced from the rest of the series. 4 stands as a bit of a soft reboot with no Umbrella corporation or zombies in sight. What is in sight is a terrific art style and setting full of excellent atmosphere and tension. Woodland Spain is truly nightmarish in this game with so many terrific set pieces and firefights. The opening shootout in the village, the El Gigante showdown, Salazar's castle, so many badass moments that are replayable and genre defining to this day.

What makes RE4 click is the synergy between your guns, your knife, and the context sensitive melee moves. This game has far more in common with a beat 'em up than a third person shooter. Much like a brawler, your goal is to cause enemies to whiff attacks, abuse i-frames, and pull off moves that do serious crowd control. The AI is designed to chase you until they're within close quarters shooting range, where they will slowly walk up to you. If you run, you will trigger their aggression and cause them to attack or chase you. You can use this to exploit the AI and quickly step back as they throw a punch at you, then knife them in the face, press the QTE button to kick them in the face, and watch them knock several enemies over. You can also shoot their weapons out of their hands and shoot each limb for a unique reaction. All of this is strategic and fun to take advantage of which opens enemies up to be punished. But considering how many enemies on the screen there are, and how many enemy types are capable of one-shotting you, you'll need to master this combat dance quick to get through its hardest moments.

The game has some of the best pacing of any game ever. You go from incredible combat scenario to scenario, many of them feeling like they could be fleshed out into their own action game. The bosses are among the best in the horror genre forcing you to adapt to different strategies. No two bosses or levels force you to do the same thing over and over. You have the greatest merchant in video game history allowing you to upgrade your gear. And when you beat the game? You can jump right back into New Game Plus with all your stuff carried over, and that awesome opening village section inviting you to try your endgame loadout once more. It is a game you want to keep popping in over and over again.

On top of the excellent campaign, you have multiple unlockable modes to play through once you're finished with it. You have Assignment Ada from the original release, and Separate Ways, which released with the PS2 port of the game. These two modes allow you to play as Ada and see what she was up to during Leon's campaign, and they have their own incentives to replay. The best mode by far is the Mercenaries mode, one of the greatest unlockables in any game. You have an arcade scoring mode where you play as five different mercs (Leon, Ada, Hunk, Wesker, and Krauser). You have four maps to choose from with tons of enemies and mini boss enemies and unique loadouts and character abilities. Even if you somehow got bored of the campaign, the Mercenaries mode can tide you over for dozens of hours.

It is HIGHLY recommended you download the [url=https://re4hd.com/?page_id=9303]HD Project[/url] mod for the PC version. It is a very faithful remaster by fans that takes the textures used to make the original game and upscales them to true HD textures. This mod also comes bundled with tweaks to make the game play better with mouse and keyboard controls which is awesome. Playing this steam port with this mod truly does make the game feel modern and refined.

If you somehow haven't played Resident Evil 4 yet, you owe it to yourself to check this game out. It is arguably the peak of the franchise, the horror genre, third person shooters, the list goes on. It is an all time masterclass in refined controls, action set pieces, combat design, dense and satisfying content, exciting pacing, and just pure unadulterated fun!

Resident evil 4 is one of the best games of all time, and I do not say that lightly. It is a masterclass of its kind and really proved the point that a game doesnt need to be all stoic and serious to be good. Its self aware and witty, and embraces its more comedic moments, I think thats what RE 5 and RE 6 got wrong, and what the remake got wrong as well, they took themselves seriously when the premise of these games arent serious to begin with!!! 

On the gameplay, I personally think its great, the tank controls really are only bothersome in professional mode towards the end... and also with the Krauser fight. The only thing that can be annoying are the QTEs but most of the ones that happen in fights you can dodge. Other than that it plays just fine. The level design and combat system are also brilliant, with various ways to stun foes, the weapon variety is also great and its super fun to figure out which weapons work best for the enemy type your going against. On the enemies themselves I do think theres some that can be rather spongey when in professional mode (mainly the dogs and novistadors) other then that the enemies are great, and theres enough variety throughout the three main areas that keep the game engaging. 

Boss battles are kind of lack luster, with some stand outs being the fight with Mendez and Krauser, most bosses are rather simple and go down pretty easy. But the villains themselves have great characterization and great banter with Leon! something that the remake doubles down on, unfortunately. :-( As for non villainous characters I think the cast is great! [b]An earthshaking classic and the founding father of the modern third-person shooter[/b]

In this, Leon Kennedy graduates from tank control cop to bonafide action hero . . . and a [i]still[/i] somewhat tankish one!  There's no left-to-right shuffle for dodging's sake, there's no shooting [i]as[/i] you move.  When you draw your gun, you plant your feet and [i]that's[/i] the patch you have pledged to defend -- and when you take off running, you fly fleetly forward like some big blonde [b]arrow[/b].  You aim your character like you aim his weapons!  Naturally, there's considerable [i]english[/i] you can put on your Leon's flight, and you can snap-turn 'im 180 degrees, too, to catch the sneakers at his back.  

The character controls are no-frills in comparison to the now, and while they might seem awkward after years of pan-dimensional navigation, your grandma could probably groove into the arcade simplicity of them in a few minutes.  The equally important part, the laser sight [b]blastin'[/b], is beyond all dissection and works like an utter dream -- especially on controllers with hall sticks -- lancing out that bold red beam in darkness and daylight, impossibly and [i]stylishly[/i].  You don't need to play this with a mouse, and for the original experience, you really should not; that laser beam really feels like an extension of your stick, and even if you can aim more accurately with the mouse, why would you [i]want[/i] to, when it destroys the tactile pleasure of it?  As for firing Leon from that metaphoric bow, it adds an immediacy to the gameplay that is astonishing to [i]this[/i] guy, who last played it on the Gamecube about twenty-something years ago.  When you take off running, you've made a commitment; when you start shooting, you've done the same.  You just throw down and [b]go[/b] and you work with whatever you've got.  There's no waffling for fine degrees of position or any mushy little glitch-dance to perform.  I can't imagine a modern game playing like this . . . but maybe they should, occasionally?

A technical marvel for its time, [i]RE4[/i] is insanely long for an actioner [i]even now[/i], boasting the kind of mad variety you usually only get in the games of your childhood dreams.  It's a supremely tuned experience with badly (but charmingly) written dialog, mushroomed to enormous proportions on a crazy-high budget (that seemed like it [i]actually[/i] all went into the game) and a cute, monkey-eared damsel whose escort missions are the most palatable in [i]video game history[/i], not only for the good sense your charge shows in the midst of a firefight, but for the ultra-cool pulp fiction rescues she sets up -- using your sniper rifle to blast off the steel bands of an imprisoning trap while she girlishly screams, shooting the legs from under drooling cult zombies that throw her over their shoulders like a sack of flour, and so on.  Gothic locales abound for the horror fan, including an autumnal European village straight out of the 19th century and a heavily mechanized castle that would have cost [b]twenty billion dollars[/b] in real life -- and the huge boss roster of gooey, expertly animated monsters keeps combat continually fresh.

You could talk about this forever:  the cheesy lines, the "balleestics," the adaptive difficulty that doesn't seem to exist unless you [i]peer[/i] extra-hard for it, the endless set-pieces of summer blockbuster scope.  But the best thing to do is to experience, or [i]re-experience[/i] it for yourself, and the way I'd recommend doing this is with the free HD texture and model pack, made by a couple Spanish bros who traveled the world to get the look of their upgrades just right.  And also a good hall effect controller, like one of those made by 8bitdo.

(So in the remake, you can't kick the doors open?  There's no "balleestics"?  They replaced cute monkey-eared Ashley with some sharp-faced little businesswoman who looks like Taylor Swift?  Why, why, why?  But I bought it anyway and will play it sometime soon, I guess.  There's no way on Earth it could [i]ever[/i] outdo the original, though.)

On February 3rd 2026 Capcom released an update to RE4 Remake that removed Denuvo, a DRM which requires a costant internet connection, and replaced it with the Enigma Protector. This DRM is supposed to prevent "cheating" (any kind of modding of the game) and it's russian developed.
Tested by the Youtube channel Digital Foundry in the video "Resident Evil 4 PC: Is New DRM Impacting Game Performance?" has been found that the Enigma Protector DRM causes an average of -10% in framerate drops, with dips of -40% in certain scenarios, way more than the original Denuvo DRM.

This is not the first time that Capcom decided to put Enigma in some of their older games: RE Revelations suffered major backlash from customers because of the major dip in perfomance, so much so they had to remove Enigma from the game for good and recently they released the original Dino Crisis series on Steam, a quick scouring of the forum will reveal a lot of customers unhappy with the perfomance of said games. You shoot a guy and his body will react allowing you to sometimes go up and hit a button to melee. You shoot a wooden door or shield, and you can break it. It's not just a reinvention of Resident Evil, but all third-person action shooters. 

Gone are the small but deadly encounters of the previous games, Resi 4 boldly opens with a horde hunting you through their warped village. Barricade the doors, the windows, and the mind; relinquish any semblance of comfort, find purchase in whatever control you can. 
It's the belly of every beast imaginable, and the only thing stronger than your enemies is your will to complete the mission. Save the President's daughter, save the world.

The interconnected labyrinths of past games are mostly replaced with funneling you through linear, layered environments: dilapidated wooden walkways, battered crenelations, contaminated labs — geography is suddenly a matter of life or death. It rarely ever feels like a hallway; the player is thrust forward with pacing so slick they won't feel a drag until the final zone, where the heightened action lasts too long and tension dissipates. 
This isn't just a byproduct of all these new systems coming together. The DLC (Separate Ways) unfortunately shows that fine-tuning is indeed a necessary ingredient. 

Throughout the game, there's that brilliant sensation of just barely getting by. Every challenge feels insurmountable, even hours after I beat them. The onslaught of enemies with increasing arsenals is a never-ending stream; metamorphosis on the player's behalf is not just ideal but necessary.
I am become Leon Kennedy, the egg-devouring, roundhouse-kicking, wise-cracking, plague-defying, destroyer of the rural Spanish populace.

Resident Evil coined the term "Survival Horror" on it's initial release when Capcom realized they needed shoppers to have a reason to purchase their games in stores. What better way than a flashy title or a few words printed at the top of the box? "Survival Horror" is what the Resident Evil marketing team came up with, and every imitator of the game has used this label since. But to kill a genre, all it takes is for the creator of said genre to switch gears and amaze audiences to COMPLETELY derail the direction a genre. 

Resident Evil 4 isn't hated for this sin, in fact it's praised for it. Horror games were completely derailed for awhile while simultaneously spawning a line of titles which I call "Horror Shooters" or "REvil 4 Clones", most of which were more fun than they had any right being. 

Corny, funny, and downright addicting, Resident Evil 4 is everything we love and hate about horror games all packaged together in goofy mess you almost feel ashamed for praising so much.

Resident Evil 4 (2005) is not just my favorite Resident Evil game, it is one of my favorite games of all time, and a huge reason for that is Leon.

From the moment the game begins, it feels special. The opening village encounter is unforgettable and still stands as one of the strongest introductions in gaming. The atmosphere is tense, oppressive, and perfectly paced. Every location feels carefully crafted, from the eerie village to the unsettling castle and the intense island sections. The game always knows when to push you forward and when to give you just enough room to breathe.

The gameplay changed the industry for a reason. Combat is deliberate and tactical, forcing you to think about positioning, crowd control, and resource management. You are never simply overpowering enemies. Every shot matters, every upgrade feels meaningful, and every encounter rewards smart decision making. The balance between action and survival horror is handled so well that it still feels satisfying even today.

Leon is the heart of this game and my favorite character in the entire franchise. This is Leon at his absolute peak. He is confident, capable, and calm under pressure, but he never loses his humanity. His dry humor and iconic one liners give the game so much personality without ever feeling forced. Watching how far he has come since his rookie days makes playing as him incredibly rewarding, and he carries the tone of the entire game effortlessly.

The supporting cast and villains add to the charm. They are theatrical, memorable, and perfectly fit the game’s bold tone. The story itself is simple, but it is told with so much confidence that it never needs to be more complex. It knows exactly what it wants to be and fully commits to it.

Replayability is another reason this game is timeless. Every playthrough feels better than the last. Unlocking weapons, mastering encounters, and refining your playstyle never gets old. It is a game that rewards mastery and respects your time.

Even after all these years, Resident Evil 4 (2005) still holds up incredibly well. Its influence on modern games is undeniable, but more importantly, it is still insanely fun to play. This is the game I can always come back to, and it reminds me why I fell in love with Resident Evil and why Leon remains my favorite character.

I also genuinely hope I get the chance to play the remake soon. Experiencing this legendary game again with modern visuals and seeing Leon reimagined while still respecting what made him iconic would mean a lot to me. Until then, the original Resident Evil 4 will always hold a special place for me.

Survival Reimagined – A Review of Resident Evil 4

Overall Rating: 11/10

Resident Evil 4 is not just one of the greatest entries in the series—it is one of the most influential and accomplished games ever made. It reshaped survival horror, redefined third-person action, and set a new standard for pacing, combat, and immersion. Set far from the familiar streets of Raccoon City, the game follows Leon S. Kennedy into a hostile rural nightmare where survival is earned through precision, adaptability, and nerve. Every system, encounter, and design choice works in harmony, creating an experience that transcends genre and era. Resident Evil 4 doesn’t simply raise the bar—it obliterates it.

Visual Design and Atmosphere: 10/10
The game’s environments are oppressive, hostile, and unforgettable. From fog-choked forests and decaying villages to castles steeped in grotesque grandeur, each location feels distinct and deliberately constructed. The atmosphere trades claustrophobic hallways for open but threatening spaces, where danger can approach from any angle. Enemy placement, lighting, and environmental detail constantly keep players on edge, reinforcing the feeling that nowhere is truly safe.

Story and Narrative: 10/10
Resident Evil 4 embraces pulpy horror and action with confidence. Leon’s mission to rescue the president’s daughter becomes a descent into cult madness, body horror, and biological nightmare. The story is delivered through memorable characters, striking set pieces, and just enough exposition to keep momentum high. It doesn’t overcomplicate itself—it knows exactly what it is, and that self-awareness gives it lasting charm. 

Gameplay and Survival Mechanics: 10/10
This is where Resident Evil 4 makes history. Combat is deliberate, tactical, and endlessly satisfying. Ammo is limited, enemies are aggressive, and positioning matters at all times. The revolutionary over-the-shoulder perspective gives players unprecedented control while maintaining tension. Crowd control, precision shots, and risk-reward decision-making form a perfect survival loop. Inventory management remains a constant consideration, forcing players to plan every encounter carefully. The pacing is immaculate—constantly introducing new threats, mechanics, and scenarios without ever overstaying its welcome.

Sound Design and Music: 10/10
Audio design heightens tension at every turn. Enemy vocalizations, environmental sounds, and weapon effects are sharp and impactful. Music is used sparingly but effectively, allowing silence to build dread before erupting during combat or boss encounters. The result is a soundscape that constantly keeps players on edge without overwhelming the experience.

Additional Modes – Separate Ways & Mercenaries: 10/10
Separate Ways adds meaningful depth, reframing the main campaign through from another perspective and expanding the narrative without feeling supplemental or disposable. It enriches the story while introducing its own challenges and pacing. Mercenaries, meanwhile, is endlessly replayable—a pure test of skill, efficiency, and mastery. It transforms the game’s mechanics into a high-score-driven survival challenge that remains iconic to this day.

Replayability and Longevity: 10/10
Resident Evil 4 is built to be replayed. Weapon upgrades, difficulty modes, unlockables, and bonus content ensure that each run feels rewarding. Familiarity breeds confidence, but never complacency—mistakes are still punished, and tension remains intact. Few games invite repeated playthroughs with this level of consistency and satisfaction.

Conclusion: 11/10
Resident Evil 4 is a landmark achievement. It balances action and horror with surgical precision, delivering a survival experience that feels empowering without ever sacrificing tension. Its influence is immeasurable, its design timeless, and its execution nearly flawless.

Final Verdict:
Resident Evil 4 stands as one of the greatest video games ever created. Through revolutionary gameplay, masterful pacing, unforgettable encounters, and exceptional replay value, it redefined what survival horror—and action gaming as a whole—could be. Few games achieve perfection; fewer still reshape the medium. Resident Evil 4 does both.
