This game should belong in a museum. This is the pinnacle example of the evolution in gaming, which plays great even by today’s standards, with a couple of nitpicks. 

The original RE4 had as many as 4 concepts. Every concept had its own build, every single one of which was eventually scrapped except the last one. The dev team actually was doubting the success of RE4, but Shinji Mikami involved, wrote the final story in 3 weeks, and RE4 took only a year to develop in the end. And despite the game being developed that quickly, we’ve got a masterpiece. 
The game has a genre of Survival Horror with elements of action. Lots of elements of action. 
It was made at the very birth of the video gaming industry in media culture. The trends were revolving around “strong”, “hot” characters, and games were made with a sprinkle of comedy, relying on the teenage audience. Leon became a badass, one-liner-spitting tough guy, and the story at times was as corny as Leon was. 

Some people prefer to call this game a “horror comedy”, which, in my opinion, perfectly describes the tone of the game. You can practically say that Capcom is one of the progenitors of the genre. It was they who released the first part of the Resident Evil series in 1996. Being the progenitors they are, they can practically form the very core of what the game of such genre should be. As I said before, this is a survival horror with elements of action, leading to the case of not the player running *from* the horrifying monsters, but instead the player running *after* them. 

If we take older Resident Evil games, or, say, Silent Hill into consideration, where you have to solve puzzles and *avoid* those monstrous creatures by stunning or running past them, in Resident Evil 4 you play as Leon Kennedy, an experienced special agent who survived the events of Resident Evil 2, where he was just a rookie cop, and who took his skills to a whole other level. Capcom turned the tides upside down with the release of RE4. Now the player can shoot enemies to actually kill them instead of stun-locking, acquire loot that now mainly consists of ammo and in-game currency called Pesetas, with which the player can buy… more guns and upgrades. 
Does that mean that the game transforms from survival horror into a typical “shoot-em-up” scenario? Not by a long shot. 

The game provides limitations in order for players not to feel like a killing machine (at least on the first playthrough). Player’s ammo is limited, guns sometimes can’t penetrate the living armor of zombies quite as good, and the enemies’ attacks waste HP quite strongly. That said, the game is far from being a walk in the park, even with the first time playing it, which restricts the player to a choice of only the easiest difficulty. The game rewards one for being clever and punishes one for being reckless, impatient, and not paying enough attention. 
A large part of the game straightforwardly depends on one having a specific gun in inventory with the respective ammo being there too, sometimes also requiring some special weapon attachments. 

The aforementioned “punishments” come as an example where if the player doesn't explore the surroundings for ammo or pesetas, one will run out of ammo pretty quickly, and one won’t be able to purchase weapon upgrades for not having enough pesetas. Or, as a simpler example, you can step into a bear trap, losing quite a bit of HP simply due to the lack of attention. 

Regarding the other parts of gameplay, the game has a very serious issue, measured by today’s standards. That being the tank controls. If you don’t have the HD Remastered mod installed, you cannot use the mouse to move the camera in the game. Leon quite literally moves like a tank, only being able to turn the camera using WASD keys. That said, if you are in the heat of a battle, you just have to run away a certain distance in order to fight back, for example. Or the way of changing weapons is only to press the TAB key, open up the inventory menu, switch, and only then go back, which sometimes puts you in quite a sticky situation. Still better than the very first PC port, which had numbers for the key prompts instead of actual keyboard buttons and which had lighting issues along with the sound lags. 

But the tank controls are not entirely a bad thing: they most certainly bring some strategic aspects to the game. There are also some clever mechanics in order to make it fair for the player. For example, at the beginning of the game, Ganados will unobtrusively alert the player from behind while getting closer to one, saying something like “Detrás de ti!”, which literally translates as “Behind you!” 

If we dive a little bit deeper into gameplay, we discover the role of a knife in this game. It never breaks, it deals damage, and it is used to break most of the crates containing loot. It is also the most effective weapon in the game. You shoot zombies, they get stun-locked, you roundhouse kick them in the face, they lie down, and you stab them to death. Bingo. 

The game’s voice acting is both a blessing and a curse for the player’s ears. We have Leon, Ada Wong, and the antagonists voiced greatly, and then we have… Ashley with her infamous “LEON, HEEEELP!” screams. While I don’t consider Ashley as annoying as most of the gamers of that time did, it is indeed quite annoying, but on the other hand, everything mentioned makes the game as iconic as it is today. Also, considering the fact that the game takes action in Spain, which leads to a point that most of the Ganados are Spanish, they all talk with a heavy Mexican accent. I don’t think I should mention that their voice-acting has been meme-d into oblivion, you would know that even without me saying it. 

All in all, it’s a very great title by today’s standards, even considering the fact that it feels a bit stretched out when you enter the game’s third location, and the fact that Separate Ways isn't as fleshed out as it could be. Pick it up and play it if you have the chance; it is simply a must-play for every gamer out there.

It starts strong, but the more hours you put into it, you start to realize how tedious it all is. Combat mainly revolves around fighting huge hordes of enemies all at once which either means two things, 1. You pull out a crowd clearing weapon like a shotgun and disperse the enemies all at once, or 2. You shoot them in the face or the leg and roundhouse kick the whole horde in front of you. You're doing this for 95% of encounters, with the other 5% being bosses or larger enemies that you shoot a few times before running right next to them as they miss whatever attack they were trying to go for. Enemies also have a nasty habit of spawning in and teleporting right behind you or just slightly out of your field of vision once you pass certain invisible lines on the map, if you place Ashley near the exit door of an area she can potentially be captured and you're given a game over in less than 10 seconds flat.

The director that chooses what weapons you can use is also pretty lame. You can't ever buy ammo so you're beholden to whatever the game decides to random drop for you at that time. It tends to prioritize ammo for guns you're using a lot or which ones you don't have a ton of ammunition for, but if you're using a handgun or the TMP, then say goodbye to every other ammo drop in the game. Both handgun and TMP ammo are marked as extremely common drops so they override most other drops you'll end up getting, meaning that you can't really experiment with the other weapons like magnums and the mine thrower unless you find ammo placed around that map deliberately by the developers. It doesn't help that both the Red9 and the TMP are some of the most consistently great guns in the game so using them just contributes to the problem.

Can you really even find items in your area when the color palette is this gray and brown? Some treasures like spinels will shine to notify you of they're location, but you'll casually stroll by green herbs, ammo boxes, and lockers that you can open since the camera is fixed at an upwards tilt, meaning you have to constantly pan the camera down just to see items that are lying on the floor. What further enhances the tedium is that most items are hidden in breakable crates that Leon has to slowly walk up towards, attack it with his knife, then pick up the item, before micro adjusting slightly to the left and doing the same thing with the box right next to you. It eats up at least 2 or 3 hours of gameplay just breaking objects for loot that is admittedly helpful, so you don't want to just leave it be.

I understand a lot of people are upset at this game for turning the Resident Evil franchise into a blockbuster action film from a horror genre, but that's just about the only thing I enjoyed out of the game. The cutscenes and dialogue is pretty absurd in a good way, but the actual gameplay doesn't match that cheesy blockbuster vibe at all. It almost feels like they played it too safe and trying to deviate away from the survival horror genre completely might have actually turned this game into something great. However, because it clings to its old principles while trying to do something completely new, it ends up as just one big frustrating mess that tries your patience more than anything.

Resident Evil 4 is an amazing game, and I can see why it's still so beloved to this ay. For a now 20 year game, it holds up shockingly well, in nearly every aspect. Once you figure out the camera controls and movement, which does take a little bit due to being kind of 3D tank controls, the game is an absolute treat to play. Much more action oriented than previous Resident Evil games (including the remakes of 2 and 3), 4 feels like an entirely different series at times. Sure Leon is front and center, and you're taking down zombie like creatures, but you're doing so 10 at a time at some points. In stark contrast to the slower more strategic combat of its predecessors, in 4 you face wave after wave of enemy, mowing them down like it's a Call of Duty zombies run. It's extremely satisfying and enjoyable, especially once you start being able to upgrade to more powerful weapons. Another side affect of this new combat philosophy is that I never came close to running out of ammo. Some of my most memorable moments in the 2 remake and 3 remake as well as Resident Evil 1 was when I had no ammo or only a handful of bullets and had to choose whether or not every enemy needed to be fought or if I should evade it. In contrast, I often had an inventory with literal stacks of every ammo imaginable. This isn't necessarily a bad thing, in fact it does suit the combat quite well, but I think it's worth mentioning. The level design was stellar. While a lot more linear than past games, it does a great job of still maintaining that cramped feel, and parts of the game do feel like classic Resident Evil in 3D. The castle especially is an absolute treat to work your way through and might be one of my favorite settings in all of gaming. The bosses are some of the best that I've played in the series so far. A couple of them do have some annoying quick time events (I recommend capping your game at 30fps to help with this) but as a whole they're shockingly great for a 20 year old game. Large parts of this game are escort missions since that's literally the point of the game and they're handled shockingly well. Ashley rarely feels like a chore to protect, and the game does a great job of giving you ways to protect her without it being annoying. Overall Resident Evil 4 is an outstanding game despite its age, and is well worth your time. I can't wait to revisit its world in the remake eventually. Resident Evil 4 Review: Redefining Survival Horror

Six years after the Raccoon City incident, agent Leon S. Kennedy is sent to a remote European village to rescue the President's kidnapped daughter. What follows is a relentless, masterful reinvention of the series, trading tired zombies for intelligent, aggressive enemies and placing players in a state of near-constant, panic-driven survival.

The Game-Changing Evolution
Gone are the static cameras and sluggish pacing. RE4 introduces an over-the-shoulder perspective and laser-precise aiming, transforming combat into a strategic and visceral experience. You can target specific limbs to disable foes, use context-sensitive actions for evasion, and manage a deep arsenal of upgradable weapons. The result is a faster, more intense, and utterly gripping horror-action hybrid.

While the classic control scheme remains (tank controls with a run button), the new camera and aiming mechanics make gameplay feel fluid and modern. The atmospheric tension is amplified by smarter enemies who work together, dodge attacks, and hunt you relentlessly.

A Masterclass in Atmosphere & Design
The game is a visual and artistic triumph. From the eerie village and foreboding castle to industrial complexes and ancient ruins, every environment is dripping with detail, mood, and staggering visual effects. Boss battles are spectacles of design and creativity, each requiring unique strategies and leaving a lasting impression.

The pacing is exceptional. RE4 seamlessly blends heart-pounding action with classic suspense sequences—like guiding the vulnerable Ashley through dark corridors—offering over 20 hours of varied, unforgettable gameplay. The new merchant system, which allows you to buy, sell, and upgrade gear, adds a rewarding layer of strategy.

Presentation & Polish
Capcom's attention to detail shines. Cinematics are engine-rendered and cinematic, voice acting is competent, and the Dolby Pro Logic II soundtrack perfectly complements the dread. The game runs smoothly, looks stunning, and supports progressive scan, though it uses a letterboxed format rather than true anamorphic widescreen.

Verdict
Resident Evil 4 isn't just the best entry in the franchise; it's a landmark title that redefined its genre. By masterfully blending white-knuckle action, palpable horror, and impeccable design, it delivers a consistently thrilling, terrifying, and polished experience from start to finish. This is an essential, genre-defining masterpiece.

[h1]★★★★★[/h1]
"Being my personal entry point into the whole series, 'Resident Evil 4' won me over by being nothing short of timeless in most of its qualities -- Achieving to bring a creative vision to life that would go on to revolutionize the industry, all while spewing charme and soul that, as some would argue, has been lost over the following years. What does that soul contain?

Much has been said about the flawless implementation of the third-person perspective into this action-driven setting or the sheer amount of games which were visibly inspired by this mechanic, especially considering how well it all holds up when playing through it today. But I find that evaluating games based on their historical impact greatly detracts from everything they are as standalone experiences. I think it has a reason why we like 'Resident Evil 4' more than we might like other games which changed the landscape in much more drastic or even lasting ways. One deciding factor for me would be the atmosphere.

The interaction of space, texture and sound-design into what we consider to be believable and simultaneously interesting places are understood perfectly and convey a continuously thick atmosphere of tension and mystery, even when an area is seemingly void of any enemies. The rustic flair of the user interface, all the ominious sound effects and the way the player interacts with his inventory or collectible items greatly add to this general sentiment of unsettledness, especially at those brief instances where the game dares to fall completely silent, almost freezing in time. It is a great sin that many modern games have lost the ability to let the player intentionally sit with the absence of these certainties and, in horror, play with the discomfort of reminding you that you are playing a game -- Anything could happen.

Of course there are many other games which manage to channel this element, though none come to mind which let you truly feel the comfort of the safe rooms, with their warm and melodically drowning ambient soundtrack, the relief of hearing the familiar laugh of the dealer as purple flames illuminate one of the only spaces in which saving your game is an option, only to take it all away again once you move on. Strangely, this aspect stuck with me more than any other and whenver I think back to playing this game, faded memories of 'Serenity' from the soundtrack haunt the back of my mind. Having to move on, act and progress on your own terms, in your own ways, free, is the strength of this medium and as much as I would appreaciate a safe room like that in my own life, 'Resident Evil 4' seems to imitiate real-life in the sense that this stagnation in comfort will stunt your progress.

The progression itself is solved through relatively simple but intertwined resource-managment-mechanics in which finding, assembling and selling diverse treasures grants you the ability to upgrade your gear or purchase entirely new items -- All in the confines of limited inventory space. These systems work very well with one another and are supplemented by scavengable loot and small puzzle sections, which are spread throughout the closed levels. Uncovering and upgrading everything, as well as mastering the combat encounters on higher difficulties gives this game a lot of replayability, even on the hardest difficulty, which is very managable if you learn to rely on your knife to conserve ammo. 

The narrative, which encompasses the main story and one additonal DLC that focusses on a new perspective, is not complex at all -- But this is not to its detrement, as the game seems self-aware enough to play into the stereotypes of the many characters and leverage their predictable traits into a charming clashing of their personalities in the vein of a stageplay and the charme of an early 2000s action-movie, oftentimes to comedic effect. This often contradicts itself tonally with the bleak setting in an interesting way, which consists of three main stages: The village, the castle and the island. This is where I think to recognize some issues;

Nearing the end of the game in form of the island, I noticed a very apparent change concering the enemies I encountered. Gone were the deranged villagers of the town, throwing their axes, angrily yelling at me in their native tongue as if I had violated their sacred space. Gone were the menacing cult-members of the castle, quietly mumbling curses to themselves as they slowly inched in my direction, seemingly devising devious and malicious plans to end me.

Instead, I was greeted with pretty generic soldiers that would dictate a tonal shift from mystery and horror to basic action. The levels followed suit and even though I very much appreaciated the subsequent attempts to return to tension and pressure by introducing the 'Regeneradors', which might even be the most intimidating enemy in the game, I found myself increasingly confronted with unnecessarily long action set-pieces that made the game feel so monotonous and predictable at times, especially in comparison to before. At their worst, these sections were chores to get through; Shooting practice to try out new weapons. At their best they made me think and wonder, what the island, covered in claustrophobic, industrial hallways and desolate military installations, could have looked like, if approached with the previous intent of creating fear and discomfort within the player forced to explore them. 

Though, nearing the obligatory climax of the story in form of a final battle, I can see it in myself to forgive this rather sharp turn into radical genre-blending and appreaciate its highlights. The flashy boss-fight against Krauser really stands out for me here.

Overall, 'Resident Evil 4' manages to capture a truly unique atmosphere and thrilling adventure featuring iconic characters and sets within the framework of crossing different genres to an extent that laid the foundation for many of the modern concepts we know and love today. It is, without a doubt, timeless."

Well, you can easily tell why this game was an instant classic, truly a bold new entry that changed survival horror, third person shooters and Resident Evil forever for better and I feel a little bit for the worse too. This was by far the most video-gamy one I’ve played in the franchise yet with the most overwhelming amount of enemies, most bombastic action yet and of course side quests and collectathons all around and it’s in those elements that this game looses the haunting, claustrophobic and scary soul the franchise had  in prior entries, don’t get me wrong action is a core pillar of the franchise but here it most certainly took the front seat as opposed to horror.
That being said what was gained by the transition is truly special, this game is truly unapologetic about itself and it’s a joy to interact with most of the game world by just shooting at everything and the goofy dialogue and quips from Leon are most certainly a welcomed changed of pay from his overly stressed self from 2. And the rest of the cast gives him plenty of material to work with as they are each great in their own right and the MGS style codec cutscene help them feel like a constant presence even when they can’t be there physically. 
While this game is not very scary it is butt-quenchingly tense at time, the iconic intro in the village, the Verdugo fight, and several of the games wave by wave fights are my favorite example of the adrenalin inducing set pieces that the game throws at you. And here’s where I’ll say something a bit controversial but I actually like having to take care of Ashley during all that madness, even if it did cost me a few attempts accidentally killing her because Leon here absolutely rises to the level Jill had on 3 of being truly hyper-competent as a protagonist here, so having someone to take care of truly ups the tension you loose when you become accustomed to the flow of combat and can kill 50 people with your eyes closed.
I also found the constant trinket hunting to be quite rewarding as I’m someone who naturally likes to poke around every last drawer, break every crate and loot every enemy, and each treasure was never too out of the way and was actually useful since you are always strapped for cash when you’re buying things from the trusty merchant. Also loved ignoring Ashley’s please for helps for a little bit because my 100th Spindle was more important.
And something that I’m insanely fond of is of course the best inventory screen design in gaming history, barring maybe the SKY UI mod from Skyrim but for anything not RPG this is to me the gold standard. I spend probably 20% of my playthrough doing inventory Jenga and I wouldn’t have it any other wise, I truly wished more games stole this system because it’s just so immersive, intuitive and just plain awesome, one more thing to look forward to when Gloomwood finally fully comes out, I guess.
Overall, while I do feel I’ll miss the more cinematic horror that the original trilogy had, what Shinji Mikami and co did here is simply too special for it not have revolutionized the industry again, with good reason. Truly worthwhile to play this gaming monolith for yourself when you have the chance, it’s not even really scary if that’s what’s stopped you from picking one up.

20 years later, original RE4 still stands as one of the greatest 3rd person shooters ever. I'm writing this review to celebrate my 100% completion, and I've never felt so satisfied hunting down achievements like this. The level of care and love that went into this game is astounding, it overflows with charm and polish in every corner. I hate that the remake sucked the charisma from each of these characters in an attempt to make the story more "serious". I think RE stories work best when they acknowledge what is happening is ridiculous and just roll with it.

I think the greatest strength original 4 has over the remake is the consistency of combat. Enemies all move in deadly but predictable patterns, making the combat the most strategic of the action-oriented entries. The sound design is also the greatest of any shooter I have ever played, every enemy has unique queues to signal their next move to those with a keen ear. When you hear a meaty explosion coming from that dead Ganado you just headshot behind you two seconds ago, you know a Plagas just spawned from it. Lets pray to god you've got a flash grenade.

Now thats not to say that RE4 has no flaws that couldnt be improved. The movement of Leon can be stiff which is a bar of entry to many modern players, but perfecting Leons movement is extremely satisfying and makes this game even more fun to return to and improve. Also there is a bug that makes QTEs way harder on 60fps (the Salazar statue run will genuinely make you lose hair if you dont know this), but you can fix this by lowering frame rate in the options.

I could gush for much longer about this classic but I'm gonna give it a rest for now. I will be coming back to replay this gem every year until I am claimed by Arthritis.

Yup, this one's a banger. One of my favourite games of all time. Better than REmake, because it's got its own identity and everything's been thought of meticulously instead of aping other current games' mechanics and bloating the game. But let's dial it back before you stop reading this. Why is this "old" game so good?

Resident Evil 4 is a classic for a good reason. This game not only kickstarted third person shooting (and inspired basically everyone of them that came after), but it's also got the pacing of a well done shooter down. The Last of Us, as bemoan as I am to mention that, and other games of Naughty Dog's ilk past 2005, owe themselves to this game, not to mention Gears of War as well (although that made it so that every third person shooter had to be a cover shooter...). If you like any third person shooter, there's a good chance you owe that to the lessons learnt from this game.

Does it lose a bit of that horror in survival horror? A little bit, definitely once you get to the island, but that's a short romp near the end that basically dials everything you've learnt up until that point to 11, so it makes sense. I would highly argue that the game still feels very much like the older games to some extent, just with a bit more action. You can't make the argument that it's going in the wrong direction, when 3 and Code: Veronica tried (and didn't succeed nearly as well due to not being able to aim freely or were restricted due to the fixed camera system) to put more action elements in the old formula. You could also probably blame Capcom for limiting REmake and 0 to the GameCube, making sure it made far less profit even if one of them was good. The formula at that point had run its course, so thinking of how to evolve Resident Evil (even if the effects of it would be more disastrous past this game) was probably the right call.

The tank controls, and not being able to move while shooting, inventory managment (tetris style management never gets old) and saving on the typewriter are some things that I can think of that are reminscent of the older style. Shinji Mikami also directed this, so it's not some other person who might not understand what the franchise is yet. Third person aiming will never feel scary, so they put a lot of emphasis on the survival rather than the horror. Unlike REmake, every hit that you get feels earnt, whether it is because Leon is dealing it, or taking it. The game has fixed rules regarding shooting areas, where shooting the head or the legs WILL trigger a melee prompt, and the melee has proper I-frames so it doesn't feel cheap when you get hit immediately after doing one in REmake. The knife is the underdog of saving ammo (and MVP of the Krauser fight), and no amount of pseudo Souls parrying will ever replace it. I never felt like the game was being too unfair outside of certain cutscenes making me get hit from enemies sneaking up on me. Dynamic difficulty exists in this game, so it can make it easier or harder depending on how well you are doing, making sure the experience is never the same, and making sure you are having a good time once you get your head around learning how Leon moves.

While some modern gamers may find this movement "limiting", it is all by design. Leon is very smooth and reflexive once you understand how he moves. He can be made even smoother with re4_tweaks, and the RE4HD Project is a must use and the definitive way of playing this game, much better than Capcom's efforts of upscaling (There is an option to use fixed camera angles during Ashley's section like it is in the Japanese version, and yes, it does become scarier). The upgrade system is rewarding and gives a great sense of progression (the Merchant is also better because he's not giving silly side quests and doesn't sound British). The puzzles are nothing to bring up comparing to the old games, but the changes to bring Resident Evil into a new direction are very good where it counts. The game is cheesy in all the right ways too, and it's not really scared of it. It's not straight camp, but Leon using humour as deflection and acting a bit like an action movie hero is probably the reason why he's a fan favourite of the franchise. Umbrella may be officially gone, but the whole franchise basically lives in that company's shadow (especially relevant for Requiem), with Leon being affected by that, and in the future too. The villains also match Leon's energy, and it's just a blast to get through, unlike the dull seriousness that modern Resident Evil likes to do so much, as if it's ashamed of its past.

The only real criticisms I have are that the additional Ada campaign doesn't feel nearly as fleshed out or as meaty in the REmake, but this game is just so good in all the right ways, a masterclass in design that should be remembered. It's definitely my favourite of the bunch, even if that may feel like sacrilege to the old RE crowd (2 is my favourite out of those ones). This is also where Mercenaries starts being fun, unlike whatever it was in 3. Wesker can't counter melees, but he's still broken as hell in this. I'll never get tired of playing this one, and I can only hope that the modern crowd can put aside their need for conformity to understand why this is an enduring legend that will live on forever.

[i]Resident Evil 4[/i] is a game that redefined survival horror and third-person action, blending suspense, strategic combat, and cinematic storytelling into one unforgettable experience. From its iconic over-the-shoulder camera to its relentless pacing and gripping encounters, it remains a landmark in gaming, combining tension, atmosphere, and action in a way few games have ever matched.

You play as Leon S. Kennedy, tasked with rescuing the U.S. President’s daughter from a mysterious cult in rural Spain. Leon is a seasoned, capable protagonist, but the world around him is dangerous, unpredictable, and deeply unsettling. The narrative is engaging and tightly paced, balancing moments of horror, mystery, and cinematic tension with bursts of explosive action. The story unfolds through interactions with memorable characters, eerie villagers, and chilling revelations that keep you invested from beginning to end.

The game’s environments are meticulously designed, from claustrophobic villages and sinister forests to abandoned castles and hidden laboratories. Each area is rich in detail, atmospheric lighting, and sound design that enhances immersion and heightens tension. Environmental storytelling is subtle but powerful — the layout of a village, the placement of enemies, and scattered clues all contribute to a sense of dread, discovery, and narrative depth.

Combat in [i]Resident Evil 4[/i] is fast, strategic, and satisfying. The over-the-shoulder camera provides precision aiming while maintaining cinematic framing, and encounters with Ganados, monstrous bosses, and unique enemies demand adaptability, quick reflexes, and careful resource management. Every weapon, from pistols to shotguns, has weight and impact, making each firefight tense and rewarding. Ammo is limited, health is precious, and improvisation is key — classic survival horror tension meets modern action gameplay perfectly.

The game’s pacing is masterful. Moments of exploration, puzzle-solving, and inventory management are balanced with high-intensity combat and cinematic sequences, creating a rhythm that keeps players engaged and on edge. Boss fights are memorable, challenging, and visually striking, testing both strategy and reflexes. The progression system — acquiring weapons, upgrades, and resources — feels rewarding, encouraging exploration and experimentation without ever slowing down the narrative.

Audio and visual design elevate the experience to cinematic heights. Every creak, distant shout, and gunshot contributes to the tension, while haunting ambient music reinforces the horror and suspense. Character animations, facial expressions, and enemy designs are iconic, enhancing the believability of the world and the impact of every encounter. The game’s attention to detail ensures that even after years, it remains visually and mechanically impressive.

[i]Resident Evil 4[/i] is more than just a survival horror game — it is a carefully constructed, adrenaline-fueled experience that balances fear, action, and storytelling seamlessly. It set the standard for modern third-person action games while preserving the essence of what makes survival horror compelling: vulnerability, suspense, and immersion.

A must-play for anyone who loves survival horror, action-packed gameplay, or cinematic storytelling — [i]Resident Evil 4[/i] is a timeless masterpiece that continues to influence games more than a decade after its release, delivering thrills, tension, and unforgettable moments from start to finish.

Resident Evil 4 is an excellent action horror game. If by the off chance you haven't played it yet and if you enjoy fast-paced third-person shooters, with elements of horror, fun gun play and a cheesy story, then this is for you. 

You play as Leon S. Kennedy, a government agent and survivor of the Raccoon City incident (Resident Evil 2). Leon has been tasked with finding the daughter of President of the United States, Ashley Graham, who has gone missing, her last sighting was in a small Spanish town. Leon must find her and bring her home. But nothing is ever as it seems, is it? A horrific cult, diabolical monsters and unspeakable horrors await you as you traverse the world of RE 4. Enter the survival horror.
 
RE4 is a departure from the earlier survival horror style of Resident Evil/Biohazard games. Where the previous games focused on large residence hub areas with a lot of puzzles and back tracking, while facing Zombies and monsters. RE4 adopts a more action-oriented approach, with a new over-the-shoulder aiming camera angle, melee attacks and quick time events and faster enemies. There is an element of back tracking in places and a few puzzles, but the game is mostly linear and mostly about shooting a range of monsters. 

You will face Ganados - crazed cultists who will stop at nothing to bring you down. Unlike the Zombies from previous games, these foes are smarter, faster and they aren't restricted to hands and teeth. They use weapons, throw explosives and even operate machines in their quest to stop you. In addition to the lowly Ganados you will fight deadly sub-bosses and even deadlier bosses. There is a weapon upgrade system, where you can collect and purchase new weapons and upgrade them, making combat more interesting and it allows to make each campaign run a bit different. 

There are four main game modes, the main campaign, and three bonus games that you have to unlock: Separate Ways bonus Campaign, The Mercenaries and Assignment Ada mini games, the mini games are based on previous battle games from the RE series, and Separate Ways is 5 chapters long and can take a few hours to complete. You can also unlock a Professional difficulty which is worth playing as it makes the difficulty feels more in line with the original Game Cube release - enemies hit harder, some take more damage, it can be quite challenging. 

I first played Resident Evil 4 on the GameCube on release day back in 2005, being a massive Resident Evil fan, I played it again and again, and then with each new release of the game: on the Ps2, Wii, Xbox 360, PS4 Switch, and now Steam. I wouldn't call it my favourite game in the series or favourite of all time, but I do adore this game and have spent countless hours playing it over the last 20 years. It is in my top 12 best games. This version of the game is just as fun, but it feels a lot easier overall - even on professional mode. The enemies hurt you less, and the game is more generous with money, health and ammunition pick ups and rocket launchers. Pro mode is more challenging, but I felt it was more inline with the original GCN hard difficulty. 
 
The story is a bit cheesy and over the top, but it's no more corny than your average Hollywood action movie. The characters are memorable, but we don't get full explanations through Leon's campaign which can be frustrating, a few holes in the story linger and questions are unanswered - Separate Ways does answer a lot of it, so make sure to play that. The music is visceral and heart pounding. The monster designs are all fantastic, and sometimes it's like John Carpenter's the Thing meets The Texas Chainsaw Massacre with how messed up the monsters are. RE4 is fun, hard to put down and well worth your time. 

There is a more modern Remake available, which will probably be you best place to start, but this classic version is still worth playing and holds a special place in many a gamer's heart.

Resident Evil 4, hasn't more been said about this game? It's one of the best horror/action survival video games ever made and currently my favorite one. Now i wont go much into detail about the actual base game, rather il talk about this port instead, does UHD hold up? Yes... and at the same time no.

So UHD includes higher quality HD graphics (duh it's in the name), much better keyboard and mouse support compared to the 2007 Ubisoft pc port (just mentioning that port gives me convulsions) and also a 60fps mode (all other versions are locked to 30), but despite all these improvements, there are some major issues:


The higher fidelity textures and effects are nice, but they aren't that much higher quality compared to the GC version honestly (plus there's also that stupid broken blur effect on the screen);

The keyboard and mouse support works well, but the inventory management keybinds are stupid (like you have to hit backspace to grab items and page down\page up to flip items, what the hell?);

The 60fps option is great, but certain animations weren't updated, so they still run at 30fps (or even at double speed) and not every QTE was retimed for 60 meaning they are much harder (like the minecart section where you have to mash for your life on PRO difficulty). Plus like, why is there no unlocked framerate option? RE1 HD and RE0 HD on steam have a 30, 60 and Variable (120) options available, so why not RE4?

If you are planning to play re4 in the most conventional and currently best way, buy this port and make sure to download the mod "re4_tweaks", it fixes a lot of graphical and framerate issues and also makes the game (somewhat) playable at 120fps. If you truly want a full HD experience id recommend "HD project" as well, its a big mod (around 8-9 gigabytes), however it makes the game look truly incredible and it also comes with the newest version of re4_tweaks, so you don't even have to install it separately if you plan to install HD project.

I rate RE4 as a whole a 9.5/10, truly a masterpiece with only a few tiny issues and this port a 7/10, its great in a way, but has some unresolved issues that could've been easily fixed.

These controls blow! 
Not far off from facing Salazar and I'm ready to throw in the towel. Do yourself a favour and go swimming with a Dolphin in the Seven Seas for the Wii version. While it was made for the GameCube and later the PS2 (in other words: designed for a controller), the WIi version is the absolute best way to play it. It plays very well as the controls feel natural. It's why it's one of the greats. 
- But these mouse and keyboard controls are absolute AS5! 
This game was never meant to have a rotating camera but that's what the mouse is doing. Leon runs whichever way HE'S facing, not whichever way the CAMERA is facing, so you need to have your mouse-hand completely still at all times except for aiming otherwise Leon is going run into doorframes, traps and enemy attacks. There's no way to set the mouse to do nothing unless you're aiming. 
- The keyboard controls are unituitive. 
With the usual WASD for movement, TAB for the inventory and ESC for pause, it makes no sense to me to have Insert and Page up to scroll across menus (why not Q and E?), Backspace to arrange items (why not Z, X or C?), M for map (why not CTRL?). The buttons are spread all across the keyboard instead of being readily accessible at your fingertips. Space does nothing in menus. Why not act as "confirm" instead of having to either go all the way across the keyboad to press Enter or take my hand off the mouse to do it. And it doesn't register the numpad Enter, either. Numbers are also not used in any way. Why can't I assign weapons or other functions to the numbers? 
- An annoyance with the sound: if the audio source is changed during the game (so if your headphones die and the PC switches to another audio source), there just isn't any sound until you reboot the game so you have to run back to a save point in silence when a key part of the game is using sound to detect your enemies, especially in the Castle area. Too bad if you're going for a low save run. Annoying. 
- While this PC version has the sharpest graphics, it's frustrating to play. Graphically the Wii version still holds up and, in my opinion, retains the charm of the original graphics. Choosing smooth and rewarding gameplay is much better than slightly sharper graphics.

Resident Evil 4 — Reviewed by Albert Wesker

Now this… this was an evolution.

By 2005, the series had mutated — shed its skin, abandoned the shambling pace of the past. Resident Evil 4 was not survival horror in the traditional sense… it was precision chaos. And I must admit — I was impressed. Not often do I say that about something I didn’t personally orchestrate.

Let’s begin with the subject of the experiment: Leon S. Kennedy.
Once a jittery rookie fumbling through Raccoon City, now he struts through Spain with the confidence of a man who’s been injected with too much arrogance and not enough common sense. His hair remains… immaculately conditioned, despite the endless bloodshed.
He’s competent, I’ll grant him that. But beneath that smug grin lies the same flaw as before — he still believes he’s the hero.

And then there’s the Las Plagas.
At last — a viral strain worthy of scientific interest. Not Umbrella’s work, of course (a pity), but a fascinating organic parasite nonetheless. The control it grants its hosts… the coordination, the adaptability — exquisite! Primitive, yes, but full of potential. Had I gotten my hands on those specimens, the world would have changed far sooner.

Gameplay? Remarkable. The over-the-shoulder perspective revolutionized the field. No longer did players feel like distant observers — they were Leon, trapped in the madness. Every headshot, every suplex, every frantic reload oozed tension.
The pacing — immaculate. The enemy variety — relentless.
It was less about surviving and more about dominating, which, frankly, I find refreshing.

Let us not forget the supporting cast.
Ada Wong — elegant as ever, though her allegiance is as fluid as her wardrobe. Always appearing at the perfect moment to complicate matters. A useful operative… when properly motivated.
Luis Serra — brilliant but reckless, much like the scientists Umbrella used to waste by the dozen.
And Osmund Saddler — deluded, self-righteous, and utterly predictable. Another fool seeking control without comprehension. I would’ve erased him myself, had Leon not done the favor.

But most fascinating of all is how Resident Evil 4 redefined fear. It wasn’t about creaking doors or flickering lights anymore — it was the pressure. The swarm of enemies. The resource scarcity. The sound of a chainsaw revving behind you as you reload just a second too late. Fear made tangible through sheer momentum.

Capcom took the formula, tore it apart, and rebuilt it into something potent. Something… inevitable.

My verdict:
A groundbreaking success — not perfect, but ambitious, daring, transformative.
Were I to rate it as an experiment, I’d call it a triumph of adaptation — the moment Resident Evil transcended its mortality.

[h1]A Timeless Survival Horror Classic[/h1]

[i]Special agent Leon S. Kennedy is sent on a mission to rescue the U.S. President’s daughter who has been kidnapped.[/i]

[h2]Story[/h2]
Set in 2004, U.S. government agent Leon S. Kennedy (Paul Mercier) is sent to rescue Ashley Graham (Carolyn Lawrence), the U.S. President's daughter, who has been abducted by a mysterious cult. His search leads him to a remote village in rural Spain, where hostile villagers, once simple farmers, now serve the cult Los Iluminados after being infected by the mind-controlling parasite Las Plagas.

[h2]Gameplay[/h2]
Resident Evil 4 is a third-person survival horror game with a stronger focus on action than previous entries. The fixed camera angles are replaced with a dynamic, over-the-shoulder view that zooms in while aiming, or switches to first-person for sniper rifles. Weapons use a laser sight instead of a crosshair, allowing precise targeting of enemy limbs or projectiles—shots to legs can stagger foes, while arm shots can disarm them—adding more tactical depth to gunplay. Players can also shoot down projectiles like thrown axes or scythes.

Resident Evil 4 lets you interact with the environment in different ways depending on the situation—kicking down ladders, jumping through windows, dodging attacks, or performing finishing moves on weakened enemies. QTEs also appear, requiring on-screen button prompts to dodge hazards like falling boulders or escape enemy grapples.

The inventory uses a grid-based attaché case where each item takes up a set number of spaces. The case can be upgraded for more room, while key items and treasures are stored separately. A wandering merchant sells weapons, first aid sprays, and upgrades, and buys treasures Leon finds. Each weapon has its own strengths and weaknesses.

[b][u]Mercenaries Mode[/u][/b]
A fast-paced, score-focused bonus mode separate from the main story. It’s designed for replayability, skill testing, and high-score competition.

[b][u]Separate Ways[/u][/b]
A story expansion and side campaign that lets you play as Ada Wong and experience the game from a new perspective. The story runs parallel to Leon’s campaign.

[h2]Enemies & Bosses[/h2]
The primary enemies are Los Ganados (“The Cattle” in Spanish), once simple farmers now infected with the Las Plagas parasite. Unlike traditional zombies, they can dodge attacks, wield weapons, and coordinate as a group. Some are capable of gruesome mutations, with parasitic creatures bursting from their heads when damaged.

QTEs are frequently used in boss fights, requiring precise button inputs to dodge deadly, instant-kill attacks.

[h2]Environment & Scares[/h2]
The game begins in a remote European countryside—a foggy, decaying Spanish village of crumbling houses, barns, and muddy streets, surrounded by farmlands, dense forests, and scattered cabins. Progress is mostly linear across three regions—Village, Castle, and Island—once you leave a major region, you cannot return, though chapters include backtracking for keys, treasures, and shortcuts. Checkpoints and merchants act as natural hubs for upgrades and resupply.

The Village features forest trails, farmyards, and a central square with locked gates and crest puzzles. The Castle is a sprawling fortress with branching corridors, dungeons, towers, traps, and frequent backtracking. The Island is a more linear mix of military checkpoints, labs, and industrial yards, serving as a high-combat finale.

The game is not very scary, as it has a stronger focus on action than previous entries.

[h2]Visual Design & Sound Design[/h2]
The graphics feel somewhat outdated 20 years later. The Village looks like a rundown, creepy countryside—old stone houses, muddy roads, wooden fences, and a generally damp, lived-in feel. The Castle is a dark, gothic fortress with huge stone walls, winding staircases, torch-lit halls, and fancy but eerie banquet rooms. The Island is cold, industrial, and military-like—concrete bunkers, metal walkways, labs with machines, parasite tanks, and large warehouses with cranes and heavy equipment.

In the Village you hear wind, creaky wood, crows, and villagers muttering in Spanish. It feels like a creepy countryside where danger can come from anywhere. Music is low and tense, with sudden loud drums when enemies attack. The Spanish mutterings of Ganados’ sound both human and sinister. Their sudden shouts puncture the quiet, signaling aggression. In the Castle you hear echoing footsteps, dripping water, and spooky cult chanting make it feel like a haunted church. Music adds deep choir voices, pipe organs, and clanging metal to sound dark and religious. On the Island you hear machines hum, doors hiss, and alarms beep, giving it a cold, military lab vibe. Music uses electronic noises and steady beats, while monsters like the Regenerador breathe heavily so you hear them before you see them.

[h2]Constructive Criticism[/h2]
The controls and movement feel awkward at first and take some time to get used to—you can’t move while aiming and shooting. The boss battle in the lake with the water monster was frustrating, because aiming was awful. I can forgive this, though, since Resident Evil 4 was the game that popularized the third-person, over-the-shoulder camera view and inspired many games to come.

The QTEs are just annoying most of the time and don't always work. There’s a part where you are running away from a giant statue, and no matter what I did I could not get past it. I had to look it up, and it turns out that at 60 FPS, you need to be EXTREMELY fast when spamming the button prompt. Otherwise, you can temporarily lower the FPS to 30 and then raise it again afterward.

A cutscene can abruptly become a QTE, giving you only half a second to react—or you die. Sometimes, even when you successfully complete a QTE during a boss fight, Leon rolls but still gets hit, which is very frustrating.

The hitbox is often inaccurate, mainly in boss fights such as El Gigante and the final boss.

[h2]The Verdict[/h2]
Resident Evil 4 remains a landmark in gaming, blending tense survival horror with fast-paced, tactical combat. Its innovative mechanics—over-the-shoulder camera, strategic aiming, interactive environments—still feel modern, and the distinct settings from village to castle to island keep gameplay fresh.

While controls, hitboxes, and some QTEs can be frustrating, these are minor flaws compared to the overall experience. For both newcomers and longtime fans, it’s a must-play that influenced countless games and still delivers engaging gameplay. I prefer the remake for its quality-of-life improvements and new features, but hardcore fans should experience the original as well.

It's almost everything you liked about the original, cleaned up and re-textured with refined systems and a little of the goof sanded off.

It's a ton of fun and scratches the same itch the original does, but it actually has modern controls and looks significantly better.

They've removed a lot of the B movie camp and feel, but the game still doesn't take itself entirely seriously. Leon's quips are reduced but not removed, and the quicktime insanity has been culled. Sound design is amazing and the atmosphere is incredible. Ashley isn't a shrieking blob anymore, and is actually kind of competent. She feels a lot more like a person than the OG, and has some enjoyable moments.

If you liked the original I strongly recommend this remake; if you have never played it then check some gameplay reviews first. Nostalga included it's a 9/10, as its own game without the bias it's a solid 8/10.

I never played any Resident Evil before, but 4 always stuck in my mind since I watch so many streams and had so much fun watching the gameplay. As a casual in general when it comes to horror games I had problem with starting it myself since I wouldn’t want to paint my pants brown.

But what a ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ good ride it was. For a game that had 20 years when I’m writing this review you can barely feel it was released so long ago.

I heard that 4 is one of the less scary Residents and leaning more into action. This didn't stop my cowardly ass to constantly feel pressured and scared to the point my asscheeks was alerting my GF as they were clapping so loud when I was shivering. First you have to learn how to fight back a constant and stressful pressure of Spanish madlads who will relentlessly chase you down like you are a tv on walmart’s black friday. Then you have to face the real spooky sections that game keeps on giving. All of them made me go “zoink scoobs” everytime any ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ just jumped at me and made me waste entire ammo on prematurely killing nearby wall in the process as I obviously couldn’t hit ♥♥♥♥ when panicking. Even on my 2nd playthrough Verdugo made my heart rate start to race with Sonic. Overall bosses in general never disappoints as they either scary or can put a really nice pressure on you.

And while I’m speaking about shooting – gunplay in this game is great. Aside from constant EQ management (as you don't have storage chest like in remake and can’t try all weapons in one playthrough) every gun feels unique. All of them have so different stats and very cool exclusive upgrades it is so much fun to commit a genocide even with your starting gun (that have bonkers exclusive btw. Got me through pro difficulty). Enemies are very responsive with where you are shooting, so you always manage to get upper hand with any loadout. I think this is the part of charm in this game since no matter what you choose, it will still get you through. Unless your aim is like general self-consciousness of your average politician – then nothing will help you.

Level design is great, but not without its flaws. Enemies tend to just spawn behind you and say “nothing personel kid” but in Spanish. Also, especially last sections of the game tend to lean too much into action shooter and being in my opinion most tedious and weakest part of the game. Nevertheless it can still manages to keep pressure and clearly reminds from time to time this is after all, a survival horror genre.

So yeah. If you are wondering if you should play OG RE4 then as you could guess is 100% worth recommending. Especially that people tends to say that remake is so different in many sections of the game. I’m yet to play the newer version but even now I feel like this game still holds on its own so well it is hard to invalidate such good experience that bring more brown colours to my wardrobe. It also have its own charm of having campy B-class action movie voice acting and story that you just can't get enough.
Even Leon clumsy movement is not that irritating since game is self-aware that you are turning around slower than any political extremist can understand a joke. It’s easy to get 100% achievements since they aren’t many of them. Even professional difficulty isn’t scary at all. It even creates somewhat different experience when you know the danger, allowing to prepare for it and receive the dopamine when you just obliterate everything with ease. Still worth playing, especially that you can get the key cheap this days.

Alright what the hell is this game? If you somehow just discovered in 2025 the existence of RE 4, you are probably way too young to be playing this, or... dude how is that possible lmao?

Anyways, this game has had a remake, which although is a blast on its own... somehow can't quite capture the feeling of the original. To differentiate both, Steam somehow thought that adding the release year to the OG was a good idea (instead of something like ''Resident Evil 4 Original Release'' or sum). I digress, this review will talk about the OG.

So, story-wise, this game is hella basic when you sum it up. President's daughter got kidnapped by evil entity somewhere in Europe lead by a psycho who wants to rule the world with a supposedly insane gift (which ends up being a controlling plagua for the aforementioned psycho leader). Your mission? yep. Save her. And kill hundreds of effected individual in the process.

The fun comes from the gameplay, the graphics and the atmosphere, the music and... well, nostalgia.

Keep in mind this game came out in the same year that GTA San Andreas came out...

The gameplay. It is a briliant use of proper tank control, pause to aim with a laser sight type of deal. The ennemies are satisfying as hell to shoot, whether in the head, the leg, the arm or the body. The PC version especially is truly the best way to experience this, using M+KB ideally! The ennemies all react differently to getting shot in various spots on their bodies. You then can melee attack them. There is a merchant system which allows you to buy and upgrade guns from various categories: pistols, shotgun. SMG, rifles, magnums, launchers... you get it. Fairly diverse options. That part, including the various unlockable weapons, adds to the replayability (I probably beat this game at least 30-40 times since its release on the Gamecube; I had a purple one).

The graphics. Now, obviously this thing has been properly enhanced somewhere in 2014 when it came out (again) on PC. If you dare play the OG PC version from 2005 - which is NOT on Steam... oh boy, that thing is rough lmao. That said, the core of the game is still from 2005, and with that in mind, this game looks damn good. Textures are sometimes hit or miss, but the world especially is impressive even 20 years later.

The atmosphere and the music. The sound FX in this and the soundtrack are absolutely flawless. Period. Hell, the remake came out with a paid DLC to add the OG soundtrack in... let that sink in.

Nostalgia. Yeah, now of course, I played this game in 2005 on the gamecube, then later on the PS2, then later on the PS3, PC, Wii, played the remake on the PS5, played the OG pc release... hell there even was a garbage ios release some 10 years ago that somehow ran decent on an iPhone 3GS. So, obviously nostalgia does drive my love for this game in a way. Is it as good as I think it is to someone who has never played it? probably not. But without this game, the gaming industry probably would not be where it is today. Hell, the remake would not exist...

If you played the remake and are debating whether to try the OG and where to play it (see the list of ports above lmao), then you are at the right place. The Steam version of the OG RE4 is truly the best way to experience it without wanting to gauge your eyes out (looking at you, 2005 PC release).

So yes, this is a really good game, even in 2025. Buy it, love it, enjoy it! Thanks for the read.

I also want to add that story is quite catching, what also makes it more interesting is probably dialogues and character uniqueness. I really enjoyed how Leon was pretty passive agressive whole time and even managed to annoy "cool" villains, villains were also well designed.

To sum up, for me this game has the best Resident Evil DNA and mastered it perfectly. It will go on my top survival horror games list. This was my very first Resident Evil game and what a game to start with. This game fascinated me at an early age. I believe I played it when I was 12, This was one of the most important gaming experiences I ever had, This game was very well received in the industry and became very influential. The game ditched the fixed camera angles and implemented an over the shoulder 3rd person camera. As soon as you start the game you are dropped into a tense situation where hostile villagers want you dead at all costs, these are not zombies this threat is different, the enemy is intelligent, then as soon as you think you are getting your bearings you hear the chainsaw revving and things only escalate from there. This game is intense, fun, and rewarding all at once. Leon from RE2 returns and his experience is quite prevalent, this is not the rookie cop from Raccoon City, this is special agent Leon S. Kennedy. He is armed to the teeth with weaponry, CQC skills and witty one liners. This game has a unique inventory system that is a game in itself causing you to tetris your items to maximize space. There is treasure hidden all throughout the game and you can sell it to the merchant to upgrade your weapons as well as buy new ones with additional weaponry becoming available as you progress through the game. This one is a pleasure to play through and to revisit on occasion. This game will always hold a special place in my heart as a significant moment in my gaming career when it became clear to me how much I could love a video game.

I've been playing the games in order and RE4 happens to be my first RE that wasn't a remake. I can confidently say that I actually like it better than the remakes of 2 and 3. 
The first major hangup for many will be the controls, they're tank controls with minimal options to change and can take a lot of getting used to. However, I found that after I got used to them I liked it better than the modern strafe system that the games and remake usually subscribe to. Of course it doesn't feel as intuitive to control, but I feel it actually echoes the fixed camera of the original games to a degree and enjoyed viewing it through that lens. 
Combat is also a bit of a coin toss, but I enjoyed it more in this game than the others I've played. Each gun feels like it has a purpose other than bigger gun has bigger numbers. What I really enjoyed is that the difficulty was high enough on the first playthrough that I actually found myself scrounging for bullets by the half way mark through the end of the game and always having just enough to get by. In a survival horror game that's a hard balance that many games fail to achieve and in the remakes I have played they seem to start missing that mark more often. It may be a boon of the more limited inventory system or actual game balancing systems but I felt it was always reasonable.
Another point that 4 has over the others is its story. Gone are the 6 million documents to scroll through from the first game (some still make it in) and the nonsensical plot progression of 2 and 3. 4 takes a path that isn't directly involved with its predecessors but instead follows a parallel path that gives it breathing room to make something new in the already existing world. Interactions between the characters themselves is fairly good if not simplistic, and I enjoyed watching most of them play out.
Unfortunately where 4 does truly fall flat is in the puzzles. I've said the same about 2 and 3, but when the game progression relies on moving through several areas it becomes much more linear and the puzzles begin to suffer. Many of them are reduced to a "find the key" or "find two halves of the sigil to continue" type beat, while others end up as 3x3 slide puzzles and the like. Backtracking is seen as tedious and making puzzles that over-arch an area is more difficult than creating these simpler, one off instances. The puzzles that are there are better than 3's and I would place them around the same level as 2's.
In the end, RE4 does show its age a bit, but I think that it actually adds to the charm of the game. This time I've only played the original and not the remake, but after viewing parts of it online, I think they both seem pretty good. My recommendation is still for this version, but if you really can't get used to the controls then maybe give the remake a try.

When Resident Evil 4 first landed on PC in 2007 (and later re-released on Steam), it brought with it the revolutionary over-the-shoulder perspective, intense action, and unforgettable atmosphere that redefined the survival horror genre. Unfortunately, its early PC ports suffered quite a bit—but Steam's updated "Ultimate HD Edition" fixed much of the damage.

✅ Pros
High-Resolution Graphics: The Steam version boasts crisp HD visuals and smoother textures, making it the definitive way to play the original RE4 on modern hardware.

Solid Performance: Runs well on most systems, with stable frame rates and widescreen support.

Keyboard + Mouse & Controller Support: Flexible control options give players freedom to choose their preferred setup.

Timeless Gameplay: Even after all these years, the tension-filled combat and pacing still hold up remarkably well.

Bonus Content: Includes fan-favorite extras like The Mercenaries mode, Assignment Ada, and Separate Ways.

❌ Cons
Stiff Controls Without Rebinding: Keyboard controls can feel clunky, especially during quick-time events, and rebinding is frustratingly limited.

Outdated Animations & UI: Despite the HD facelift, some character animations and menus clearly show their age.

Audio Bugs & Inconsistencies: Certain sound effects and music transitions are jarring or missing—remnants of its rocky PC port history.

Occasional Crashes & Glitches: While not game-breaking, some users have reported crashes or bugs depending on system specs.

In 2005, Resident Evil 4 didn’t just reinvent a franchise—it reshaped an entire genre. What began as a troubled development cycle turned into one of the most influential games ever made. It ditched the fixed camera angles and tank controls of the past, introduced a revolutionary over-the-shoulder perspective, and seamlessly blended survival horror with kinetic action.

Nearly two decades later, it’s still a masterclass in pacing, tension, and pure, chaotic fun.

You are Leon S. Kennedy, now a U.S. government agent, sent to rural Spain to rescue the president’s daughter, Ashley Graham. What follows is a descent into madness, featuring parasitic cults, chainsaw maniacs, ancient castles, and one-liners so cheesy they’ve become iconic.

The plot is simple but unforgettable—elevated by its characters (Luis, Ada, Salazar, and the incomparable merchant), over-the-top villains, and a tone that walks a tightrope between horror and camp with confidence.

Resident Evil 4’s biggest innovation was its third-person, over-the-shoulder camera—a now-standard design choice in modern action games. It gave players precise control, allowing for tight, satisfying gunplay while retaining a deliberate sense of vulnerability.

Combat is strategic and tactile. Enemies react to where you shoot—kneecap a ganado to set up a suplex or blast a parasite-ridden head for maximum tension. You’re always making micro-decisions under pressure, especially as ammo and herbs stay limited enough to keep you sweating.

The game constantly reinvents itself with unforgettable set pieces: defending a cabin alongside Luis, dodging lasers in a trap-filled hallway, or battling a lake monster with harpoons. It’s relentlessly creative and never drags.

Capcom nails the mood. The opening village assault sets the tone immediately: you're outnumbered, outgunned, and alone. From there, the environments evolve—eerie farmland, medieval castles, creepy laboratories—all drenched in atmosphere and full of tension.

The sound design is subtle but effective: distant chainsaws, guttural enemy chants, and oppressive silence in just the right places. Graphically, it pushed the GameCube to its limits, and while it's not cutting-edge today, the art direction has aged surprisingly well.

There’s a lot to do after finishing the story. Mercenaries mode is a high-score arcade blast, Assignment Ada and Separate Ways add more story and perspective, and New Game+ lets you blast through with upgraded gear. Add in unlockables like the Chicago Typewriter or infinite rocket launcher, and you've got dozens of hours of replay potential.

And of course… "What're ya buyin’?" The Merchant’s shop, upgrade system, and inventory management (a.k.a. Tetris with guns) are satisfying in their own right.

It’s no exaggeration to say Resident Evil 4 influenced everything from Gears of War to Dead Space to The Last of Us. It was the moment Capcom proved that horror could evolve without losing its soul—and it set a new gold standard for game design.

Even after a critically acclaimed 2023 remake, the 2005 original remains a must-play. In many ways, it still feels ahead of its time.

Resident Evil 4 (2005) is lightning in a bottle—a rare blend of innovation, polish, and pure entertainment. It balances intense horror with crowd-pleasing action and never lets up. Whether you’re revisiting it or playing for the first time, it remains an unforgettable ride.

A genre-defining classic that’s just as fun, freaky, and fresh today as it was in 2005.

Once a big time boss rolls around though, your best option is to stay put, look at a certain pixel on the screen and swing your knife a couple of times--looking at you Krasuser. Resident Evil 4 was the game that got me back into gaming. It was the game that brought me crawling back to my GameCube to finally complete Resident Evil Code: Veronica. After completing Resident Evil 4 for the first time, I ended up completing it multiple times on multiple platforms.

Resident Evil 4, I believe—along with many fans—shaped gaming forever. It brought a new way to play, with a third-person view centered more around action but still maintaining pure fear in a completely different way.

This game is one of the best games of all time—immortalised in horror, action, and suspense. RE4 did what no game had done before: it introduced a sliding difficulty system that wasn’t selectable at the beginning of the game. Instead, the game dynamically adjusted the challenge depending on how well you played—making it harder or easier based on how many times you died or struggled at a certain point. For example, when you entered the castle, there would be more or fewer enemies depending on your performance.

Over the years, I’ve played all sorts of video games, but RE4—and the Resident Evil series in general—has made the biggest impact. I'm sure this game has inspired so many developers who grew up playing the first Resident Evil game.

I was five years old when I crept downstairs. The creak of the stairs echoed as I lifted my foot off the last step. I positioned myself in the perfect stance to open the door into the living room—just like Jill opening the first door in Resident Evil (1996). I didn’t want my father to see me watching him play, afraid I’d be told to go to bed.

I watched intently as he died to a zombie. He reloaded the game and entered the first door leading to Kenneth’s body. The iconic cut-scene played—I couldn’t contain my fear. My heart pounded in my little chest as the zombie turned to face Jill and the scene ended. I ran back upstairs and hid under the covers, terrified it was going to get me.

My father heard me run upstairs. He came to check on me and asked if I was watching him play. I asked what it was, and he told me it was a new scary game he got for the PlayStation.

“Do you want to watch me play? It's very scary though,” he said.

I said yes—and I’m glad I did.

“Don’t tell your mother,” he added.

Of course, I told her the next day. Kids can’t really keep secrets. My own daughter can’t either. And to this day, I still think it was the coolest thing he ever did. He showed me gaming. Forever.

My father wasn’t very good at it—and still isn’t. He can’t play Resident Evil anymore. He sticks to getting killed on Battlefield over and over again, but he enjoys it.

But in that very moment, I knew something important about myself:

I've invested hundreds of hours into playing RE4 across multiple platforms. Easily one of the greatest games of all time. Here's a few recommendations for this version:

#1. Go into the options menu, controller setup, keyboard & mouse, and swap from classic to modern aiming mode (in less you want the clunky feel of the original console versions). This will likely require you to adjust your in-game mouse sensitivity along with it. Be aware that your mouse sensitivity greatly affects your aim with harpoons during the Del Lago boss encounter (it's not exactly a 1:1 transition from normal gun aiming to harpoon aiming).

#2. Next, go into brightness adjust and bump the brightness from 00 to +25. For whatever reason the PC version looks way darker than it should be. It's also a little high contrasty, so you might want to slightly lower your monitor's contrast.

#3. For video settings, either turn off anti-aliasing completely or set it to 4x. The effect of AA is most noticeable on the inventory screen. 4x removes jagged edges almost just as well as 8x, but they look a little less blurry on 4x. Turning it off completely gives the most crisp look (i.e. no blur), but edges will still be jaggy and pixelated. Lastly, turn off motion blur (in less you like that sort of thing).

#4. If you're comfortable with modding, I highly recommend downloading a mod to remove film grain. It's VERY strong in this game and it looks so much cleaner and better without it. The mod re4_tweaks accomplishes this (among other useful things). If you do use re4_tweaks, you shouldn't need the 4GB download in less you're utilizing other mods. Additionally consider turning off mouse turning (it's enabled by default), because it's actually pretty useful to be able to look in another direction while you're moving. And besides you can always manually turn with the keyboard anyway.

Aside from all the above I just want to throw my 2 cents into two very long standing internet debates. First, Ashley is fine, leave her alone already. If she dies or gets abducted it's 100% on you because you were acting foolish. Her yelling was intentionally obnoxious in order to get your attention so you don't game over unncessarily. And secondly, no, the Red9 is not the best handgun in a standard playthrough. It's the Blacktail. When both are fully tuned, the Blacktail has a bit more DPS, faster reload speed, and most importantly a much higher capacity (which is going to lead to more damage over time). Sure, the Red9 does have more damage-per-bullet than the Blacktail. But that only matters if you care about conserving ammo. And even in that case, a fully tuned Handgun is superior. If you only do headshots with it, it has the highest kill-per-bullet ratio of all the handguns (according to the RE wiki).

In my opinion, it is one of the finest Resident Evil games, Although the movement may feel somewhat annoying. understandable given its release many years ago, it remains both highly engaging and challenging. If you are seeking an enjoyable experience, I would certainly recommend playing it.

A Masterpiece That Changed Everything

When Resident Evil 4 launched in 2005, it didn’t just reinvent the franchise—it reshaped the entire action genre. Capcom took a bold leap, trading in the fixed camera angles and tank controls of past entries for a revolutionary over-the-shoulder perspective. The result was a game that felt faster, sharper, and more intense than anything the series—or gaming as a whole—had seen before.

From the eerie, isolated village to the gothic nightmare of the castle and the militarized madness of the island, Resident Evil 4 constantly escalates. Each area is a masterclass in pacing and environmental design, and the transition between survival horror and high-octane action is handled with expert finesse. It never loses its tension, even in its most bombastic moments.

Leon S. Kennedy’s mission to rescue the President’s daughter could’ve been a throwaway setup, but Capcom infused it with memorable characters, iconic boss fights, and a perfect blend of horror and humor. Enemies like the relentless chainsaw-wielding Dr. Salvador and the grotesque Regenerators remain etched in players’ memories for a reason—this is fear and adrenaline done right.

The game’s weapon variety, upgrade system, and tight combat loop keep things compelling across its 15+ hour runtime. There’s a tangible sense of progression as your arsenal grows, and encounters that once felt overwhelming slowly become opportunities for creative domination. And with extras like Mercenaries, Assignment Ada, and Separate Ways, the game offers serious value well beyond the credits.

Even after all these years, Resident Evil 4 hasn’t lost a step. Its controls remain responsive, its pacing impeccable, and its design influential. For those who want more, mods and randomizers inject fresh unpredictability—but even without them, the core experience is so finely tuned it’s easy to see why it’s still beloved.

Verdict
Resident Evil 4 is a landmark achievement in game design. Its blend of action, horror, and over-the-top spectacle set a new standard—and it still stands tall today. Few games are this fun, this polished, or this unforgettable.

Resident Evil 4 remains an important title in video game history, even years after its first release. It changed the way many third-person horror games were made, offering a mix of action and tension that was new at the time. At first, I thought about playing the remake version, but my laptop does not meet the system requirements to run it smoothly. I also read that many people consider the original version just as strong as the remake, especially when enhanced with the mods mentioned above.

In conclusion, Resident Evil 4 was a major step forward for its series and had a strong effect on many games that followed. It mixes survival horror and action in a way that still works well today.
