As someone who got into Resident Evil for the horror with REVII in 2017, Resident Evil 4 is an absolutely legendary video game. If you're not too familiar with Resident Evil 4, it was responsible for the third person over the shoulder camera perspective. Essentially the first to do it and the one to pave the way for the third person shooter genre. Every third person shooter game post RE4 in 2005 followed this blueprint. Not only did RE4 change the video game industry, it also changed the series itself. For the better (and worst) making it truly iconic and what is now the Skyrim of Resident Evil. You'll see many and I mean many ports of this game all over the place. 

Pros: 
-Gameplay is fun and extremely addictive. 
-You're given a large arsenal of weapons compared to previous titles.
-The story while sometimes not so serious is a fun time no matter the situation. 
-Extra content post game content includes Professional difficulty, bonus costumes and weapons, The Mercenaries, Separate Ways, and Assignment Ada.

Cons: 
-QTEs are increased with button mashing because of the 60 FPS boost.
-Personally the later part of the castle section drags and the island is a mixed bag of action and slight horror.
-Separate Ways in RE4OG post RE4R kind of falls flat in comparison to it's Remake DLC counterpart but has it's fun sides.

      Overall Resident Evil 4 is a non stop roller coaster of fun from beginning to end and is without a doubt one of the best video games ever made. If you love less action and survival horror then this might not be for you. If you love action and horror then you'll have fun. On another note. I highly recommend that if you do yourself a favor and buy this, then download the "HD Project Mod". It's a mod that feels like a true remaster in comparison to the default HD PC port. The HD Project Mod is an incredible mod that was also a decade in the making. It improves the graphical quality, adds unique settings including an FOV slider, and many more great additions of course fixing QTE problems. Please download it if you can. Anyways get out there and roundhouse kick and suplex some ganados while trying to save the president's daughter. It'll be a blast.

Okay, scratch everything you thought you knew about survival horror! Resident Evil 4 (2005) is here to redefine 'intense' and inject it directly into your veins! You're Leon S. Kennedy, special agent extraordinaire, and you're off to rural Spain, not for tapas, but to rescue the President's daughter from some seriously unchill villagers.

These aren't your grandma's neighbors. They're wielding farm tools with homicidal glee and shouting in Spanish like they're starring in the world's most terrifying folk festival. And the rest of the enemies? Let's just say they've got more parasites than a poorly-maintained petting zoo.

The action is relentless, a glorious ballet of bullets, roundhouse kicks, and desperate escapes. Leon's arsenal is a masterclass in video game logic, a collection of ridiculously oversized weapons that somehow all fit into his magical briefcase. Seriously, that thing's bigger on the inside.

From battling giant lake monsters to outsmarting pint-sized Napoleons, Resident Evil 4 is a non-stop thrill ride. It's funny, it's frantic, and it's an absolute blast. If you haven't played it, you're missing out on a cornerstone of gaming history!

My, my. Coming back to change my review. I bought RE4 with RE5+RE6 in a bundle and tested it a while back, hated it, dropped it and now I picked it back up. Idk what it is about this game. I kinda hate and like it at the same time.

STORY
The Story is simple: Save Ashley and learn more about the villains and the las plagas virus.

CHARACTERS
Leon is pretty cool and got some funny one liners. Ashley is cute, sometimes a bit loud when she's consistently screaming "LEOOON!", but overall I really like her. There are certain parts of the game where you can actually play as her, which is nice. Both of them are not interacting as much as they do in the remake. Sad.

GRAPHICS
The graphics are old, really old. They're not looking good and they're taking away the fear factor, because some monsters are just not that scary to look at, but you get used to it while playing and after a while you see a certain charme in it. 

CONTROLS
The controls are so bad, my god. The camera movement is - like the graphics - really old and clanky. It took me a long time to get used to it and I'm still not good with them. I had to walk slowly and adjust my camera after every corner and in stressful fights it's even worse. 

GAMEPLAY
Sometimes you get quick-time-events where you have to dodge attacks with a key-combo. This combo pops up really quick, so the first times it was a quaranteed miss. These combos can change keys aswell. Sometimes they want you to do a mousekey-combo and sometimes a keyboard-key-combo. 

LANGUAGE
My native language is german and for the first half of my first playthrough I actually played it in german. The voiceover is still in english, but the subtitles are in german. And some of them are just NOT WHAT THEY'RE SAYING. So I recommend playing it in english.

DIFFICULTY
It's doable and not that hard. Even the professional playthrough went relatively smooth.

GAMETIME
My first playthrough was on normal mode and it took me 20:00:45.
Then I played "Seperate Ways" (Ada's campaign) which took me 04:30:26.
And then I did another playthrough on professional, which took 16:59:14.

ACHIEVEMENTS
It took me two playthroughs of the main game and one playthrough of Ada's Campaign to get all achievements.

PRICE
I bought RE4 in a bundle with RE5 + RE6 for 15,02€ (which is around 15$ aswell) and I would recommend buying it in bundles.

Resident Evil 4 is in my opinion one of the greatest games of all time, the gameplay was revolutionary at the time, the graphics far exceeded its predecessors, and it gave us a more mature and skilled Leon.
The enemies in RE4 were much smarter than the previous 3 games as they were infected with parasites rather than a zombie virus, which made them smarter and gave them the ability to wield weapons. The enemy types are all unique and provide different challenges such as the Dr. Salvadors and their one-shot chainsaw attacks, or the Regenerators requiring you to shoot multiple parasites to defeat them. 
The bosses are also unique and fun, from Mendez splitting apart midway through, to the terrifying U-3 encounter, to cheesing Salazar with an RPG, to Krauser's knife stun lock, every boss has different techniques and tricks that make them enjoyable every time you play.
The characters also stand out in the game, Leon is an amazing protagonist, Ada's interactions with Leon are flirtatious and antagonistic (towards Leon of course), Salazar is annoying to the point of being quite funny, and Luis is one of the best side characters in all of Resident Evil.
The extra modes in the game are also quite enjoyable, mercenaries is always a delight and RE4 does not disappoint, Assignment Ada, while not being canon, is an enjoyable game mode where you play as Ada collecting Las Plagas samples, and the Separate Ways story mode is an amazing story expansion that shows the game from Ada's perspective, giving more boss fights and implementing sparring use of her grappling gun.
The game is not as much a survival horror game as it is an action shooter, but it does balance a sprinkle of horror within the game, with several parts such as the U-3 boss, the oven man, and of course, the Regenerators, provide the horror aspects that Resident Evil fans long for in each game.
The biggest flaw in the game is Ashley's AI, she commonly puts herself in the worst possible positions throughout the game, walking into beartraps, crouching down and stopping when an enemy gets close, running right into the Las Plagas tendrils that protrude from Ganado heads, and at times running in front of Leon as he makes his shot. Ashley does become much more manageable if you unlock the Knight costume, which makes her invincible.
Overall, Resident Evil 4 is, not without reason, most people's favorite Resident Evil game, it has a fun story, challenging but fun gameplay, and a decent mix of horror and action.

A Timeless Classic
No matter how many years pass, Resident Evil 4 remains a legendary piece of gaming history. From its immersive atmosphere and intense gameplay to its unforgettable bosses, everything about it is incredible.

The story follows Leon S. Kennedy on a mission to rescue the president’s daughter from a mysterious cult. Along the way, he encounters iconic characters like Ada Wong, whose role is further explored in the extra modes. Leon’s cheesy one-liners and the game’s tense yet action-packed narrative make it an unforgettable experience.

Gameplay & Extra Modes
The over-the-shoulder camera revolutionized third-person shooters, making combat feel intense and strategic. The enemy AI is smart, inventory management is satisfying, and exploring the world is rewarding.

Beyond the main campaign, the game includes Separate Ways, which expands Ada’s story, and Assignment Ada, a short but fun challenge. These modes add more depth and replayability, along with The Mercenaries and unlockable weapons.

Why It’s Still Worth Playing
Unlike many modern games that last only 7-8 hours, Resident Evil 4 offers a lengthy adventure with plenty to explore. It’s not overly difficult unless played on higher modes, but it always keeps you engaged. The sound design and eerie atmosphere enhance the experience, making every moment feel tense.

Final Verdict
An absolute classic that still holds up today. Whether you're a longtime fan or new to the series, Resident Evil 4 is a must-play that set the standard for action-horror games.

Resident Evil 4 is not just a game that has survived decades—it has rightfully become the benchmark for action-horror. Even years after its release, its influence on the genre remains undeniable. It set new standards for game design, and its balance between intense survival, dynamic combat, and horror atmosphere still feels fresh today.

The story is simple but presented with cinematic flair: special agent Leon Kennedy is sent to a dark Spanish village to rescue the president's daughter. But he has no idea that he will face a nightmare beyond ordinary zombies. The Los Illuminados cult, parasite-infected villagers, and terrifying mutants turn every encounter into a true test of survival.

Gameplay is what truly makes Resident Evil 4 iconic. The over-the-shoulder camera, groundbreaking aiming mechanics, melee combat, and constant resource scarcity create tension that lasts until the very end. Every gunfight requires tactics, and the variety of weapons and upgrades adds depth to the gameplay.

But the real magic lies in the atmosphere. The darkness of abandoned villages, the eerie silence of Salazar’s castle, the cold corridors of underground labs—it all leaves a lasting impression. The soundtrack, sound design, and intense horror moments make you feel like you are trapped in this madness.

Resident Evil 4 is not just a game—it’s a legend that has stood the test of time. Its remakes and ports only emphasize how essential it is to the industry. Even if you've played it dozens of times, it will still make your heart race.

I managed to pull through, partly because RE4 is a bloody masterpiece, here's why:
+ meticulous level design. the game looks as messy and detailed as real life. Lots of different environments: barns, church, caves, castle. There's some backtracking involved in the story, and it's done well. Also there's lots of crates with loots which reward exploration. Also egg laying chickens! i really felt like a young boy during Easter collecting all those chicken eggs. the eggs saved my life many times.
+ RE4(2005) looks and sounds amazing. It rarely felt like I was playing a 20 year old game. It's that immersive. The cinematography is damn impressive, with lots of memorable action scenes, like the ones with the fish, or the helicopter, also the duel between Leon and that other person. All the animations look very realistic, which more than makes up for the low graphics fidelity.
+ excellent combat. you can choose to play more safely and use more ammo, or you're like me who's too frugal to use limited items, so you shoot the zombies in the leg, then slice them like vegetables as they lay on the ground. This is very satisfying, and also risky when there's a lot of enemies. But you have the ability to E Kick a staggered zombie which knocks back a whole group of zombies, and then you can slice multiple lying zombies at once! Boss fights are designed very well. Creepy and challenging at first, but doable once you figure it out. The detailed, fluent animations and sounds are what allows the game to stand the test of time. If you're more into the story, you can buy a rocket launcher to deal with the bosses quickly. But it takes up 8x2 of inventory space and costs 30,000 Pta.
+ gameplay progression is very compelling. Enemies become stronger and weirder after each chapter, but you get new weapons and upgrades in order to keep up. At least, if you've found enough coins and treasures to afford them. This feels way more organic and realistic, compared to the countless games where you gain levels from earning EXP.
+ very disgusting enemies, if you're into that. you do get used to it if you're not. the bosses in particular are gross AF.
+ writing is kinda terrible, but it's "so bad that it's good" type of terrible.

It's like a deranged level of choosing style over comfort. This is the first Resident Evil game that I have ever owned, and man it was a blast! If you are tired of some of the current industry trends in video games (graphics over game play, multiplayer/online only, micro transactions, etc) then this game is a great vacation. It's a cliche to say, I know, but they really don't make games like this anymore. There is a reason why the game has been ported to so many platforms (started on Game Cube, then ended up on PlayStation 2, Windows, Wii, iOS,  Zeebo, PlayStation 3, Xbox 360, Android, PlayStation 4, Xbox One, Nintendo Switch, and Oculus Quest 2 according to Wikipedia) it's really 'effin good!

The main character, Leon Kennedy, has quickly become one of my favourite video game protagonists. His dialogue is so corny, but I love it. I think you'll find it hard not to smile at some of his lines. He's a smooth talking, bad-a**, secret agent who doesn't give up against overwhelming odds. I honestly can't think of anything I dislike about him. He's just a really fun over the top character, and I'm all for it. The dialogue in general is over the top, in a way that I think has a significant "cool" factor but is self aware, and does not take itself overly seriously. You may also notice some familiar voices, such as a particular squirrel from bikini bottom, or your friendly neighbourhood Nord. Ashley can be a little bit annoying at times to deal with I'll admit, but I found that you never have to deal with her for too long before the game separates you from her. 

The game play uses something called "tank controls" which involves using WASD to move and the mouse to aim and shoot, with the caveat being that you cannot move while shooting or reloading. I had a hard time with it at first, and if you have never played a shooter with a similar control style (like me at the time) it's going to feel clunky at first. Don't let that stop you though, you get used to it I promise, and eventually it feels completely natural to control. Landing your shots is essential to survival, for conserving ammunition as well as keeping enemies at bay. It can make for some really tense moments when you have one magazine left and you need to land all your shots to survive. I played through the game on normal the first time, which has adaptable difficulty. This means that if you're doing well, it'll crank up the difficulty, but if you're dying a lot, it will tone it back. It's really seamless, and can be helpful for your first play through. Once you beat the game once, you unlock the hardest difficulty, professional mode, as well as the option to do new game+ among other things. Professional mode is what normal mode would be, if the difficulty was always cranked to the max setting, and was what I played it on my second time through. I enjoyed both modes a lot, and see the value in each. Beating the game also unlocks a game mode called separate ways, which goes through the story again, but this time you play from Ada's perspective which was really neat to see, and which I would also recommend playing through.

The game is from 2005, the graphics are not going to be hyper realistic, but I could honestly care less. Personally, I think graphics are the most over rated part of what makes a game good, and I'm not impressed by the industry's shift in focus towards it over refined game play and user experience. I think it has aged well for how old it is, and has some notably decent looking graphical effects (fire from torches, curtains billowing in the wind, etc). I would also mention that the soundtrack has some really unique tracks that I think suit the game well, with a good mix of horror and action themes. 

The bottom line is, if you aren't bothered by the older graphics, the nuances of games from this time period, enjoy over the top action-horror, and are looking for hours of game play from an amazing single player experience, buy this game, you won't be disappointed.

Can't really say anything that hasn't already been said about the original Resident Evil 4. It is truly a masterpiece that everyone who enjoys games should try playing at least once in their lifetime. This may seem biased from a massive survival horror fan like myself but Resident Evil 4 really does live up to the love that everyone gives it. 

The story is simple enough to understand for anyone to enjoy, Leon who has been seen previously in Resident Evil 2 has been trained into a full on mega soldier with the reflexes of Bruce Lee in Enter the Dragon. Leon has become a completely different person compared to the events of the previous games and it really shows in the events throughout the story. You set out on a simple mission, find the presidents missing daughter inside of a village hidden away within Spain. I would go a lot further into this but believe me when I say it gets so much better and is worth experiencing without knowing anything at all. Before I move on I must say that the dialogue is peak writing and the way Leon reacts to his enemies throughout the story is absolute cinema. 

The gameplay is terrifying. You have to ADS to reload and you can't move an inch either when doing this, this is made even more excruciating when you have an unupgraded rifle and a catapult is prepared to give your skull and new pavement to rest upon. There are no crosshairs either when you play, instead you get given a laser that you have aim that is in justice, a lot more accurate but harder to use with how the camera works in this game. Did I forget to mention that aiming down sights also means you can't move at all? All of this is brilliant as in each encounter you really have to play when is the best time to reload and prepare to fight as if you didn't look behind you expect the hand of God himself to send you packing back to your last checkpoint. I find all of this a very intriguing mechanic towards making the game scarier by using the way that your character does the most basic of tasks, shooting things. 

Resident Evil 4 is so replayable even after being out for almost 20 years now which is insane. Normal difficulty does not hold your hand, thanks to the time it was released where games were expectedly much harder even the base difficulty will give u a little struggle here and there. But my god Professional difficulty really does the name justice, it really tests your knowledge of the game and how to conserve your resources for the extremely hard parts later in a run. We all know I'm talking about Water Hall and for anyone who doesn't know what this room is I envy you.

This is one of those objectively good, classic games, that i absolutely can't stand to play and will most likely never finish.

The atmosphere is fantastic and the dialogue is hilarious and cheesy, so it should be right up my alley, but the controls absolutely massacre this game for me. 

More than a few times I've had the camera pointing in one direction, squeezed the trigger to aim, and had my camera snatched away to face where Leon is facing, disorienting me and throwing off my aim, and the control stick sensitivity is just never right. I can't seem to get a happy medium between too sensitive and too stiff. Or had Ashley nabbed by an enemy, before i accidentally shoot her in the face because Leon shakes like a jello cake on an old washing machine. 

The argument in favor of these controls is always "Yeah well the game is built for them so get over it", and while yes, the game is in fact built around these controls (Most of the time), these controls are still awful. and I'm not gonna sugar coat it. The game suffers because it is having to compensate for these controls. Enemies have to be slow and predictable, and the combat can never take place too far or require too much precision, because Leon just can't do it. The few times where it tries to do something more than the controls allow, such as the water room where the game wants to have a big action hero shoot out while you solve a quick puzzle under stress, it falls apart, and you can see this in how veteran players speak about these areas in the game. The water room is the most universally despised section of this entire game and it's one hundred percent because the game tries to do something that it's controls just don't allow for. It always inevitably ends up with the player cheesing the area and kiting the enemies into a room to funnel them. The remake is so much better in many ways, the enemies are faster, but Leon can move and fight his way through them with a little effort. Remake Leon makes this room feel like something out of a john wick film. OG RE4 Leon feels like Barney Fife by comparison.

This is a game that you should definitely try once in your life, maybe you'll get over the dated controls. If you do you're in for a classic game with a lot of good cheesy dialogue and puzzle solving. But if you don't, that's okay, and don't let any RE super fan tell you otherwise, they're not good controls, they never were, and they never will be. If you can't hack it, play the remake, it's fantastic.

Resident Evil 4 isn’t just a game, it’s a revolution. 
When it was first released in 2005, it redefined the survival horror genre, introducing groundbreaking gameplay mechanics and a bold new direction for the series. 
Even today, it stands as a timeless masterpiece that continues to influence action-adventure games across the industry.
The over-the-shoulder camera was a revelation, offering a level of immersion and precision that felt entirely new. 
This innovation transformed the series’ combat, striking a perfect balance between tension and action. 
Fighting off waves of Ganados, hostile villagers under the control of the Las Plagas parasite, was an exhilarating experience, combining strategy, resource management, and split-second decisions. 
The satisfaction of landing a headshot or perfectly timed kick is unmatched.
Leon S. Kennedy, returning as the protagonist, is effortlessly cool and charismatic. 
His one-liners and stoic demeanor provide levity amidst the relentless terror, making him one of gaming’s most iconic characters. 
The supporting cast, including Ashley Graham and the enigmatic Ada Wong, enrich the narrative, while memorable villains like Ramon Salazar and Osmund Saddler deliver campy, larger-than-life performances that perfectly complement the game’s tone.
The pacing of Resident Evil 4 is impeccable. 
From the eerie opening in the desolate village to the high-octane battles in the castle and island, every moment is packed with tension and excitement. 
The game constantly evolves, introducing new enemies, weapons, and challenges to keep players on their toes. 
Boss battles, such as the fight with El Gigante and the nerve-wracking duel with Krauser, are thrilling set pieces that remain etched in memory.
The atmosphere is another highlight, with detailed environments that ooze dread and foreboding. 
The haunting music and sound effects amplify the suspense, creating an unforgettable sense of immersion. 
Add to this a vast arsenal of weapons, a clever merchant system ("What’re ya buyin’?"), and plenty of secrets to uncover, and you have a game that invites endless replayability.
Even years after its release, Resident Evil 4 remains a pinnacle of gaming excellence. 
It’s a game that dared to take risks and succeeded in every way, leaving an indelible mark on the industry. 
Whether you’re a fan of survival horror or simply love great games, Resident Evil 4 is an experience that’s impossible to forget.

Resident Evil 4 (2005) is one of the most iconic and influential entries in the survival horror genre, fundamentally changing the gameplay approach and setting of the series. Released initially on the Nintendo GameCube and later on other platforms, it quickly gained cult status. Here are the key aspects that are often highlighted in reviews of the original game:

Revolutionary Gameplay: Resident Evil 4 significantly altered the gameplay mechanics by abandoning the fixed camera angles that were a hallmark of previous installments. Instead, it introduced a dynamic over-the-shoulder camera view, which improved the combat system and made the gameplay more action-oriented while retaining survival elements.

Story and Atmosphere: The game follows Leon S. Kennedy as he travels to Europe to rescue the U.S. president's daughter, Ashley Graham. The atmosphere of the game also shifted, becoming darker and more intense, with a greater focus on action and tense moments. Unlike earlier entries, Resident Evil 4 balanced horror and action, making it more of a thrilling action-horror experience.

Enemies and Level Design: The game introduced players to new enemy types, including the "Los Illuminados" infected, as well as massive bosses and creatures. Each level was carefully designed to offer unique environments, keeping the gameplay fresh and engaging throughout the entire game.

Exploration and World Design: Although not an open world, the game’s level design encouraged exploration. Players could search various locations for hidden items, weapons, and secrets. The weapon upgrade system added an element of strategy and resource management to the gameplay.

Sound and Music: The sound design was top-notch for its time. Environmental sounds, music, and enemy noises helped create a chilling atmosphere. The sound of enemies approaching or the ticking of a clock in critical moments added to the tension and suspense.

Innovations in Controls and Combat: The game introduced a tactical approach to shooting, improving aiming mechanics, which was a major innovation for the series. The combat was more dynamic and engaging, with cover mechanics and diverse weapons offering players more tactical options in battles.

Replayability: After completing the main story, Resident Evil 4 offered additional modes and unlockables, increasing its replay value. These extra features kept players coming back for more.

Resident Evil 4 (2005) is not just a successful game, but a breakthrough in the genre, setting new standards for action and horror games. Its influence is still felt in modern games, and it continues to be regarded as one of the best titles in gaming history.

It's gonna be difficult to review this game as what can be said about it at this point? 

I have probably run through this game well over 100 maybe even 200 times across all its various ports. From the Gamecube to the Ultra HD Steam version, I've seen a lot of RE4. Don't let that 300 hour number fool ya - I've probably got well over 1000 maybe more on this game combined with all its versions. 

I think what makes this game hold up so well is the fact that it is so simple. It's not too hard for newcomers (especially if you have played a third person shooter before), and it's not too easy for genre vets as the dynamic difficulty can deliver surprises. The mechanics are easy to use. It's primarily just moving and shooting. Get to one area, clear it out, get to the next area. 

Unlike previous Resident Evil games where enemies were to be avoided, here in RE4, the enemies are the puzzles. Dispatching them and getting from point A to B is the puzzle. How do you do it efficiently/correctly/consistently? And how can you improve it? What weapons should you use? How should you upgrade them? 

As it turns out, the answer to all those questions is... whatever works for you. This is greatly benefited by the satisfying gun-play. The guns in this game have a certain charm to them that makes each of them unique to use. It's not like in previous RE games where you would find the shotgun and pretty much barely use the handgun anymore. Here, every weapon can be useful in any scenario. 

I would absolutely love if Capcom gave this game the Dead Rising Deluxe Remaster treatment. Add some QoL to the gameplay (moving while shooting, switching weapons via the D-pad, and cut out some of the fat: Dos Gigante fight, Novistador enemies, and the entire island). 

The 2023 remake greatly disappointed me with its shift in gameplay to utilize the knife more. I absolutely hated that. Why remake a game that is all about the guns and make the knife the big thing? What were they thinking turning the combat into a QTE fest of parrying? Ugh. Just awful. 

But that's the risk you run when remaking something that was already good - there isn't much to change other than maybe some superficial details here or there. If the Remake focused on gunplay (and actually had consistent aiming, i-frames, proper wait/follow-me commands for Ashley - y'know, all the good stuff this game had), I would have enjoyed it way more.

Ever since the remake's release, I have found a new love for this game that wasn't there before. I have grown to appreciate its design way more mechanically and understand why it works so well and has held up over the years. And if it's not the gunplay that serves it well, it's the added benefit of its comical performances.

Paul Mercier's portrayal of Leon Kennedy simply is too good. It's almost like he knows he's the protagonist of a video game. Nothing gets in his way and he exudes confidence. It's shocking to me that Capcom thought that the Remake needed new dialogue and new actors - they really could have re-used the audio from this game and it would have worked far better. 

The story is of course nonsensical - a roller-coaster of attractions and events that really could only happen in a video game - but that's part of the fun. It doesn't take itself seriously, and none of the characters try to make it serious. Trying to bring seriousness into it (like the Remake did) takes away the charm. 

The best way to pay homage to Resident Evil 4 isn't to remake it. It doesn't need one. Yes, there is some age to it (tank controls, graphics, etc.), but that's superficial. Like I said, a Deluxe Remaster would serve this game's legacy far better than whatever Capcom did with that Remake. 

I wholeheartedly recommend this game to anyone who wants a fun roller-coaster to playthrough. I definitely recommend it over the misguided remake. And if tank controls scare you, try control Type II - it's not a total fix, but it makes the control scheme more modern.  I also recommend installing the HD Project as it not only greatly improves the textures for the game, but also adds re4tweaks - a sort of limited game modifier that can tweak certain aspects of the gameplay (debug menu, skip the intro, fixed camera in Ashley's segment, auto-complete QTEs). 

If you have already played through this game multiple times as I have, and just need a reason to go through it again, well, how many ways have you tried to challenge yourself playing it? No yellow herbs? No weapons upgrades? Knife only? Pistol only? No reloading? No merchant? See... that's one of the the best aspects to this game that the remake also fails at - it's actually fun in this game to limit yourself. The gameplay is just so tailored to any experience you want and it's consistent enough for you to know how to react. 

I cannot express my love for this game enough. Pick it up, play it, have some fun.

As a veteran of RE4, I must say that I'm shocked to discover that I actually prefer the remake to the original. The remake simply has more reason to explore and find items, has better level design, a better story, and much more modern controls. However, the original RE4 has slightly slower gameplay and values taking refuge in certain choke points whilst you shoot all of the enemies rushing towards you; a different but more realistic gameplay approach. The game also has that traditional old game charm (can't believe games like this are considered "retro" now) where the color pallet is colorful, but still dark enough to maintain the tone at the same time. The game doesn't take itself serious, but it's also not necessarily a comedy either (though the writing can be so corny that it's funny sometimes). There's just something about the vibes of games from this generation of gaming that are so novel and cool, I can't quite describe it.

Of course, this game originally came out on the gamecube so the controls are very much something to get used to if you're playing on controller; which is most definitely the definitive way to play this game since the game is designed solely with controller in mind. This game's tank controls help give you a sense of panic, but it still gives you enough time to react since the enemies move slower as a result. It's quite an unconventional and unique combination that actually works out in the game's favor.

This game is where the resident evil series started to turn more into an action series rather than a survival horror series so if you've never played any version of RE4, keep that in mind. It's more of a action game with horror elements rather than a horror game with action. 
The separate ways dlc comes with this game and I gotta say, separate ways for the RE4 remake is definitely better. Much of the content from the separate ways dlc in the remake is present in the main campaign INSTEAD so it's not all doom and gloom.

The original RE4 definitely takes significant inspiration from action movies that came out around the time of the games release such as the matrix and even older blockbusters such as the type that arnold schwarzenegger or sylvester stallone would star in. It has cheesy one liners, mini guns, and explosions, yet it somehow also maintains a "survive in the woods" aesthetic similar to the first evil dead. You can tell that they just threw random ideas at the wall and kept whatever seemed fun. That doesn't mean the game is bad, quite the contrary actually.

Some parts of the original are easier than the remake and some parts are harder. This game also has a dynamic difficulty feature that adjusts difficulty in real time based off how well you're doing in game and I'm not sure if the remake has that feature or not but I'm pretty sure I remember hearing that it wasn't in the remake. It helps balance the game and you don't even notice that the game is changing difficulty when you play either.

So the big question remains: Is the original RE4 worth it in 2024? Does it hold up?
It holds up for the most part in that its still a very fun game but the remake is probably more worth it if you're more used to playing games that came out in the last 10 years, hate tank controls with a burning passion, or if you can't stand gamecube era graphics. just keep in mind that you can't move while aiming in this game, the camera movement is EXTREMELY limiting, and you aim with the left stick on controller instead of the right stick. Considering that this game was so popular that it essentially INVENTED the third person shooter genre, I'd say it gets a pass though. I mean hey, on the bright side there's no weapon bloom because this game had the cool stylistic choice to make it so that you aim with every weapons laser sight instead of using a dorky crosshair that's stuck to the center of the screen when you decide to aim. It's a very cool and immersive way to make your character aim a gun in a video game and I don't think we give this game enough praise for that.

Buy this game if you have nostalgia for the original, have nostalgia for this generation of games, want a more campy and OG RE experience, like action games, or zombie games. If you want a scary resident evil experience, buy resident evil 1 or 2 instead.

BEFORE YOU BUY HOWEVER, READ THIS: There is a bug in the mine cart level during the QTE after you jump off the mine cart and have to spam a button to pull yourself up. The QTE requires DOUBLE the button presses in order to be successful. It really sucks and the only way to fix it is to temporarily put your game at 30fps in the game's main menu. It's not the end of the world but it certainly is an inconvenience.

The gameplay itself is a symphony of tension and exhilaration, wherein each confrontation with the ungodly Ganados doth test the mettle and wits of the player. The camera, steadfast o’er Leon’s shoulder, doth immerse one fully into his plight, whilst the arsenal of weapons grants choice and strategy in dispatching foes. Truly, the combat is as a dance of death, both graceful and grim.

The artistry of the setting is no less a marvel. The sinister village, the decayed castle, and the foreboding island are rendered with such grim splendour that one might feel the chill of their darkness upon one’s very skin. The atmosphere is thick as London fog, each corner pregnant with the promise of peril.

The characters, too, are a gallery of vivid souls. Leon, the stoic yet sardonic hero, doth carry his burden with aplomb. Ashley, though a damsel oft in distress, is endearing in her plight. And let us not forget the villainous Ramon Salazar, whose theatrical malevolence is as delightful as it is detestable.

Yet, all is not without blemish. The escorting of Ashley, though integral to the tale, doth occasionally test the patience of the player. And the quick-time events, though thrilling in their moment, mayhap be seen as the bane of immersion.

In summation, Resident Evil 4 is a masterstroke, a game that hath not merely endured but flourished in the years since its release. It doth combine the pulse-pounding thrills of combat with a narrative of gothic intrigue, ensuring its place as a timeless jewel in the diadem of gaming history. Hie thee hence and partake of its splendour, for it is truly a marvel to behold!

The last two thirds are enjoyable at times, but RE4 has so many fundamental and frustrating flaws, that I'm [i]baffled[/i] by its 'GOAT' status.

 - There's a completely broken quicktime event which occurs at the end of a lengthy and challenging minecart combat section. The only fix is to change the FPS limit to 30, which, of course, you can ONLY do by exiting to the MAIN menu, and with RE's fixed save points, your last save was a long time ago. I literally wasted AN HOUR OR 2 of gameplay. Absolutely shocking; almost deserves the thumbs down for that alone.

 - Thin and cliched story

 - First third utilises an unengaging 'running - shooting - picking up items' gameplay loop. Almost gave up entirely on it, but thankfully, the last two thirds are much heavier on puzzles (the highlight of previous games), as well as interesting environments.

 - Camera movement isn't linked to where Leon's facing, and when he's on his own, the FOV is too narrow and he covers too much of the screen. This bizarrely makes such basic activities as being able to move around and see the environment you're in, feel much more cumbersome than they should. 

 - Ridiculously long, about TWICE as much as it should be, just gets old and stale.

 - They don't always get the balance right with boss fights. Some involve a lot of trial, error and respawning.

 - The inventory doesn't automatically condense all items in one area to make space, so in order to accommodate a large item, you have to manually move many small items around to make space, which is far more cumbersome than it needs to be. Baffling.

 - Ammo drops become infrequent towards the end, but the game provides all ammo types, even for guns you don't own, and you can't buy ammo. There's a wide variety of guns to choose from, so what this should theoretically encourage, is for a player to strategically pick the few which they like, and which suit their playstyle. I didn't think pistols were useful past the game's halfway point, roughly. Yet, I still get pistol ammo drops, despite not owning a pistol, and running out of ammo for all the guns I DO own. The game is forcing me to buy a gun I don't even want. Dumbest issue.

 - Quicktime events often don't give you enough time to respond, or they're not responsive enough, since I often failed at events after clicking the right buttons / pressing the right keys. Also, they sometimes appear out of nowhere during cutscenes, catching you off guard.

Niet voor niets dat Capcom hier in 2024 een remake van maakte, maar was dit per se nodig? Naar mijn mening niet, ook al komt dit spel uit 2005, de gameplay is nog van deze tijd. De wapens zijn responsief, de enemies zijn nog steeds eng, vooral die ene in de koelcellen in de kelder van het kasteel. Ik kan echter niet ontkennen dat de graphics er misschien wel gedateerd uitzien, edoch geeft dit enig gevoel van nostalgie.

Het is zo'n spel waar je eigenlijk zelf alle controls uit moet vogelen, voor mensen met een 60% keyboard kunnen de knoppencombinaties af en toe nog wel hinderlijk zijn. Als je je spullen bijvoorbeeld in de inventory wil draaien moet je 'Backspace + Fn Backspace' doen. Wat mij ook gehinderd heeft zijn de knoppencombinaties bij de quick-time events. Het is namelijk een afwisseling tussen beide muisklikken en X + C tegelijkertijd indrukken, dat gaat af en toe vrij lastig als je maar 0,8 seconden hebt om te reageren. Ik ben toch geen F1-coureur! Het is een afweging die je zal moeten maken, wil je dit spel spelen. Je hebt de keuze tussen kut-knoppencombinaties maar wel goeie aim, waardoor je minder schaarse resources verspilt, of je kiest makkelijkere knoppencombinaties, maar wel embarmelijke aim. 

Vervolgens wijd ik een stuk aan het plot. Het doel van dit spel is eigenlijk om de dochter van de president van de VS te redden, Ashley. Zij is ontvoerd en meegenomen naar een gek dorpje ergens in een uithoek van Spanje. Daar komt onze hoofdpersoon in het verhaal, Leon S. Kennedy. Hij moet Ashley redden, maar komt er al gauw achter dat de dorpelingen besmet zijn met het Plagas-virus, een parasiet die ervoor zorgt dat de grote schurk, Osmund Saddler, jou kan sturen. Lijkt net de 5G-chip van de coronavaccinatie, they did know! Afijn, de bedeoeling is dus dat je Ashley redt, maar daartussen zitten nog zes boss-fights. Deze boss-fight zijn allen even uniek. Bij de ene is het run-and-gun, terwijl je bij de andere juist een put met lava moet openen, zodat diegene erin valt.

Kortom kan er gesteld worden dat Resident Evil 4 een pareltje is in de gaming-industrie, ondanks dat het spel uit 2005 komt. Mijn vingers doen zeer van het typen, dus scheid ik er maar eens mee uit.

Crazy to think this game is going to be 20 years old soon. It's innovations are still fresh in 2024, so it doesn't feel like something from yesteryear. Within the franchise you have the TPS shooters still sharing 80% the same formula and mechanics of RE4-the remakes from 2019 onward being the most recent. Outside of the franchise, the number of games that had its developers cite RE4 as a direct influence litter the decade of 2005 to 2015. The Last of US, Dead Space, Gears of War, Uncharted. Even the Bioshock devs talk up the RE4 connection in terms of open map design.

	Then there are the franchises indirectly influenced by RE4. You can basically throw every single third person shooter into this pile. Play GTAIII and spend an hour shooting stuff. Then play GTAIV (or V) and do the same. Night and day; TPS before RE4 were generally janky and placed the camera directly behind the character. RE4 places the camera more on the shoulder and lowers the FOV and zooms in on the reticle when aiming. It's as innovative a mechanic as z-targeting was in Ocarina of Time. 

	RE4 was a phenomenon during its time. But it did have detractors. Fans of the classic franchise preferred the emphasis on puzzles and 'survival' in its predecessors. 'RE4 is a good game, but it isn't RE' was the sentiment. And I have to agree; as compared to its predecessors it was a totally different formula. Some called it 'evolution', but in retrospect the era from RE4 to RE6 were rightfully criticized for being heavy on the action and sparse on the puzzles, survival, and exploration-series staples.

	Thankfully it seems like a balance has been reached by RE7. But there are a few other flaws worth pointing out that are more apparent now. The maps can instill claustrophobia at times, and I've had my fair share of damage due to the small spaces. Or even getting boxed in by enemies. And it becomes a bigger issue when Ashley joins you a third of the way in. 

	The escort aspect of the game has her follow you into battle (with no weapons). She can take damage (and die) or get kidnapped (and net you a game over). Ashley's 'LEON!' yell became a meme during it's time for how annoying she and the escorting could be. Yes, she will take damage in the smaller areas of the castle. And it is annoying to waste healing items on what is an anchor.

	That said, Ashley joins you a third of the way through but regularly 'disappears'. And even when she doesn't, there's usually a place to stash her safely into. As much as I'd like less Ashley it's still commendable to have escort mechanics work this well in 2005. Ashley and puzzles aside there's really not a lot to fault the game for in its play elements. It feels like nitpicking. The mine launcher is situational. The TMP is mediocre. Fair points, but it feels like grasping for something to critique. I think the only other fair criticism centers around the writing.

	This game came after CV, which was the first RE game to get us out of Raccoon City while still continuing the plot threads. Claire returns, in search of her missing brother. Wesker returns, in a superhuman, virus-infused form. And Chris comes out of hiding, in an effort to rescue his now missing sister. All happening with the backdrop of Umbrella's founding unfolding, and the quest for a scientist to cement his family's legacy within the corporation (via child clones). 

	All good stuff that reasonably moves the franchise forward. Originally CV was supposed to be RE3, but they kept that title for the PSX line of games. Whatever the case, RE4 came out afterwards, and it abandons most plot threads from CV and/or just reiterates them. Wesker is back at the very end, doing the same thing he did in CV: collecting viruses for an as-of-yet unknown organization. And...that's it. The main plot deals with rescuing the president's daughter from a religious cult using a parasite to control and expand its adherents. 

	And it works, there's nothing wrong with the game. But writing is second, with this feeling like a spin-off of the main franchise. I'd say they had a difficult task in moving the franchise past Raccoon City, but CV already did that. Funnily enough, RE5 would continue what CV started, which further makes the plot in RE4 feel odd. It's unrelated to everything before and after it. 

	Thankfully the game gets everything else right. Writing aside there's no concrete criticisms you can throw at the game. It uses the tank controls from the old RE games, but in third person. When aiming you stand still and move the reticle around. It's slow, but it works with the zombie-like enemies of this franchise. If you've played the newer games it feels a little odd at first, but easy to get used to.

	The game is split into three 'worlds': the village; castle; and Island. The village has larger, more open environments with options for the player in battle. The castle presents enemy variety and more Ashley involvement. As well as some unique set pieces. The Island throws ammo and enemies at you, abandoning all pretense of 'survival horror' and becoming a shooter. 

	Past the main campaign you get the mercenaries mode, which is a short arcade game set in a small play area where you rack up kills. It illustrates how well-crafted the shooting is, and I remember wasting days on this mode. You get to play as other characters, each with unique weapons and melee attacks. There's also the Ada campaign, as well as 'Separate Ways', which was a PS2 exclusive campaign. Then there are the unlockable weapons for a new playthrough.

	So popular was this game that in their frequent playthroughs people found that you could complete the game using only the knife. Knife only runs were a staple on Youtube at the time. You can easily find people still arguing between the different weapons. And it's had plenty of mods created for it over the years. Its popularity is cemented. A '10/10' is rare for me, because it has to be impeccable quality and/or innovative. But RE4 is easily one of those games for me. 

	I can't speak to the remake's quality or comparison to this game (yet), but that's irrelevant since this game stands on its own as a must-play anyway.

Tip #1: While standing on the docks, shoot the water enough times for an achievement
Tip #2: Crows drop items and money
Tip #3: Press the delete key or bumpers to rotate items while moving them
Tip #4 Press 'interact' twice to kick open doors

Disclaimer: I touched it up in case any one else wants to read it, but you can ignore the rest of this review. It contains mostly useless info and info that the game feeds to you over time, but I'm keeping it intact for comparison between my style and skill as of 2024 and any future writing I let loose onto the web.

Movement - Is pretty good for the most part. You walk like a tank, vault over objects, and climb ladders. Taking cover behind objects can be a bit awkward because of the limited movement (unless you get to interact with an object to take cover). It isn't the most complex or refined, but it does what is needed to get the job done. Easier interactions with some objects would be nice though.

QTEs - On controller, the QTEs provide some appreciated interactivity and tension, but there's no option to turn them off, so if you're bad at mashing, you'll have to find another workaround. On keyboard & mouse, the QTEs are a bit confusing in their instructions, so it can be difficult at first to figure out what to press. The QTEs on keyboard are exponentially harder to complete than those on controller, so I'd reccomend utilizing turbo inputs and/or a spare controller for QTEs if playing on mouse & keyboard.

Combat - Is a little slow, yet action packed. Since your movement is limited and you have to be stationary to shoot, you are forced to observe your surroundings and manage your enemies carefully (or recklessly if you have the resources). Enemies will try to grab you, kindly amputate you, block attacks, throw weapons and explosives at you, dodge your bullets, fire bullets and bolts at you, and call for backup (so they can be ignored by their comrades), but you can stun them, stagger them, and hit the weapons out of the air or out of their hands and even get them to kill each other in some cases (Note: hand axes are ethereal and out to get you). When an enemy is stunned, you can perform a melee attack on them by pressing the interact button at a close enough range. These melee attacks and their effects depend on how an enemy was stunned, what enemy it is, and what character is being used (ex: Leon can suplex enemies to prevent resurrection, Ada back kicks them to get some much needed personal space, and HUNK snaps their necks to instantly kill them without triggering ressurection). Aiming can be a little difficult sometimes because there is no 3rd person reticle, you just get a laser or a scope. Traps are placed around the map and can be used to your advantage (except for bear traps) while providing interesting decisions regarding the manipulation of enemy pathing, killing enemies while conserving ammo, and acting as a hazard for you to avoid. To swap weapons, you have to open your inventory, which kinda sucks, but it gives you some time to plan your next move. Each weapon is fun to use and serves a purpose. The handguns are most useful for stunning enemies and quickly dispatching weak enemies, shotguns are good for crowd control and knocking enemies on the ground, rifles and magnums are excellent at killing every enemy; but have fairly scarce ammo, and the knife is good for conserving ammo; but lacks range and damage. Other weapons include the TMP which is not a bad weapon, but is certainly outclassed by most other fast firing weapons; the mine thrower (which-out of fear of lacking ammo-I didn't use); the crossbow (which I didn't use due to inventory space), and the rocket launcher, which can one shot most every healthbar, but takes up a lot of space and can only be used once before having to obtain another.

Camera - Is okay overall. It can be hard to see sources of danger due to its positioning that doesn't like to be changed manually. Sometimes, while in combat, you may accidentally do a 90-180 degree turn after closing the inventory if using a mouse.

Inventory - Is pretty good. Your storage uses a cell system in which every item takes up a certain amount of space and you have to manage where it is placed (ex: eggs take up 1 cell of space, while a rocket launcher takes up 16 cells of space). It would be nice if the item shapes weren't restricted to just squares and rectangles, because item storage basically boils down to "where do you want your stuff" most of the time instead of making you put your belongings together like a puzzle.

Horror - Is kinda there in spirit. It has horror elements in the atmosphere and some terrifying enemy designs, but it isn't very scary as everything can be dealt with easily if you have the knowledge and ability to aim. The tension is pretty good and there a good few scenarios that will test your ability to act and think under stress.

Story - Overall, is riddled with plot holes and nonsense. It's entertaining and fun, but there isn't much aside from some decent world building, cheesy one liners, some cool and nice moments, and likable characters that don't get enough time and dialogue. If it made more sense and the characters were better developed, it would genuinely be a pretty good story.
Disclaimer: I don't speak Spanish, I'm just going off of my current knowledge of the language... The main enemies are those affected by Las Plagas (which means "The Plague") and it is obviously not a plague (even when you consider its discovery, they clearly knew it was a parasite before naming it). My other issue with the Spanish language in this game is that the characters speak Latin American Spanish instead of Castilian Spanish, despite the game taking place in Spain.

Difficulty - Is disappointing in variety, but otherwise well executed. There are 3 difficulties, easy, normal and professional. I haven't played easy mode. Normal is pretty hard, but well balanced and makes for an enjoyable time, and if you're ever stuck on a boss or just want to skip them, you could use a rocket launcher to instakill them (unless it's Del Lagos, multi-phase bosses, or the final boss). Professional is the "hard mode" that's unlocked after beating the game. The only things that change in professional mode are that you cannot buy the tactical vest (it reduces damage taken by 30%), and DDA (dynamic difficulty adjustment) is turned off, so enemy health, damage, and placement will always be at its hardest. It's a difficulty that should've been available from the start. If it changed the game in a way that forced you to play differently or give you new situations to deal with, then it would be a different story, but it doesn't. Professional is just normal mode, but a bit more punishing.

Upfront, as an assiduous Resident Evil fan, this is hands down the best game of the franchise. The amalgam of horror, along with the amazingly fluid motion of the gun control, is an utter satisfaction to the player. Moreover, although mostly independent from the other games story-wise, the plot is truly engaging and urges you to learn more about what's behind Ashley's kidnapping. The action is definitely one of Resident Evil 4's main focuses. The large number of enemies swarming you at certain moments requires not only good aiming but also strategy. Although the aiming may be fluid, I find it a bit slow compared to other games. Nonetheless, it does not hinder nor detract from your gaming experience. The character control is also pretty solid, and this applies to all characters. However, you will struggle with camera positioning at times, especially in close quarters when you're overwhelmed by enemies. Aside from that, the gameplay is top-notch.

The only thing I find genuinely bad game design is all the QTEs. Set those to be automatically passed (tweaks!) if you find them too frustrating, but try it with them on.

This being remade before the first game or Code Veronica is absolutely ludicrous.
All they did is add more graphics, paint everything important yellow, and make it less silly (which makes it less fun). They made Leon less stupid and cocky. Being able to investigate things and his response usually being "what is this for?" is the best.
The self-satisfied, oblivious, nature of him is part of the charm!

In Resident Evil 4, Leon Kennedy takes his first European vacation, trading the urban chaos of Raccoon City for the rustic charm of an infected Spanish village. 

The plot boils down to this: The president's daughter, Ashley, gets kidnapped by a creepy cult. What does the government do? Do they send an entire elite task force? Nope. They send one guy armed with nothing but a handgun and a knife. 

Ashley spends 90% of her time screaming "LEON!" at top volume, or standing directly in front of your line of fire. The game quickly turns into an escort mission, where you’re constantly yelling “stay there!” or “get behind me!” as she runs headfirst into danger like it’s a national sport. She has the stealth skills of a rock and the survival instincts of someone walking into an obvious trap. And of course, just as you’re fending off a horde of angry villagers, you’ll hear her classic, spine-chilling line: "Leon, HELP!"

Resident Evil 4 redefines the term “tactical combat.” Here’s the strategy: shoot them in the leg, and then, while they’re stunned-kick them in the face. Repeat. 
The boss fights remain thrillingly intense, pitting you against everything from giant lake monsters to grotesque mutated creatures. Every boss fight feels unique and requires a mix of strategy, quick reflexes, and a whole lot of bullets (or, if you're brave, knife slashes), each encounter is memorable and packed with tension.
Quick Time Events (QTEs) in Resident Evil 4 are like surprise pop quizzes in high school. The game throws these at you when you least expect it, turning every cutscene into a potential thumb workout.

The Merchant, the true MVP of Resident Evil 4. He’s always lurking in the shadows with his raspy voice and endless stockpile of guns, grenades, and healing items. I don’t know where he gets his supply, or why he’s immune to the nightmare happening around him, but I do know one thing: when he says “What’re ya buyin’?” I feel safer than in any other moment in the game.

A massive part of RE4’s vibe is in its sound design. Whether it's the chilling silence before an ambush, the distant groans of enemies, or the haunting, low hum of the castle halls, the soundscape wraps you in a blanket of tension. If you thought the rural village and medieval castle were unsettling, wait until you hit the island section. Suddenly, you’re thrust into a high-tech lab, and the vibe shifts into full-blown sci-fi horror.The game expertly switches between moments of spine-tingling tension and heart-pounding action, all while keeping you engaged.

Resident Evil 4 HD doesn’t just update the visuals, it also brings back the excellent Mercenaries mode, where you can test your survival skills against waves of enemies, along with the Ada Wong-centric “Separate Ways” campaign, giving you more reasons to dive back into the horror. These extra modes add even more value to an already packed game.

In the end, Resident Evil 4 HD is the action-packed, zombie-blasting vacation. It's got suplexes, weird cults, and somehow, Leon’s hair still looks incredible. Just remember: always watch out for the guy with the chainsaw, and for the love of all that’s holy, keep an eye on Ashley.

Resident Evil 4 is a complicated game. Within it's historical context, it's up there as one of the most influential games out there, as well as one of the most culturally significant. I think it's worth playing for that if nothing else, although luckily it is an absolutely wonderful game nonetheless.

 It's great strength is easily it's combat. The guns feel utterly sublime and they all play a very distinct mechanical purpose. The encounter design is often spectacular, with smart enemy placements that really well utilise your limited movement capabilities to force you to make interesting choices. Because yes, the tank controls and not being able to move and shoot are both good design choices that set the game apart from the pack even today and that are really well built around by the rest of the mechanics. 

The game also has great vibes, using a lot of Resident Evil trappings to make something, that whilst not quite scary, still has a great horror feeling. A lot of the performances are also iconic, helping to make up for a very under baked and uninteresting story by just being a good time. Not Ashley though, she is utterly insufferable in this game. 

That's the good stuff, however as this game has become more divorced from it's historical context, it's shortcomings have come more sharply into focus, those being, the second half of the game, from when Ashley first gets kidnapped in the castle. Nothing from the castle interior on looks as nice as the village, plays as well as the village, or is as well designed as the village. It's too easy, and the strong progression drive with tons of new weapons, getting your case to an acceptable size, getting the bulk of upgrades you are going to get all happens in the village. Later sections have their moments, like U-3 on the island, but they are overall much weaker.

A lot of other RE games suffer from this as well, however RE4 is a lot longer than most of those, and it's also a steeper drop in quality than, say, RE7s second half, so it is a bigger deal here. Despite that, I still really love this game and it ended just in time to not lose me from that love, and I'd probably still rank it among my favourite games.

The best action you are gonna get out of any RE game. Love that there is an emphasis on player expression. There is a wide variety of weapons and you can make use of every weapon however you like. Combat is stupid fun and it progressively gets harder but not in a bigger health bars kind of way, it pushes you to become a better shooter and be more efficient with your ammo as new enemies appear with armors on different parts of their bodies, shields and weapons ranging from melee, ranged, explosive or incendiary. You can parry melee attacks with your knife, shoot axes mid-air coming towards you, shoot the dynamite or the molotov before the enemy throws it at you, quickly equip your rifle with a long distance scope and shoot the crossbow enemies sitting way behind the battlefield, find the small angle to shoot the feet of the enemies with shields so you can kick them in the face. RE4 (2005) is the fourth numbered entry in the Resident Evil franchise, but strays off the beaten horror path to focus more on action, which would have an effect on the series as a whole due to the enormous influence this game has had on both the Survival Horror and Third Person Shooter genres. 

Resident Evil 4 takes place in 2004, tasking gov. agent Leon S. Kennedy with rescuing the US president's daughter from a cult in a remote village in Spain. He has to jump through flaming hoops, all while wisecracking, humiliating the enemy faction responsible for the region's cult activities and doing some sightseeing on the side. 

The gameplay is like clockwork, even 19 years later. It is the single most important game at the time that popularized the over-the-shoulder shooter genre that would influence future franchises like Dead Space and Gears of War. You control Leon using the classic tank controls from a new perspective, making it somewhat easier this time than the older games, as well as stopping to aim and shoot with a red dot laser guide at enemies. Shooting enemies in certain areas (head, joints) will stun them, letting you walk up to them and perform a finisher move that can knock down several enemies at once. You can kite enemies around and parry incoming projectiles by shooting them and use a variety of items in your inventory such as grenades to assist you. Some vestigial survival horror elements are still present, such as inventory and resource management, as you'll have to use your ammo carefully to get around groups of enemies. You're introduced to an attache case-style inventory system for the first time, with grid slots you can sort items in to get the best fit. Almost like tetris. The game features a variety of puzzles that you can solve to move forward or to even acquire rewards. The game also has a focus on item collection in the form of treasures you can combine and sell at the suspicious-but-charismatic Merchant's many pitstops, who will offer you items and weapon upgrades at a cost. New to the series is an overhaul melee system, as while you still have your trusty knife, which you can use to slash away at enemies dealing chip damage, precision aiming is rewarded by stunning enemies, by either shooting them at the joints or head, and allowing you to come up close to them and trigger a melee finisher move by pressing the interact button to knock the foe down, and even sweep other enemies if they're grouped close enough together. When it comes to side content, RE4 brings back the Mercenaries mode introduced in RE3: Nemesis, letting you play as a host of characters, such as Leon, Ada, HUNK (of RE2 fame), Jack Krauser and even Albert Wesker. Although this iteration of it, and the ones moving forward, is different from how it was in OG RE3, where while you did rack up points for killing enemies, you could also rescue hostages to increase your tally further. Here, you make full use of the new melee system to optimize your enemy routing, and pick up power-ups along the way to extend your playtime. It is a very fun addition to an already amazing game.

The story, while being a fairly by-the-book adventure romp, is extremely cheesy and campy, to a ridiculous degree, to the point of being like an B-list action flick, that makes it timelessly memorable. The main villains are all larger than life yet still sinister, and Leon seems to have taken lessons from Spider-Man in quipping, with many funny interactions with his enemies, taunting them over the intercom. It doesn't stop the story from having its darker moments, and some of the death animations are pretty gruesome, but the game has decided on a lighter tone compared to its predecessors. The story is notably more streamlined to focus on the thrills, which is not a bad tradeoff, but the same tone would not return again in later games, as they opt to be more serious narratively, instead.

RE4 is an all-time great, even if it set a bad precedent for the series going forward, but it doesn't diminish its achievements by much, and remains one of the best games ever made, which is unlikely to change. Absolutely worth full price, maybe even too cheap for how fun it is, but it also goes for really cheap during the frequent Capcom publisher sales, so keep an eye out.

There really is not much to say about Resident Evil 4 that hasn't been said, but if you somehow haven't played this game with the Community HD Texture Pack mod, it is like experiencing this game for the first time all over again. It's just unbelievable what those people have achieved with it, and I would consider it required installation if you have played this game for hundreds of hours, or if it's your first time. It's maybe the single best remaster I have ever seen for a game, and this is something I could easily see myself paying for if it were sold for money (you can donate to the group to keep the servers up). Installing the mod on Deck was a surprisingly easy process, and is how I revisited this game. It's just insane to be playing the absolute ideal version of RE4 on a handheld wherever you want, and you can pretty comfortably play this game at 1080/60, mostly maxed out settings with this mod on Deck. It's great for when you want to play on a TV or monitor, which I highly recommend you do. This is maybe some of the best texture work I've ever seen in a game, and it should be appreciated at high resolutions.

As for the game itself, I replayed it recently with this mod on Professional difficulty and let me tell you, this game is hard as hell on Professional. It plays a lot closer to OG Resident Evil in this regard where you have to be far more mindful of your resource management and enemies can one-shot you like you're a balloon. It's not my favorite form of difficulty modifiers (enemies take way more bullets than normal, while you can die in three hits with a maxed out health bar), but it does balance itself out where you're picking up way more money than on the base difficulty. It's still a little frustrating when you're stuck and trying your hardest to work with the more sluggish controls, but I do think it makes you appreciate the level design; often times more fair than unfair. Kind of reminds me of Doom Eternal, which is either a good thing or bad thing depending on how you felt about that game. The Island section -- and parts of the Castle -- weren't well balanced for this difficulty mode, and will probably frustrate you unless you know this game inside and out. But in general I would still say this is probably one of the greatest games ever made and it should be required playing for just about anyone.

Resident Evil 4 is the classic Gamecube entry into the legendary Resident Evil franchise that I wanted to hate due its clear shift into a more action oriented formula. Unlike the slow, methodical, foreboding horror of its predecessors, this one is less focused on ammo conservation, and veers directly into frantic arcade-like shooting and melee. Despite my fervent disapproval (at the time) of changing Survival Horror as I knew it, RE 4 stands out as a thoroughly enjoyable, well crafted game with just enough spookiness mixed into the action so that it can still be considered a proper horror title.

As for -this- PC port.. There are several notable features it has going for it over the Gamecube original. One is the option of using "HD" textures. I use the word HD loosely because in 2024 the "HD-ness" of said texture mode still looks....well, pretty bad and low res! You can however play the game in a smooth 60 frames per second which is such a massive improvement over the original's 30 fps cap.

One annoying issue I've run into though is concerning the game's audio, and its lack of any audio options. Myself and apparently many others have run into audio bugs including the game running at very low volume despite the PC volume being turned up almost to 100%. I haven't found a reliable fix or workaround for this unfortunately, and am forced to take my chances hoping that a notification doesn't come on while I'm playing at max volume and blow out my eardrums!

Other than that, it's Resident Evil 4 from 2005 with added 1080p, 60 fps, and just slightly better textures. That's all you really need to know in order to buy this! If you're a fan give it a go. If you've never played it, you could do worse than this version unless you want to spring for the new remake that changes quite a bit of this one's spooky, whacky charm to be more realistic and drab.

The kind of game that could only result out of years of trial and error, experimentation and a willingness to take risks to reimagine and reinvent a franchise for a new audience. The game is so successful at delivering a perfectly paced, exquisitely themed, stupidly self-aware and delightfully interactive digital rollercoaster that it is hard to truly say it makes me miss Resident Evil's survival horror days.

Still holds up to this day and I find that I prefer it to the remake because there were things done better in some regards, like the scene setting, the credible world design and clever interweaving of tutorials where they managed to hide them in plain sight. 

The facial expressions are so good and perfectly display the intended emotion, and I feel that this version of the game managed to better blend the lighthearted and serious moments far better. 
This is why it was released so many times before a remaster was even talked about, it didn't seem to need to be, much like Resident Evil 1 and the gamecube version, changing things can change everything.

Some of the negatives I have about this version are easily fixed with some mods, and some mods are recommended for the best experience, such as re4hd. However the two things I still struggle to get a feel for are related to the controls
[list]
[*] The awkward tank controls not being something I ever liked are something that I think I [b][i]could[/i][/b] come to get used to if it weren't for how sluggish it is overall with no way to really speed this up or resolve it. I don't think anything would be lost in the experience if modern movement controls were somehow an option for this version, and I think even then it could still be retained. If the controls were modernised for movement out of combat but when in combat they became stiff and close to how they are at the moment (with a slight speed boost as mentioned before) I feel like this could work as it would suggest tension and stress, keeping the intended claustrophobic panic and feeling of fear. This is just my thoughts on it though
[*]The other issue I have is more so related to the fact that I think the controls for aiming weapons on the Wii were incredible, so there's not an all around fix that could translate this to the PC version, but I do think it could be emulated if gyro controls could be used for aiming if a controller that supports this was being used. Most games that support this don't make it a mandatory method of aiming which is for the best considering those who don't enjoy it, but for precise aiming there is nothing like it.
[/list]

Like I said, these issues are really just personal but I do truly think adding the ability to have these choices, more so the second would enhance the experience [b]dramatically[/b].

Regardless, this game is one I would recommend to everyone as an absolute must play during your lifetime. Don't skip it for the remake or if you have already played the remake still don't skip it!
