I've always been a casual fan of the Resident Evil series, I wouldn't call myself a hardcore fan but I've played enough in the series where I look back generally with good memories of it.
The first game I've played in the series was RE3: Nemesis back in the early 2000's, I still remember Nemesis jumping through the police station window and scaring the hell out of me as a kid, a couple years later and my cousin and I are playing co-op on RE5, I have good memories of this game although I remember the story being kind of meh, next is RE: Revelations (3DS), this game I loved and was a stand out on the 3DS being one of the most visually impressive games on the hardware and followed by RE: Mercenaries 3D (3DS) which was a really fun game, I remember Krauser being broken in this game having infinite Arrows with his Bow, and finally RE6, this game I don't remember completing at all, I played a couple missions here and there then I walked away and for the past few years I've watched a few games be release and just kind of been meh on the series. I don't know what got me interested but I decided to buy Resident Evil 4 Remake and it turned out to be one of the best purchases I've made in a while, it was easily my GOTY last year over Baldur's Gate 3, but before I could dive in with RE4R I had to play the original to get the full context and I got to say this is easily one my favorite games.

Resident Evil 4 (2005) is a great game and its influence on the gaming industry cannot be understated, it's 3rd person over the shoulder aiming was revolutionary at the time and has set the standard for 3rd Person in gaming, I was surprised how much this game holds up in 2024 being a game released in 2005, it was also a departure from the survival aspect of the Resident Evil Series shifting to a more Action Horror which changed the series going forward, it explains why sequels never quite lived up to RE4 as Capcom struck gold without understanding what made RE4 great at the time.

Resident Evil 4's Story is fantastic, the campy nature of the Story is really fun with great memorable characters, it comes off as a campy B movie that doesn't take itself seriously coupled with great Music and Sound Design, Gameplay and Art Direction, you get a great game. Leon is one of my favorite characters in gaming now along with Adam Jensen, Link and Cal Kestis.

The Music and Sound Design in this game is great, apart from a few actual songs here and there, the music in RE4 is mostly these cords that sustain a low note followed by ambient noises that surrounds you building upon the horror and tension of the game, Salazar Castle is a great example as the music is comprised of cult like chanting and humming that feels oppressive as you're surrounded my cultists.

The Gameplay is a stand out, people can be mixed when it comes to Tank controls but the movement in RE4 is fantastic, when you understand the limits of the controls it oddly becomes more intuitive to use if that makes sense? this game can gets tense and the gunplay in here is fun as you'll be dealing with crowds of Ganardo's and other infected monsters, being a survival horror game you'll be managing your inventory, Ammo is easy enough to come by but not enough to go wild in a fight as you'll be conserving ammo, the game encourages you to aim for limbs to stun enemies to then follow it up with a melee attack to save on ammo, or funnel enemies into areas with environmental dangers. The amount of variety in enemies in this game is pretty impressive too on top of the regular enemies having variety in the types of weapon they use, you also have to worry about special infected enemies which can be bullet sponges if not dealt with appropriately, some of the mini bosses are challenging too and pretty terrifying, Regenerators are easily one of the scariest creatures in gaming. The game has QTE's in it which I'm personally mixed about although I don't mind QTE's in cut scenes as it makes the story more engaging.

Art Direction is also pretty good, games tend to become dated visually especially in the mid 00's (I'm looking at you Oblivion), the Art Direction in RE4 holds up pretty well especially with the HD update, it's not a crime to the eyes to look at when playing.

Overall I'm glad I took a chance with Resident Evil 4 Remake, it's changed my perception of the series going forward and I can't wait to see how they adapt RE5, Resident Evil 4 is easily in my top 10.

Resident Evil 4 remains a timeless gem, delivering a thrilling experience filled with memorable locations and cinematic cutscenes from beginning to end. Despite its age, the game's charm and excitement have not faded, making it a joy to revisit.

It's easy to overlook the fact that **Resident Evil 4** still employs tank controls, lacking the ability to strafe and featuring aiming mechanics best suited to the left stick. However, these quirks only add to the game's nostalgic appeal, reminding players of its roots in survival horror.

The PC port's 60FPS enhancement brings smoother gameplay but comes with its own set of issues. Some button-mashing Quick Time Events (QTEs) become nearly impossible to complete, which can be frustrating. Thankfully, installing the "re4 tweaks" mod offers a plethora of fixes, including the option to auto-complete QTEs entirely—a feature that streamlines the experience without compromising the challenge.

Personalizing the gameplay experience is made easier with tools like Steam Input, allowing for custom mapping of controls. I found mapping the weapon hotswapping feature to X+dpad particularly useful, enhancing fluidity during intense encounters.

While occasional crashes may occur even with the mod installed, I discovered that disabling Steam Overlay resolved the issue entirely. Though it required a bit of tinkering, the effort was well worth it for the opportunity to relive such a beloved classic.

In conclusion, Resident Evil 4 continues to stand the test of time as a masterpiece of the survival horror genre. Despite its technical quirks, the game's immersive world and gripping gameplay make it a must-play for fans old and new. Whether you're experiencing it for the first time or revisiting it after years, the thrill of Resident Evil 4 is as potent as ever.

[h1]OG > REmake[/h1]

Upon its release, I purchased Resident Evil 4: Remake and lost interest only a week or two later, never understanding why. Haven't played it since.

I even purchased the Resident Evil 4: Remake (PSVR2) version and found myself bored when I reached the castle. Never completed it.

I recently replayed the original Resident Evil 4 (Having completed it several times over the years), and I now understand why I prefer this version. There was no need for a remake, as this one still holds up really well. The remake improves certain things, but OG RE4 feels better regarding pacing, gameplay mechanics, and overall feel. 

[h2]MODERN = DULL, DILUTED & NOT ALWAYS NEEDED[/h2]

The industry is different these days, and games generally aren't produced by passionate developers for an equally passionate crowd but to attract as large an audience as possible. I get it ($$$), but as a result, ideas and identity get watered down. These days, AAA devs just integrate ideas from other games into one package, resulting in a homogenized product; everything plays, feels, and looks the same. Nothing has an identity and feels distinguishable. 

There's also this belief that because a game is "modern," it's an improvement from the past, which I don't think is true. Sure, the engines used are much more refined, but "Modern-day" gaming continues to show that devs and publishers don't care if you're actually enjoying it.

You bought their product. They win.

They're pushing out a derivative product to appease corporate overlords rather than constructing a cool concept or passion project. This is why folks describe games today as "Soulless" because that's precisely what they are. They know the gaming community has an impulse problem and take advantage of it.

Not only do most games these days look and feel identical, but they all operate under the same design principles of adding sections that feel like busy work and padding out game time instead of just making the damn thing fun. 

I wholeheartedly believe THE PACING IN the Resident Evil 4: Remake IS TRASH for this reason. 

[h2]CLASSIC: STANDS THE TEST OF TIME[/h2]

I was surprised that I enjoyed the original more. Still, there's a reason the original RE4 has frequently been released for different systems since 2004. We'll likely not see any remakes or remasters for the RE: Remake version.

I'm not exaggerating when I say this is probably one of the best games of all time.

This game marks the turning point when RE became a primarily action based series, meaning that survival horror is less emphasised and the scare factor is minimal(seriously, walking around the RPD in RE2R for the first time is scarier than anything in this game.) I only remember one time I ever ran out of handgun ammo, and that was at the start of the game. 

However, this game is still amazing, the gameplay is insanely fun, the shooting is fantastic, and I think being stuck in place when shooting enhances the gameplay more than it hinders it. The merchant system is great, it's always lots of fun to sell treasures and go shopping with the fat stack of cash you just picked up at the end of a tough section. It's satisfying as hell to finally be able to pick up a new weapon or upgrade and see the major difference between now and then when you use them. Inventory sorting is also a lot of fun.

Overall, I don't really have anything bad to say about this game, some people might consider the gameplay aged and out of date, but I believe it's a lot of fun once you get used to it. The many environments and enemies are interesting to fight against, and while the story isn't crazy in depth(it's a resident evil, it'd be more surprising if it was), it's still pretty intriguing, and had some fun characters. I've heard the remake is just as comparably an amazing game, so I'm excited to play that sometime soon too.

TL:DR: While it strays from being a traditional RE game, this game is absolutely one of the best in the series and is 100% worth playing, even if you've played the remake.

[h3] Resident Evil 4 HD Edition ★★★★★ [/h3]
Resident Evil 4 HD Edition is a great action horror game that has been wounded by time, but can hold quite well with the help of mods.

In Resident Evil 4 you mainly play as Leon Scott Kennedy, an agent in a mission to recover the recently kidnapped daughter of the United States president, Ashley Graham, and for that you must explore a remote coastal village in the Spanish countryside, open old wounds with familiar faces, and meet new ones, shoot, kick and suplex your way through hordes of bloodthirsty locals and horrific creatures alike, manage your attaché case of collected valuables, ammunitions, explosives, herbs, and barter for new and better weapons, tools of the trade for the one man army that is Leon S. Kennedy, [b]this is a horror game, but for the monsters.[/b]

RE4 main campaign is structured by missions, every mission has small closed-off areas that are stringed together to form something greater, each area requires growing amounts of proficiency and focus in different aspects of gameplay, or put a new spin on it, they manage to surprise and entertain at every turn while scaling the difficulty in such way that you always have the tools to push through, even if costly, almost all areas have non-combat puzzles, secrets, and valuables for trading and upgrading, every single area will root themselves in your brain, and despite having a mission based campaign, the missions themselves don't follow a hard structure and some outright offer different routes, you may explore, backtrack, flee or just run for the next exit!

The graphics have seen better days but they don't hold back this action-horror game, the story is complemented by many cutscenes and documents scattered about, and the tone can go from serious and spooky to funny and cheesy and regardless of the tone, Leon seems to be enjoying every bit of RE4 himself, the sound design is superb, all foes have audio cues related to their awareness, position, actions in a way that complements both gameplay and setting, the songs are typical of horror media with lots of droning and loud thumping that are contrasted by some action oriented themes, long periods of silence or the relief inducing tones of safe rooms.

Even after you are finished with the main game, there are plenty of in-game unlockables, a new difficulty, weapons, costumes, two new side campaigns, an arcade mode with plenty of action and new characters and so many more in-depth mechanics to learn, [b][u]unfortunately, this version of the game is quite broken on modern machines, [/u][/b]quick time events are an old design relic that may bug out completely, the game may crash or softlock you, in many cases the game can't be finished if you don't install mod fixes, [b][u]I strongly recommend the installation of RE4_TWEAKS[/u][/b] and suggest Resident HD Project, despite that, this game is genuinely fun, challenging, and with the help of mods it manages to hold up quite well even today.

Honestly, I think the only downsides it has is that the mouse sensitivity feels a tad bit off at times, and there are other times where the framerate will just die when there's a lot of particles on screen for instance - though, I assume that's something present on the original release as well.
But overall, if you can look past the jank (and you absolutely should - it's a game from 2005, for Easy Pete's sake) you'll have a great time with RE4.

This is probably the most "iconic" of all of the resident evil games. This "original" release was the first of the Resident Evil games to use the "Over the Shoulder" camera view rather than a fixed camera for each location which is probably why it really stands out against the older games. The graphics are still a big step forward from Resident Evil Code Veronica X (not available on PC).

The game is also much more "linear". You will rarely have a choice about what to do next. The story line doesn't quite have the same "feel" as earlier games, though if you play the extra game [i]Separate Ways[i] that unlocks after completing the main story line, the ties to earlier characters and story lines gets fleshed out a bit better. They sort of give you a mix of Camera Control and Tank Movement Control - which can be off putting to gamers use to playing the latest games - but which you will eventually warm up to (just leave the camera alone and let it follow you around).

Several of the sequences are truly ground breaking for their time and a blast to get through. The game relies heavily on Quick Time Events (QTE) tied to many of the cut scenes and action sequences. The game was designed originally to run at 30fps but by default will run at 60fps today - this sometimes creates issues with the QTE elements giving you half of the frames to get the buttons pushed. The game can be run at 30fps to address this, but the graphics tear a bit on modern systems at this rate and just aren't as smooth. You can not toggle this setting while "in a game" and must quit the game back to the main menu to use the options then - for some sequences this means you will be playing in 30fps with worse graphics for a period of time.

The game is certainly still playable in 2024 and still quite fun and exciting. However, it probably falls quite short of the experience of playing the remastered version. Because of this it is probably only really viable for either die hard fans of the franchise (or this game specifically for the memories) or if you got the game in a bundle (came with our Humble Bundle in late 2023). If you are only going to play one of the games and didn't pick this game up in a bundle of some sort, then I would recommend the remastered edition.

Resident Evil 4 (2005) – The Grandpa Who Keeps Crashing the Family Reunion

Look, I love Resident Evil 4 (2005). I do. It’s the wild, campy uncle of the survival horror genre — the one who shows up with roundhouse kicks, a suitcase full of grenades, and absolutely no respect for OSHA regulations. The story is still iconic: creepy village, cultists, a U.S. agent who can suplex monks, and a president’s daughter with zero survival instincts. It’s pure chaos, and I adore it.

BUT.

Playing the original PC port in [current year] is like trying to run Windows XP on a NASA supercomputer. I’ve got a high-end PC that can render a small moon in real time — and somehow, this game crashes every 20 minutes like it’s punishing me for not playing it on a GameCube. I save more often than Leon reloads his Red9. I fear the “Alt+Tab” more than I fear chainsaw man.

Graphics? 6/10. For 2005, it looked fine — but in 2025, it looks like everyone’s made of slightly damp cardboard. Ashley looks like she was textured with a cheese grater. The water effects scream “Windows 98 screensaver.” And don’t even get me started on the lighting — the whole game feels like it was lit by a single, underpaid candle.

The remake, though? Absolute glow-up. Leon’s hair has more physics than the original game had polygons. Everything’s shinier, punchier, and somehow Ashley became less annoying (slightly). The combat is smoother, the pacing is tighter, and nobody crashes during a cutscene. It’s like comparing a black-and-white TV to a 4K OLED. The remake is the stylish younger sibling who does yoga and owns a bidet. Meanwhile, 2005 Leon is out here yelling “Where’s everyone going? Bingo?” in 144p and crashing your desktop.

BUT THE SOUL IS STILL THERE. The original RE4 has that campy, over-the-top charm that the remake — while phenomenal — doesn’t completely replicate. It’s weird. It’s cheesy. It’s art. Just… art that was held together with duct tape and a lot of prayers.

Final Score: 6/10. Masterpiece in spirit, disaster in code. The remake is the slick modern reboot. The original PC version? A lovable, buggy mess that’ll crash just when you’re about to save, like the true survival horror experience it was meant to be.

[h2] GOOD [/h2]  
[list]  
[*][b] Timeless Gameplay [/b]  
Despite its age, the original Resident Evil 4 port still delivers tense, satisfying action that made it a landmark in the genre.  

[*][b] Classic Mechanics for Purists [/b]  
While dated, the tank controls and ability restrictions may actually appeal to fans seeking an authentic old-school experience missing from the remake.  

[*][b] Surprisingly Competent Companion AI [/b]  
Ashley’s AI is refreshingly reliable for the era, adding to the game’s playability and reducing typical escort frustration.  
[/list]  

[h2] BAD [/h2]  
[list]  
[*][b] Clunky Controls [/b]  
No strafing, no walking while shooting, and the infamous tank controls make movement feel stiff and unwieldy—new players will struggle to adapt.  

[*][b] Technical Aging [/b]  
Even as a port, the visuals and interface show their age. There’s no escaping that some elements just don’t hold up compared to newer releases.  
[/list]  

[h2] Final Thought [/h2]  
Resident Evil 4 (2005) remains a survival horror classic worth owning—especially for franchise veterans who appreciate its unique mechanics. It isn’t modern or polished, but its pure, tense gameplay is still compelling. An excellent buy in a bundle or solo, as long as you’re ready to wrestle with its nostalgia-fueled quirks.

Resident Evil 4 stands as a landmark in the survival horror genre, redefining the series and setting a new standard for action-packed gameplay intertwined with intense horror elements. Released in 2005, this game has retained its status as a classic, captivating players with its gripping storyline, innovative mechanics, and chilling atmosphere.

One of the most striking aspects of Resident Evil 4 is its departure from the fixed camera angles of its predecessors, opting instead for an over-the-shoulder perspective that brings players closer to the action. This change not only enhances immersion but also allows for more dynamic combat encounters, as players must carefully aim their shots while facing hordes of grotesque enemies.

Speaking of enemies, Resident Evil 4 introduces some of the most memorable foes in the series, from the relentless Ganados to the towering monstrosities known as El Gigante and Verdugo. Each encounter is a test of nerves and skill, as players must conserve ammo and strategically use the environment to survive.

The game's story follows series protagonist Leon S. Kennedy as he investigates the disappearance of the president's daughter in a remote European village. What starts as a routine mission quickly spirals into a nightmarish descent into madness, filled with twists, turns, and betrayals. The narrative is expertly paced, keeping players on the edge of their seats from start to finish.

In addition to its compelling story and tense combat, Resident Evil 4 boasts stunning visuals that still hold up today. The detailed environments, eerie lighting, and grotesque character designs combine to create a truly atmospheric experience. Whether exploring the decaying village streets or navigating the labyrinthine corridors of a sinister castle, every location feels meticulously crafted and dripping with atmosphere.

Beyond its single-player campaign, Resident Evil 4 also offers plenty of replay value thanks to its Mercenaries mode, which challenges players to survive against waves of enemies within a time limit. This mode adds an addictive arcade-like experience to the game, encouraging players to hone their skills and compete for high scores.

In conclusion, Resident Evil 4 is a timeless classic that has left an indelible mark on the survival horror genre. With its gripping gameplay, unforgettable enemies, and immersive atmosphere, it remains a must-play for fans of horror and action alike. Whether you're a seasoned veteran or a newcomer to the series, Resident Evil 4 is an experience that should not be missed.

I am aware that Capcom shot itself in the foot with the stupid DRM decision, but this is a review for the game, not the company.

I cant believe how much I enjoyed this game. Even though i put it off for so long because I was afraid of the stupid tank controls, I decided to give it a go, 20 years after its release.

I was afraid I wouldn't get past the first level because of the controls, but after 15 min I got the hang of it and after 1h I barely had any issues with them at all

The good: 
- It has perfect save points in order to make it just a bit challenging and not overly annoying.
- even though the movement and camera work are similar to controlling a tank, the game is built around this. You won't get cheap deaths due to game exploiting this type of controls
- its challenging, yet fun. Its long, yet expertly broken down into bite sized levels so you wont feel overwhelmed
- it balances quite good intense action with breathing room areas
- it awards you for exploring the game world
- weapons feel good and impactfull.
- some boss fights are really challenging, but in a fun way


The bad
- you need to learn resource management and abuse the knife. Some areas of the game can be extremely hard if you lack the proper resources
- most QTE are crap. I died more because of QTEs than because of the infected.
- if you are watching a cut-scene, keep your hands in the controls. A QTE might start during it and if you miss it it's either 90% of your hp gone or insta kill
- i've seen people suggesting to play with 30 fps because the QTE scale with frame rates. More frames, more and quicker button mashing (some QTEs were pure cancer on 60 fps)
- a proper tutorial is lacking. For example: i had to google search how to rotate inventory items. And i wasn't even aware I could do this for more than half of the game
- some bosses are a bit unfair and if you want an easy life, you need yo learn how to cheese them
- the story is...so-so. Main villain has some questionable decision making

The so-so
- controls are hard at the beginning, but its not a negative since the game does not abuse your lack of experience. You get enough space between you and enemies for most of the game. And enough time to react to danger
- graphics are outdated, but still look cute. After all, its a 20 year old game
- escort game-play is not my cup of tea, but the game handles it very well. You can order the VIP to cover, hide and stay in order to keep them out of danger. VIP is not brain dead as well and it can dodge enemies.

Alright! Resident Evil 4 revolutionized the survival horror genre with its over-the-shoulder camera, which brought players closer to the action and terror. This perspective shift wasn't just a visual change; it altered the entire gameplay dynamic, making encounters with the Ganados more personal and terrifying.

The game's pacing is another high point. It masterfully balances moments of high tension with periods of calm, allowing players to catch their breath before plunging them back into the fray. This ebb and flow creates a rhythm that keeps players engaged from start to finish.

Then there's the arsenal and the attache case inventory system. It adds a layer of strategy to the game, as players must manage their limited space while choosing the right tools for the job. It's like a puzzle within the game, and getting it just right feels incredibly satisfying.

Let's not forget the setting and story. The eerie Spanish village, the mysterious castle, and the ominous island all have their own unique horrors and backstories. The narrative hooks you with its twists and turns, and the characters, especially Leon S. Kennedy, have become iconic in the gaming world.

Lastly, Resident Evil 4 has set a benchmark for future games in terms of boss battles. Each boss fight is a spectacle, requiring players to use their wits and reflexes. These encounters are not just battles but memorable experiences that stay with players long after the credits roll.

So, while I can't pen a full review, these points definitely highlight why Resident Evil 4 is a gem in the gaming world. It's a mix of innovation, storytelling, and pure adrenaline that's hard to beat! Resident Evil 4's impact on gaming is one reason it deserves the Game of the Year title. It influenced a multitude of games that followed, introducing mechanics and storytelling techniques that are still used today. Its legacy is visible across the industry, marking it as a title of significance.

The game's replayability is another factor that sets it apart. With unlockable content, such as new costumes, weapons, and the challenging Mercenaries mode, it offers reasons to come back time and again. This longevity is a testament to its quality and appeal.

In terms of technical achievement, Resident Evil 4 was a marvel at the time of its release, pushing the hardware to its limits with detailed environments and character models. Its visuals and audio design created an atmosphere that was both beautiful and haunting, immersing players in its world.

The game also boasts a narrative that is engaging and filled with memorable characters. The dialogue, while occasionally campy, has some iconic lines that fans still quote today. The story is a roller coaster that complements the gameplay perfectly, making it a complete package.

Finally, the game's ability to evoke a range of emotions – from fear to triumph – is unparalleled. It's a journey that takes players through moments of vulnerability and empowerment, leaving a lasting impression. For all these reasons, Resident Evil 4 stands out as a deserving candidate for Game of the Year, even amidst tough competition. let me tell you, the graphics in Resident Evil 4 were mind-blowing for its time! I mean, seriously, it was like stepping into a whole new dimension of gaming. The level of detail in the environments and character models was insane. You could see every little crease in Leon's jacket and the grotesque details on those terrifying Ganados. It was like playing a horror movie come to life!

And the lighting effects, man, they were on another level. The way the shadows danced and flickered added so much atmosphere and suspense. It made every dark corner feel like a potential jump scare waiting to happen. Plus, the game had some seriously intense set pieces that were just jaw-dropping. I remember being blown away by the explosive action and cinematic moments.

Even the little things, like the way the rain splashed on the ground or the way the fire flickered and cast realistic reflections, added so much to the immersion. It was like the developers went above and beyond to make every pixel count. And let's not forget the attention to detail in the character animations. The way Leon moved and reacted to his surroundings felt so natural and realistic.

Honestly, man, Resident Evil 4 was a visual feast for the eyes. It pushed the boundaries of what was possible at the time and set a new standard for graphics in gaming. [h1]Jinkies Scoob, this resident sure is getting evil – and there is more than one![/h1] 

Resident Evil 4 is one of, if not [b]THE[/b] most popular game of the franchise. While it strayed away a little from being an eerie and atmospheric horror experience towards more of an action title, many people still believe it to be the best game of its times and one that would keep this title for a long time. The game not only greatly influenced the survival horror genre, but also defined how the third-person camera format would look like for the next decade with its over-the-shoulder angle. 

Leon S. Kennedy, known from RE2, is once again one of the unluckiest video game characters I’ve ever seen. As a survivor of the Raccoon City incident Leon received special training from the government. A while later he gets the position as the bodyguard of the USA president’s daughter. First day of the job and guess what? Before he could even meet the girl, she gets kidnapped and imprisoned in some rural village in Spain. 
Although the writing of dialogues in this game (at least in the English dub) leaves a lot to be desired (unless you enjoy the corniness), the story generally does the job pretty well. We have recurring characters, menacing main adversaries and a goal that is something more than just “survive/escape” this time. 
In terms of horror the village surely is the most haunting area of the game. Traveling through the foggy PS2-looking forest while being stalked by creepy farmers armed with sickles and axes was the most intriguing part of the game for me and it makes a great, terrifying first impression, especially counting the initial attack in the village when you can barricade yourself in a house. The vibe of this place (together with the lake area) is amazing and very eerie. 
I feel like the other acts of the game kind of lose this charm. The castle and the island are still alright, but besides a few highlights they’re not as scary. 

RE4, after a bunch of different prototypes, ultimately became an action shooter. Although the previous formula had its advantages in terms of a horror experience, I consider RE4 to be a step in the right direction ([strike]even though 6 was a "fu.ck, go back" moment)[/strike]. Especially, how the gameplay of this game is so da.mn good. Skillful players can utilize kicks to knife opponents conserving ammo or run when they know the confrontation is not worth it, while others can just blast away and pray, they’re not going to run out of bullets. Exploration is also key, because not only do you need to look for ammo or herbs to mix, but also money and valuable items to sell so you can upgrade your guns. I really liked the idea of combining treasures to sell them for a higher price to the sus arms dealer. 
Key items and treasures don’t take inventory space, but everything else you need to pack and use wisely as you have limited space. This micromanagement is important because you have to make decisions whether you want more healing items, guns or a rocket launcher so you can easily deal with a boss. 
The game has puzzles, some better, some worse, but generally they are all rather alright. 
QTEs were done in a cool way – they can catch you off guard as they also appear in cutscenes. 
While a big chunk of the game is an escort mission, I never really understood why people always complain about Ashley. She mostly stays literally glued to your back and when you absolutely have to shoot in her general direction, she ducks to make things easier for you. Also, there is really not that many areas where she can possibly get hurt. Most of them aren’t that hard or have a dumpster in which you can leave her. There are really far worse escort AIs out there (she does yell a lot though). 
The gameplay is juicy, but since it is a bit of an old game there is some stuff that is not up to today's standards, for example the lack of strafing or being unable to move while aiming. 

I already wrote about the aesthetics and that they complement the horror atmosphere. Graphically the game looks bearable (unless you play with the motion blur on you psychopath), but you can see time doing its thing. Enemy and parasite designs are sick, I especially liked the Verdugo. 
Musicwise there is of course the iconic Serenity along with a few other tracks that are very cool, like the ending theme. 

For me Resident Evil 4 almost strikes the perfect balance of action and scariness in a survival horror game. If tone down the explosions a little bit and get rid of the minigun fellows [strike] and generally the entire god d.amn island warzone section[/strike] I think it’d be perfect. I was actually kind of baffled when they announced the remake of this game because besides some mobility restrictions, this is still a very playable game today. At least more playable than Code: Veronica. 
A definite milestone that not only defined the genre, but somewhat the industry too.

(Played with RE4 HD Project)

[h3]Deeply flawed PERFECTION.[/h3]

OG RE4 comes from the heels of one of the strongest strings of amazing videogames in 2004, only missed by a few mere months by releasing in early 2005. This game is near perfection in my eyes, great variety of enemies, great sense of progression by finding loot to upgrade your weapons and one incredibly shlocky plot carried by it’s batsh!t silliness.

It’s really stupid and I absolutely love it with every fiber of my being.

This amazing game is only paired back by a [b]deeply mediocre port[/b]. Consider this game’s porting history like the “botched Jesus painting” meme, once considered the pinnacle of gaming on GameCube and [b]especially on the Wii[/b], it was severely downgraded for the PS2 release and unfortunately it was the basis for the very first port made by Ubisoft, also the first DMC 3 port and Onimusha 3 on PC were handled by them. It was so infamous that it drove Capcom to handle their own PC ports themselves ever since.

This port by comparison is a MASSIVE upgrade compared to that absolute mess from Ubislop, but it’s still marred by issues that were never fixed since it’s release, like for example, by uncapping the framerate to 60, a lot of things broke, like animations speed and ESPECIALLY quicktime events became insanely hard. Also some minor issues like color correction and some upscaled muddy textures that apparently were good enough to be considered “HD” by Capcom.

And that’s not even mentioning the framerate issues this game has been plagued by since release, check the Steam community tab and you’ll see PLENTY of performance guides to mitigate the slowdown in this game, especially for laptop users.

My recommendation would be, either play the Wii version through Dolphin and crank it up to 4k… Or be willing to download some mods to fix this game, like [url=https://github.com/nipkownix/re4_tweaks]re4_tweaks[/url], not only fixes all the previously mentioned issues, it also lets you uncap the framerate to cap it youself to 60 with a third party tool like MSI Afterburner or Nvidia/AMD’s own tools, completely eliminating the slowdown issues.

Also I greatly recommend checking out the [url=https://re4hd.com/]RE4 HD Project[/url], this is a [b]TRUE HD remasterization made by fans[/b] that ALSO fixes a lot of the underlying issues and it also comes bundled with the previously mentioned re4_tweaks tool in one fell swoop, although it’s a hefty download of around 30 GB, but the massive bump in graphical fidelity makes this an essential download.

In conclusion, in my heart this game is a [b]near perfect 10/10[/b], insanely enjoyable and silly storyline, great variety all around, really tight gameplay with an excellent challenge curve, good amount of content and lots of replay value, but [b]be aware[/b] that this might not be a smooth experience from a fresh install and some assembly might be required.

After playing Resident Evil HD Remaster and Resident Evil 0 Remaster before, I was really looking forward to this Part of the Resident Evil Franchise because of 2 main aspects; the infinite save function without Ink Ribbons and the third-person perspective.

So far all good, right..?

Well not quite..

[h3]Controls[/h3]

The controls wasn't quite like I expected(from Resident Evil 2 Remake for example) because I still was kinda restricted while playing this game with keyboard and mouse.

The fact that you have to use WASD for movement AND camera positioning was really frustrating because on controls you can easily move around without any problems but on keyboard and mouse, ugh.. it was a real pain in the a** for me.

The next down site especially for keyboard and mouse players is, that there are many situations throughout the game where you have to press either Left Mouse Button, Right Mouse Button, both Mouse Buttons OR "X" and "C" together to dodge certain attacks + you have a extremely short window of time to react like 1 to 2 seconds which is hard frustrating if you don't expect to dodge a attack while you use WASD for running.

If you get into a choke hold, you have to move your mouse very fast very wide left-right like 30 cm to get out of the chokehold which is sooo annoying.

[h3]Ashley[/h3]

Ashley becomes intentionally separated from you several times throughout the game which I personally was laughing my a** off every single time, maybe my humor is broken a** hell but you might think that the very first rescue of Ashley is the only one, but god no, this girl gets separated from you several times - this is why I personally just love that game, every time Ashley became separated from me, I was thinking "ah sh*t here we go again" lmfao.

There is also a funny "easter egg" line from Ashley which is kinda rare.

You can kill Ashley while she's carried by an enemy. So be careful!

[h3]Gameplay[/h3]

The game is veeery stressful on some stages and you quickly become overwhelmed.

[h3]Enemies and Bosses[/h3]

The "Regenerator" and the "Iron Maiden" are in my opinion the most annoying enemies(also besides the bosses) in the entire game because they tank sooo much ammo especially if you don't have the "Infrared Scope" where you can see they weak spots of them, to kill them faster.

The "Krauser" boss was very annoying because he moved so fast that it barely possible to hit him except for the part where you have to kill him.

[h3]Bugs[/h3]

» Sometimes I was unable to sell my stuff because when I selected a item and pressed "Yes", nothing happened.

» Frequently my shots just went through the enemies instead of hitting them which was also very annoying and a waste of ammo.

» When I dodged an enemy attack, my camera perspective sometimes became very weirdly depositioned so that I had to repositioning the camera with my mouse to see and continue the fight which is hell of annoying.

[h3]Graphics[/h3]

There's not much to say except that I love game with this type of old graphics.

[h3]Rating[/h3]

Although the controls are a** especially for keyboard and mouse players, I'd give that games a solid 8/10!

[h3] Despite Leon slaying throughout, I struggled to express myself in Resident Evil 4's restrictive and awkward controls. [/h3]

Failing to find joy in a bona-fide classic is always a disappointment; Resident Evil 4 (RE4) is a game so critically acclaimed that it's difficult to have an opinion on. I've shared fantastic moments with RE4 lovers in-person in coffee shops, to over Twitter, who gush over its iconic and creative set-pieces and boss fights. In many ways, I share their sentiments and have found new aspects to love about the game. But ultimately, I struggled to keep myself going half-way through. 

I love the holistic ways in which RE4 builds tension. Each aspect of the gameplay services a feeling of vulnerability, from the slow movement controls to lack of hipfire. Leon can't move while reloading, and most levels are claustrophically boxed-in offering the player little space to dodge enemies. RE4 is about managing situations, considering your environmental space and creating bottlenecks to eliminate your targets. Quick reflexes and an itchy trigger finger leads to frequent deaths, and instead creating environmental bottlenecks and landing precise shots will award you the best chance of survival.

This difficulty creates an undeniably immersive world. Several enemies can kill Leon in a single hit on regular, and you're constantly toeing the line of having 'just' enough ammo to get through the next room. This creates a feeling of apprehension whenever you walk into an arena or bossfight, knowing you'll be pushed to your limits.

Whilst I appreciate what these features bring to the game's horror, the sluggish control scheme felt like I was always battling against Leon. When several enemies are running into the player's face, capable of killing you in a single swipe, it's frustrating to have Leon passively walk step by step backwards with zero urgency or agility. This does create tension, but because of the lack of control over Leon rather than the enemies themselves. 

The visuals, while sharp and with great UI scaling on modern resolutions, also lack much of the lightening features present on the original Gamecube version. Most people will likely play the stunning RE4 remake, but it's worth noting the PC port is very minimal here. There are barely any adjustable graphics settings, nor support for English subtitles. Controller support works out of the box, which is great, but mouse input features some of the strongest mouse acceleration you'll ever experience.

I am 32 years old.

When we were going through our separation, I felt lost and unhappy. I was self-destructive. One day, I was so angry with everything spiraling out of control that I punched a concrete wall in a moment of overwhelming emotion. This resulted in breaking my fifth metacarpal in my right hand—the hand I worked with, played games with, and used to carry my children to bed—the hand I desperately needed to ensure I could continue providing.

Upon learning the severity of the self-inflicted damage, I became almost suicidal. Keep in mind that just a few months before this, I was the happiest man, with no history of depression or anxiety. I had never experienced anger outbursts, nor was I the type to break down and cry, but I was in a tough situation that truly prevented me from seeing the light on the other side.

With nothing better to do, I looked for a game I could play WITH ONE HAND while recovering. Somehow, I stumbled upon this game and read some of the comments. I decided it was worth a try... I must admit I didn't beat the game, nor did I play as much as some of you. In fact, I may have played this game for only a day or two. That being said, after doing so, I had a new joy and hope for life. I managed to leave behind the pain and suffering that had been thrust upon me. I could experience the joy and happiness of other people. I relaxed for 5 ♥♥♥♥ minutes listening to this music, long enough to realize that I would be okay.

After realizing this, I turned off the game and went back to work. My hand hurt a lot, but I was motivated. I stopped feeling so sorry for myself and became the father I needed to be at that moment, not the weak boy I was behaving like.

Today, I am close friends with the mother of my children. We don't fight, argue, or say hurtful things to each other. We are parents and friends.

Now I have 3 children. My third child is, wait, ALSO 4 YEARS OLD. The woman I am with was going through a very similar situation at the time of my separation, and we just unexpectedly stumbled into each other's lives. We have been dating for a year and are very happy together.

Moral of the story: you never know what life has in store for you, and if I had given up when all odds were against me, I wouldn't be where I am today. This silly little game helped me realize that.

So a quick backstory about my life -- when I was kid, I watched some childhood friends of mine play this game. It completely had me anxious and scared as a kid experiencing this kind of game around the 2000s when this game came out. I've always wanted to play this game since then and I finally got the chance to do so this year. 

The positive side of things for this game in my opinion is the atmosphere, the level designs, the different type of enemies you run into, the story, and certain game mechanics that called back to its predecessor games with the limited capacity with an on-the-go item box that is expandable. I really liked the idea of being able to buy upgrades in certain areas of the game and having certain safe spots like that to prepare for the next part of the level. It has a nostalgic feel that makes me recall the days when I was kid and is very much a slow burn, anxiety-intensive horror game. I appreciated how in the extra section of this game there was another perspective to fill in the holes and really give you a complete story for why things were happening in the game. 

On the negative side -- I thought there were some cheesy and sometimes cliche lines that really didn't fit into the game or to Leon's character. It felt really out of character and perhaps that was just a thing of its time, since this game came out originally in 2005. It didn't take away from the story or disrupt it, the lines or comments just felt unnecessary in some parts. Especially when some of them were mainly sexual innuendos and/or sexist comments in some parts. On a side note, this has been fixed by the developers in the Resident Evil 4 Remake.

Personally this is one of the best games in the Resident Evil series. 
I'd rate it a 9/10.

GENERAL TIPS:

You don't have to have played the others in the series to enjoy RE4. They play nothing alike and it's not as strongly connected plot-wise to the other games.

The absolute hardest part of the game is the very first time in the town when you start the game. There is a shotgun in one of the houses to help you out.

Always scan your area for breakable boxes and other pickups.

With solid positioning you'll never be in a place where the tank controls will be a hindrance. Keep a clean exit behind you and check back there every once in a while.

Buy the treasure maps to each area, but be mindful that you'll be locked out of older areas as you progress and any left behind treasure will be lost. Also, some treasure can be combined with others to make them more valuable, so you might want to hold on to them until they're fully combined.

Ashley's AI is pretty good and she's pretty resilient against enemies, just try not to hit her yourself. There are also a few dumpsters in the game you can stick her into to keep her safe while you clear the area.

When you find yourself under siege in a certain house, you can push the cabinets against the windows and doors to buy time. Also, shooting an enemy while they're climbing on a ladder or through a window knocks them outside.

If you find and shoot all 15 blue medallions in the farm and cemetery, you get a better version of your prize.

You earn a bunch of extra cash by getting a Perfect in the mini-game shooting ranges whenever you find one. Another good way to make money early on once you get the boat is to kill big fish and sell them. Tossing junk into the lake will cause the fish to come to you.

After the boat trip, get back on the boat and head towards the blue light for a hidden shop.

Near the end of the castle you'll see a giant disgusting cone hanging out of the ceiling. There's a lot of money to be made by shooting it down.

Chickens can lay eggs if they are undisturbed for a few minutes.

Once you pick up the Blue Medallion notice, the Medallions will be shown on your map.

There is no guaranteed 2nd drop of the Blue Eye treasure, don't feel like you missed it.

Combat & Enemies:

Pistol + melee will be your weapons of choice for most of the game. Get good at popping enemies in the head or legs then running close and hitting/knifing when they're stunned. It does loads of damage and is a great way to push a crowd of enemies back.

Regular enemies are defenseless against knife swipes while climbing up a ladder, climbing over a barrier like a window sill or a fence, or during their standing up or jumping down animations. Unarmed enemies can also be knifed freely over a barrier, as they cannot grab you over it.

Flash grenades instantly kill any parasite monsters that pop out of enemies' heads, and are also effective against crows.

Leon can do a suplex by shooting the shins of monks, closing the gap and then hitting the action button.

If an enemy swings at you, simply stepping backwards is usually enough to make them miss, with the exception of pitchfork-wielding and unarmed enemies.

Kicking is your friend, abuse it. You get invincibility frames with it as well.

Shotguns are much more effective at clearing crowds than the TMP.

Try to avoid reloading in front of bosses.

Try to save a Rocket Launcher for the part where you fight a boss with liquid nitrogren all over the place.

You can shoot (or even knife!) weapons enemies throw at you out of the air. Likewise if you shoot dynamite in the air or in enemies' hands, it'll explode early.

Weapons & Items:

On normal difficulty, pick the weapon that looks like the most fun to you as the game won't be too hard. Keep a shotgun, pistol, and rifle. Magnums are great for a few bosses ("Prepare for your Death, Leon") but shouldn't be used against regular enemies. If you want the most powerful of each slot, the Red9, the second shotgun and the second rifle are your picks.

The bolt-action rifle is slower but much more powerful than the semi-auto rifle, making it useful for far-off enemies. Buying a scope is optional as you can usually do fine without.

You can get a free Broken Butterfly magnum with some backtracking in the second main area.

Unless you're really having trouble, hold off on upgrading your weapons until chapter 3, as newer, better ones become available for purchase at that point.

Generally firepower upgrades get more bang for your buck. Also, upgrading your ammo capacity fills your ammo.

Yellow herb + green herb = maximum life increase + a heal.

What an absolute experience I just had with this game. This being my first Resident Evil game, and also my first ever horror game in general, I had no idea what expectations to be had for getting into this. I am simply astonished. Who knew that video games can give such a brilliant cinematic yet interactive experience? Who knew that there could be such perfect harmony between narrative, presentation, and gameplay? Resident Evil 4 has completely changed the way I look at video games from now on. I will admit, I am not much of a gamer at all besides my investment in franchises I’m already deeply connected to so what and how I gush about this game might not seem that all that new or impressive to most people.

Firstly, I have to talk about its presentation. It perfectly captures this liveable yet spooky setting in the countryside of Spain and the locations like the village, castle and island are all so distinct from one another yet they blend so well as a cohesive visual identity to Resident Evil 4. Despite how dark the game gets due to its setting being at night at times, there is just clarity in everything I can do, see, and interact with. It is easily distinguishable from what's just background and what I can interact with yet somehow it never looks out of place in keeping my immersion with the game. Though the immersion doesn’t just end at the visuals because what strikes me even more is the chilling sound design. The creeping atmosphere with the haunting sound effects makes every walk through a corridor or road so daunting. What’s even scarier is when I know there’s enemies ahead with the whispers and weapon sounds making the inevitability of combat all the more tense. Every time I boot up this game I am just drenched in cold sweat with how engaged I am in playing as Leon with how real it makes me feel being in the world.

But I wish I knew more about this world. Being the 4th entry in the franchise, it definitely seems connected with the previous games with characters like Ada Wong and Krausser seeming to mention events from past games. It is okay though, the bottom line of Leon investigating and trying to recover Ashley is an intriguing enough hook with what seems to be some political struggle going on in the background which interests me enough to definitely check out the other games. These characters are fun to follow though, Leon has this cool no-nonsense behaviour that of an actual military personnel but can also goof off if the situation allows it. My kinda guy. I was incredibly worried that since the game is essentially one giant escort mission that Ashley was going to be super insufferable but turns out she is alright. Yea she cries out for Leon a lot when she’s captured, but she’s helpful in her own right and can banter well with Leon in the more light-hearted scenes. This is a detailed review of Resident Evil 4 (2005). 

If you have the attention span of a TikTok doomscroller, you might want to click away now. 

But for those who haven't played this masterpiece and want a detailed, spoiler-free review: 

here it is.

The Experience

After playing through the entire game, earning every achievement, completing the Mercenaries mode to unlock the Handcannon, and beating the game on every difficulty five times, I can confidently say that RE4 (2005) is a masterpiece. It excels in nearly every aspect of the gaming experience to ensure you have an enticing, fun time.

Main Story

The Main story is fantastic. The gameplay, though simple, is the most addictive in the franchise (trust me, I’ve played the RE4 Remake). While the writing might seem "mid" to modern players, its cheesiness is exactly what makes it so entertaining. For Resident Evil fans, this is the Resident evil writing.

The atmosphere is frequently chilling and occasionally absolutely frightening, marking a shift from prior RE games. The game utilizes amazing sound design and level layouts (reminiscent of the RE1 Remake) to create a vibe unique to the RE0, RE1 Remake, and RE4 era.

Graphically, the game moved away from pre-rendered backgrounds in favor of full 3D models. While these look solid in the HD Edition, the RE4 HD Project Mod (the biggest mod in the game's history) makes the environments look realistic and jaw-dropping. I definitely recommend checking that mod out.

DLC: Separate Ways & Assignment Ada

The DLCs Separate Ways and Assignment Ada are included with the main game. They are excellent additions for people who want to experience the original settings from a different perspective, offering faster pacing and fewer horror elements than the main story.

Mercenaries Mode

Before debating the genre, I want to focus on the Mercenaries Mode—the "cherry on top" of an already great game. The modern Mercenaries style seen in RE5, RE6, and RE8 made its debut right here. You start with Leon and four maps, and from there, the rest is history.

The Genre Debate: 

There is a big debate over whether this game focuses more on action or horror. In my opinion, this game provides more tension than the older titles. The enemies are much faster and more intelligent than "braindead" zombies. The atmosphere often baits you into scares, and the creature designs are truly unsettling—often more intimidating than those in previous games. You have to strategize how to take these monsters down; that is the horror. The action comes from the fact that you can dispatch enemies with ease using kicks and the abundance of resources dropped by foes or sold by the Merchant. If you are careful with your knife and melee attacks, you will basically always have the resources to kill every monster.
So, what genre is RE4? 

It is perfected, balanced Action-Horror.

Conclusion
This game is an amazing, scary experience on your first playthrough and becomes even more fun on subsequent runs. It is a perfected action-horror experience with extra modes that round out the package beautifully. It is my favorite Resident Evil title and my favorite video game of all time.

10/10

[h1] Resident Evil 4 HD: An Upscale More Than A Remaster [/h1]

Alright, let's get this straight - Resident Evil 4 HD is like that expensive imported sports car you've been eyeing for years, but when you finally buy it, you realize it's just had a fancy paint job and nothing else. It should have been Resident Evil 4 Remastered, but it's more like Resident Evil 4 Upscaled. And honestly, it's a letdown.

Don't get me wrong, Resident Evil 4 is a classic. It's often hailed as one of the best action games of all time, setting the standard for third-person shooters. But this so-called HD version doesn't do it justice.

The biggest problem? The visuals. They've simply upscaled the GameCube version, and it shows. The game's textures were designed for a maximum resolution of 480p, and this "HD" treatment just makes them look chunky and outdated. The whole point of Resident Evil 4 is paying attention to your surroundings, but when the grass looks like Lego and the textures blend together, it's a mess.

The tank controls, a point of contention among fans, are showing their age. And the game's visuals make them even less forgivable. When you scrutinize the intricate details of Salazar's castle or Lord Sadler's portraits, you realize that they look worse, not better. Leon's character model, though iconic, is now too in-your-face. This "premium" download should have offered more.

But let's not forget why we love Resident Evil 4. It's a thrilling, action-packed adventure filled with monsters, incredible boss fights, and the unforgettable merchant. Leon's mission to rescue the President's daughter, Ashley, keeps you on the edge of your seat. You not only have to save her but also manage her during the game. It's tense, and it works.

And then there's the combat. Resident Evil 4's over-the-shoulder viewpoint and pacing have influenced many games since. The game introduces its mechanics gradually, then thrusts you into a village filled with hostile villagers. The tension and excitement build as you face one enemy after another.

The game's brilliant context-sensitive melee moves add depth to the combat. Rather than running from the action, you often rush headlong into the fray, delivering roundhouse kicks and desperately trying to create some breathing space.

The game's superb boss fights are like a battle royale of grotesque monsters. Every encounter is unique and challenging. Take the Garrador, for example - a blind enemy with an acute sense of hearing. Each time you face it, the circumstances change, keeping the game fresh.

Sure, this HD version tweaks some encounters for the better, like the sewer battle with Salazar's insects, but overall, the visual upgrade is lacking. It doesn't make the cut. For those who've played this gem multiple times, Resident Evil 4 HD falls short.

If you're a die-hard fan and haven't revisited Resident Evil 4 since its release, consider the Wii version. It's cheaper and the pointer controls work great. But this so-called HD upgrade is nothing more than a disappointment. Resident Evil 4 deserved better, the fans deserved better, and Capcom should have done better.

So, Resident Evil 4 HD - it's still a fantastic game but not the definitive version it should be. 

Capcom knew this and with the 2023 rerelease, I've experienced so many slice of life upgrades that I would rather point people to that version rather than this. But hey, this game is cheap and holds closer to the original. 

Do you value true form closer to the original RE4 experience? Get this game. 

Do you want the modern experience of RE4 with a lower difficulty and added slice of life fixes? Get the 2023 version.

Resident Evil 4 sees the return of Leon Kennedy as he's tasked to rescue the President's daughter, who has been abducted by the resident of a mysterious Spanish village. Resident Evil 4 (2005) marked the beginning of the more action-focused era of Resident Evil, where gameplay took more of a turn to gunning down endless waves of enemies and less of a focus on survival horror elements. This isn't to say that horror elements are no longer present, they're just toned down to compensate for increased action movie elements. This includes the dialogue, which is both famous and infamous for being so incredibly B-tier action movie it's become the subject of many a meme. Leon throws out quips like a major league baseball pitcher and rarely ever shows a moment of fear towards the situations he finds himself in. You'll also be given sections where you have to guide Ashley around by the hand, sometimes literally. People who have played RE4 before may know that Ashley will find herself in trouble at a moment's notice, but I surprisingly didn't find too much of an issue with this, so my immersion wasn't broken too often by repeated instances of "LEON! This change not only enhanced aiming and combat but also brought a newfound sense of tension as players faced relentless hordes of infected villagers. The inventory system, weapon upgrades, and resource management elements added depth to the gameplay, making every decision count. The game's controls were intuitive and responsive, contributing to its overall excellence.

The game's memorable antagonist, Osmund Saddler, added depth to the storyline, and the overall presentation was top-notch.

Horror (5/5):
Resident Evil 4 masterfully blended action and horror. The relentless pursuit by infected villagers, grotesque creature encounters, and the eerie ambiance of the environments kept players on edge throughout the game. Jump scares were expertly timed, and the tension was maintained from start to finish. Resident Evil 4 is a prime example of how to create a truly terrifying experience.

The game's replayability was enhanced by its multiple difficulty levels, unlockable content, and New Game+ mode. In summary, Resident Evil 4 (2005) is a true masterpiece that left an indelible mark on the survival horror genre. Its gameplay innovations, captivating story, and spine-tingling horror elements have solidified its place in gaming history. Even years after its release, it remains an essential title for anyone seeking a truly immersive and terrifying gaming experience. Ah, Resident Evil 4, a game that many praise as a masterpiece of the survival horror genre. But allow me, kind sir or madam, to don my critical hat and present to you a perspective that may have eluded the masses.

M'lady and gentle-sirs, the lauded Resident Evil 4, in my humble opinion, falls short of the lofty accolades heaped upon it. It is a game that has become an icon, yes, but not for the reasons one might expect. Instead of championing the survival horror formula, this entry seems more inclined to embrace a misguided action-oriented direction.

First and foremost, let us address the protagonist, Leon S. Kennedy. While he may have become a beloved figure in gaming, I dare say his character arc in this installment is nothing short of lackluster. Gone are the days of genuine tension and fear; now, we have a one-liner spewing hero who's seemingly impervious to danger. Where, oh where, has the subtlety of storytelling gone?

Furthermore, the enemies, commonly referred to as "Los Ganados," are a far cry from the unsettling horrors of past Resident Evil games. They're not so much terrifying as they are an inconvenience, constantly pestering you as you make your way through the mundane environments. The tension that once defined the franchise has been replaced with relentless action, and it's truly a lamentable departure.

And let us not forget the egregious inclusion of quick-time events (QTEs). Oh, how they plague this game! Instead of allowing players to immerse themselves in the world of survival horror, Resident Evil 4 often opts to interrupt the experience with these infuriating button prompts. It's an affront to the art of gaming!

M'lady and sir, in conclusion, while Resident Evil 4 may have garnered widespread acclaim, I must respectfully dissent. It is a departure from the series' roots and a betrayal of the very essence of survival horror. The once-heralded franchise has, in my view, lost its way, and this entry is emblematic of that lamentable shift.

This review is based on the RE4 HD Project (including re4_tweaks), available as a free download. I've never played RE4 (original or remake) before, so I went in totally blind. I tested the first hour or so using controller, then switched to mouse and keyboard.

+ Goofy (one might even say Fun™) story and characters, doesn't take itself too seriously. Lots of cheese and tropes pulled from Hollywood movies of the era, plus nods and inspiration from other games.
+ Engaging third-person combat with an emphasis on aim (without being too punishing).
+ Good overall difficulty curve, introducing you to basic mechanics and enemies while slowly increasing the heat over the course of the game.
+ Large mobs and boss fights tend to prioritise strategy. A little bit of foresight goes a long way; there were only one or two encounters that felt cheap.
+ Resource management is a large part of the game. You can't buy ammo. Instead, you'll be relying on enemy drops and map exploration. Panicking during one encounter and wasting your ammo might lead to additional hardship an hour or two down the line.
+ Taking the extra time to explore the maps tends to lead to items, treasure, or ammo. Holding on to certain treasure/items and knowing when to combine+sell is its own rewarding mini game.
+ Got some rare things on sale, stranger! Stronger weapons, upgrades, and items are available at your friendly neighbourhood merchant. Again, knowing when to buy/sell is key.
+ About the right amount of level variety. The middle part of the game taking place in the castle is the highlight of the game.
- Bullet sponges. I was a bit confused by how this seemed to change at different points and wondered if this was part of the RE4HD mod. A little bit of research later shows the game has a dynamic difficulty setting hidden from the player; if you're not taking damage and hitting most of your shots, enemy aggressiveness and tankiness increases automatically. There were a couple of moments where it felt absurd - even with weapon upgrades and headshots (or even point blank hits), certain enemy types were taking a looooong time to go down.
-  QTEs were getting out of hand towards the end of the game. I had four QTE prompts back to back in a 15 second period during the sequence with the three falling containers.
- There's no quick weapon swap. If you do run out of ammo, or need to switch targets that needs a different weapon, you're going to be constantly in and out of the attache case screen.
- There are lots of moments in the game where you get to a typewriter (save point), go through a door, and there's immediately another typewriter. During the last stretch of the game, the typewriters seem to dry up.
- This is probably just me, but I was getting a bit impatient/burned out towards the end of the game. "Too much of a good thing."

I'm not the biggest fan of the RE series, but I would definitely recommend this instalment if only to experience a little bit of gaming history. I would also strongly recommend the RE4 HD Project which drastically transforms the graphics for the better. It's a hefty download (30GB+), but absolutely worth it. Look up the video by Nerrel on YouTube to see a comparison and better appreciate the work that went in.

[h1]Notes[/h1]
I've already played this on my PS2 when I was younger, so my experience may differ from someone playing the game for the first time.

[h1]Overview[/h1]
One of the best and most famous games of the Resident Evil franchise, in this game Leon will have to save the president's daughter, who was kidnapped by a mysterious cult located somewhere in Spain, whilst trying to survive another biohazard controlled by that group.

[h1]Gameplay[/h1]
Such as other games from the franchise, the main point of the gameplay is fighting monsters and exploring, the combat isn't very dynamic, since Leon can't dodge and will stop moving while aiming. There is a good variety of guns and enemies through the game, and you'll find yourself having to manage your inventory and combining herbs to make more powerful healing items, mechanics you may already be used to if you played other Resident Evil games. All guns have laser aim (except for the ones with scope), and Leon seems to be always trembling while aiming, which is realistic in a way, but may be frustrating since it may lower your accuracy.

[h1]Graphics[/h1]
The game uses 3D graphics, considering it was originally a PS2 game the graphics are pretty decent, with good models and animations, but it does have some textures that seem a bit crappy.

[h1]Audio[/h1]
The game's background is mostly silent, which makes a quite tense and creepy atmosphere, but there are still some memorable music, such as the one that plays in the safe rooms. The sound affects are very well done and the characters are properly voiced.

[h1]Price[/h1]
The game is already pretty old, and there's even a remake of it now, so it could be cheaper, but even so you can say the price is fair for the content it provides.

[h1]Difficulty[/h1]
You can choose the difficulty before starting a new game, but regardless of that, the game has adaptive difficulty, which means it will try to be always challenging but never overwhelming. I heard somewhere that adaptive difficulty is turned off in professional mode, but since I already had past experience with this game I had no problem on normal mode, so the professional mode wasn't much different from it, so I can't really say if that's true.

[h1]Duration[/h1]
The game has an average duration, it isn't necessarily long, but it may still give you some good hours of fun before running out of content, especially if you're a completionist.

[h1]Replayability[/h1]
You unlock professional difficulty after finishing the game on normal once, so you can play it for the challenge. The game also features New Game+, where you can start the game again with all your equipment and money from the previous run. Completing the main game or the mini-games unlocked after beating it once also unlock new outfits and weapons (those new weapons, however, are only available on new game+ runs).

[h1]Achievements[/h1]
You'll get most of the achievements naturally as you progress through the game, the rest are easy to get as well, with the only arguably hard being the "Finish the game in the highest difficult" one.

[h1]Problems[/h1]
[list]
[*]Even though the game events are located in Spain, the ganados speak mostly Mexican Spanish.

[*]While I don't particularly see it as a problem, some people may not like the adaptative difficulty.

[*]Some cutscenes are not synced with the audio.

[*]You are unable to play the game at 60fps, even though it has an option for it in the menu.
[/list]

The game is really good. Graphics, gameplay, audio, pretty much everything holds up to date; the game has really aged well. Controls worried me at first but they actually work very well. The controls are robust, yet the controls provide a unique experience that you just don't get anymore.

The graphics are amazing for a 2005 game. The motion capture is extremely fluid; complemented with the lively facial expressions that are almost as good as modern games (and better in the case of games like Assassin's Creed). The environments are well designed with intricate detail everywhere you look, although I didn't like how almost everything in the village was brown. The environmental designers could have gone for a bit of orange and yellow if they wanted the game set in Autumn.

Resident Evil 4's audio design isn't easy on the ears, and that's a good thing for the most part. Getting into combat gives this eerie rumbling that makes you feel unwelcome, but it is played too much to the point of being annoying. The voice acting as heart and soul poured into it, and not just the main cast. The Ganados, Zealots and Soldiers all have pretty good voice lines. I especially like when the Zealots perform their zombified chants (my personal fav is 'Cogedlo'). All the guns have good audio direction. Big guns and good guns are beefy, small guns and weak guns have sound that is respective to their status. Ambient noise wasn't noticeable, which is what I like. The only audio that I hated was the Attaché Case's selecting of an item. I hate the metallic sound it makes.

I love all the characters. The Merchant is the best; his awesome voice and his epic lines getting me pumped to continue playing the game. Everyone is funny in their own way. Chief Mendez who doesn't even talk is still funny yet intimidating with how he just stares blankly. Salazar and Leon's beef is actually treasure as is Leon's beef with Saddler. The cheesy dialogue is really what I like to see in villains, especially the anti-American rhetoric. It manages to be funny constantly without overstaying its welcome.

It might seem odd with this game having tank control, but it really is a unique experience that you don't really get anymore. You have three speeds: walk, backwalk, sprint. It allows for really consistent, well-thought-out moments of evasion. While baiting out and dodging an attack might not be deeper than walking forwards then walking backwards, it still feels satisfying when you pull it off correctly, i.e., in the right situations. The Merchant system works superbly, especially as it is intertwined with the exploration. You explore to find resources and treasure/money. You can sell anything you own that isn't a key item. As you progress, money is easier to come by, allowing you to purchase the goodies that pack a punch. This includes guns as well as upgrades. The system is paced in a way that fits so well with the difficulty. You get progress just as the game does, no need to grind for a stupid amount of money or to get a high enough level. You earn enough money as you go along and exploration isn't necessary, it just gives those with a 'lack of skill' a boost. Guns are great. You've got your pistols which are weak 90% of the time but are useful for stunning and performing melee attacks. Knife helps you save ammo (not that you need to) and is vital in some parts of the game. Shotgun destroys at close range and provides easy area clearance. Rifle is for long range high damage. TMP is crowd control - good for stunning lots of enemies who are overwhelming you. Magnums have a kick and RPG is the boss killer. You can't go wrong with that, mate. Ashley controls surprisingly well; never really had a problem with her. The enemy variety is big and it's really good. This game always manages to shake things up with different enemy types. Even the island which has a bad flow has great enemy variety and placements.

Unfortunately, there are a few criticisms, but they are pretty minor and few in quantity. Firstly, ammo is just way too abundant. I was never running out of ammo unless I exclusively used a single weapon for a long period of time. It really hurts the resource management in the game. On the other hand, healing items are relatively scarce, which is a good thing in my opinion. There was also this one cutscene that really annoyed me. When Leon and Luis are tied up, a guy with an axe (that we never see in-game) attempts to murder them. Leon and Luis were tied up for a reason and Leon was injected with las Plagas. They weren't even attempting to escape, they were just talking. I also think the island section drags on for a bit too long, making the flow feel a bit incoherent.
