[h1]An amazing blend of action and survival horror and a classic game![/h1]
[h3]Unfortunately, its jank can be offputting.[/h3]

Resident Evil 4 was a game that both intimidated me and infuriated me before I even played it. On one hand, the game's action looked overwhelming and terrifying to deal with. On the other hand, I knew it still used tank controls, and I had always hated them even though I grew up with the original Tomb Raider games. Because of both of these perceived issues, I had never played the game as a kid.

This kept up even after I got into Resident Evil once more as an adult, as even though I was more comfortable with the action-oriented nature of the game, the controls still put me off. I also had this odd idea that RE4 was not a true Resident Evil game since it drifted away from the claustrophobic hallways and dark rooms of the first four games and the most recent game at the time, Resident Evil 7.

Then RE Village happened. That game changed my view of action horror, and the only thing keeping me from playing RE4 was the tank controls and stationary aiming. I was running out of excuses not to play this game and stubbornly holding onto anything that would keep me from doing it. And then the remake was announced, and I was out of excuses. I had to play the original

So one day in 2022, a friend and I took the plunge, playing concurrently. And I'm extremely glad we did. Just as the accolades for this game say, it really is one of the best games of all time.

For those who might not know much about Resident Evil, the fourth game serves as a bit of a soft reboot. Instead of focusing on Umbrella Corporation and the damage the T-virus does to the areas in which it spreads, it takes a familiar protagonist, Leon S. Kennedy of RE2 fame, and sends him to Valdelobos, Spain, where the daughter of the US President has been taken.

Valdelobos is a small village that's still developing, and it's quite a change from the feel of the mansion of the first game, the metropolitan setting of the second and third game, and the more industrial setting of Code: Veronica. The differences are immediately more noticeable, as is the fact that the game starts during the day.

But the most notable change is that to an over-the-shoulder camera. As I said earlier, it keeps the tank controls, but now the camera never moves from behind Leon during normal gameplay. Aiming is also pinpoint now, rather than the point-and-shoot mechanics of the previous four games, though you still have to be stationary while shooting, something that the devs did account for with enemy movement and aggression. I was worried the Ganados would be just as aggressive as the enemies in Village, but I'm glad they weren't.

When it comes to moment-to-moment gameplay, RE4 shares quite a bit in common with Village. Both have an attaché case where items have to be arranged in a grid, both have high-action setpieces with crazy amounts of enemies, both have an unwinnable ambush at the beginning of the game, and I could go on. It's quite clear how much of an influence the game has had on the series. Even in the RE2 and 3 remakes, enemies are far more aggressive than in the original versions, and there are far more of them.

I was also surprised at how "survival horror" it felt at times. I had a few times where I was tight on resources in ways that I didn't expect. There were several times where I had to make healing items last or aim extra carefully because I'm on my last couple dozen handgun rounds. The powerful feeling of the weapons is also a huge plus. None of the weapons in any of the original games or in the "revival" games feel particularly weighty like the guns in RE4 and all the remakes do.

The story is pretty standard fare for a Resident Evil game. Turns out that this small village is home to a cult called Los Illuminados (not [i]the[/i] Los Illuminados; that's just saying "the the enlightened") who found a parasite that they've termed "las plagas"—wow, creative. Their leader, Osmund Saddler, controls all the villagers with telepathic powers, and his whole goal is to [spoiler]eliminate the US and put his cult in power[/spoiler]. It's really cliché, but that's par for the course for Resident Evil.

It's very cheesy, and it's honestly got a ton of charm. Quotable one liners like, "Your right hand comes off?" and, "Where's everyone going, bingo?" constantly show up. The whole game feels like a silly B movie, even more so than the previous games. The cutscenes are regularly more bombastic than the gameplay, and the radio calls give me some serious Metal Gear Solid parody vibes.

The merchant is also a wonderful addition to the game. You know nothing about this man, but as he approaches you with, "Over here, stranger!" you can't help but be intrigued. He is an enigma, but he endears you with his unique accent and charm.

There's a lot to love here, but there are also a few things that royally frustrated me during my playthrough. As I've said multiple times in my review, the tank controls and stationary shooting are already a point of contention for me. Because of those controls, you can sometimes find yourself in less-than-stellar positions, and it can be hard to escape from a corner if you don't have shotgun ammo or a grenade. Since there's no way to block incoming attacks, you can often get staggered by multiple enemies in a row and take a ton of damage before you can recover, and before you know it, you've lost half of your health.

There are also a lot of rooms and corridors that are pretty empty and seem to serve almost no purpose other than as filler. Nearly every room in older Resident Evil games and RE7 has some kind of purpose, ammo, or item, but quite a few areas have no function beyond just being another room. It's actually a problem that Village and the RE4 remake run into, as well. I suppose they needed to pad it out in some ways if they wanted it to be longer and larger than any other game in the series so far. I just wish they could've found more meaningful ways to do it.

But now comes the criticism everyone's probably been expecting: Ashley. Unfortunately, she is just as bad as you'd expect, if not worse. At least to me, Ashley in this original game is an unlikable brat who does nothing but get in your way, in both the story and gameplay. She has a couple redeeming moments, like her more levelheaded demeanor in some later parts of the game and her solo section in the middle of the game, but overall, escorting her always feels like nothing more than a chore that you're forced to do.

I would wholeheartedly recommend this game, though, even if it's not a 10/10 for me. And this is a 10/10 for a lot of people out there. Your experience could be different from mine, and you could love every aspect of this game. In fact, I hope you do.

The best 60fps version of the game, since you can choose between mouse+keyboard or a controller, and you have all the inherent PC/Steam advantages such as modding and being able to play on any PC. However, this version has no new content compared to any version since the PS2 version, and it still falls far short of the Wii version due to the Wii version’s superior motion-control aiming.

A word of warning on the 60fps: while it makes the game look much nicer and makes aiming with a controller much easier, it introduces a load of glitches. Enemies can run through fire (which almost ruins fire grenades), button-mashing QTE’s are twice as hard, and the enemy AI is a bit messed up in general (for example, it’s far more aggressive than the old versions and has a tendency to do things like spin on the spot or freeze). The 60fps ports also don’t have the graphical features which made 30fps tolerable on the old versions, so you’ll have to play 60fps and put up with the glitches.

Overall, you won’t go wrong with this version and it’s probably the most accessible for beginners. However, the best vanilla experience is still by far the Wii version so I’d get that one instead/as well if you own a Wii. If you have already played RE4 before, you might want to only get this version on sale and only if you intend to do PC/Steam-specific things like modding. For example, I only ever play the Wii version unless I want to play Randomizer mod or I'm not at home or something like that.

Resident Evil 4 Ultimate HD Edition, a port of the Xbox 360 version, which was based off of the 2007 Wii version, which takes the not pre-rendered cutscenes from the GameCube port and the content from the PS2 port. What a history. 

Well, it's at least a complete version of the game. However, by itself it does have some glaring flaws, such as not all textures actually being HD like the name implies. This is is only the tip of the iceberg, as there's noticeably 60fps related issues. Some are minor like ammo drops and other miscellaneous interactions, however by far the biggest change is QTEs. Because of the way older games were made, increasing their framerate increases the literal speed at which the game runs at, like in an emulator. This is similar to the Super Mario 64 PC port in that the doubling of frames requires the doubling of inputs to keep up with the additional 30 frames. Combine this with Professional mode's decreased QTE leniency and instances such as getting knocked off by Del Lago a second time practically impossible. 

Fear not, as the RE4HD Project and RE4 Tweaks fixes these issues, enables additional customization/functionality, and is free to download. There's legitimately no reason not to get them (other than the former requiring ~40GB of storage).

 Overall, the port does it's job. Resident Evil 4 Ultimate HD Edition gets the game onto Windows and it runs. Honestly, aside from the QTEs the port does a good job of being playable and allows for a unique experience using a keyboard and mouse. The game is smooth and feels like an upgrade compared to playing on console. I definitely recommend this port, even with the remake out as of writing. If you haven't played the original you are missing out and there's plenty of fun to be had. For any remake fans, there's *spoiler alert* a skin that makes Ashley invulnerable turning the game into a cakewalk! I got this on sale for at $4.99 so I can't say I wasted my money in any capacity. $20 is a bit pricey IMHO for such an old game, especially for a digital copy. I know I just said I got it for less but considering the remake is out and some of the flaws... it's still a good game. You might get stuck on a section or two but you'll make it through this awesome adventure. On sale, you can't go wrong.

The constant barrage of quick time events (and bugs associated with them) is honestly the only bad part about this game.

I'd always heard about Resident Evil 4 and how great it was, but never got to play it since it was locked to old consoles I never owned.

And after playing it, I can see why everyone loves it so much. It's got solid gameplay, and interesting story, and decent voice acting.

The addition of a shop and economy is also a neat touch, rewarding exploration a bit more directly with the occasional cache of coins laying around.

The tank controls take a bit of getting used to (as does the static aiming), but after adjusting to them it's not bad. Definitely not ideal, but vastly better than the fixed camera of the first 3 games.

I do recommend the remake over this, but buying both versions is a good choice (and what I did).

Solid 8/10. 2 points taken off for the constant QTEs (and random old game jank that gets annoying).



==Separate Ways==
A solid expansion of the story by letting us see what Ada was up to the entire time (always love it when games give you multiple viewpoints).

However, the limited technology of the time really holds it back imo. Ada is shown to be very acrobatic in cutscenes, and while she does move faster in gameplay it doesn't quite feel like I'm playing the Ada from the cutscenes. The tank controls contribute to this problem, but as I said I think most of it is just because that's about the best they could do in 2005 with the available hardware (and disc space).

The story itself is interesting, and fills us in on who Ada is working for, why she's on the island, and the various ways she helps out Leon throughout the entire game.

Even the Merchant is there - and overcharging us because his "shop isn't set up yet". Also doesn't offer tune ups like he did in the base game.

But anyway, this is just an extra mode you unlock after beating the game, and I recommend giving it a shot. Only a few hours long & fills in some extra details in a neat way (as well as giving us a bit more insight on Ada's character).

But it's still a solid 8.5/10. Give it a go (no reason not to).



==Professional Mode==
Yeah I don't like it. Makes everything a bullet sponge and leads to lots of frustration.

I think the main issue is the limited movement the game offers while designing enemies around a more robust movement system, leading to artificial difficulty that ends up making this more more frustrating than it should've been.

But if you want to 100% the game, you'll have to beat it on Professional. If you can deal with the bullet sponges it's not bad, but I still hate it when games just scale up health for difficulty rather than doing something interesting.

The original RE4 still holds up as a timeless masterpiece, even with the fancy new remake (which I also love). It's been a long time since I've played a game this consistently engaging and competently-made. Sure, it's not perfect - the tank controls are dated, the script stilted, and some gameplay segments undercooked. And it's not so much a survival-horror game as it is a horror-flavored action game; the scariest part of this game is probably the controls.

But what it does provide is an incredibly immersive atmosphere, effected by some truly sublime audiovisual design as well as incredible variety in its gameplay. For all 18-20 hours of its campaign - one of the longest linear campaigns I've played to date - RE4 delivers a constant stream of new ideas and challenges without ever growing stale. The Salazar castle has quickly become one of my favorite settings in all of gaming: a massive gauntlet that is almost overwhelming the first time around, it mixes its dark fantasy setting, almost akin to Zelda's, with the pulp sensibilities of Indiana Jones or Tomb Raider. It's such a ridiculously compelling concept.

This game also surprised me in another way: its sheer replayability. Unlike the earlier RE games, RE4 has a substantially long campaign. But like the earlier ones, it maintains that arcade-y encouragement of multiple playthroughs so that you can shave down your times, refine your strategies, and play with new weapons. I almost never replay games, but I've finished 4 consecutive playthroughs of RE4 and I'm on my 5th now with no signs of slowing down. I can't stop playing the thing.

tl;dr: Even if you've played the remake, the original RE4 is absolutely still worth playing. It lives up to its title as one of the best action games ever made.

When it comes to this RE4, it's generally a mixed bag for me.

To say that it wasn't an iconic staple for modern third-person perspective shooters would be incorrect. Resident Evil 4 is extraordinary in many aspects, but for me is dragged to the floor by additions or exclusions that give it a weird place in the series. Is it worth it? Yes, very much. However, it's hard for me to say it's the best experience from the franchise.

The Good:

Action-Paction
RE4 functions super well as an action title, and I think the gameplay is engaging and thrilling for new players. When I think fondly of this game, I remember staying in areas and killing enemies until the music would stop or taking down bosses and sub-bosses as fast as possible. Combat is where most of the development effort went, and it feels nice to sweep through a chapter killing any enemies that get in your way.

THE INTRO IS SO GOOOOOD
They say that the first few minutes you experience a game are supposed to introduce you to the world and mechanics of the title. And I have to say, RE4 has one of the best intros by game design. In most traditional entries, even RE7, you start with the pistol first, and with a little bit of exploration eventually, finding a shotgun. Since RE4 is action-oriented, instead of waiting for the perfect time, you instantly get a new weapon telling you that this is not going to be the same game you’ve played several times, and I love that. The intro is when this game feels the most like a survival horror experience. No more rooms with one or two zombies, now you have to fight the horde barely escaping alive by the skin of your teeth. Though enemies die quickly, their mass will overwhelm you if you aren't careful, so nonetheless, it's very thrilling the first time around.

A1 Bosses
Bosses, RE4 has some of the most iconic of them. El Gigante, Del Lago, Krauser, Bitores Méndez, and one of my favorites in the entire series, Verdugo. Of course, this game has its stinkers like Ramon, and at least for me an incredibly anti-climatic Lord Saddler. However, I can't hold that against the game though because every Resident Evil has its horrible boss once in a while.

A1 Enemies
The enemy design is some of the best I've seen in the franchise. Yes, I am saddened that Zombies, Lickers, Hunters, and all the great enemies from the previous games are gone, [spoiler]after the end of Code Veronica and the end of Umbrella.[/spoiler] But man, the enemies complement the new gameplay so well for the simple fact that they are unexpected, and serve as elements of surprise. You never really know how an enemy will function until you man up and fight it. In addition, RE4's use of colorization and art style make even the everyday Ganado a little bit disturbing. I will say it's more jarring to look at them than it is to be pursued by them unlike the Hunters, or the Lickers. They aren't too scary.

The Bad:

QTEs
Starting, RE4 came with the introduction of these horrible QTEs which serve as a skill check that is SUPPOSED to heighten the tension of this game but if you ask me they are not implemented well at all. Don't get me wrong some QTEs make sense I guess? But god, they are more painful than anxious. At points in the game, you'll probably forget that they exist at all only for them to come back and bite you with a literal mere seconds of reaction time almost like Capcom wanted you to die to replay the scene again.

The Inevitable Gameplay Snooze Fest
Do you remember what I said about the intro to this game? RE4 has great gameplay that's fun and interesting, but when its novelty wears off, jeez the final hours of this game become the biggest drag ever. Nearing the end, drained of interest, I was waiting for the end chapter screen or the final cutscene to play. Everything starts to feel like a loop. Go to a place, kill enemies, activate something, back to step one... Very Point A, Point B. It doesn’t change all too much.

This Game Is Barely a Survival Horror Game
One thing that infuriates me about RE4 is that there is never a challenge or a moment of despair in this game. I told you the intro is the most survival horror this game will ever get. In the previous games, it felt like an escape room to get away from the danger. Unlocking rooms, getting better equipment, and eliminating threats cautiously. RE4’s solution to that is to kill everything. There is no more strategy for winning. Weapon progression is locked behind how much money you have. RE4 believes that if there is at least some presence of survival horror then it passes because it’s barely a survival horror game.

Horrible Atmosphere

This is subjective, but the aesthetic and atmosphere of this game are probably some of the worst in the series.

RE2, you enter a police station for help where cops who are more armed than civilians are seemingly claimed by the undead in an already apocalyptic city applying pressure and making the odds of survival hopeless.

RE1, a mansion that is confusing, navigating it could feel like a maze at times. There's very little explanation of why you are here and the only information you are given is expressed in hard-to-understand notes capitalizing on its fear of the unknown.

RE4’s village is a good introduction, but its enemies, no matter how they look, aren't adding too much to make the place feel disturbing or scary. When it becomes night, the game does amp it up a bit leading up to the big fight with Mendez. 
Salazar’s Castle has big rooms with many enemies, and it does that a lot, over and over again. The maze was a nice switch-up, and the lava room was cool, but that was about it.
And lastly, the Secret Base, was when I stopped caring, but the Regenerator was terrifying, a very excellent addition. In conclusion, this place threw away the horror aspect of the game and went straight for that action.

I think RE4 had ideas, but let's be honest, the castle could be set in a broken insane asylum and the entire cohesion would make sense. You could say that about any game in the series, it's just that this one specifically doesn't contextualize these areas well with its main cast of characters. The Illuminados are simply just there for Leon the stomp on and to be the reason why all of the conflicts are happening. They aren’t interesting in the slightest.

Lore
Oh, that’s right, they do have lore in the files but since there’s so much action the only place to put files is at the beginning of every chapter which creates this mangled sequence of events.

Strange Characters…

It effortlessly combines heart-pounding action, relentless suspense, and a captivating storyline to create an unforgettable gaming experience. After hearing many things about the RE4 Remake, I went and played the original for old times' sake. There are a few things that spring to mind with this particular entry in the RE series:

a) This was the game that changed the overall feel of the RE series, moving from the slow paced survival horror style the series was originally known for, into a more action oriented experience, for better or worse.
b) The game was an amazing showcase in visuals and sound at the time of release.
c) It features perhaps the most simple story in the series: Save the girl!. Which makes sense since the game focuses on action.
d) It made a more prominent use of QTEs (Quick Time Events), which Capcom had dabbled in previous titles such as Dino Crisis, so you had to pay attention and react fast!
e) It features a huge arsenal of weapons that can be upgraded, this encouraged variety in repeated playthroughs for sure!
f) It was and still is a huge game, packed with lots of content!

Although nowadays it is posible to play a remake version of the game, and added to the fact that I like some of the older games' pacing a lot more (I simply love the PSX versions of 1 and 3, as well as the RE1 Remake for the most part!) this was and still is a true classic title and one of the best videogames ever made, despite being almost twenty years old! Whether its remake reaches that status or not, it is too early to tell. 

Be sure to try it alongside with the incredible RE4 HD Project mod for an amazing update to the game's visuals and a variety of added fixes and QOL enhancements!

The following review is an excerpt from my piece on both Resident Evil 4s. This excerpt covers my full thoughts on the original game.

When I started [i]Resident Evil 4 (2005)[/i], I noticed the controls were weird. Tilting the joystick forward moves Leon forward, and tilting it left and right turns him from side to side. The player can make him do a quick turn by pushing the joystick back while pressing X. (on a PS5 controller). The player has to hold down the left bumper to pull out Leon’s knife and then use the right trigger to swing it. It is not possible to move while aiming a weapon. The controls are clunky. But this control scheme works remarkably well for an action game with roots in survival horror. Enemy encounters are always tense because it is not easy to get away from them. This puts pressure on the player to make decisions and make them quickly. “How much ammo do I have left for each gun? What kind of weapon do I want to use? Should I try to kill this enemy or run past it to conserve ammo? Do I want to heal now and get some health back or wait until I find a red herb and heal fully?” These are all questions I have to ask myself while trying to land shots on enemies, and it keeps the gameplay constantly engaging. Even though[i] Resident Evil 4 (2005)[/i] is the game that took the series away from its survival horror roots, the clunky controls help maintain the previous games’ tension in an action context.

The level design is varied and supports the controls' playstyle. The game has three main areas, the village, the castle, and the island. They all have their own unique set pieces, puzzles, and enemies. The village eases the player into the game as they learn the controls. The enemies are relatively simple. Most of them are plagas-infected villagers. Eventually, Leon will encounter chainsaw-wielding enemies that can kill him with a single attack. Some enemies carry throwing axes or dynamite sticks, but it is nothing the player cannot handle with a bit of planning and perseverance. The castle adds cultists with new weapons, plagas-infected dogs, suits of armor, and wolverine-like beasts that can slice the player in half if they aren’t killed using the weak points on their back. This area is filled with puzzles that use both Leon and Ashley, encouraging experimentation and exploration.

The game’s final area, the island, houses the game’s most action-packed moments. It feels like a warzone. The enemies are much more challenging now, and some have guns. The player has to duel Jack Krauser, another highly trained soldier, to the death. It also is home to an underground lab filled with Regeneradores, the only enemy in the game that legitimately scares me. The whole level builds to one final interaction with Lord Saddler, the game’s main antagonist, and the final test of the player’s skill. The game remains fresh and exciting to play throughout all three of these areas. There are no dull moments in [i]Resident Evil 4 (2005)[/i]. It’s filled with meticulously crafted level design and has a campaign that could only be rivaled by [i]Metal Gear Solid 3: Snake Eater[/i], another masterpiece from that era.

[i]Resident Evil 4's[/i] gameplay is at its best when fighting bosses. The tension felt when fighting regular enemies is not even comparable to the bosses. The bosses test the player’s mastery of the game’s combat. Leon is just one guy with a few guns, and the bosses are giant monsters of bioterrorism. The bosses require the player to get aggressive even though they seem outmatched. Players must land shots on the bosses, often at specific weak points, while dodging melee and projectile attacks, manipulating the environment to their advantage, and managing resources. Every boss is well-tuned to the game’s combat, and they are all thrillingly fun to fight (except for U-3, that boss sucks).

While [i]Resident Evil 4's[/i] gameplay is just about perfect, the story is a little dated. Most of the characters are paper-thin. They have a pretty standard representation of their archetypes. Ashley is a scared and sometimes irrational young woman who acts like a spoiled teenager, fitting for the President’s daughter. Luis is a side-kick Leon can never truly trust, and he’s “great with the ladies” (In 2005, this just meant he would make uncalled-for comments about women’s bodies, apparently) Ada is a femme-fatale foil to Leon. She’s intelligent and charming and can easily manipulate Leon despite her betrayal of him in [i]Resident Evil 2[/i]. The game’s villains are also one-note. Lord Sadler is the mastermind behind the organization, a zealot cult leader who controls just about everything. Ramón Salazar is the clear standout; he’s short, has a silly hat, and antagonizes “Mr. Kennedy” throughout the castle. Bitores Méndez is just… sort of there?

The plot itself is relatively simple. Leon Kennedy, a survivor of the Raccoon City outbreak from [i]Resident Evil 2[/i], now works for the feds and needs to save President Graham’s daughter, Ashley, from a cult in Spain. There is a bit more to it that ties the game into Resident Evil’s greater lore, but most of it is not explored in the game’s original release. What [i]Resident Evil 4's[/i] plot lacks in complexity, it more than makes up for in charm. The game is full of B-movie humor, witty one-liners, and over-the-top scenes. So while I would not nominate the game for “best writing.” It more than gets the job done; the story presentation fits the game perfectly.

After rolling the credits on [i]Resident Evil 4[/i], I was thoroughly impressed. Despite being an eighteen-year-old Nintendo GameCube game, the gameplay had me just as engaged as the modern third-person shooters it inspired, like [i]The Last of Us[/i]. I could easily see why it’s regarded as one of the best games of all time, and I think it is easily one of, if not the best, game on the GameCube.

Resident Evil 4, the iconic survival horror game, continues to captivate gamers even after all these years. As a long-time fan of the franchise, I can confidently say that this installment is an absolute gem. It seamlessly combines heart-pounding action, immersive gameplay, and a gripping storyline that will leave you begging for more.

One of the standout features of Resident Evil 4 is its revolutionary over-the-shoulder camera perspective. This perspective revolutionized the way we experience survival horror games, providing an unparalleled level of immersion. The controls are smooth and responsive, allowing you to navigate the treacherous environments with ease while delivering precise aiming during intense combat encounters.

Speaking of combat, Resident Evil 4 introduces a revamped combat system that elevates the franchise to new heights. Every encounter feels intense, with enemies displaying an uncanny level of intelligence. Their unpredictability keeps you on the edge of your seat, making every encounter a thrilling test of skill and reflexes. The variety of weapons at your disposal is impressive, and each upgrade feels satisfying, empowering you to face increasingly challenging foes.

The game's atmospheric settings are nothing short of breathtaking. From the eerie and foreboding village to the hauntingly atmospheric castles, every location is intricately designed with attention to detail. The graphics, even by today's standards, hold up remarkably well, thanks to the HD enhancements and improved textures of the 2014 PC version.

But it's not just the visuals that shine; the narrative is equally captivating. You assume the role of Leon S. Kennedy, a charismatic protagonist tasked with rescuing the President's daughter from a mysterious cult. The storyline is filled with unexpected twists and turns, keeping you engrossed in the game from start to finish. The campy feel of the story and dozens of memorable snarky lines by Leon are legendary.

Furthermore, the replayability factor in Resident Evil 4 is off the charts. With multiple difficulty levels, unlockable weapons, and bonus content (Assignment Ada, Separate Ways and Mercenaries), there's always a reason to revisit this masterpiece. Especially the addictive Mercenaries mode provides a thrilling challenge outside the main campaign.

In conclusion, Resident Evil 4 is a timeless classic that deserves a spot in every gamer's library. Its seamless blend of heart-stopping action, immersive gameplay, and entertaining narrative will keep you hooked for countless hours. Whether you're a die-hard fan of the franchise or new to the series, this game is a must-play.

This is the real Resident Evil 4. Everything in this game looks and sounds truly authentic. 

The strongest point is the atmosphere that is quite sensational. The audio and visuals are brilliantly calibrated to really immerse you into the areas you're in, whether it is to make you feel safe or fear. The game can be quite straightfoward but with rewarding exploration around. The inventory system is so innovative and easy to handle, you'll see yourself taking your time and liking to sort out your items as you like. The meet-ups and interactions with the merchant to get better equipment truly add up to the adventurous feeling of the game. Every character you meet have their own natural charm, they all fit nicely into the game's story and they also all deliver a great voice acting. Their dialogues are legit, and have not been written according to modern sensitivities like is the case in the remake, characters're all pretty lively in their own way. Cutscenes and enemy introductions are quite spectacular too. You progress thorought the game with a feeling that there could be a showdown at any time, so you can either play safe by dodging enemies or just clear areas to facilitate your exploration. There is an undoubtable tactical aspect in the gameplay that you must experience by yourself. There are also bonus gamemodes that you unlock upon completing the game that lets you play other characters with their own specificities. There are so many more positive things that could be said about the game itself, about the weapons or the balance...

In conclusion, you can tell it's been made with true passion and care for artistical detail to give the player an overall sensation of progression in a hostile rural environment. Everything just blends in together to give you a powerful journey into the many surprising areas of this game that are well thought-out. Resident Evil 4 is very satisfying to play unlike the remake, it hasn't been polluted by the low standards of modern gaming that only thinks in terms of graphical and control improvement to the detriment of the overall "soul" of a game.

[h1] This game is important. [/h1]
Let me just start by saying that I first played RE4 like 3 years ago, so nostalgia doesn't play any part in this review. But I grew up playing RE2 & other early 3d games so I'm used to the concept of tank controls & other old game design quirks. Now this game is great. Amazing, even. A cornerstone in the survival horror genre, and for video games in general. But it's nowhere near perfect.
[b] Let's start with the positives: [/b] the controls are fantastic. Shooting enemies feels responsive, and the combat in general is really satisfying once you have it down. The graphics still look pretty damn good, aside from some low res textures. Sound design is peak, I'm a major audiophile and this game pushes all the right buttons for me: the gun sounds, having each foot make a different sound when you walk, enemies screaming threats in spanish & they distinct sounds to telegraph their attack, etc. Love the setting of rural Spain & the castle, really meshes well with the more macabre elements. Also love that it keeps that same Resident Evil campy cheesiness, while still maintaining a horror atmosphere.
[b] And now for the negatives: [/b] the story is sh!t. You know it, I know it. It really starts to dip near the final act (basically the entire island section). And yeah, RE games haven't exactly been known for having Shakespearean writing, but I feel like this is the one where ♥♥♥♥ just truly goes off the rails. And there are a few parts that still make me cringe to no end, specifically the chopper gunner segment and anytime Krauser is on screen. Ada's character in particular is just really annoying to me. I kept thinking she'd have some sort of tragic backstory or some underlying motive but no, she's just mysterious and aloof for no reason other than it makes her cool and sexy ig? (which it does tbf) And the only gripe I have with the actual gameplay is that some of the bosses are just a slog to get through, makes having a rocket launcher a necessity. Aside from all that, this game still holds up incredibly well, and even if you've played the remake you should really give it a go. 10/10

My opinion on RE4 has changed a lot since its original release in 2004. Back when I first played the GameCube version I hated it, it represented the biggest change in the series away from what I felt was true survival horror: careful item/ammo management and avoiding combat encounters.

I've since replayed the title many times over the years across various platforms (Wii/Ps4/etc) and now finally replayed the Steam version with the added fan project - RE4 HD (which in my opinion is now the definitive way to experience the game, link here - https://www.re4hd.com/)

If you've already played RE4 on other platforms and are wondering if the Steam version is worth it, with the above texture and upgrade pack along with some decent achievements I'd say it's probably worth it for you, especially if you can get it on sale from its usual $20 price tag.

If you have played other RE entries and somehow avoided 4, you need to fix that and buy this game right now. Its absolutely a classic and while I was initially not a fan of the heavier combat focus, it makes for a much more replayable game these days.

While i might sound silly, the item box system is one of the best changes ever made to the series. Instead of just dumping items in boxes scattered around, you carry an attache case and play almost a mini-game of tetris style item stacking to be efficient, which is oddly enjoyable. The merchant system is also cool, showing up at the most helpful times to offer a really deep weapon upgrade system that makes scouring for treasure worth it as you can really deck the guns out with improved power, reload speed, etc.

Puzzles are nowhere near as frequent or interesting as some of the older games, but again that was not the focus and you wont really notice it after some time. The improved environment interaction like blockading doors and knocking over/using ladders makes the encounters deep enough to not really care about puzzles in between

Dealing with ashley can be both fun and annoying. On pro, having to balance fighting off enemies and also ensuring she doesnt get attacked/carried off adds a lot more stress and therefore intensity, but sometimes can feel overwhelming. Luckily you can mitigate this in a lot of areas by having her hide in containers

Controls are as tight as ever, sound and graphics are solid and the gameplay feel is second to none. One of RE4s best assets is the satisfying enemy feedback from weapons and the head-popping effect when landing headshots is still the best. 

Its hard to find too many flaws in this game but if there are any, its got a little too much padding and I think what is ultimately around a 14-16 hour game (for first playthrough anyways) could have easily been half that. The second half of the castle section and the entirety of the Island area is largely uninspired, uninteresting and feel like a slog compared to the excellent pace of the Village areas and first foray into the castle. Some if this might have been the fact I played it twice almost back-to-back as you have to in order to unlock and then beat Pro mode for one of the achievements. Still, towards the end of both playthroughs I really found myself wanting the game to just be over, and even with the updated assets the later areas feel more rushed and much less atmospheric/interesting. 

Very few games can match the atmosphere of RE4s opening but the same can be said for the latter if RE4 itself.

Overall, solid version made better with a fan patch, worth it if you have played this game before and just want to revisit and a no-brainer purchase for survival horror/action fans who have someone not played this game in the 20 years since release

Controls are understandably clunky and the green filter is awful but the combat has an arcadey charm that makes it a fun game to play. Escorting Ashley isn't as annoying as what people said as she always follow the instruction given and is smart enough to crouch down when you shoot. Character interactions are fun to follow, with cringe dialogues (in a good way) which are signature of its era.

In general, the game has definitely shown its ages but it still aged much better than most of its contemporaries.

A MASTERPIECE in Survival Horror. I've beaten this game many many times and each is just as enjoyable as the last. The atmosphere and sound design is second to none. It's incredibly how much music and sound effects add to the experience. The sound of heads popping never gets old. Each enemy encounter is carefully crafted so that it feels tense and scary. Its cast of characters is charming and likable from the start till the end. Leon, after the incidents of Raccoon city is tasked with rescuing Ashley Graham, the President's daughter after she mysteriously disappeared and was found in a small village in Spain. Now much more roughed up, smart and stronger, Leon displays a cool "Action hero" attitude which makes the whole experience enjoyable all the way through. Never one to miss the chance, he will occasionally add a sarcastic and sometimes funny remark to situations. Though disliked by many, I find Ashley to be likable even if a little bland with not many character traits. The gameplay loop while simplistic, never gets old. Shoot, dodge and survive your way through the endless hordes of enemies as you try to uncover the mystery of it all. I truly believe this game DID NOT need a remake because it still holds up remarkably well. If you think tank controls are bad or being stuck in place while shooting is "bad game design" then you clearly don't know what you are talking about. This is definitely a certified classic of gaming. Wether you're into shooters or not, wether you like horror games or not, the original Resident Evil 4 is one of those classics that you should absolutely try for yourself at least once in your life.

The game itself is a blast. The story is pretty alright, it knows how to have a serious tone while still throwing jokes here and there and smacking some impressive situations to keep you excited and engaged.

Voice acting is medium, mainly because of the latin american voices for rural spanish folk, which you'll very easily identify if you ever heard an actual spaniard talking, but it adds up for the humor in some way.

Gameplay is solid. Aside from the tons of details that will add to your playstyle, allowing you to engage your foes and fights in different ways, the variety of tools at your disposal is quite impressive for a game of it's age. You may feel the dated controls being somewhat uncomfortable at first, but you'll easily get used to them in a couple of hours, which won't be near enough to get you through 20% of the game, because you're looking at a pretty long game if you take your time exploring every corner and trying to get everything the game offers you.
You're out for at least a 10 hours run as your first time if you really wanna experience the full game.

All in all, the game is GREAT, even if you're not a Resident Evil fan. It's a great mix between action and horror, with a neat plot which also allows for new players to hop in to it, since the main plot is entirely from scratch in this one. Definitely recommended, even considering the remake is out there.

I'd recommend to look for some tweaking mods online, they're rather easy to find and install. Considering the game's from 2005, you'll probably thank those mods, mainly because they'll fix your typical screen resizing issues along with unstable framerates, but also because they'll tweak and optimize the gameplay a little bit so it feels more comfortable and less clunky.

Why are you still reading this? Go get yourself a copy and try it out, this game's not iconic for no reason!

Resident Evil 4, released in 2005, is a landmark entry in the survival horror genre that pushed boundaries and set new standards for action-packed gameplay, atmospheric storytelling, and intense suspense. Developed and published by Capcom, the game managed to revolutionize the series while retaining the essence of its predecessors.

Graphics (9/10):
Resident Evil 4 showcased impressive visuals for its time, utilizing the "over-the-shoulder" perspective that provided an immersive view of the environments and characters. The character models were detailed, and the design of the rural Spanish village and eerie castle created a foreboding atmosphere. While the graphics may show their age today, they were cutting-edge at the time of release.

Sound (10/10):
The sound design in Resident Evil 4 deserves a perfect score. From the spine-chilling echoes of distant footsteps to the unsettling creaking of doors, every auditory element contributed to the sense of impending dread. The voice acting, while sometimes criticized for its campiness, has become iconic in its own right and adds to the game's charm.

Gameplay (10/10):
The gameplay of Resident Evil 4 was a significant departure from its predecessors, introducing a more action-oriented approach. The "over-the-shoulder" perspective allowed for greater control and precision during gunfights, while the new inventory management system added a strategic layer to combat. The game masterfully balanced tension, exploration, and combat, keeping players on the edge of their seats throughout.

Storytelling (9/10):
The game's narrative was intriguing, centered around protagonist Leon S. Kennedy's mission to rescue the President's daughter from a sinister cult. While the plot occasionally dipped into campy territory, it effectively combined horror and action elements, leading to memorable encounters with iconic enemies like the chainsaw-wielding Ganados. The plot twists and reveals kept players engaged, even if some story elements felt far-fetched.

Overall (10/10):
Resident Evil 4 remains a cornerstone of gaming history, garnering acclaim for its innovative gameplay, atmospheric presentation, and unforgettable moments. Its impact on the survival horror genre and the gaming industry as a whole is immeasurable. Despite the passage of time, it still holds up as a captivating experience that should be played by both series veterans and newcomers alike.

In conclusion, Resident Evil 4's exceptional graphics, immersive sound design, revolutionary gameplay, and compelling storytelling make it deserving of its reputation as one of the greatest video games ever created. With a near-perfect balance of action and horror, it's no wonder this title continues to be celebrated by gamers worldwide.

First of all, I did not have any of the problems described in the other negative reviews related to performance, slowness, or game not booting. Apparently these problems have been patched. In any case they weren’t a problem on my system.

Second, this game was one of my favs on Wii, I beat it in normal and torment modes.

What is my feeling of this version? 
I really think the graphics, music, and atmosphere still hold up. The zombies are pretty sluggish compared to what I remember, but I’m sure it gets tougher as the game advances and I’m pretty sure I could enjoy this game a lot if I simply could operate Leon Kennedy.

What makes it impossible to operate Leon Kennedy?
-> No, it’s not the fact that you cannot fire and move at the same time.

-> On the controller aiming is quite jittery, but I suppose it probably could be corrected by fiddling with the controller adjustments in Steam, since aiming with the mouse is smooth.

-> The real dealbreaker for me is the fact that you have to move and rotate view using only one single stick. Said differently, there is no strafing and the right stick does not allow to change the direction (instead the right stick makes a C-turn, see below). I guess when I was younger I just played and adapted, but still, I kind of remember the impression it gives of always running heads down into walls constantly.
If you have play any more recent games like RE2R, or Revelations 2 where you move and rotate with 2 sticks, it feels extremely uncomfortable, it’s impossible to see say what’s just right behind a wall without walking an awkward circle around it (or using C-turn). It gives me a slight motion sickness.

Why C-turn is not an answer: when using C-turn, Leon gives a glance in the direction of the right stick. Fifteen years ago, this was a great feature. You can C-turn and aim, thus shooting in one direction that would have normally been impossible  without actually rotating your full body in that direction (which would require at least 2 full seconds since you can’t just rotate on your feet). While this was cool as a way to compensate the problem of not being able to rotate, it now feels just unnatural and clumsy.
Moreover, the C-turn is almost fixed-length, although it seems like you can control is sligthly (again maybe this is problem of sensibility/dynamics of the right stick and could be corrected in the Steam options, but I can already guess that it will be a real pain of trial and error to fix).
Finally, the C-turn gives a big camera movement, so it adds plenty of motion sickness to the already existing motion sickness.

It’s possible that the C-turn was better on the Wii, and thus compensated better the absence of rotation, but I can’t be sure.

Anyways, i will just wait a few years for the price of the remake to drop.
In the meantime, I’ll blow the dust on Revelations 1, Revelations 2, RE1R and RE2R.

Resident Evil 4 revolutionised 3rd person survival horror when it released on the GameCube back in 2005 and went on to influence titles such as Dead Space whilst revitalising its own stuttering series.

It did this by moving from a fixed camera to one that floats behind the player's shoulder. This made the combat much more exciting and dynamic, increasing the scope of the arena and improving player mobility. Enemy AI that could dodge and behave unpredictability as well as the ability to shoot enemy projectiles out of the air made the combat a joy to play, with this new perspective putting you right in the action. The action is also really well paced with peaks of intensity bookended by calmer sections and boss fights.

The gameplay has held up really well although the inability to fully rotate the camera does restrict visibility somewhat and the quick time events during cut scenes are something I didn't particularly like when I first played RE4 in 2008. I don't mind the QTEs that occur during gameplay as much because they tend to be used to avoid enemy attacks as there is no dedicated dodge button. The ledge climb button mashing QTEs can piss off though. Even the parts of the game that involve escorting Ashley are rarely frustrating as you can order her to hold back or to hide in a bin. In fact, many parts of the game where you have to watch out for Ashley just add to the chaotic, exhilarating nature of the combat.

A lot of the tension and fear in this horror game comes from the peaks in the action, as you barely hold off hordes of villagers with your rapidly depleting supplies of health and ammo. Highlights for me are the opening village assault, the defense in the cabin with NPC Luis and the horde of cultists that attack you and Ashley in a large castle room. Then there are the relentless and seemingly indestructible Regenerador's who embody the feelings of panicky ♥♥♥♥♥♥-ness I felt while playing the game.

RE4 also comes across as fairly self aware when it comes to the games story and characters, embracing the camp and silliness inherent in a series that usually takes itself so seriously. Resident Evil is a series known for its bad dialogue and RE4 embraces this, with ladder hating Leon in particular -in this game a 12 year old boy's idea of a 'bad ass'- delivering his daft lines earnestly, with a mostly straight face and just the right amount of sarcasm. Squeaky voiced midget Salazar is another highlight and the moments when the villains take over your walky-talky are wonderfully camp with over the top villainy. Not to mention the cockney pirate merchant.

The plot itself is your usual RE fair; there's an evil group bent on world domination by way of a deadly virus. But RE4 shakes things to here too by moving away from Umbrella, the T-virus, zombies and the USA, to a religious cult, parasites, crazed villagers and "Europe". The exact setting is unclear but the parasite hosting villagers speak in some sort of Spanish, so chances are its Spain. A very rural, backwards Spain by all accounts but it's certainly a nice change of setting and vibe. There's also the presidents daughter to rescue, so just another day for our glossy haired, roundhouse kicking hero.

Despite all the the tongue in cheek elements the game still has loads of atmosphere with its grainy graphical style and rustic visual design. There are creepy forests, ramshackle villages, a misty lake, crumbling ruins, gloomy castles, grim concrete fortresses and clinical, claustrophobic labs. Lots of grim visual touches too; the villagers 19th century clothing is blood spattered and filthy as are their homes. There's general decay and mess in the villages which is contrasted nicely by the cleaner, more ordered areas in the castle. It appears that classicism has finally come to Resident Evil but it also shows how the leaders of the cult are more in control of their parasite than the mindless villagers. There's also some great body horror as hosts become infested with parasitic appendages, heads and limbs explode and mangled flesh glistens.

The sound design is also fantastic, from the kaw of crows to the moans and chatter of enemies, their screeches and screams when they spot you and the slow, monotonous chanting of the priests. All this audio adds to the atmosphere and in practical terms it helps you locate enemies when the camera isn't helping, allowing you to swivel and face incoming foes when you hear running footsteps or groans and squelches fading in. The guns are also suitably loud and meaty sounding as bullets thud into body parts. Ashley yelling "Leon!" constantly whilst often helpful can get annoying, but kudos to the audio of the oozing, twitchy Regenerador's, making them all the more frightening.

So if all that hasn't made it clear, I love Resident Evil 4 and think it's well worth playing, even with a PC port that's far from perfect. It's constantly surprising you and while there are a few sections of the game that haven't held up as well, or are frustrating (I'm not a huge fan of the truck section or the U3 mini boss), it's mostly great, a true survival horror that's creative, tense, horrifying, entertaining, silly and utterly charming*.

* While I haven't played the remake I'm a little worried that some of this charm and campy fun might be missing from it. It looks to be back to that dark and serious Resident Evil which to me isn't the RE4 I love. I did thoroughly enjoy the RE2Make though so will still be checking it out.

Resident Evil 4 revolutionised 3rd person survival horror when it released on the GameCube back in 2005 and went on to influence titles such as Dead Space whilst revitalising its own stuttering series. 

It did this by moving from a fixed camera to one that floats behind the player's shoulder. This made the combat much more exciting and dynamic, increasing the scope of the arena and improving player mobility. Enemy ai that could dodge and behave unpredictability as well as the ability to shoot enemy projectiles out of the air made the combat a joy to play, with this new perspective putting you right in the action. The action is also really well paced with peaks of intensity bookended by calmer sections and boss fights.

The gameplay has held up really well although the inability to fully rotate the camera does restrict visibility somewhat and the quick time events during cut scenes are something I didn't particularly like when I first played RE4 in 2005. I don't mind the QTEs that occur during gameplay as much because they tend to be used to avoid enemy attacks as there is no dedicated dodge button. The ledge climb button mashing QTEs can piss off though. Even the parts of the game that involve escorting Ashley are rarely frustrating as you can order her to hold back or to hide in a bin. In fact, many parts of the game where you have to watch out for Ashley just add to the chaotic, exhilarating nature of the combat.

A lot of the tension and fear in this horror game comes from the peaks in the action, as you barely hold off hordes of villagers with your rapidly depleting supplies of health and ammo. Highlights for me are the opening village assault, the defense in the cabin with NPC Luis and the horde of cultists that attack you and Ashley in a large castle room. Then there are the relentless and seemingly indestructible Regenerador's who embody the feelings of panicky ♥♥♥♥♥♥-ness I felt while playing the game.

RE4 also comes across as fairly self aware when it comes to the games story and characters, embracing the camp and silliness inherent in a series that usually takes itself so seriously. Resident Evil is a series known for its bad dialogue and RE4 embraces this, with ladder hating Leon in particular -in this game a 12 year old boy's idea of a 'bad ass'- delivering his daft lines earnestly, with a mostly straight face and just the right amount of sarcasm. Squeaky voiced midget Salazar is another highlight and the moments when the villains take over your walky-talky are wonderfully camp with over the top villainy. Not to mention the cockney pirate merchant.

The plot itself is your usual RE fair; there's an evil group bent on world domination by way of a deadly virus. But RE4 shakes things to here too by moving away from Umbrella, the T-virus, zombies and the USA, to a religious cult, parasites, crazed villagers and "Europe". The exact setting is unclear but the parasite hosting villagers speak in some sort of Spanish, so chances are its Spain. A very rural, backwards Spain by all accounts but it's certainly a nice change of setting and vibe. There's also the presidents daughter to rescue, so just another day for our glossy haired, roundhouse kicking hero.

Despite all the the tongue in cheek elements the game still has loads of atmosphere with its grainy graphical style and rustic visual design. There are creepy forests, ramshackle villages, a misty lake, crumbling ruins, gloomy castles, grim concrete fortresses and clinical, claustrophobic labs. Lots of grim visual touches too; the villagers 19th century clothing is blood spattered and filthy as are their homes. There's general decay and mess in the villages which is contrasted nicely by the cleaner, more ordered areas in the castle. It appears that classicism has finally come to Resident Evil but it also shows how the leaders of the cult are more in control of their parasite than the mindless villagers. There's also some great body horror as hosts become infested with parasitic appendages, heads and limbs explode and mangled flesh glistens.

The sound design is also fantastic, from the kaw of crows to the moans and chatter of enemies, their screeches and screams when they spot you and the slow, monotonous chanting of the priests. All this audio adds to the atmosphere and in practical terms it helps you locate enemies when the camera isn't helping, allowing you to swivel and face incoming foes when you hear running footsteps or groans and squelches fading in. The guns are also suitably loud and meaty sounding as bullets thud into body parts. Ashley yelling "Leon!" constantly whilst often helpful can get annoying, but kudos to the audio of the oozing, twitchy Regenerador's, making them all the more frightening.

So if all that hasn't made it clear, I love Resident Evil 4 and think it's well worth playing, even with a PC port that's far from perfect. It's constantly surprising you and while there are a few sections of the game that haven't held up as well, or are frustrating (I'm not a huge fan of the truck section or the U3 mini boss), it's mostly great, a true survival horror that's creative, tense, horrifying, entertaining, silly and utterly charming*.

RE4 is a game you either love or you don't. The latter applies to me. Although objectively I can see that this game is good, I unfortunately have to label it as not good. Why is that? Well, first of all, Since this game presents itself as a Resident Evil game, I also have to rate and judge it as a RE game. And in my opinion this is not a RE game. #1 It has absolutely nothing to do with Raccoon City or any of its events or aftermath. #2 It has nothing to do with S.T.A.R.S at all. #3 It has nothing (or not enough) to do with Umbrella. #4 The puzzles are laughably simple and remind me of the Duke Nukem games (get the red keycard here and find the door that matches it). #5 The connections this game tries to make to the stories of the past are rather far-fetched and above all superfluous. In addition, they are anything but interesting and/or an enrichment to the overall storyline. #6 The music is a completely different experience than in the previous parts, and left no memories or feelings on me. #7 The story (rescuing the president's daughter) is for me just as simplistic as the Super Mario Bros storyline, save the princess from the castle. And is therefore rather RE unworthy. #8 I personally think the controls are terrible and are completely different from the originals. #9 Organizing your item box is an unnecessary activity that disrupts the experience. And unlike the previous parts, they feel more like a burden than a usefull addition. #10 The treasure chests you find and the items enemies drop in the game make this game look and feel like an arcade shooting gallery. And that leaves a bad taste in my mouth. It makes the franchise ridiculous. #11 The merchant also does not belong in a RE game, and also gives me the feeling of a shooting gallery or a casino. I would have been fine with all of this in an additional mode like mercenaries, but not in the original storyline. #12 The one-sided color palette makes this whole game boring and above all unattractive. #13 the enemies are non iconic, and they have left no impression on me. #14 Leon is an uninteresting character who should have made way for a better well-known character who does have some charisma, such as Criss Redfield Or Barry Burton. #15 This game has too many ridiculous fight scenes that are more reminiscent of a japanese anime than a RE game. And so, little remains of the franchise's extremely Western face. #16 Ramon Salazar was a ridiculous character who doesn't belong in a RE game. 

I could have been fine with all of this, if this game had stood on its own and hadn't carried the name Resident Evil on it. In which, incidentally, all references to that franchise were omitted. Had this been the case, I might have even been full of praise for this game. 

Objectively, this is not a bad game at all. But you have to ask yourself as a developer.. If you think everything has to be different than you did in the original games, then why do you want to make another Resident Evil game anyway?? Just make something really different and leave the original franchise alone. 

Because I don't want to kick this game completely into the ground, I will therefore also drop two reviews here.

As an objective game:
9/10

As a Resident Evil game:
3.5/10

It's a harsh judgement. But in my opinion it is the naked truth.

Reviewing this game in 2023 means answering the question "Why should you get this over the remake?" 

Here are my 23 answers to this question:

1) This is the best Resident Evil of them all. This masterpiece by Shinji Mikami was revolutional at the time and influenced the direction for Capcom for decades to come - every RE game after that is in some way a derivative of this one.

2) This is the best place to start. If you'd like to get acquainted with the classic RE hits, but couldn't possibly stomach the fixed camera angles from the PS1-era, this one is for you.

3) It aged like fine wine with all the care from the community. Download RE tweaks to fix some bugs and the HD mod to update graphics - and you essentially get a modern game, not to mention several times cheaper.

4) Combat is tactical and consistent. Every shot makes the enemy stagger, knee shots slow them down, headshots open them up for melee attacks. Unlike the remake's random-based combat, combat in the original is responsive, predictable and fun.

5) Gunplay is designed for an action focused game. Every gun comes with a laser sight out of the box, making aiming easy and bullets going where you want them to. Submachine gun has a mild spread and manageable recoil, acknowledging the fact it fires 9mm bullets, while one from the remake clearly fires .50 cal. 

6) Movement is fast and fluid compared to the remake. This shouldn't be a thing, given the tank controls and inability to move and shoot, but here we are.

7) The difficulty is fair. Enemies on Professional hit hard - but so do you. Highest difficulty is balanced around your skill and not around you having an infinite rocket launcher, like it became customary for Capcom's recent remakes.

8) Every weapon is viable. There is no crafting, so you don't need to dedicate space in your inventory for crafting materials, furthermore you don't need to choose between a pistol/shotgun/magnum or rifle/smg based on resources they use - just use what you want and the game will adapt.

9) There is no durability on your knife and body armor. The only purpose of this mechanics in the remake is an additional money sink.

10) Rocket launcher does not cost the annual US defense budget - offering you an option to get through a particularly obnoxious boss should you need it.

11) There is no predatory monetization here. You get all additional content with your purchase - some of which the remake offers as DLC, and some that it doesn't feature at all. Likewise, there are no pay to win microtransactions here - no cheat items, balance breaking overpowered weapons on sale et cetera.

12) There are no speedruns here - you get all unlockables by simply completing the game on all its difficulties as well as the additional content. 

13) This is a self-aware B movie. The game acknowledges the fact you can't be scared with a machine gun and does not try to be a horror. It isn't overly serious or pretentious. It's full of silly jokes, one liners and goofy features.

14) This game constantly keeps you entertained with its wide array of unique setpieces, like running away from a giant boulder - meanwhile the remake is a tedious exercise in repetition: shoot the medallions - 5 times; kill the rats - 3 times; restore the power puzzle - 3 times.

15) There is more choice and player's agency - to escape the village you can choose to fight Bella sisters or El Gigante, or even both if you'd like the loot.

16) There are more areas and rooms to explore - cut in the remake with nothing to replace them with.

17) There are more weapons - throwing an incendiary grenade to insta-kill a dozen crows for massive loot? Homing mines? A laser beam? Yes please!

18) There is more attention to the story here and much more notes and dialogs in general - with the focus on the plot rather than meaningless trivia like Luis' journal or Leon's PTSD. 

19) The characters and their motivations are much better presented here. For example, Saddler is an over-arching presence throughout the whole game and comes across as a pragmatic criminal mastermind rather than a mindless religious fanatic.

20) This game is based - it was made in the day and age when sexualizing females was the norm and fan service was commonplace. Leon flirts with the ladies, and they flirt back. Ada wears her iconic femme fatale red dress. Ashley wears an actual skirt, which you can actually look up and see actual panties. Luis references Ashley's "ballistics". Ashley is a damsel-in-distress rather than a "strong female character", and offers Leon "overtime" for the rescue.

21) Voice acting is great here - it was made before they started cutting costs by hiring non-union talent. Every character brought to life sounds distinct and memorable.

22) Design decisions are meaningful - for example, you meet the dog during the first 5 minutes, and the encounter serves as an introduction to the concept of traps. In the remake, you just randomly meet the dog some 30 minutes in, the encouter is out of context now and is easily missable. 

23) The level of interacting with the enviroinment - you could destroy doors in 2005, which is no longer possible in 2023.

[h1]A Great Game That Should Have Never Been Resident Evil.[/h1]


After nearly twenty years since playing it at release on the Gamecube, I return to [i]Resident Evil 4[/i] with this port.  The game almost entirely holds up, with my opinion of it being mostly the same: a great game with some nagging flaws, the primary one being that it should've never been [i]Resident Evil[/i].

RE4 is a great Action/Adventure game, and excelled on the Gamecube where it was designed with the limitations of its controller in mind.  It transfers pretty well to mouse and keyboard, with an obvious drop in difficulty.

However, it is no Survival Horror game, as the core series had been up to that point.  No sense of terror, no fear, no real inventory management, no needing to pick-and-choose your battles to conserve ammunition - just kill all enemies, advance to next area.  The tone is also vastly different, getting pretty goofy in story, characters, and scenarios.

All of this works well in its own game, but poorly as [i]Resident Evil[/i].  This should've been an original game (like the earliest development version turned into [i]Devil May Cry[/i]), or a side-game, like [i]Survivor[/i] or [i]Dead Aim[/i].

For the flaws outside of being placed in the wrong series, the most glaring - from 2005 and today - are the Quick-Time Events.  RE4 is another great showing that only the Yakuza Team should be doing QTEs in games.  The QTEs in RE4 range from pointless to frustrating, with little in-between that is actually interesting.  Aside from that, the aiming can still feel overly stiff, and getting insta-killed by an enemy because you're stuck in a reloading animation is always irritating.  Thankfully, the rest of the game is so well done these are just some dark spots on a real gem.

So if you want a great and rather unique Action/Adventure game, [i]Resident Evil 4[/i] is definitely worthwhile.  If you want an actual Survival Horror game, the HD port of the remake of the original [i]Resident Evil[/i] game is on Steam, and arguably the best entry in the series.

No doubt this game is recommended. Its one of the best titles in the Resident Evil series, has legions of loyal fans, and is a nostalgia bomb that just blew a ton of money into Capcom's pockets.  At the time of writing this, Capcom just released their remake and to celebrate I thought I'd take a trip down memory lane with the original. 

First lets get a few things out of the way:

1. Download the HD modpack. It makes Capcom's own attempt at a remaster look incredibly terrible. The insane amount of professional work done by the small modding team makes the game look incredible. So good it makes this game look acceptable as a last gen title, instead of a remaster from 2 gens ago. I cannot sing enough praises to the makers of this mod...simply incredible.

2. Shame on Capcom for totally looking like a bunch of fools. A 2 person team made your lazy port look disgusting.

With that out of the way...if you're a resident evil fan from the beginning, you know this title was kindof a shocker. WTF happened to umbrella? Whats up with this parasite crap? Leon is Rambo now? Over the shoulder camera angles? Did I honestly buy a Game Cube?  

All these were honest questions for an age where we were locked into locked camera angles and stiff gameplay. Resident Evil 4 delivered us from all that but it wasn't without a cost. This game is Survival Action, not Survival horror. If you're looking for the scaries then wait for the remake to go on sale or play the remakes of 1,2,3 or 7 and Village. Don't touch 0. Pretend it doesn't exist. Anyways, despite this sudden departure from slow moving exploration in a survival horror atmospheric setting, we now get intense action in a survival horror setting with horrible one liners in the best way possible. 

I'm serious, the voice acting should be cringe but dang it, we know it and we love it. Ashley is as annoying as ever. Rambo-Leon watched Cobra, True Lies, and Terminator too many times, and he's got the superhuman acrobatics to back it up. A 20 year old mini me played by a 70 year old man is threatening the world and panty shots from a 12 year old playing a college girl was acceptable because Japan be Japan. You might think I'm ranting here but this game is just a blast back to a different time. Its weird thinking about it now that I've entered my middle ages but here I am. Looking back on a great game and thinking you should too.

Buy it when it goes on sale, mod the hell out of it, and enjoy a trip back to a different time.

Resident Evil 4 is one of the greatest video game experiences I have ever had the pleasure of playing! For years I have heard people describe this as one of if not the "BEST" game ever made, and sure that did raise some eyebrows as how can a majority of people claim to share the same opinion in this day and age.

However while not ranking as my #1 favorite game of all time, this is definitely up there as this game had me hooked! I started it one night and finished it the next day I legitimately could not put this game down. This game that originally launched as an exclusive for the Gamecube back in 2005 still holds up to this day, and while the remake of it just came out a few weeks ago at the time of writing this, I feel like it still can stand on its own as its own experience. 

The control scheme being a little bit clunky at times wasn't a negative for me as it played fine once I got used to it, it was just a bit foreign at the start using half of the controller's triggers and bumpers for guns only and the other half for the knife. The "corny" dialogue in this game is quite charming, as I am a big sucker for cheesy/corny action stories, and while I loved Leon in RE 2 remake I see why this is the game everyone loves him from the most. I am excited to play the remake in the near future to see how it compares but man was this game phenomenal all the way to the end! 

Please if you haven't already or if you plan to only play the remake I highly suggest you play the original as this game is worth every penny!

This is one of the few games I've bought more than once. I first bought it for the PS2 back in the 2000s. Good stuff. My favorite RE by far. Bought it again for the PS3 in the early 2010s. I appreciated being able to play it again in widescreen and without the bitcrushed visuals and audio. Bought it a third time on Steam back during the Covid lockdowns. I enjoyed being able to blast Ganados in 60 FPS. Recently reinstalled it since a remake came out. I'm sure the remake is a masterpiece too, but this RE4 redefined both the series and video games in general. Not as intense as Capcom's own Devil May Cry, but easier to learn than DMC, and still more intense than nearly other action game of its era.

Some people say this isn't "real" survival horror. I disagree. Nothing is more horrifying than the words, "Not enough cash, Stranger."

A few other notes: Blacktail > Red9 (but that's just my personal preference), Ashley isn't annoying, I think the B movie nature of the script works in the game's favor, Krauser is delightfully OP in Mercenaries, grenades are your best friends, and learn to conserve ammo if you hope to beat Professional mode.

The base game is great outside the movement. However, it has some additional issues if you are playing the original un-modded version. Mouse movement is rough, using the A & D keys to turn stinks hard. Some of the enemies don't mesh well with the slow movement, inability to dodge, pushed up camera FOV, and camera resetting each time you aim (IE, dogs and bugs). All this is remedied (mostly) with the tweaks mod that allows for changing the FOV and movement controls. Using the mouse to look around is sooooooo much better than the original. What do you know, its nice to be able to look around and see if someone is creeping on you. Especially because the sound design on the game isn't the greatest. Unlike games like B4B, where you can hear every enemy approaching by sound only, this game enemies creep up almost silently. It's something I never noticed before I played on PC, because on PS I was generally playing through speakers and not headphones. 

Anyway, some enemies take way too many shots still and the first playthrough kind of sucks because you are forced to use crappy weapons or waste money upgrading them to only sell them later. Wish the dealer sold more items and didn't hold back. It's only relevant on the first playthough though. 

The mod though, helps incredibly. It helps to make even the first playthrough fun (usually it is a bit of a slog because you literally have nothing and the stuff available to you stinks).  It's just annoying having to shoot an enemy 10 times in the face and they are still walking around (professional mode). I like shooting guys, not really into the kicking or knifing portion of the game.  Also, should have had an option to buy ammo from the dealer. 

Anyway, the game if released as only what you get from Steam, I don't think it is good, and it all comes down to the movement. However, with the tweak mod, it makes the game everything I thought I was getting when I bought this on PC.  I can deal with jank but at some point if moving around isn't fun, I can't stand the game.  This is one game (base game unmodded) that fits that mold. Walking around, or simply looking around sucks. With the mod, it makes it all better. 

Last thing, the boss fights are pretty lame in general. I hate being the slowest person on the battlefield, and I hate having quick-time events breaking up the shooting.  You get either/or/or both in each instance. 

So good job to whoever made that mod. It took me from never wanting to touch the game on PC, to actively finishing everything.  I can't stress enough how much movement needs to be good in a game for me to enjoy it.  

Looking back, I used to think RE4 was my favorite RE game, but I actually think because the movement is so bad that it's actually 3rd now. I have to decide if I like RE revelations 2 or RE5 better.  RE Revelations 2 has my favorite game mode of all time, but the story is kinda not fun to play though, and gunplay is tight whereas RE5 is great except for the 2 player thing, unless you have 2 people playing.   (speaking purely as if you bought the game from steam and started playing, no modding...with mods RE4 would probably still be at the top).
