The original Resident Evil 4 was a staple of my childhood, and with the remake coming out a couple days back I decided to revisit the PC port on Steam, and I was not disappointed. The story, mechanics and gameplay has all aged really well. The HD graphics for the steam version makes the game look very good for originally coming out in 2005. I had no delay or performance issues playing the game. 

You are unable to move when shooting, which usually would be a complaint but this game was clearly designed for that in mind. It never felt unfair, nor did I feel like I needed to move when shooting.

My only complaints with these game is that the bosses are too easy, and a lot of them can be killed either instantly or very fast with a magnum or rocket launcher. I felt like the minibosses were harder than the actual chapter bosses at times. The increased FPS (30 boosted to 60) also messed up the tick rate so a lot of the quick time events are bugged out. It's not uncommon to fail a button mash because of this, and my friend and I both had to replay the statue section several times.

This aside, this is a great game and a fantastic port!

With a series as hit or miss as Resident Evil, I think this is the only game in the series to be as good as the original. While it leans more towards being an action based third-person shooter, it keeps the campy horror atmosphere of the series, and is pretty much a gold standard for the action horror genre.

This version of Re4 is easily the best version, as it not only has the best graphics out of all of the ports, it also keeps all of the bonus features of each version, and with mods there are even more QOL improvements and additions (I'd highly recommend re4 tweaks). There is easily 100+ hours of content here, with not only the highly replayable story which will take ~10-15 hours to complete, but 5 bonus modes with unlockables to obtain. 

Overall, Resident Evil 4 doesn't continue the survival horror legacy of the previous entries in the series, but instead crafted a new unique experience that attempted to appeal to a wider audience, and succeeded. I wouldn't recommend it as a survival horror experience, but rather as a one of a kind action horror game that even future RE titles would never surpass.

Resident Evil 4 is a game that has stood the test of time, but the same cannot be said of the PC ports.

The original PC port done by Sourcenext was so bad it didn't even have mouse support, so a separate studio - QLOC - was commissioned by Capcom to make this version. While this port is a great deal better (mouse+keyboard support, no additional bugs/crashes, all post-launch content, the option to play at 30 or 60 fps), it doesn't have the sort of graphical settings you would reasonably expect from most games on PC.

So what sets this version apart from the other releases? Resident Evil 4 has been ported to basically every other console by now, so why would you buy [i] this [/i] one? Well, because this one is on PC, there's mods to sweeten the deal.

"re4_tweaks" is a must-have modification for this game. It offers a variety of toggleable options (accessible through an in-game control panel) that allow you to customize the game to your liking, ranging from small cosmetic options (e.g. disabling film grain, changing your camera's FOV) to huge game-changing modifications (changing your QTE keys, automating button mash QTEs, making Leon turn with the mouse.) It can even improve performance on low-end systems by swapping out RE4's archaic frame limiter with a modern, more streamlined implementation. re4_tweaks is to Resident Evil 4 what dsfix was to Dark Souls: Prepare to Die Edition.

The other major modification worth mentioning is the Resident Evil 4 HD Project, but my laptop isn't powerful enough to run it. Suffice it to say that Albert Marin and Cris Morales put a lot of blood, sweat and tears into it over roughly eight years of development, so if you have a computer that isn't a decade old it's worth checking out.

First of all, I already purchased the RE4 Remake, but after playing the Demo I'm starting to doubt whether or not is it going to be as good as the original, but even if it ends up failing at that, we still have the original. Also yes, I'm a big Resident Evil fan, and I have a lot of nostalgia for both og Re2 and Re4. With that out of the way my review is the following:

The Original RE4 is my 3rd Most Favorite Game of all time. Along side Majora's Mask and Metroid Prime. So it's safe to say that the game is pretty good. The game has a cheesy plot with a badass but goofy protagonist and the game's pacing it's always cycling between action and silent set pieces to keep things fresh.

The mechanics of the og Re4 are still amazingly tight even to this day, shooting certain parts of the enemies to open them to a special attack to inflict area of effect damage, or cause the enemies to be pushed backwards has always, and will always be satisfying. The shooting is great, the weapons are powerful and the sound design is superb. 

My only real complaint with the gameplay is the tank controls, but I will talk about that in a bit.

Now, the GameCube version was good, but the Steam Version with the HD Texture Pack Project made by literally Chris and Albert (No pun intended) is pure perfection. 

The Texture Pack not only makes the game stunning to look at, but also includes some amazing tweaks such an FOV Slider, Better Mouse Camera and Mouse Character Movement (YES, it allows You to control Leon's movement with the mouse) 

So basically the Re4 Texture Pack, gets rid of the tank controls and allows You to control Leon's Movement Camera with the Mouse, which to be honest makes the game way easier, but much much more enjoyable to play.

Also, this Leon's Personality and One liners is something that the Remake will not be able to fully replicate. They already ruined the "Where is everyone, bingo?" Scene by making it three times longer, and by changing the scenery/cinematography making it look worse than the original.

So yes, in short, I love Re4. It's Capcom's Skyrim at this point, since they keep re-releasing the game every few years. But how could they not? Re4 is just that good, and even if they mess the Remake up, the Original game still holds up great to this day.

[b]Resident Evil 4[/b] is an all-time classic, and oh my god, I love it with all my heart. Back when I first played it, I didn’t really have a game I could call my favorite — this was basically the start of me being a gamer, haha. I had played a few games before, and they were cool, but nothing crazy. This one, though? It’s mesmerizing in almost every way, from its presentation to its gameplay. It’s one of those games I can always come back to, on any version or console, and it still hits.

The atmosphere is incredible. My favorite part is still the village section with its thick, tense vibe, but the rest of the game is amazing too. And the story? [i]Resident Evil[/i] has never been about story first and foremost, but it was still grounded enough to work. [b]RE4[/b] is kinda wacky and a little cringe in a good way. Leon says some funny ♥♥♥♥, which is great — at least it’s not as cringey as [i]Code Veronica[/i]. And the visuals? The GameCube really flexed its capabilities back then, and this 2014 port looks really good.

Gameplay is just phenomenal. Gunplay feels tight and satisfying, all the weapons feel great, and the animations and sound design are top-notch — seriously, just watch the Red9 reload animation. Combat is a standout too. Enemies here are much smarter than in previous games, which makes sense — these aren’t exactly zombies. They react to your movements, and their bodies respond to every shot. Shoot them in the hand and a weapon will fall, or a bomb in their hand might blow up. Shoot their knee, and you can perform a suplex, or kick them in the face — you name it. You can also cut enemies with your knife, adding another layer to the gameplay. Looting different areas, selling treasures, and upgrading your gear with the Merchant were a fresh twist for the series.

At some point in the story, we’re rescuing Ashley, which means you’ll have to escort her for part of the game. This adds another layer to the gameplay. Yeah, she might scream if she’s carried by enemies because she can die and you need to heal her, and she does some stupid stuff in the story sometimes, but I personally never had a problem with her — at least gameplay-wise, she never bothered me.

QTEs show up occasionally, and honestly, they’re fun. There aren’t a ton, and some are a little ridiculous (looking at you, Salazar Statue), but they break up the action in a cool way without feeling overwhelming.

Boss fights are another highlight. They’re better than anything the series had done up to this point. I mean, in classic survival horror, I was totally fine just standing there and shooting bosses because they were cool — but [b]RE4[/b] takes it to another level. The Krauser QTE fights, for example, are crazy and insanely satisfying.

Level design and pacing are fantastic. Yeah, the game is linear, but it’s linear in a smart way — every zone, every encounter feels carefully crafted so you’re never bored or overwhelmed. Every location has perfect pacing, kind of like the original [i]RE2[/i] — nothing overstays its welcome, and every part of the game just flows perfectly. There are puzzles, which are… kinda meh sometimes, and yeah, a lot of people hate the island section (myself included back in the day), but it grew on me. (The turret section on Professional mode was still ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥, though.)

[b]RE4[/b] isn’t really a game about exploration and survival like the old titles. It leans more into action now — yeah, it still has survival elements, but the focus has shifted. Enemies drop loot, which encourages you to fight them instead of just avoiding them, but unlike later games like [i]RE5[/i] or [i]RE6[/i], which completely forgot what it means to be a [i]Resident Evil[/i] game, [b]RE4[/b] balances this quite well. It still has that classic [i]Resident Evil[/i] crunch and tension, just in a more action-oriented package.

The inventory system is amazing too. It’s creative and super satisfying that you can rearrange items however you want — it’s basically a little mini-game on its own, which makes managing resources way more fun.

All in all, [b]Resident Evil 4[/b] is a masterpiece. It’s fun, tense, sometimes ridiculous, but always a joy to play. It’s the perfect mix of action, horror, and charm, and honestly, it’s a game I’ll never stop coming back to.

Resident Evil 4 is a game that holds more sentimental value to me than any other. This is the game that got me into gaming as a whole, into survival horror, into this series. Over the course of the many ports and various versions of this game, I have probably sank well over a thousand hours into Resident Evil 4. 

This was the first game of the series to play without fixed camera angles, and introduce more action and campy dialogue, whether that's your cup of tea or not, this game does a pretty okay job combining these with a little horror, but for the most part, this is a glorified action game. As a Resident Evil game, it's actually one of the longer entries in the series. There are various bosses to fight and weapons to collect.

I think this is a must play for anyone that is interested in the genre or the series, so I won't go into too much depth with my review, but at the time of me writing this, a full remake of this game comes out in about ten days. Whether or not you believe this game needs one or not doesn't matter to me, but I think we should all come together to agree that this game fully *deserves* one, and with all the many hours I have spent playing the original, I just don't find much joy in it anymore, so the upcoming remake is sure to reignite the spark I once had with it.

Only the games available on steam. I do not have rose-tinted nostalgia sunglasses on so it is getting my unbiased opinion from my POV.

The Good: 
Really lengthy game and incredibly well paced, you won't get bored. Incredible price for all the game-play you get and replay-ability. Gameplay is a mixed bag, I had fun when I got use to it but it was a very hard learning curve to me, it was about chapter 3-2 till I got use to it. It was pretty fun taking crowds of villagers and kick flipping their as*ess. Enemies didn't feel boring and felt like JUST the right amount of enemies and the difficulty. Overall a very fun game when you get use to it. Gotta give credit where credit is due, I know I probably can't say much good since I've played many games just like it but I know this was basically the first that set the standard for all those other games. So i admire this game a lot for inspiring dead space, love me some dead space. So it holds a very high praise from me for establishing a gold standard.

The Bad:
The port to PC can suck major doo doo, man... Quick time events really messed me up a lot in this game due to my computer deciding it will be "X, C" and/or my mouse. It screwed with me a lot. basically died at every QTE and went through trial and error till I got it. There seemed to be a bad film grain filter? Depending on what areas I was in, the film grain would become more pronounce and distracting. Good or bad, the boss fights were very easy, get the rocket launcher and become a one-hit wonder lmao. Compared to the previous titles this was a huge jump in gameplay, I was use to the few enemies but they hit hard and the more terror involved rather than action. (I know I won't like 5 & 6 for this) So it was quite the learning curve compared to the other games and I still enjoy the the more horror in the previous titles. Gameplay was fun, story was odd? story is of course there but I wish it was built off a lot more, I want to know more about basically all the characters and want to see them more. I hope the Remake adds more. Also really lacked puzzles, I like my puzzles...

The Ugly:
Words can't describe how annoying I think Ashley is, using the same two lines over and over, she is so whiny. Every time she wines Leon's name, I hope she gets taken away from me.

Conclustion:
Overall I will give it an 8/10, It's very fun to play but not exactly what I want out of a Resident Evil game. I know people would want me to give it a 10/10, but it's just not what I exactly want. If the remake adds a bit more horror, puzzles and more characterization for every character, think I would really enjoy it.

[h1]TLDR: The granddaddy of every single modern third-person shooter, RE4 is an absolute classic that aged like fine wine. It’s fun, the gameplay is nuts and feels oh-so-satisfying. It’s also the Resident Evil that almost killed the series as we knew it. Fact of the matter is, it’s a Resident Evil in name only. If you’re coming from the classic RE games you should “Forget the concept of Survival Horror” as the back of the PAL cover puts it. [/h1]

This version of RE4 is the second PC port and is based on the PS3/X360 HD release. It is far better than the first PC port, but a lot of effects are still missing, there's a few bugs and the textures have been upscaled poorly. To address those issues, you should use the "RE4HD" mod even for a first play through. 

I remember playing the demo at my local game shop and thinking "This is going to be the best RE bar none". Sure, the demo level had atmosphere and felt brutally difficult. That feeling worn out very quickly when I got the full game and beat it in one seating. I expected a Survival Horror. It took me years to truly appreciate it for what it is: the birth of Action Horror. Still… I can’t deny it: it was innovative and I had fun with it back then, and still do to this day because it has something special.

That something special is the gameplay loop: shoot dudes, get ammo to shoot more dudes. Grab a treasure, sell it to the merchant. Get a bigger weapon and kill bigger dudes. Rinse and repeat. It is very repetitive, but the moment-to-moment gameplay has that "hunter/hunted" dichotomy that makes it feel great. It has been done better since, but RE4 is a very specific, early-2000 breed of 3rd person shooter: animations that still feel very satisfying and stylish, corny and often funny dialogue, charismatic lead characters dropping one liners all the time and of course: non-stop action. Hideki Kamiya’s influence can be felt throughout.

With a Remake on the horizon, perhaps you’re thinking about playing the original and yeah, you definitely should! It’s a piece of gaming history that would influence a lot of games that, in turn, influenced many other games. RE4 has a legacy like few games do. If you haven’t played it yet it’ll feel familiar while still being its own thing. RE4 is nuts and should be experienced by anyone - including people like myself who hated it for killing the classic survival horror formula. I’ve made peace with that game since and I can say that it is absolutely worth your time and money. Absolute classic, absolutely recommended!

RE4 did for the third-person shooter what Quake did for the first-person shooter. That being, they both revolutionized the way their respective subgenres looked and felt to play for generations to come. 4 is certainly one of my all-time faves, as of now. 

Funny story, this game was not only the first in the series I played (I first played it in 2021), it was my first exposure to Resident Evil over a decade before that. When I was a kid, my family and I were at a party, and the hosts' eldest son had a Gamecube. The two games I remember being shown off then were Smash Bros. Melee and RE4. The chainsaw death on Leon scared the piss out of me and turned me off of RE and violent games for years. After years of mere exposure effect to RE material, I ended up enjoying RE4 very much, and saw for myself why people loved it.

The story and humor are cheesy, the characters lovable (or despicable) in their own ways, and the gunplay fulfilling across the myriad of arms to choose from and upgrade. Organizing the inventory was a good way to relax in between fights. Escorting Ashley wasn't so bad for me (most of the time— the professional difficulty always makes the escorts more of a schlep). The treasures I could find throughout the game world made the experience one I could enjoy countless times. 

I ended up putting quite a few playthroughs into this PC port, as well as the VR version on the Quest 2. As it stands, the Quest 2 version is my favorite gameplay-wise, and despite it cutting out some of the more perverse dialogue (I can see the reason for these changes, but I found some of the dialogue funny). Aside from that, I originally thought this game doesn't need a remake (1 month away from release as of writing), but can see now how the upcoming new version strives to improve upon and streamline the original's quirks and flaws— I dig this game, it holds up, but it's not perfect. Still, the option to go back to this original game will exist once the remake comes out.

[h1]Resident Evil 4 - A Game Changing Masterpiece[/h1]

So after finishing the clumsy and troublesome Resident Evil 0, I finally got my hands on the next installment in the RE series - the almighty Resident Evil 4. Now, for this game of course I had very high expectations because many RE fans claim that this part is the best one in the series, and also other people that have played only this RE title consider it as one of the best games ever made. Are those claims justified? Damn sure they are.


The developers acknowledged the fact that all previous installments followed the same formula - slower horror survival games with fixed camera and limited action, so they wanted to present something new to their fans and refresh the interest in the series - and surely they did a great job. The gameplay got changed completely, and thus in this RE for the first time the 3rd person camera was implemented. This brought a whole new level to the overall atmosphere. That being the case, the environment was more realistic, because it featured 3D models for the first time.

Gameplay is as fun as it gets, but it can be troublesome at the beginning - at least it was for me. I was so irritated by the fact that I replayed the first entry to the village for like 3 or 4 times. Mostly because I started playing on gamepad (which I used for every previous RE) and it was just so hard for me. Not that it can't be played, but in this RE you can aim precisely for the first time ever and I found that using mouse was so much easier. You can try out both and see for yourself (if you are a console player, you won't have any problems, I'm sure). And also I got owned a couple of times, not knowing that enemies can now throw things at you and that you can't dodge them as easily as in the previous games.

So much new things were carried out in this RE - new inventory format, the ability to collect money and buy weapons, kicking away stunned enemies, not needing a certain item (ink ribbon) to save your game etc. Each of the above proved to be a great asset and something that you would want to have in previous RE titles as you were playing them. 

Another great innovation is the introduction of the quick time events, because they bring the unpredictability to the gameplay. I was caught off-guard many times because they can occur during a cutscene, which I wasn't expecting at all. 

The only thing that I can say is a con for me is that the survival horror and scary ambience were pushed away by much more action-oriented approach. It is not necessarily bad, but it is just what the series was known for a long time. Even with that in mind, the game is still amazing. 

Graphics - it certainly aged well when you consider the fact that the game was released back in 2005. The cutscenes are the best so far, with many different camera angles and very dynamic moments. 

The story - it's typical Resident Evil-like. Cheesy and not so deep with some illogical moments, but hey, if you played the series from the first RE like me, you got used to it and you will enjoy this one as well. This is also the first time that the setting is away from the premises of Umbrella Corporation and you are not fighting any zombies at all, which is also a new thing in addition to a whole new gameplay.

For me, I'd say that Resident Evil 2 (1998) is still the best RE game, because it captures the survival horror segment the best and also had a handful of scary moments, which I really can't say for RE4 because I wasn't scared once during my playthrough, BUT that doesn't take away anything from this game, and it still is a masterpiece. 

This game was so brilliant and influential, it inspired some big titles such as Dead Space, The Last of Us and Bioshock. The 3rd person and the use of the 'over-the-shoulder' camera were revolutionary for the gaming industry. 

Tier list update until I finish all the Resident Evil titles (the main titles):
RE2 (1998) > RE4 > RE (1996) > RE3 (1999) > RE: Code Veronica

[h1]Walking Where I Do Not Belong: The Air of the Forastero[/h1]

I recall a scene from [i]Band of Brothers[/i] in which certain American soldiers felt almost at home. Upon arriving in the Netherlands, they remarked that the people treated them kindly and, moreover, spoke their language — English. Something similar occurs here. In [i]Resident Evil 4[/i], I travel in a car with two Spanish police officers, and they speak my tongue. For a moment, it feels as though I might wander through Spanish lands as if they were my own.

Upon my arrival, choosing without hesitation to proceed alone, the place reveals itself as desolate — submerged in a sylvan landscape where eyes and ears remain unseen, yet ever-present. A local receives me, but I realise at once that I cannot wander as though I were at home. Here, hostility is palpable. There are no folk who would welcome an outsider — especially an intruder who failed to ask leave. Instead of an apology, he attacks me. I was taught to defend myself, and so I continue on my way.

Here, I hold no authority, nor do I come to impose. Yet I witness the hecatomb brewing within the village; many were merely attending to their chores. A villager sights me and cries out “un forastero” — a stranger. I understand the word, but it is the atmosphere that truly strikes me. Perhaps it is because I have trespassed into another’s home. And yet, instead of apology or explanation, the horde known as the Ganados lunges at me, for I am an intruder who does not align with their communal rhythm.

I find myself fascinated by this exposure of voices. I speak in English, while the villagers speak in Spanish. At times, their speech becomes a strange repetition, as if language itself were refusing dialogue. Further on, I meet Luis Sera. This encounter unsettles me. He speaks my tongue; he informs me; yet he is Spanish. He does not merely receive me — he asks something more unsettling: “Who is the outsider?”

The word outsider resonates deeply. It implies one who stands apart, unaccepted, or who distances themselves by choice. What I find most compelling is the aim of the parasite — Las Plagas — within these lands. It seeks a closed unity, and the village becomes its most refined expression. It forges a sequestered community, excluding even Luis Sera, stripping him of belonging. He, too, becomes a stranger — a forastero — because of the plague.

It is clear that the village, in its near-religious purity, pursues an end, as Osmund Saddler declares. Yet his intent is ritualistic when he asks us who the outsider truly is. Luis Sera speaks their tongue, but he resists the cult. The village reveals obedience — but is obedience all I wish to see, as far as my eyes can reach? Without domination, the village might simply remain bound together, imperfect and alive.

Perhaps Saddler seeks to impose a vision of his world. I am drawn to the ambiguity of this place; no explanation is given. Having been healed of a wound, I imagine the parasite in control — yet Saddler is keenly aware of public life. Still, I, Leon, am not exempt from criticism. I am reminded of Eightball in [i]Full Metal Jacket[/i], claiming to bring democracy to Vietnam. Is that truly what is required — there, or here?

Resident Evil 4 dismantles this tension not through cliché, but through two moments of quiet superiority. The first is Luis Sera himself. He recalls what the village once was — tranquil, untainted by grand ambitions. Imperfect, yes; and precisely for that reason, complete. In his memory, it was a happy place. For this, he pays dearly: the outsider is always a threat. He dies.

The second moment is decisive. When I am controlled by Saddler, he strips me of every vestige of power and imposition.

I resist.

Not out of rebellion, nor disbelief in the divine, but in refusal of the forced expulsion the plague seeks to enact — a unity that erases plurality. Biology yearns for a single mass of flesh. Yet the village is saved not by obedience, but by resistance. The struggle shifts when the leader of the plague yields to the presence of the outsider. An outsider to the parasite, perhaps — but not to the village itself. It would be a contradiction for the village to have laboured all along to become a lifeless unity, where all are one.

During my stay, the village remains the place where the notion of the outsider is felt most profoundly. Ritual and heritage may endure, but when a leader seeks absolute power, harmony shatters. It is difference that makes communication possible. Luis Sera is the true peril to the plague, though he is the least of outsiders, guiding us even through his ghastly death. Ashley is a companion. Ada is more an outsider than we are. The rest is obedience.

The terror here is not the village itself — that is merely the air we breathe, the atmosphere that enfolds us — but the terror of the outsider, and of biological unity.

Back to topic, The game is an award winning game from the RE series that manage to make a name of it as some people call it the best game of all time including its own series and after playing the game was only I may tell that they are not lying. Due to its over popularity, the game was released to multiple platform and among those steam manage to be one of it.

[h1]Foreword[/h1]
This game holds a special place in my heart!
It wasn't my first Resident Evil, but it was my favorite nonetheless.
Of course, I've already played RE1 and 2 on the PSx and I liked them a lot.
Code Veronica X also liked me a lot. But RE4 was different. As was customary in the past, I started this game blindly. I expected a typical Resident Evil game and got a masterpiece of the extra class.

[h1]The game[/h1]
Compared to the previous Resident Evil games, the fixed camera angles that were typical up to that point were completely removed. Third person was included in the RE games for the first time. The first big surprise. The game is much more action-packed and has therefore given me even more fun. Unfortunately, the horror aspect suffers. There are only a few passages that are a little creepy. However, the atmosphere of the game is not less good, it is just different. Probably Metal Gear Solid ⅔ also contributed to the fact that I liked this type of game better than the typical RE gameplay.

[h1]The HD version[/h1]
This is an HD remaster from 2014. However, this is not particularly great. Unfortunately, there are bugs here that did not exist in the original. I don't remember which ones exactly, as it has been a few years since I last played it.
In addition, the textures are not high-resolution and even at the time of release, they looked old. But fortunately there is a real HD mod that eliminates all bugs and makes the textures shine in a new glory. [url=https://www.re4hd.com/?page_id=9303] Download HD Project [/url]

[h1]Control[/h1]
Unfortunately, the control was not overhauled and the game feels somewhat outdated due to Leon's stiff movement. But the mod has also been revised. Shooting and moving at the same time is not possible, however. That would change too much and affect the balance. For that reason, I think it's good as it is.

[h1]Conclusion[/h1]
A must for any horror, action and Resident Evil fan. On offer, the game only costs 4.99€ and you can't do anything wrong - I think. The remake is coming soon and it would be interesting to draw a comparison. I'm mega excited about the remake!

Well, it's my favorite game period, so of course I'd recommend it to anyone who appreciates good game design, well-balanced action and corny Evil Dead-level humor. Should you wait for remake instead of playing the original? God no, the modern tendencies will not be able to give you the same experience. And while the remake looks impressive (knife chainsaw parry is something I always needed in life), the beauty of the original in many aspects cannot be replicated with modern technologies. 

What is this beauty, you ask? Well, there are small details which would make zoomers seethe and gaming journalist cry bloody tears. The combat mechanic itself is great in that it doesn't give you too much control over character while at the same time providing you with all the moves you need to kill, stagger and melee your enemies. Any other way it would ruin the balance which tuned-in perfectly for maximum fun (did I say I've played it, like, 20 times on more than 5 platforms?). The other thing is atmosphere which is made using the old-ish baked-in lighting. The colors pop, the simple bloom and fog effects give an eerie vibe and it all feels melancholic, desolate and rather Innsmouth-y. And then there are sounds. The music is great and sound effects for everything, from shooting and hitting the enemies to navigating through menus, feels satisfying as all hell. Oh, and the menus, the interface. You know, I feel really sad seeing the minimalistic interface of the latest RE installments making its way into RE4make. I mean, they all look like the variables of the Last of Us interface, as well as myriad of other games like that. The identity, man, it's being lost as we speak if it hasn't been already.

In order not to mop on the fact that nowadays games lack a certain something, let me instead say that classic games like this are always with us despite any attempts to replace them with remakes. And there are people making them better than ever. Take a look into the Resident Evil 4 HD Project and be sure to play or, most likely, replay RE4 with this mod. The work that was made by this mod's author is of the epic proportions and it makes the game look as good in HD as it looked back in the day on GameCube hooked to a CRT screen.

tl;dr: play the game, enjoy it and probably replay it later.

Resident Evil 4 is a game way ahead of its time, even though it was made in 2005. Unlike its predecessors, a lot of innovations were made in this game and it is still playable even today.
Although the game is a horror game, the action I experienced in this game was indescribable.

Moving camera while moving the character feature was first introduced in Resident Evil 4 if I remember correctly. But although they created a fighting mechanism for the first time with this feature, we can fight very fluently. 

Capcom's investments in motion capture and facial animation have revolutionised the game world. Facial expressions are really marvellous for 2005, and not bad for 2023. Cutscenes are really tremendous. We watch the cutscene like watching a film. Especially when the camera following the knife and stuff in conversations, it's really awesome.

There are also very interesting death scenes in the game. In places where I could pass without dying, sometimes I died on purpose just to see the death animation. It is obvious that they added too many details in the game. For example, if I wasn't an achievement hunter, I wouldn't have seen what happened when I shot into the lake 6 times. Also, Leon's jokes, funny personality and being a very good main character are very nice. 

Some cons are that the game is too brown for some reason lol, and the same sound effect is sometimes heard 35 times. I know I've praised the game too much, but that doesn't make it any different from any other Resident Evil game. Also, the game is from 2005, I can't say you should play the game just because it's so good for its era. Apart from that, it's a very good game and I can't wait to play the remake. First off: get the HD Project mod. It rules.

God this game rules. The gameplay is just satisfying in a way that's a little hard to describe, kind of similar to how Mario games just feel better than many of their competitors. The way you juggle enemies and switch through weapons reminds me of the OG Doom, and the game does a good job of keeping you on the razor's edge of item scarcity, meaning the traditional survival horror feelings (popularized by RE1) are never exactly gone, even if they're diminished in this action-forward direction. This game is nearing 20 years old now and still dominates game design trends (think Gears of War, Dead Space, The Last of Us, etc) because it's just that good.

The story is...weird. Mostly, it's fun in a knowingly cheesy way. Leon spouts off one liners so badly that he comes off as an endearing weirdo, and characters like Salazar and Luis (mostly) are absolute joys to bounce him off of. The thing is, the plot itself is very 'pulpy spy thriller' except its made circa 2005, meaning there's a strong post-9/11 Islamophobia streak to it that sort of comes with the territory. The game's about a religious society trying to destroy America, you travel through sandy ruins, the word "terrorism" is directly invoked, etc. It's not directly Islamophobic, but in trying to go for a stripped-from-the-headlines plot it definitely feels present. The other thing with the game is, Ashley.

Ashley is just bad. She has basically no character beyond screaming for Leon and, at the end to prove how much of a cool boy you are, flirting with Leon. She, a teenager [EDIT nope she's 20! This is apparently a common misconception that I also fell into. This doesn't really affect the rest of this paragraph besides turning my feelings from 'this is very distasteful' to 'this is typically distasteful'. Like the post-9/11 stuff, it's honestly more a reflection of 2005 culture than the game itself], is sexually harassed by the otherwise delightful Luis (and the game itself via a badly named achievement). And, most infamously, she's the subject of a game-long escort mission. That last part actually bothered me the least. Ashley during gameplay quickly fades into the background beyond some strategic decisions to keep her out of a room before combat, which made me feel smart whenever I thought of it. Still, the target demographic of this game is clearly teenage boys, and Ashley is clearly designed with that audience in mind.

Still again, it cannot be overemphasized how good the moment-to-moment combat of this game is. The on-the-fly prioritization of enemies, creating distance, and tracking projectiles make for a wildly engaging gameplay. Decisions are always being made. Also, when the story isn't creeping me out, it's a ton of fun, with dumb lines improbable flips and cool fights. Overall it's a very, VERY strong package. The phrase that keeps coming to my mind is one that over the years has become nothing more than fun trivia: "only for Nintendo GameCube." Though it's been ported to a million systems, RE4 was originally a GameCube exclusive, and it feels like one. It has the classic Nintendo polish you expect from a Zelda or Mario title. RE4's reputation has been tainted somewhat by its sequels, which took the action direction and drove it, I'm told, straight off a cliff. But I think it deserves to be remembered as a minidisk set next to Super Smash Bros. Melee and Metroid Prime, a standalone game that stands by itself as an instance of pure mechanical perfection.

The gameplay, while a little old and awkward feeling at first, becomes something you quickly get used to and start enjoying. There's just the right amount of story in this game to give your actions weight, and it's like you're playing the hammiest, cheesiest 2000s horror movie ever without feeling stupid or like a waste of your time. Resident Evil 4 has the balls to be fun and goofy where every other game wants to be bland and serious. It walks a tightrope act of balancing a bunch of different mechanics and ideas together, yet never once comes close to falling over. Overall, this game is well worth your time and money, especially when it goes on sale for $5 USD.

I played the "original" Resident Evils - 1, 2, 3 and C:V - when I was a kid and young teen, and loved them despite their faults. When I saw pre-and-post-release screens of RE4, and I saw browns and greys and unfamiliar enemies and an OTS camera, I wasn't excited. I was one of [I]those[/I] guys. I liked the fixed-camera perspective; it defined the series' gameplay for me, made RE what it was. I wanted to see them iterate on C:V's approach, where the environments were fully rendered and the cameras - still fixed - could move dynamically. The benefit of the fixed camera lay in its ability to frame environments as a director might, to control the way the player takes them in and engineer tension (for example, if the camera is fixed outside the window, we feel as though we're being watched; if it's close in, we feel claustrophobic). People think of it as "outdated" now, as though it was born from technical limitations and nothing else, but it was a model with thought put into it. It was almost a genre unto itself.

So I sat on RE4 for years, almost on principle. A decade and a half now, in fact. People praised it, called it the peak of the series. It breathed new life into RE as a franchise, and became the model of the series going forward. It inspired copycats by the dozen.

And I don't like it.

I feel bad saying that. I wonder whether I'm still biased by the frustrations I had fifteen years ago, sad that the series abandoned its roots. I likely am. But I tried my very best to go into this with an open mind; I had heard so many good things about it, after all, and I eventually came to love other OTS action survival horror games, with Dead Space even becoming an all-time personal favourite. I enjoy the RE2 Remake, and I was skeptical of that too at first. Perhaps those later games learned from RE4's flaws. Perhaps I just think RE4 aged poorly.

The camera is too tight, the FoV too narrow. The game lacks colour, the aforementioned ubiquitous browns and greys from the screenshots seeming all the more drab when playing. The environments seem uninspired, flat and linear, with no pretense of exploration or discovery: complete this action set-piece, move on to the next. It feels stiff to control, a relic of the older games that worked with their slower, more methodical gameplay, but doesn't work so well here. It feels arcadey, with slightly too-long gauntlets of individually unthreatening enemies spitting corpse money at you, a core complaint I once had with Dead Space 3. The antagonists are too cartoonish to be intimidating, lacking the iconic appeal of Umbrella or the Nemesis or even the lasting neo-ironic appeal of Wesker's ludicrous shades-clad supervillainy. The minor enemies, too, are unmemorable: zombies are one thing, as they're what the series was founded on, but give them weapons and they're just slow-moving regular people (context is everything). The game feels overlong, the final few hours leaving me sighing in frustration with every new map I knew I would have to slog through. It became a chore.

And it doesn't feel like Resident Evil. It feels like some other thing. And that's what bothers me the most as I'm writing this: because I feel like I was right all along, I can't escape the feeling that I'm just biased. That maybe there's just a smug told-you-so voice somewhere in the back of my mind sneering at all of the game's perhaps forgivable flaws and telling me they're worse than they are.

But it isn't all bad. I enjoy Leon's sassiness. Aside from the drab colour, the game looks pretty good for the time, the models expressive and characterful. Ashley, despite her occasionally irritating shrill voice, is a surprisingly manageable escort character and almost never gets in the way or detracts from the experience. The boss fights are better overall than those of older RE games, which were mostly just high-damage ammo and herb sinks. When the game peaks, it can be fun, and while it can drag, it's never truly boring. The inventory system is well designed, and I like that the knife doesn't take up any space. For that matter, I like that the knife is a viable option during gameplay in general.

So perhaps it's just not my thing. Maybe I tried it too late to enjoy it, or didn't play it in the right frame of mind. Maybe I shouldn't have played it right after a playthrough of the pretty excellent RE1 remake. Or maybe I'm just a stupid dumb idiot who doesn't like nice things.

One of the best, if not the best, game of the PS2 era. 

Without a shadow of a doubt the most important and genre-defining third-person shooter ever made. So culturally impactful that its influence can still be easily recognized today.

A entry that drastically reinvented a creatively stagnant franchise and was so successful and complete that from then on Resident Evil could only go downhill, until it started to cannibalize itself.

It's a testament to the quality of the work that 20 years after its release, they still haven't managed to recapture the same brilliance of this game.

RE4 it's one of the most creative and replayable games of all time. It's [i]still[/i] immensely intuitive and easy to return to. Its sense of [i]style[/i], striking art direction, solid mechanics and impeccable pace still make the game perfectly accessible and incredibly enjoyable on almost every front. 

A spectacle that delivers everything the franchise has always delivered and much, much more. From visceral and atmospheric horror to brutally competent over the top action. A sublime and sadistic blend of claustrophobia, teenage bravado, nerve-wracking tension, split-second decisions and surgically cathartic bursts of violence and slapstick comedy.

A gameplay based on tight, highly dynamic, tactical challenges that revolve around enemy interaction, resource management, precision and positioning. Elements that are constantly and inventively put to the test throughout the duration of the experience in almost every insane possible way, resulting in something immensely fresh and unique, not yet replicated at this level of competence and variety.

It's a type of combat that empowers you to play in the face of danger and feel awesome for it.

Shoot enemies in the legs, knock them down. Shoot the weapons they're carrying. Shoot the projectiles they throw at you. Stun them with headshots. Set them up for a powerful melee attack with splash damage. Slam them to the ground with shotgun blasts. Finish them off with your knife. Pick them off from afar with your long-range rifle. Blow them up with their own bombs. Make them jump, hit them in the air and make them fall to their deaths. Make traps. Outmaneuver them, outsmart them. 

Herd them all into one place, throw a grenade, and watch them burn while you reap the rewards.

Celebrate every critical hit.

Savor every upgrade you earn.

It's visceral, intense combat, backed by a strategic dimension so versatile and deliciously challenging that it never gets old. Everything works exactly as it should, with the reliability it should. The core gameplay is so solid, so elegant that simply doesn't age. The balance is flawless.

Add in an impeccable paced, straight to the point exploration that balances these more intense moments with resource-gathering, a healthy dose of purposeful backtracking (And optional content), simple puzzles and fun narrative segments, and you've got a killer combination.

Even inventory management comes with a layer of meaningful strategic decisions that add flavor to the game.

As good in its quiet moments as it is in its more explosive ones. Incredibly immersive and engaging. 

This is the kind of game that you remember enemy encounters and specific situations. The positioning of certain items. You remember the geometry, details and the mood of the places you visit. The hidden secrets.

The atmosphere... The music.

It's a game that you [i]internalize[/i].

And best of all: This was the first time in the franchise that they knew how to embrace the ridiculousness of the premise. 

The level of absurdity and self-aware sense of humor is... [i]pure bliss[/i]. 

So many fun characters. So many iconic lines.

Villains are megalomaniacal weirdos from a saturday morning cartoon, who like to tease and give you every possible chance to ruin their plans. Heroes have the depth of a puddle, but they exude so much charisma and coolness that is almost painful.

And everything is executed with a explosion of confidence rarely seen, that it fits perfectly. 

Despite being pure nonsense.

It's a tone that captures a unique combination of Hollywood blockbuster clichés and the drug-infused theatrical madness of anime.

It's the glory of stupidity executed with talent and heart. 

Fun for fun's sake. 

Soulful dumb.

A big and memorable experience from start to finish. A string of very distinct locations and set-ups that just keep getting crazier and more fun. By the time the game is over, you get the feeling that they've squeezed the most out of these mechanics and tested you in every way possible. 

And you can still be surprised by how dynamic and unpredictable some of these situations are.

And what about the delicious spice that is the other game modes? New and grueling difficulties, fun costumes with mechanical functions, ridiculous weapons that completely break the game, minigames that are so well done you could just play them forever. How about self-imposed challenges? How about a speedrun? 

I remember reading a review that said that [i]"Resident Evil 4 was so good, it was everything it could have been. Everything that could have been done, they did the first time!".[/i]

And i agree.

Resident Evil 4 is an extravagance and excess in the best sense. 

You never know what's coming. Resident Evil has never been so exciting and fresh.

So, yeah... Play it, play it as many times as you need to, explore every corner and climb the highest difficulties. Get good. Get hooked on the completely free optional content, try out mods and marvel at how much value and fun you can extract from this 20-year-old thing. Buy copies for your friends. Become an evangelist. Appreciate all the subtlety and timeless and inspiring creative drive that went into building such a resonant piece of culture for this medium.

And then play it some more.

It is a masterpiece in any sense of the word. 

P.S: Look out for the HD PROJECT MOD.

P.S.2: The sequence where they give you an RPG for free is still one of the best gaming moments I've ever had. It's like all the systems in the game connect into a wonderful whole in the form of a gift, a choice and a very satisfying long-term reward.

Resident Evil 4

The definition of a survival action horror game, changing the gaming industry and changing the identity of the Resident Evil franchise for a number of years.

Story - This game follows ex-rookie cop Leon S. Kennedy a survivor of the Raccoon City outbreak, who is now an expertly trained special agent for the President of the United States. He is tasked with a mission to save Ashley Graham, the daughter of the president, who has been mysteriously kidnapped and is held captive in Spain. As Leon explores, his mission gets more complicated than he could ever imagine. However, he is not alone and will be introduced to new friendly faces that help with parts of his mission and new unfriendly faces that cause more problems to delay his objective.

Combat - Leon is always outnumbered. He has to use his tools to his advantage. Environmental interactions like blocking doors, vaulting over obstacles or even climbing up and down terrain/ladders to get better positioning. This is important as enemies (the Ganado) can grapple, sprint, dodge, throw axes/sickles, and open doors, even vault over obstacles themselves. They stop at nothing to dispose of their foreign intruder. Ganados react to where you shoot them (limbs specifically). Capping an enemy in the head or kneecaps can briefly stun, which allows for a melee attack follow-up, if you are close enough. These have wide range and can cause much needed crowd control/space in the hectic fights. 

Item Management - Leon is attached with a small Attache Case. Enemies will drop ammo from time to time along with gold, there are many wooden crates/boxes and chests spread around the areas you can explore for additional healing/ammo/gold. As you progress you have opportunities to upgrade the attache case from the iconic merchant/weapons dealer (you'll be saying his voice lines, once you meet him) of RE4 and increase your storage to help lighten the load. You will still be faced with the decision of taking  ammo over health, vice versa. In some cases, wishing you had more of something when a boss fight comes around.

Weapons - Leon has a diverse arsenal of weaponry to experiment at his disposal, he will have to accumulate them on his journey. Combat Knife, Grenades, Pistols, Shotguns, SMG, Rifles, Magnums, Rocket Launchers ( along with a few hidden weapons post completing the game on normal and pro mode). Each weapon has different handling (speed of aim, accuracy of the laser) that helps them have their own identity. Resident Evil 4 is my favorite game. It is the game that I've finished multiple times with every weapons. I've got it on every consoles that it came out. That includes Gamecube, PS2, Wii, PS3, and now PC is my last port. I know every treasure location, and know every scenario that the game throws at you. It's my favorite game just by how many times I've finished it, and it always finds a way into my heart. It was the game that me and my cousin took turns playing, where we decided on every weapon we got and each of us pick up where the other one died. We would have loved RE5, yet that is not the game that we played on that old PS2 we boot up every weekend. The game we played is Resident evil 4.

I like the variety and usefulness of every weapon and how they all have their own attraction for different people. Do you like the Blacktail for it's slick and black design, effective is a wide range of scenarios. Or do you want to feel the power of the Red9, with a firepower that surpasses the basic shotgun? Let's look at the rifles. You might like the semi automatic rifle, that fires off rounds quickly to get head-shots off multiple enemies. Why pick a slower bolt action rifle? This is what you would say until you dedicate some time into it, where you realised that a fully upgrade bolt action rifle is more powerful then even a magnum, and can down even the regenarators, a powerful enemy, in a few hits. After using it, you start to get used to the bolt action and slowness of the weapon, since your trading speed for more power. Which one is the best? Don't let tier list deceive you, because it comes down to you and your wit. You'll need all the weapons to survive this gruesome night.

And this night is quite gruesome and horrific. You enter into a village and immediately have to fight off a group of angry villagers defending their chickens, which you will happilly take their eggs and kill the livestock. Yet they don't quite like that and attack you.  If you try to go into a house to defend yourself, you get attacked by chainsawman and have to use the shotgun that you found, and thankfully the villlagers are too stupid to use despite having one, since no other enemy in the game figures out how to use a gun until resident evil 5. On that note, why does no one question Resident evil enemies having firearms in their house, but have a problem when they start using those guns on them? Yet you eventually escape, but that was just the beginning. You soon meet a centipede monsters, bugs, a right hand that comes off, and other horrific monsters to deal and contend with. On your first playthrough, you'll find yourself tensed and always on edge. 

Some people might say Resident evil 4 isn't horrific, and it's a silly action game with cheesy dialogue. I could make the point that back when this game was released, my young 12 years was always scarred of the Las Plagas, and hate them, along with the bugs. You may say that that was a simpler time, yet all games, especially horror games, become quaint over time. What once terrified on first playthrough is just another day upon another. I played Dead Space multiple times and it loses it's scariness after the first. Yet I don't call them horror games based on how it can keep my in fear. I call it horror remembering those moments that compelled fear out of me. It's a game where death can happen to anyone, where enemies don't die simply by shooting the head, something  that shook all of us who thought shooting the head was the best strategy. It's setting ranges from eerie, to unsettling, to outright horrific. It's a good action game with great horror themes and atmosphere that makes you feel vulnerable and alone, rather then a bad-ass. This is embodied by the character you play, Leon.

Leon is the character that makes you think this game has silly dialogue.  There's that opening scene where Leon ask, "where everyone is going, Bingo?" You might think the line is a bit corny, yet I beg to differ. He delivers this line after and intense wave upon waves of enemies barrelling down his neck. Every house he runs into to find security, they just barge right on in.  He has a few close encounters with the Chainsaw man, and it seems like there was no end. Until the Church bell rang, which makes everyone stop and leaves. What made everyone stop? To play Bingo?  The joke makes you think of those kind of people who always goes to bingo, and it does bring some levity to this intense scene of mobs descending on you. Yet he does not say it as a comedian, but as a man who just survived a mob. You can even hear the tiredness in his voice, as though he is recovering from a load of adrenaline pumped into his body. His jokes play off the enemies, and scenarios. It's enjoyable, yet it never subtracts from the tense atmosphere that the game has. He's not like some who are just experiencing this horror for the first time. He's like you and me who have played plenty of horror games, and kinda know a bit of the flow. We can feel tense, and shocked by what we see, but it never burdens us to the point of being moody, so that we don't make some jokes in this hallowed night.

The game ran great on Linux with Proton and controlled fine on the Steam Deck with one exception. Using the volume buttons at any time locks you into keyboard controls regardless of what control scheme you have selected. This prevents you from aiming and moving straight in the forward direction. You can move in an 'S' pattern back and forth to move forward and press aim immediately followed by the fire button to fire. This can help if you are near a checkpoint or typewriter. The only solution I came up with was exiting and relaunching the game. This bug is quite annoying consider there's no audio options in the settings menu.

Chapters 4-3 and 4-4 both have quick time events that involve mashing the X button to climb. This did not work in 60 FPS and Leon would consistently fall. You can only change the game to 30 FPS from the main menu. Later sections might have the same bug; after the second QTE I played the remainder of the game in 30 FPS. This issue is not a Linux specific issue.

I think it would have taken me about 13 hours to beat the main story line if it wasn't for the issues mentioned above.

From the frost-bitten terrains of HowlStrom, where the winds howl and shimmering ice cascades across the landscapes, I, Kiba Snowpaw, an Ice Wolf of 36 winters, bestow upon you a tale unlike any you've heard. A gaming veteran of numerous years, I've ventured through worlds beyond imagination, but today, let us embark upon a tale where fur meets fear.

Enter the realm of Resident Evil 4.

To a mere human, this may seem like just another survival horror, but to an old wolf like me with a keen eye for detail and a flair for drama, this game becomes an odyssey of survival and intrigue. I approached this title, not just as a game, but as a fusion of stories told over flickering flames in the coldest nights of HowlStrom.

The Howl and Echoes of Leon's Journey

First and foremost, Leon S. Kennedy isn't just any rookie cop, but to me, a lost pup in the midst of chaos, trying to find his way. His mission - to save the President's daughter from the clutches of a mysterious cult - echoes the age-old stories of heroes venturing into the unknown to save a loved one.

As Leon navigates through hauntingly eerie villages and confronts the Plagas-infested villagers, the intensity reminded me of the fierce blizzards of HowlStrom. Every corner turned, every door opened, is like venturing deeper into the snowstorm, uncertain of what lurks behind.

The environment, to say the least, is chillingly detailed. The same ice that courses through my veins felt palpable in the cold dread that this game consistently delivers. The music, an eerie serenade, is reminiscent of the haunting howls that resonate across the icy plains of my homeland.

Battle Claws and Firearms

Leon's arsenal, varying from the traditional handguns to the cataclysmic rocket launchers, reminds me of the diverse powers at the disposal of the creatures of HowlStrom. Just as we adapt our magic to counter the adversities of our world, Leon too must strategize and select his weaponry wisely, adding a layer of depth to the gameplay that I found immensely satisfying.

However, there were times my furry paws craved the feel of a controller over the keyboard and mouse. The experience was reminiscent of the first time I conjured ice magic; powerful but needing finesse.

From the Eyes of an Ice Wolf

The tale woven in Resident Evil 4 is intense, with drama echoing in every gunshot and every whispered word of the Los Illuminados. Though the game's title may hint at a chilling horror, which it very much is, to an Ice Wolf like me, it felt more like a rite of passage, a challenge to be overcome.

If you're wondering whether to take this journey, I, Kiba Snowpaw of HowlStrom, would howl a resounding yes. Dive into this masterpiece, and you might find yourself, as I did, lost in a world of drama, action, and unparalleled suspense.

Final Frosty Verdict

Resident Evil 4 is not just a game; it's a saga. From its detailed graphics to the intricacies of its story, it's a title that stands tall, even by HowlStrom standards. If I were to rate it, I'd give it a solid 9.5 out of 10 frosty paws. It may not be as cold as the winds of HowlStrom, but it sure does give you the chills.

Till the next tale, may your paths be clear, and may your games run glitch-free.

After 17 years with an absurd number of ports and re-releases, Resident Evil 4 stands as one of, if not the finest action horror game ever made, this is not news, and I would be genuinely surprised if you have not played it in some form or another. After watching the trailer for its 2023 remake I was curious to revisit this gem and see if it holds up under scrutiny.

The short answer is a resounding yes, there is no doubt that it is a masterpiece, and I will try to elaborate on why. Resident Evil 4 is very polarising however as one could argue that it is inherently a bad horror or even Resident Evil game and quite frankly, I would agree with you, the plot connections to the first three entries are so menial that characters could be swapped with no change to the story and be considered a new franchise in itself, and the combat/gameplay is so far removed from what came before that game director Hideki Kamiya accidentally made a prototype for Devil May Cry with the game's first prototype which to those unaware is a hack and slash predominately melee combo-based experience… so needless to say traditional survival horror was not the objective here, If you look at Resident Evil 4 with this mindset of a survival horror experience you will undoubtedly be tremendously disappointed, however from the perspective of a campy self-aware immaculately designed over the shoulder shooter I don't know what else to say…..other than it doesn't get better than this.

The plot is laughable, campy, and cliché and I unapologetically adore it, with our modern era of refined plots full of melodrama and social messaging, it is so refreshing to play something that has the clear objective of being a fun time, with its hilarious dialogue, absurd set pieces, Saturday morning cartoon villain, and, Super Mario brothers esc rescue the princess plot. One could say that the narrative is bad by all definitions, but nothing embodies the feeling of laughing at a campy movie with a friend through gaming like this, and it very much falls into the so bad it is good territory. Leon Kennedy embodies the ideal American action-hero trope perfectly, however, Ashley Graham, the president's kidnapped daughter is obnoxious and frustrating to listen to, the two main characters here have little to no chemistry however the pacing is so aggressive, fast, and intense presenting the player with increasingly outrageous scenarios that this doesn't present itself as much of an issue, especially with the laughable amount of times Ashley is kidnaped by an overly convenient set of traps leaving the player to their own devices.

The gameplay/level design is simply outstanding, it is the perfect blend of arcade esc combat, exploration, and tension. it serves as a major contrast to the shoddy narrative, and I personally feel that this combination of stellar pacing, excellent levels, and a self-aware plot is why I find Resident Evil 4 so intriguing. The combat is intense and satisfying with Leon firmly planting his boots in the ground while shooting, adding an extra layer of tension while infected villagers lumber towards you, the iconic example being the infamous doctor Salvador sprinting towards you while brandishing a chainsaw. The weapons feel positively devastating with enemies stumbling and staggering with each shot, melee kicks serve as an excellent addition and add an extra layer to what is on the surface a simple combat system. The basic enemy variety (excluding the boss encounters) could be better with some noteworthy but sparse exceptions including the regenerators and garradors. I adore the developers manipulating the player's expectations after blowing enemies' faces off by sprouting out disgusting parasite monsters to replace them, this is ingenious and one of my favorite details. The game features an economy system with treasure and jewels which can be exchanged for weapons and equipment by the iconic and mysterious merchant character whom I cannot help but mention his voice acting and delivery is cheesy in all the right ways, and he fits this games tone and atmosphere like a glove.

Resident Evil 4 established many gameplay trends regarding over-the-shoulder shooting which was subsequently used in games like Gears of War and Dead Space however it is infamous for popularising "quick time events" in which the player mashes a particular button a repeated number of times to complete a particular scripted action, while quick time events usually take away control therefore taking me out the experience, the implementation with certain ones in 4 is admirable often acting as dodge maneuvers for certain boss fights, however, most fall into the category of obnoxious cutscene button prompts, or tedious input mashing with some hilarious backdrops, (if you have played the game, you know what moment I'm referencing).

The environment, presentation, sound, aesthetic, ambiance, and atmosphere in Resident Evil 4 is simply unrivaled despite the graphical limitations of the GameCube console. I cannot emphasize enough how perfect the opening village section is, it gives the player complete control and agency, and is enhanced with its bleak moody autumn color pallet, rotting village, dreary lake, dense forests, moody graveyard, and atmospheric church there is no doubt in my mind that this is my favorite opening segment in gaming, the pacing is immaculate the two boss encounters are exciting, and the opening village section is perfect throwing the player into the deep end right of the bat building tension only to be relieved upon hearing an iconic campy one-liner. The following segment in the castle is a fun change of scenery while dramatically amping up the camp of the plot, the environments are gorgeous and offer an impressive amount of variety, especially considering the confined setting. Unfortunately, the final island segment of the game feels padded to match the same runtime of the first two areas, it features bland environments, however for me personally it has four major highlights that warrant the slog through, these being the U-3 boss, the introduction of the regenerators, Krauser's fight and, the final boss and subsequent jet-ski escape. The ambient background sounds and music, particularly the serenity track is immaculate.

Resident Evil 4 also features a slew of bonus content including two separate condensed campaigns starring Ada Wong and the excellent mercenaries arcade mode the two of which would quite frankly have been sold as paid DLC in today's gaming climate. In conclusion, the package here is just stellar and if you for some reason have not played this game, I urge you to try it as soon as possible, it is by no means perfect, but the pros certainly outweigh the cons making it a perfect campy action experience in my eyes.

Back in early 2000s I played a lot of the original Resident Evil 1, 2 and 3 on PlayStation. But, for whatever reason I haven't touched RE4 when it was released in 2005. 17 years later, and after playing the remakes of RE2 and RE3 I decided to give RE4 a go.

Here's my verdict: [b]This game is amazing.[/b]

To start off, I will say that I played it with [url=https://www.re4hd.com/] Resident Evil 4 HD Project Mod [/url] which is a must for updated visuals and various tweaks.

During the first chapter of the game I struggled with controls (you cannot move while aiming), lack of ammo and many deaths, but as soon as I got the hang of it, a simple mechanic started to unveil itself: stop, assess the situation, aim for the head, shoot, rinse and repeat. It takes a bit getting used to. Also, make sure to use your knife whenever possible.

Gameplay-wise, It always pays off to go and search for loot. Every peseta and gun upgrade will make your playthrough easier as the game likes to throw various [i]gotcha![/i] moments which, with a bit of bad luck, you won't survive. Luckily, you have autosaves during some crucial moments, though make sure you save as often as you can.

Having played RE7 and RE Village before this, I can clearly see the path Capcom has chosen with some elements such as upgradable weapons, weapon parts and combinable treasure. These alone add immensely to game replayability - no wonder why it's a fan favorite.

Without spoiling too much for those who haven't played it yet, the story is over the top but you have to remember that this was the standard for early 2000s games, I mean, every game out there tried to copy The Matrix and John Woo during cutscenes. 

I'm really looking forward to the newly announced remake which should be out in March 2023.

The game that changed things forever. 17 years ago, RE4 breathed new life into the Resident Evil franchise by pioneering a brand new style of gameplay with the over-the-shoulder camera and free aim system, something that has been copied by hundreds of games since. 
RE4 was an upgrade in many ways. Leon was more skilled and competent than he had been in RE2; the Ganados were more coordinated and dangerous than the zombies; the environment was completely different and the gameplay mechanics were vastly improved over the old system. 
Even to this day, Resident Evil 4 holds up as an amazing game that any gamer worth their salt ought to play at least once. The bosses are varied in their designs; the enemy synergy is damn near perfect, you have freedom to customize your playstyle and nothing quite beats that first Village fight. 
Resident Evil 4 is lightning in a bottle, a stroke of absolute genius on Capcom's part and a landmark masterpiece in gaming history. It doesn't take itself too seriously either, which is in contrast to a lot of the dark, edgy, serious games of the current era. 
The game isn't without its faults, of course. Many things could be improved upon, such as the removal of the unnecessary QTEs and giving the player more fluid movement and gameplay mechanics, as this game will feel stiff for some. The Separate Ways mode for Ada, while being a lot of fun, is disappointing due to Capcom's refusal to remake the cutscenes for it, as they continue to be 480p video files whereas all other cutscenes in the game are rendered in real time in-game. 
The Mercenaries mode, despite lacking a little in character and map numbers (5 and 4 respectively) is arguably the greatest Mercenaries in the entire RE franchise, striking a perfect balance between difficulty and strategy, with World Records still being set 17 years since its initial release. 
It's no secret that Resident Evil 4 is my favourite Resident Evil game and one of my favourite games of all time. This game is a must-play, whether you're a fan of RE or not.

Quintessential. Nearly everything in this game has purpose and adds to instill a specific feeling. The action is tense and extremely fun, the inventory management and preserving resources remains engaging to this day, and this might be the best version of quick time events integrated into gameplay. The game effortlessly balances the fear due the atmosphere with how funny the dialogue is. The dialogue being so cheesy and funny helps to reset the tension, keeping the pacing well balanced. 
While the controls can be weird if you aren't used to tank controls, it isn't inherently worse. Mastery of these controls is extremely satisfying, and it proves that having a homogenized control scheme isn't always going to be a good thing if someone wants their game to achieve different things. I would recommend a controller though, the game was designed around using a controller and doesn't have great keyboard and mouse support.
Also check out the Resident Evil 4 HD Project if you've got a decent PC. While it can fix a few issues with the PC port like the timings for the quick time events, it dramatically improves the games visuals in nearly every way.
Even if the Remake comes out and is a fantastic game, the original will always be a fantastic game and worth playing on it's own merits. Don't let the possibility of a remake have you miss out on peak video games. The game is iconic for a reason.

RESIDENT EVIL 4 is amazing. Everything about it is great.
Leon S. Kennedy returns 6 years after the disaster of RACCOON CITY in RESIDENT EVIL 2.
He's sent as a special agent to retrieve the US President's daughter, Ashley, somewhere in Spain. He winds up in a village where all the villagers want to kill him. That's right, it's not zombies this time around, Leon has to deal with real, alive, living people who have rational thought. The opposite of what he went against in Raccoon City.

Leon is as amazing as ever in this game, and just like RE2, this game really makes you love him. He's a complete badass who nobody can truly defeat. In RE2, Leon's first day as a rookie cop in RC is when disaster is upon the city. In RE4, 6 years later, he's basically a veteran & knows what he's doing with every move. I mean, he went from being in a disaster on his first day as a cop, to working as a special agent to retrieve the President's daughter. After only 6 years, that's pretty amazing.
With only a handgun, he does some pretty great things. Like I said, complete badass.

This game introduces The Merchant, who appears all over the game. You can sell to him for PTAs, you can buy from him, or tune up your guns to raise their firepower, capacity, reload speed & firing speed. You can also buy gun mods, like Gun Stocks from him, but when you combine these with your guns, they remain in your inventory instead of becoming a part of the gun item itself, so it can mess with inventory management/inventory space a bit.

RE4 is quite long, my final clear time was nearly 12 hours, so you will definitely be spending quite a bit of time with this game, but it is absolutely amazing & you will love each second that you spend with it.

For Halloween I decided to play through a few Resident Evil games, and one that I have started multiple times but never finished was Resident Evil 4. Luckily, with the absolutely jaw-dropping HD textures available now, I was finally able to finish the game. It's amazing how re-texturing the game with high-quality assets makes the game look on par with those from the PS4 generation, rather than from the PS2/Gamecube generation which it came from. 

But how about the gameplay itself? Well....alas RE4 has unfortunately aged not as gracefully in this aspect. I know many claim RE4 as the best in the series, but for someone completing it for the first time in 2022, I don't quite agree. The game is still very fun to play, but there are just so many aspects that are not as well-put together:
- awkward tank controls which are greatly improved in subsequent sequels
- puzzles are far below the levels of REmake or RE2
- too many irrelevant and unmemorable bosses. Compared to, say, the utter unhinged level of Wesker in RE5, I just found these bosses very generic
- Ashley is just plain annoying. From her endless shouting of "Leon!" to the mundane spiel of rescuing her, then losing her, then rescuing her, then losing her, ad nauseum
- too many shooting gallery moments, like the ski lift section or the Ashley driving the truck section - the latter I especially dislike once the truck is parked and you have to pull switches while Ashley keeps crying "Leon!"

And overall the game just went on for too long. Unlike REmake or RE2, the game doesn't feel cohesive thematically and visually, lurching from medieval-esque town to castle to horror section then to some sci-fi industrial island. It doesn't feel like they belong in the same game somehow. REmake especially stands out as an absolutely perfect game with a level of cohesion unlike the rest of the series.

Despite all the negatives above, I still enjoyed the game:
- Leon's quips are entertaining
- Ada Wong is back, and she's better than ever
- Jack Krauser boss fight is a real standout - lots of fun
- Luis is great as a character
- the village section still remains very memorable, especially when chainsaw guy appears
- invisible bugs are scary (until you can tell what they look like disguised)
- fight in the cabin is tense

But as you can see those moments (except Krauser) happens in the 1st half, and overall it is the 1st half that stands out to me most. Still very fun, but I'd give this a 7/10 for being a good, but not amazing, entry in the RE series.

While it does overstay it's welcome just a bit, RE: 4 is a must-play for fans of the the terrifying, yet often-ridiculous, Resident Evil series. Looking at it's release date, RE: 4 was clearly a title that helped define the entire shooter genre. It has numerous weapons to choose from, meaningful weapon upgrades, and of course plenty of bad guys to kill.

As many will tell you, it is a departure from the typical series formula in that it is much more action-oriented and fast paced.  Gone are the jump scares and sparsely-located resources that made the earlier titles so gut-wrenching.  Instead, you are given tons of ammo and explosives along with plenty of cannon fodder to use them on.

Despite the horrendous controls that I can begrudgingly forgive due to the game's age, my only real gripe is the length.  I clocked 15 hours which is right in-line with the average time on HowLongToBeat.com.  Given the game's lack of complex systems, it started to feel like quite the slog around the 10-hour mark.  The final 2-3 hours in particular are quite draining with the game design going full-on "Call of Duty" which was just too much, in my opinion.

This is a legendary game that is tons of fun once you get used to the disastrous controls and I look forward to playing the remake with a modernized touch.
