Throughout October I've been playing all of the RE games, starting with 1, then 0, REmake2, REmake3, and now 4 (completing Revelations next). 

This is by far the worst of the RE games so far, which is good that it's getting a REmake pretty soon. 

Story is decent
Very little backtracking required
Enemy diversity is really good
Weapon choice and customization is really good
Decent boss fights
Longest single play through RE game so far

...and that's the end of positives about this game.

This game marks a change where RE tries to be more action and less horror. It is the least scary/tense of the games, and part of the problem is a total lack of atmosphere for most of the game. Coming from Tyrant(RE2) and Nemesis(RE3) chasing me constantly, this was a good thing personally, but detracted from what makes an RE game stand out compared to other action/survival horror games.

Other negative changes in this version compared to the franchise as a whole:
Inventory management but not resource management (SO much ammo/health)

Almost no puzzles(?!)

The game is bloated with quick time events (Press X to not die), which really destroy immersion.

Large sections of the game turn out to be trench warfare, murder fests, with dozens of (diverse!) enemies rushing you. Which is action-y but really gets boring the 7th time, and worse the next 5 times it happens.

If you disliked helping escorting Sherry (RE2-Claire) then you will really hate escorting Ashley as it becomes at least 1/3rd of the gameplay, sticking her in a corner while you mow down waves of enemies.

There is a mandatory kill count, in that you must kill them to progress, that runs over 150, compared to past games the goal might have been to kill as few enemies to preserve bullets.

The worst thing by far though is the controls. Perhaps this was really good when ported to the Wii. I played on PC and used a steam controller, and I don't know if that was part of the problem, but I've played them all so far on Steam deck or with steam controller and this one was AWFUL. There were no improvements from past games, and most things were worse. No strafe, no dodge, aiming is not precise, and Leon is SLOW.

Overall the other games are much better, If you can only buy one RE game, REmake-2 is the best in the franchise (up to this point) IMO, with story, characters, diverse locations, medium puzzles, progressive difficulty, and more, but it is scary af.

Okay, but really. Here's the cons:
QTEs: They're janky and unnecessary.
Graphics: You need the HD mod because the HD edition is half-assed, but modders are amazing. The mod fixes most major issues such as QTE glitches at 60 FPS.
The Castle: Is so freaking long. Why??? Overstays its welcome.
It's Old: There are definitely moments where the game shows it's age, but it's not often. Some casual sexism and outdated stereotyping. It's more meme-able than anything else.
Story: There's some plot holes. Not many.
Subtitles: There are none. This is the big one. (EDIT! For my d/Deaf, HoH, or just prefers subtitles crowd: the RE4 HD project includes some as of version 1.1. You'll want it no matter what, so grab it.)

Overall though? This is my favorite game. The story is simple and very reminiscent of early 2000s action movies. It's tongue-in-cheek humor directly pokes fun at them. The gameplay is clever and smooth with a little bit of weirdness. (It's rarely a problem, but I have died because I couldn't open the inventory while in the stumble animation.) The story is simple with a few strange moments. (Krauser is confusing if you didn't play Darkside Chronicles, and who did? Luis is a strange situation if you're not into reading files. Nothing major.)

If that doesn't convince you: I'm a filthy casual gamer, I have horrible coordination, and I hate escort missions. I've played this five times. Three times on easy, and twice on normal. I'm sincerely considering playing on professional (and I did. It was terrifying, and I loved it.) Ashley is whiny but the best escort AI I've seen, Ada's unbearably cool, and the boss fights (barring the underwhelming final boss) are amazing.

Pro tips if you're getting stuck: the knife is OP. Play it like a stabby game. Bring a rocket launcher into your boss fights. Don't stick with the base weapons, and get the Punisher for free.

Now buy it. Particularly on sale. It's only, like, $5 on sale. Worth every penny.

This likely has to be among my favourite installments of the [i]Resident Evil[/i] series, alongside [i]RE:1[/i], [i]RE:2 Remake[/i] and [i]RE:3 Remake[/i].  I would sing my praises on the overall gameplay, story, characters, and more; however, I feel other reviews have already expressed all that I would have to say.
Although, I [i]will[/i] emphasize a few notable elements that especially stood out to me over the progression of several runs through the game.

Primarily, this installment has a considerable amount of replay value.  Of course, with the Extra Modes as well; however, the main story alone is enough to keep you replaying the game.  And I can acknowledge that the development of good replayability, let alone a video game, takes enough effort and creative gymnastics as is.  And this game, along with its monumental performance as an instalment in the [i]Resident Evil[/i] franchise, is an exemplar of such.

Now... While I all too frequently find myself sighing and rolling my eyes and guffawing at the absurdity, uncanniness, or tackiness of some quips or one-liners, whether by Mr. Backflipping Kennedy himself or other cast, I can't deny the fact that it holds its own distinctive charm.  Especially in comparison to other video games, let alone media.

[b]And[/b] in conjunction with that note about charm and particular characteristics, I [b]immensely[/b] took appreciation in the aesthetics, the atmosphere, the tone.  This can often make or break the overall UX of a game, but they absolutely nailed it for this one.  Between moments of suspense or brief stillness.  And the accompaniment of the environment around you.  [b]Especially[/b] reminiscent for me; the silence of the long corridor of the Salazar Castle, as you progress to attain the King and Queen's grail, with vaulted ceilings, ornate carpeting over herringbone wood floors, painstakingly meticulous engravings in every surface from wall-to-wall, candelabras lining the moldings of each wall, velvet and gold furnishings, tall windows with garnet drapery lazily rippling with the breeze, the ravens calling in the distance, as the moonlight washes every surface in silver.  I will shamelessly admit that this Spanish Gothic-Regency maximalist aesthetic will always claw at my heart.
It's a bit of a shame that much of this style, both in terms of aesthetic and character cadence as aforementioned, has long gone by the wayside over time, but I can, at the very least, still appreciate the fact of its existence and impact.

Any few criticisms I may have would be the audio mixing and, oftentimes, delayed or absent QTE prompts.  If there were any option in the settings to adjust the music volume, I think that would have made a world of a difference, so that I may not have to resort to turning down the system volume and sacrifice character voice volume + ambient volume.

Personally, I would place this game at a solid 8/10.

A fantastic action game that rewards exploration and planning. You are allowed to wander about as you please, despite having a main objective. There are treasures, keys, ammunition, guns and enemies to find. The environments are relatively small, but they are unique enough to remember and provide different challenges. The boss encounters all require their own strategies and mechanics that are not necessarily found in other parts of the game. Dealing with normal enemies also requires strategies. You can stagger individuals by shooting them in the leg or in the head, allowing you to dispose of them with your combat knife, or giving yourself time to deal with other targets. 

Controls are a bit better than on the Playstation 2 since you can now use a keyboard and mouse, but feel exactly the same. QTEs are forgiving. Graphics have been improved, but can be improved further with the installation of the HD Project (https://www.re4hd.com/). Sounds from guns have impact without being improbable, and music and ambient sounds are good, too.

The story is alright, but flows logically. The writing is a bit cheesy and redundant. None of this gets in the way of enjoying the game, but an editor could have found employment here.

To say Resident Evil 4 redefined survival horror would be an understatement. RE4 redefined video games entirely, and for the better. Traveling to a village in Spain, it doesn't take long for everything to go to crap. 
Villagers are screaming at you and swinging their pitchforks like you're the monster. Worst of all? They wear bags over their heads and chainsaw you like a blonde oak tree.

Absolutely incredible. It might take a while to get used to the tank controls and tight camera angles, but even 17(!) years after the original release it manages to hold up as likely the best third-person action experience I've ever had. Feeling equally as ground-breaking now as it did then, Resident Evil 4 is a must-play.

Resident Evil 4 (2005) is still one of the best games I have ever played and easily one of the strongest entries in the Resident Evil franchise. Even after all these years, the game holds up incredibly well thanks to its excellent gameplay design, atmosphere, and pacing.

The gameplay is near perfect for what the game is trying to be. Combat feels tense and strategic, with enemies approaching in smart ways that force you to think, manage space, and use your resources carefully. The controls may feel dated at first, but they are intentionally designed to create tension, and once you get used to them, everything clicks beautifully. Every encounter feels fair, challenging, and rewarding.

The level design is outstanding. Whether you’re exploring the village, the castle, or the island, each area feels distinct and memorable. There’s always a sense of mystery and danger, and the game does a fantastic job balancing action with horror. Even though Resident Evil 4 leans more into action than earlier entries, it never loses its creepy atmosphere or survival horror roots.

The story is simple but extremely effective. Leon S. Kennedy is a fantastic protagonist, the villains are memorable and entertaining, and the game never takes itself too seriously. The dialogue is iconic, and the mix of tension, dark humor, and over-the-top moments gives the game its unique charm.

Visually, the game is obviously dated, but the art direction is so strong that it still looks great today. The environments, enemy designs, and animations do an excellent job creating an unsettling mood. The sound design is also excellent, with eerie ambient sounds, satisfying weapon effects, and a soundtrack that perfectly supports the atmosphere.

Replayability is another huge strength. Mercenaries mode is incredibly fun, and replaying the main story on higher difficulties or with upgraded weapons never gets old.

Overall, Resident Evil 4 is a masterpiece of game design. It understands exactly what it wants to be and executes it almost perfectly. This is the gold standard that later action-focused Resident Evil games failed to live up to, and it fully deserves its legendary status.

[i]Resident Evil 4[/i] is probably the best game ever made. Yeah, I said it. And it's true, probably! There really won't be another game like this in a long time, and very few games period come close to the majesty of this experience. 

Where do I come from on this? Well, I've beaten [i]Resident Evil 4[/i] about eight times over. Once on Gamecube, twice on Wii, three times on Playstation, and three times on PC. As a result I probably have a combined 100-something hours in this game, and you know what? It never got old! How is that possible? How can I beat a linear, action-focused game almost ten times and never get bored? The answer is polish.

Re4 is remarkably polished for its age. The graphics, gameplay, and general design of the game are so incredibly well done that it's almost like it came out a full five years before it was intended to. It looks better than some early-generation Xbox360/Ps3 games, for crying out loud! Not only are the textures, animations, particle effects and environmental design immaculate, but the detailed environments and haunting mood lighting make for a very engrossing experience. Gameplay is similarly excellent, with snappy and precise-feeling controls. Enemies are reactive in interesting and fun ways, dodging and weaving inbetween your shots to throw off your aim. The amount of enemy types, unique situations and setpieces the game throws at you is just fantastic, and even when it loosens the leash and lets you fight a simple shooting gallery, it never gets old. The crunchy, wet sound of a head exploding in this game is burned into my memory.

Another thing Re4 excels at is pacing. If you ask someone who thinks this game is the best ever made why its so good, they often cite the pacing. Re4 throws so many new ideas and locations at you at such a constant rate that its impressive as hell. In the first level alone, you: shoot some guys, jump out a window, fight an entire village, explore a creepy farmhouse, escape from a boulder, dodge some dynamite chucking dudes and get knocked out. The game gleefully skips from concept to concept, making the most it can of its linear design. There's never a dull moment, especially since Re4 isn't afraid to throw some genuinely messed up stuff your way. Since this is a [i]Resident Evil[/i] title without manual saving being tied to a resource, it is more than willing to kill you stone dead if you aren't paying attention. The Dr. Salvador villager, aka the [i]second enemy type in the game[/i] only has one attack- a chainsaw swipe that instantly kills Leon no matter how much health he has. This is but a taste of the fear that Re4 will inject into you.

Once you've beaten the lengthy campaign, Re4 unlocks a bunch of bonus content too. There's Assignment Ada, a short little jaunt through the final section of the game to beat it as fast as possible. Later versions of the game (including this one) also added Separate Ways, a side campaign that's about half as long as the main story. King of them all is The Mercenaries, a high-tension score attack mode where you can play as five different characters on four different maps. This mode is capital-A ADDICTIVE, with lots of content to unlock and some unique things to experience. Also on board are a boatload of awesome unlockable weapons. 

While I'm excited for the upcoming remake, I doubt it will ever meaningfully outdo this game. Re4 is just so well done in so many ways that I really can't recommend it enough. I adore this game, and will probably continue to play it for the rest of my life. While the [i]Resident Evil[/i] franchise is stacked with some of the best games ever made, [i]Resident Evil 4[/i] stands tall as arguably *the* best game ever made. You owe it to yourself to play this.

The protagonist of the recently remastered RE2, Leon S. Kennedy, is our player-character, smirking, overconfident and insanely insecure. He's sent to "Europe" to rescue the president's daughter because there are no princesses left in the world to save and soon finds himself butting heads, fists and feet with zombie cultists in service of a mysterious Lord Sadler. 

The first thing you might notice about RE4 is that the writing is a tiny bit ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ awful. Or great, depending on your willing to embrace the camp. Leon liberally showers quips and jokes throughout cutscenes to prove to everyone (and himself) how cool and smooth he is. This is a staple of the Resident Evil series and I'd hate it in most other places, but there are a few key details that go into making this work. First, Leon is obviously insecure, so you're laughing at him, not with him (this is also true of the villains - the ones who think they're high and mighty still get dragged into petty arguments). Second, that the voice acting and writing are garbage, so it sounds like children on the school yard coming up with insults rather than Aaron Sorkin dialogue. Third, villains, monsters and fight scenes are so absurd and creative that any bravado feels like the product of being completely incapable of processing social cues rather than keeping a straight face. Or maybe unwilling, since they all have their internal narratives they want to maintain. None of these characters act like real people, which is to its credit.

And yet this tone in cutscenes is never detrimental to gameplay. It wouldn't be as scary if Leon constantly quipped while being chased by a chainsaw-wielding cultist, so hey presto, he keeps his smug mouth shut. The only parts that get translated to gameplay are the ones that are needed - the resilience of the cultists, Leon's acrobatics, Ashley (the president's daughter, you find her early on)'s personality that affects her behaviour in combat. The biggest holdover is Leon's flamboyance with his roundhouse kicks or suplexes against stunned cultists, which still work because it's either a nice punctuation on an enemy's death, or an ego-shattering failure as they just get back up.

The majority of the tone in combat is being anxious and stressed out of your mind by the hordes and hordes of pitchfork-wielding cultists pressing in from every angle, constantly turning on tank controls to run away and get some space, then turning back and taking aim while standing stock still. And it works, it really does. The early game, for example, extracts every bit of complexity it can out of aiming while standing still - your 9mm has different effects depending on where you hit a cultist. Yes, headshots do the most damage, but they leave them grabbing their heads and flailing, so it might not be the best for consistent damage or large groups. You could shoot their legs out from under them and get them on their knees, then shoot them in the head to make them fall over, give yourself some breathing room. Or, if there's too many of them, you could do one of those roundhouse kicks on a kneeling enemy and knock over a whole bunch of them. But careful - that might mean getting into melee range, so it may be best as a last resort. The game is filled with little strategies like this that expand in number along with your weapon selection, that change based on the situation - your ammo, the enemy types, what weapons you have, what ammo you're trying to save, everything. And they're all decisions to be made in the brief window before you're caught up to again.

But RE4 also knows how to pace itself. There are plenty of decent stretches of time with no combat to speak of, just time to loot, reload, organise your inventory and recover as best you can. Then after a nice calming walk, you're back to being locked in a cabin, shoving shelves in front of windows fighting off another horde,  trying and failing to aim in two places at once. Every climactic moment hits as hard as the game wants it to. If you want a nice display of what not to do, play Ada's little side-story once you've finished the main campaign and see how your focus slides off the screen while you shoot gangs plopped every 10 metres. it uses the same levels with none of the discipline.

I will say, one aspect you might be disappointed about when you play this game is the horror. It depends on what you find scary. My favourite kind of horror is hair-wire tension, where tiny sounds and movements - cracking twigs, creaking floorboards, etc., feel just as intense as an explosion going off in your face because that's all you have to focus on. [i]This review is based off of playing on a Steam Deck.[/i]

[h1]Introduction[/h1]
The genre-defining colossus that is Resident Evil 4 not only mastered the franchise's formula but established an eerie setting, accompanied by horrifying visuals, great action, improved boss fights, precise aiming, and a classic RE storyline. RE4 ultimately influenced the evolution of not only the survival-horror genre but various others as well. It also popularized the "over-the-shoulder" camera view that is incredibly prevalent in nowadays’ third-person perspective games.
https://steamcommunity.com/sharedfiles/filedetails/?id=2866244154
[h1]Story[/h1]
Six years after the events in Raccoon City, former police officer Leon Kennedy is now a federal agent. He was sent on a mission to rescue the U.S. President's missing daughter Ashley from a cult located in a rural village in Europe. This village is affected by a sickness driving its inhabitants to act much like the people back in Raccoon City when the original outbreak happened. While traversing this village, Leon comes to meet a lot of faces, some familiar, some new.
While being an intriguing setting and concept, the story is nothing remarkable, though that is not to say that it is terrible. It is enjoyable and full of cheesy RE quips while still being thrilling with every twist but could also be considered corny.

[h1]Gameplay Analysis[/h1]
With this installment, the gameplay fundamentally changed with a complete revamp from the fixed camera angles to the over-the-shoulder perspective; this included many quality of life changes such as faster, smoother, and more fun action. However, the notorious tank controls remain unchanged, which can make movement feel clunky. While aiming, you can adjust your aim; but cannot move, which admittedly feels outdated and causes awkward but strategic situations, forcing the player to either quickly move and avoid incoming damage or aim for the legs and kick the enemy to the ground. However, the combat is still entertaining; it is by no means perfect and is simplistic, but it has charm.

Ashley becomes an ally with her own health bar, that you must keep her safe. Specific scenarios allow you to play as her, which usually is a brief, but pleasant change of pace. It can, however, feel limited gameplay-wise, but ultimately is different and fun.

The type of enemies you face are varied visually and mechanically, from mere ganados to cultists to huge troll-like nightmares, each with a different strategical approach needed. Boss fights are straightforward, as they usually rely on one or two quirks that the player has to interact or play around. This results in bosses being refreshing but also a fun action spectacle. They are tough enough to stay engaging, but easy enough that you can enjoy the absurd monster battle thrown at you.
https://steamcommunity.com/sharedfiles/filedetails/?id=2866270388
Quick-time events are new for the franchise and are a hit or miss. When implemented correctly, they add to the moment making it more intense and memorable. However, for the most part, they end up feeling painful and annoying to do as they cause instadeath and force you to replay from the nearest checkpoint. The QTEs are also bugged at 60 FPS, causing them to be 2x speed, which furthers the frustration.

Exploration feels not only rewarding but also enjoyable, as opposed to games nowadays that use scavenging as a distraction or time waster. In RE4 it makes for a simple yet delightful experience. What sets it apart from other games is that because of its linear nature, it always feels like you are moving towards your objective. Regardless of how much you wander around exploring, it never feels wasteful or unrewarding, ultimately helping the pacing feel great. Though if you prefer a system geared toward open world exploration, you might not like it.

Resources are usually within breakable barrels, pots, chests, need to be shot down, or locked behind a puzzle. Interaction with the merchant plays a pivotal role in managing your items. You can sell your acquired goodies to a merchant at every savepoint, where you can purchase weapons, upgrades, and healing items.

Inventory management features a more robust grid system with individual items occupying different amounts of space. Only weapons, ammunition, and healing items are kept in your inventory, while story items and treasures are in a separate menu. Having a different menu for non-gameplay-related items helps the management element feel like a proper mechanic you can work around without it being frustrating, which also results in easier and faster access to your items.


[h1]Additional Content[/h1]
Once you finish the campaign, you can experience it from Ada's perspective in Separate Ways. Furthering her mysterious qualities and finally giving more clarity on what Ada was up to, who she is and who she works for. This supplemental campaign is by far the most in-depth and well-made of the bonus content.

Assignment Ada is a short but enjoyable minigame where you play as Ada and have to collect samples of the virus and escape with them. In Mercenaries, you slaughter through waves of enemies trying to achieve the highest score within the time limit across different maps and characters. This is not only satisfying but incredibly fun if you favor combat. If none of that interests you, you also unlock the ability to replay the game on a harder difficulty. 

[h1]Visuals[/h1]
For its time as a GameCube game, it visually and aesthetically looked great, but does it withstand the test of time now that it has had an HD remaster? The textures have been almost completely overhauled, with higher fidelity such as environments, characters, and in-game objects, and it also fixes a lot of texture stretching.

Fortunately, it still looks adequate; the environments are unique and visually pleasing, while props and characters are brimming with attention to detail. Everything has this distinctive horrifying visual aesthetic that the HD textures even enhance. Unfortunately, the textures do not meld well with the old environment models, as they make the models stand out and feel dated, but overall it’s a nitpick. 
The enemies look terrifying and unnerving; mere villagers look like unhinged and alarmingly zombie-like beings, while the actual monsters foster elements derived from nature that result in uniquely disturbing and horrifying designs.
https://steamcommunity.com/sharedfiles/filedetails/?id=2866317390
[h1]Audio[/h1]
Dialogue tends to fall flat outside cinematics, sounding either repetitive or mediocre. As opposed to conversations during cutscenes or interactions on the field radio, these exchanges always felt solid and genuine while having the classic cheesy RE-styled remarks and memorable moments.

The soundtrack is choreographed well and supplements the eerie setting and action blend that Resident Evil is known for. It consists of pieces that keep you on your toes, while at times becoming a grand track, enhancing an encounter.

[h1]Steam Deck Specifics[/h1]
Performance is outstanding with the Deck, maintaining glorious 60 FPS at the maxed-out settings (HD textures enabled) and no adjustments to the performance tab, resulting in ~4 hours of continuous playing, with almost no hiccups or stutters.

The game did, however, very rarely bug out and constantly switch between mouse and keyboard and controller layout causing everything to be jittery and unplayable, only fixed by restarting.

[h1] Final Thoughts [/h1]
A fresh take on Capcom's beloved franchise, it has a perfect blend of horror and tense action gameplay enhanced by an enjoyable easy-to-follow storyline, situated in an incredibly eerie setting. If you enjoy horror or action or are simply a fan of RE, there is something here for everyone.

The bad; Serious frame issues (but only happened once during my 4 playthroughs [only through chapter 4.1-4.4]), There is no independent volume control for the game in the options, for some reason the sniper rifle animations are stuck in 30fps regardless of what graphic settings you use, to unlock the costumes/tommy gun you have to play Seperate Ways (The Ada Playstation exclusive port dlc which comes with every port now), the Seperate ways cut scenes are compressed to all hell since they use the originals instead of just making new ones with the engine, the grain filter isn't able to be switched off (you can only add more filters from the menu), to use the new weapons you unlock you have to play through the same save again so you can't change difficulty.

Personally I found this game, which used to be my favorite Resident Evil, a slog on my playthroughs. I've beaten it on professional on the gamecube and 360 port and didn't have as much trouble with stunlocking as I did with this one. I had two previous playthroughs on here stopped at chapter 3-1 and I remember why doing new fresh runs after that. The first two chapters feel more "survival" even though they are really easy parts to get through. The more you play the easier it gets once you remember all the mechanics and where everything is. Chapter 3 onward is where the game turns into a firefight with loads of ammo and tons of enemies. That might be a turn on for some people getting into this but it really doesn't feel that great for the main game, more like a mercenaries story at that point. Chapter 5 is probably the weakest part too with tons of military infected and miniguns shooting at you. Latter half of the game ends up feeling like work but not that rewarding. The real reward is playing through the game on a new round playthrough where you get the OP weapons and infinite ammo for some guns. Most hardcore Resident Evil fans are probably going to remember this game for the Mercenaries mode and it's still just the way you would remember it but I feel like it's almost not worth playing anymore since it's an old formula now and online gaming exists. Even with the new Resident Evils that have come out I feel like I'm less interested in the Mercenaries mode unless it's multiplayer like Revelations 2 (not really even merc-mode). This is still a banger though and the only reason I complain about it so much is because I do enjoy the game so much. 100% worth picking up if only for nostalgia but honestly it's one of the best Resident Evil titles out there, just very solid. I think this game will be put to rest though once the new Resident Evil 4 remake finally comes out, hopefully all the silly issues will be fixed and they will go the route of RE2make and change the game play for the better.

[h1] Hesitant Eagle 4 [/h1]

Is it bold of me to claim Resident Evil 4 as not only [b]THE BEST[/b] one in the entire series, but [b]THE BEST[/b] action-horror game ever? Honestly, I don't care... because I know it's true.
If you're making a "Top 10 all-time best games ever" list, and Resident Evil 4 isn't on there... then you straight-up failed as human being. You'd be a broken person. Oh yeah and better add bingo to that list while you're at it.

The amount of time & effort put into making this game just right, to be as refined & enjoyable as possible continues to prevail even nearly two decades later. Resident Evil 4 is one of the most polished experiences you can achieve on the market, it's a game where naming a simple down-side to anything regarding the game becomes a surprisingly big hurdle.



[h1] Gameplay Masterpiece [/h1]

The gameplay of Resident Evil is more groundbreaking than an earthquake.
When controlling Leon "Sex Appeal" Kennedy, it's like slipping into your own clothes. Controlling Leon is so seamless & natural, that rarely did I feel like I had to like THINK about the controls, but instead everything just happened in an almost instinctive way.
Looking, shooting, and running; all feel so fricking smooth, it's unnaturally natural, almost uncanny. I feel like I'm actually Leon whenever I hop into this game!
I feel like I'm an actual secret mercenary, as Leon constantly runs around with his weapon ready, and how he has all these incredible moves to deal with the enemies. And the satisfaction of popping someone's head off with a sniper-rifle is insanely satisfying, just like when you group up a ton of enemies and just throw a grenade in the middle to see them fly out to all sides! It's like the gameplay equivalent of watching fireworks.

When you want to shoot, you're completely stuck, just like when reloading. So it creates all these creative situations where you dabble between optimizing position or shooting, and when to reload, and when to swap weapons, and when to heal, and when to throw grenades... It's just such a dynamic system which enforces creative gameplay to survive, where you have to play to your optimal survival. You can't rely on running around some guy in circles while shooting, as that's physically impossible in this game. The smart toggles between prioritization never gets old or stale, especially as the game continues to throw new enemies & their personal prime strategies to eliminate them as optimal as possible, especially in tight, stressful, and uncomfortable situations where you're flocked & weary.
Resident Evil 4 just shines during combat, as it's its peak. No doubt.
Nearly every fight has a unique twist or gimmick that makes it memorable all within the confines of the core mechanics. And those gimmicks are explored and then discarded to make way for the next idea, and it ends up in this really neat gameplay loop of hopping into the next long series of “rooms” with entirely unique and self-contained encounters.

And the inventory management from the prior trilogy still continues on here, and while it's not as hefty, it's still a task which craves a smart mindset of trying to continuously perfect your inventory, as you need to keep a balance between keeping spare ammo, but also not filling your inventory with it. So you're pushed into switching weapons, both as what's most useful during current combat, but also having a balance between your different types of ammo. That's a duo I ADORE!
And the changed inventory system is straight-up phenomenal. Trying to Tetris all your resources & item into this tightly limited area creates an experience I've never encountered before.
This explodes in perfectionism even more once you meet Ashley, as since she's constantly behind you, it does so it's not really any sort of escort mission, as there's no bullsh!t AI to micromanage -- Instead it feels almost like a secondary resource management to attend to, because you now have to prioritize whomever needs to be healed when low, and whether she should follow, hide, or just stand... Simple enough. But you also have to keep an eye out if she's being captured, which can create hyper-stressful situations as you try to rescue her if captured WHILE dealing with your own squad of enemies; it means you have to zig-zag around and try to duo management them both, or focus on one only... It's crazy how epic it is!
I'm here gobbling over all this, just because how fantastic it is!
And she's not like some annoying ass companion character like Atreus from God of War 2018 or something despicable like that... god no. Ashley is actually an interesting & likable character; who the game encourages you to like, beyond the matter of the fact that Leon cares about her.
And I simply adored whenever Leon & Ashley interacted within cutscenes, as it was genuinely heartwarming. I care deeply about both characters. Like the little fist-bump Ashley does when you kill someone is just so adorable<3
And I would've never cared about her to the extent of which I do outside of gameplay, if I didn't have to during gameplay too. And I feel like that's something games nowadays are still struggling to adapt & learn from; even nearly two decades after Resident Evil 4 perfected it...



[h1] Sound-design [/h1]

Extraordinary, brilliant, magnificent...
The sounds of Resident Evil 4 are at such a level that I can barely compare it to anything else. Its satisfying *PLING* when hitting a coin, or the insane *BLAM* when getting an explosive headshot, or the haunting chanting of the cultists, or the sweet sounds of your guns reloading, or Leon screaming "Ashley!", or the external "ssssssshhhhhh!!!!!!!!!!ttttttt" sound YOU make when hearing a chainsaw turning on... it's just so freaking crazy how high-quality every sound has been constructed at.
There exists catchy songs, yeah, but Resident Evil 4 creates catchy sound-effects; ones stuck in your head for eons to come after playing this game. While I'm writing this, I have all these different sound-effects on loop in my mind, and I'm not even really annoyed, as they're really good! And satisfying!

The music of Resident Evil 4 is beautiful yet broody. Each song seamlessly play in the background, unnoticeably due to how in-line with your situation & circumstances they are. And while most of them only really work in-game, as externally they sound kind of dull without the gameplay... well, except for 'Serenity' with its melancholic aura.
'Serenity' is maybe the most defining song from Resident Evil 4, not because how in-line it is with its gameplay counterpart, no -- It's because how it symbolizes the breaks in-between such, the relief of safety. When you enter a room for the first time, and just instantly hear 'Serenity' begin to play, your entire stress built up within you flows away.
It's like a Pavlovian treat which'll steadily create a conditioning of your brain to produce instant dopamine once the song plays. No joke.
But much like how the presence of music is important, the lack of such is much too. Resident Evil 4 perfected the art of silence, as most of the game there's always a gorgeous tune in the background playing which you never really pay attention to; but the second it goes away every instinct in your body activates in fear. You know something wrong, something's gonna happen, and SOON. You'll be on your tippy-toes constantly, and make you weary of everything around you. Suddenly you trust nothing! And this is something the newer Resident Evil games don't understand, so they never have any music thinking you'll always be on your tippy-toes when in actuality you therefore never will be.



[h1] Conclusion [/h1]

I got Resident Evil 4 for the PC through a Humble bundle, and am so glad I did. I had written it off as unplayable when I gave it a shot on my Xbox, as in my opinion this game controls like ass using a controller. However, I decided to give it one last shot on PC, and ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ I am so glad I did. Resident Evil 4 hasn't aged the best in every single area, but its somewhat clunky systems form a surprisingly tense action-horror experience where resources are certainly more plentiful than previous games but also disappear faster than ever. Having the ability to precisely aim with the mouse is MUCH more of a godsend than you could imagine if you haven't tried playing this game before, and having a dedicated quickturn button was a bonus. In short: if you held off from this game because of the controls, give it a shot on PC. I also highly recommend the original to anyone who's played the remake, as more is different (especially after the halfway point) than you might expect, plus you get the shockingly good cherry atop the cake that is Separate Ways. Besides the fun (if somewhat dated) gameplay, there's also a really cheesy main story that has such an absurd charm to it that I just can't help but love. Considering all of the above, the surprisingly addictive New Game Plus, and more bonus features like The Mercenaries and Operation: Ada, there's a lot to love here.

My only issue is how comically difficult Professional mode is. I get it, it's the hardest difficulty, but some of the areas in the last chapter are a completely different level of brutal. The segment with Mike in particular was a nightmare, causing almost 20% of my deaths in the entire run. It really soured my experience by the end, which was very unfortunate. The rest of the game more than makes up for my skill issue, I guess.

TLDR; the original RE4 is a fantastic, somewhat cheesy experience that definitely shows its age but is nonetheless still worth playing, arguably moreso if you really enjoyed the remake (plus, you get Separate Ways, which rules).

This game really shines with the atmosphere it creates. There are so many moments where it makes you feel like you are really helpless and fighting against a horde of zombies. One of the first big moments for me is the first time you run into Dr. Salvador in the village. He's a chainsaw wielding enemy who can kill you in one hit! If you're not careful when you run into him you will die! Another is in the castle when you first fight Novistadors. These grasshopper like enemies can cloak rendering them invisible and you'll have to rely on your ears to hear them and shoot them before they get the jump on you, which really helps create a sense of tension. And of course the final big one is on the island when you first fight Re-generators. Oh my god! The atmosphere, the music, that horrible sound they make!!!! I was legitimately terrified the first time I fought one!  The fact that they are so hard to kill without a certain upgrade and that you have to fight at least three of them before you can get that upgrade only ups the terror factor for me!!

As far as combat goes you have a good choice of weapons at your disposal. II'd say decide early on which weapons you want to use and stick with them. You can upgrade the weapons at the merchant and with enough upgrades each weapon gets an exclusive perk that can help you even more. Or you can try beating the game with only the handgun and the knife if you want a challenge!

The only negative thing I have to say about the game it the QTE's. They were a sign of the time when this game was created and unfortunately I feel they are the worst part of the game. Also one thing I should let you know about in regards to the QTE's. If you are having trouble with them (ie: No matter how fast you are pushing the buttons you always seem to fail) then try reducing the frame rate down to 30 (I believe it's set to 60 by default) Apparently there's some sort of bug where since the original game was capped at 30 FPS the QTE's may not work properly when you set the frame rate higher. I was having particular trouble with the sequence with the Salazar Statue chase where no matter what I did I couldn't beat it. But then I switched the frame rate down to 30 and was able to beat in first try. So yeah be aware of that going in.

Aside from that small hiccup, I love this game! It's definitely worth playing and I will likely play it many more times!

[h1]Resident Evil 4 (2005)[/h1]

Resident Evil 4 marked the beginning of a new era for Resident Evil, focusing more on action while trying to maintain a horror atmosphere. There's not much that hasn't been said about this game already: it's considered one of the best Resident Evil games. Even Capcom is aware of this, having ported RE4 more times than other RE games combined.

Of course, even with its accomplishments, I'm of the opinion that it isn't a flawless masterpiece but still a top-tier RE game.

[u]Story + Characters (Possible Spoilers!)[/u]

[spoiler]The whole story of RE4 is pretty simple: Leon S. Kennedy, one of the Raccoon City Incident survivors, is sent to Spain to find the US President's missing daughter for his first mission as a US government agent. In a new phase where Umbrella is practically gone and focuses on smaller bio-terrorist organizations, RE4 does well with progressing in this stage of the Resident Evil timeline although it doesn't try to tie with earlier games that much.[/spoiler]

[spoiler]RE4's story has great pacing in the Village area, the Castle area is long but mostly enjoyable, but then bogs down slightly in the Island section where it feels like they made it so Leon could just have a final showdown with Saddler, who does all this for world domination basically. However, I do like the tie-in with Wesker and his subordinates providing Tricell a sample of a dominant species Plaga for research which would eventually lead to the events of RE5.[/spoiler]

[spoiler]Leon is by far the best character overall in this game. Before RE4, Leon was a pretty obscured character who only had a major appearance in RE2. I would argue that RE4 propelled Leon into the iconic popularity he has with fans today, including me. Leon's best scenes either have him showing how much he's improved from his rookie cop image to an American agent badass or making corny quotes that are the best in the series.[/spoiler]

[u]Gameplay[/u]

Resident Evil 4 uses an over-the-shoulder camera for the base vision for the player. This is far better than fixed camera angles because the game's pacing is far faster than the earlier games, which is balanced by the freedom of your movement, the amount of ammo you receive, and new mechanics which assist in giving you more options to bypass/dispatch enemies. The game also has a dynamic difficulty mechanic which changes the difficulty of the game depending on "how good you are doing".

Aiming feels outdated; you can't walk while aiming and you can only turn your aiming reticle. This makes shooting in tight areas difficult and you can sometimes get hit once or twice before you get a shot off.

You are mobile in your movement and can even dodge some attacks if given a QTE prompt. It's possible for even the newest of players to bait out enemy attacks and bypass them if you want to preserve ammunition. Most enemies can now be temporarily stunned by shooting them in certain parts or affecting them with a specific weapon, giving your shots strategic value according to where you land them, allowing you to run past them or even be given a chance for a melee attack.

RE4 balances this mobility with it's enemy variation, with each enemy having strengths and weaknesses. Most of the enemies in this game are not like slow-moving zombies, they can close the distance much faster and even engage at range with throwing weapons or crossbows. Enemies that are slower will often have the ability to heavily damage or instantly kill you. Most major encounters, you will be fighting more than five enemies at a time and the game balances this by giving you more ammo and explosive weaponry to deal with all of them. Even so, it's not uncommon to use dozens of bullets in these set pieces so you still have to manage your resources to prepare for these battles. QTEs are a thing in this game too although they do feel outdated at this point.

RE4 also includes a Merchant character who can be interacted with to either buy or sell items. These range from new weapons to larger inventory cases. You can also upgrade your weapons firepower, reload speed, firing speed, or capacity by expending currency you receive from fallen enemies, loot drops, or treasures, requiring you to make choices on whether its important to upgrade weapons or buy supplies. The attache case is the inventory system which all of your resources are put into - as big as it looks, weapons can take a good portion of the case and you get a lot of ammunition + healing items from drops which can take up space quickly which requires you to still manage your inventory. Any key items or treasures you receive are put into another separate inventory which I'm not a big fan of.

One unique gameplay aspect that RE4 has is [i]Ashley[/i] as a companion. Putting aside the "Ashley is useless" jokes, Ashley is actually a well-programmed AI companion. She consistently sticks close to Leon, ducks so you can shoot over her, will usually yell for Leon when in danger, and can be ordered to wait (even hide) so you can deal with threats ahead. As a result, Ashley's an additional challenge that requires you to escort her and one that's decent; if she dies, it's usually because you weren't careful enough and not the AI screwing you over.

Replay value is pretty generous. There's Professional mode, unlockable weapons and costumes to play with, and even has abundant extra content such as Separate Ways, Assignment Ada, and the Mercenaries. All of these are unlocked by beating the game once or completing the extra content.

[u]Graphics & Sound[/u]

Despite the efforts of the HD remaster, there's really only so much you can do to make a game made in 2005 look graphically pleasing. That being said, even if the graphics are relatively dated, RE4's HD remaster did a really good job in making RE4 less of a pixelated mess (most prominent in the PS2 version). The textures are smooth and the HD remaster improved in the shadow and fog effects that RE4 had huge issues with in its 2007 PC port (which I used to own).

Sounds in this port are the most refined compared to others. Sound effects and voices are quite crisp now and it doesn't sound so damn muddy that you'll be wondering if your speakers are acting up. These are particularly important since it helps with audio cues to determine where enemies are if you are unable to see them and to determine what kind of enemy it is.

[u]Conclusion[/u]

Resident Evil 4 is still one of the best Resident Evil games for its fun and engaging gameplay while maintaining with a plot that doesn't try too hard to be complex, balancing between the seriousness of being in a secluded area controlled by a cult and that Resident Evil "campy" tone that is typical now. It began an era in which 3rd person perspective would be typical of Resident Evil games for almost a decade. 

I would definitely recommend it to anyone who is into Resident Evil or enjoys action horror in general.

There was an especially awful sequence on a mine cart in Chapter 4 that takes what feels like forever, just to die at the end to a random QTE I did not expect.

While it may seem like I hate this game, something kept me playing (albeit with long breaks). Between the goofy ass story and overwhelming sense of relief and satisfaction I get from making progress, I can still say I had quite a bit of fun. Don't get me wrong, I still prefer the PS1-era games, and I do blame RE4 for taking the series in a direction I really didn't like (sorry, but RE5 and 6 are just awful). Played this game for the first time very recently and I have to say... I completely get why this game is foundational for a lot of horror video game fans, even if the game itself isn't really scary. The gameplay is surprisingly solid despite the controls being intentionally more inconvenient than in a non-horror setting. There is also a lot of opportunity to "git gud" and do a ton better on a second run. Lots of opportunities to learn from mistakes and build upon them.

If I were to point out any flaws with the game, it would mostly be small things. The three biggest I can think of are...

1 - The game has MANY points of no return. Normally this wouldn't be too bad but the game doesn't always make it obvious when they will happen, and sometimes they can happen surprisingly suddenly. These points of no return can prevent you from getting bonus treasure and loot, and while it will rarely ever stop you from completing the game it can be a bit frustrating.

2 - Random QTEs in cutscenes. Don't get too comfortable in cutscenes because many of them have at least one QTE (Quick Time Event) in them that, if failed, almost always result in an immediate death. This will rarely be more than a nuisance but these QTEs are FAST and can sometimes send you straight to a real bummer of a checkpoint.

3 - Somewhat spotty checkpointing. The way checkpoints seem to work is that they will set you at the start of the area you entered, which in some cases can mean losing 5-10 minutes of progress if you are particularly unlucky. 

Overall, though, the issues I have are greatly overshadowed by the parts that were really fun. There's a surprising amount of decision-making and resource management as well as many opportunities to make every subsequent run a bit better than the last. Better money and resource management, knowledge of handy weapons and items, and more can pay dividends for those willing to learn this classic.

I attempted to play 5 first, which was outright horrible, so I'm pleasantly surprised that 4 was actually a decent game.

This game was released in 2005, the games aged but actually handles rather well. 

Pros:

-Standard RE mechanics:  You can't move and shoot at the same time. Resources are limited. Storage of said resources is also limited.

-new game modes released upon completion of game which would be considered DLC packages by todays standards.

-This game's voice actors are top notch, however the writing can be cheesy at times. Kinda wonder what went wrong between RE4 and 5.

-"Can I offer you an egg in these trying times?" You get eggs fairly often which you can use to heal your low hp ally without wasting your actual HP items. 

Cons:

-Can't start on the hardest difficulty, you need to play on Normal difficulty first making the first play thru kinda simple.

-intentionally horrible user interface: 
Quick-equipping an item has been a game mechanic since the 80's so I'm surprised that in this 2005 game, you cant hotkey an item. I cant believe that the RE designers wanted you to pause the game, and select the item you wanted every time you wanted to use something other than the item you are currently using. Wanna throw a grenade? pause, item screen, weapon select, equip. Wanna swap to your shotgun? pause, item screen, weapon select, equip. Wanna heal? you get the idea. I want to believe that this was done intentionally so that the game is harder on the player, but really it's just annoying, there's no extra difficulty here, if anything it helps the player as there's no weapon swap time.

-The "react" mechanic: during cutscenes you'll have to "react" by pushing a button before a timer runs out which is pretty standard in games however this game did it rather poorly. it's always one of 4 buttons, X, C, LMouse, RMouse, and sometimes it's a combination of 2 of those keys. The game won't punish you for hitting all 4 at once, so you may as well just do that since the react time is so brief. I died more during cutscenes than any other point in the game until i realized this.

Neutral:

-Roughly half of the game is a giant escort mission, so if you hate those types of missions. This probably isn't the game for you. I will say that the person you escort is probably the best non combatant companion I've ever had, they are very well designed. 

-Shopkeeper wont "sell you ammo" but he will sell you larger magazine sizes, and don't you know it, he'll throw in a full clip of ammo too. Do with that info as you will. By the middle to late game I had to often leave ammo and grenades behind, seems kinda like an overlooked mechanic in a game that's supposed to be about resource management.


Altogether it's a great older game, I just feel like the designers could have tweaked a thing or two to make the game better, and would have really made it stand the test of time.

INTRO.
Resident Evil 4 will always hold a special place in my heart, being both somehow my actual first RE game (how is this even possible, given that OG versions of RE1,2, and 3 were also on PC?) & my favorite RE game. For a long time, RE4 to me was the best RE game, until recently RE2 Remake came along & flipped my world upside down. 

RE4 a long time ago was brought to the PC at retail (on disc in 2006) & while it certainly was a great game, that RE4: OG PC Version was best played with the controller since the PC controls were a mess (i.e. not mouse-friendly, it lacked mouse-look & you had to use the cursors keys or whatever you mapped them to for aiming) & was unfortunately a very bare bones port of this classic.

[snip]

ULTIMATE RE4.
You have plenty of options here in RE4: UHD [Steam-version] here on PC...such as support for higher-resolutions (such as 1080p); AA features; old graphics textures and new graphics textures options; 60fps support this time around is allowed (the original RE4 PC port was locked to 30fps, BTW); & a few other graphical features. 

Oh, and there's even support for Achievements here on RE4: UHD on PC, which is always welcome to keep players Achieving things in-game and also for replay-ability.  This game straight-up supports the mouse now & mouse-look out-the-box & it plays great, playing how you'd normally play a modern RE game since say RE5. Sure, you can still use a gamepad, if you like - and I use the old USB-based Xbox for Windows PC Controller here, BTW - but now having mouse/keyboard support feels great just for aiming down the barrel properly right out-the-box, as you'd expect from any other PC game with shooting. 

Performance was perfectly fine on my aging gaming laptop with an i7 4720HQ, 16 GB RAM, 2 TB HDD, 4GB of VRAM on the GTX 960m & W10x64 at 1080p30fps. I also could easily max this out on my old gaming desktop at 1080p60fps loaded with the following specs: i7 950, 16 GB RAM, multiple HDD's, GTX 970 & W7 x64 - and this new RE4: UHD version ran smooth as butter & both ran & looked much better than the original version of RE4 from retail on disc.

RE4 TWEAKS.
Using a mod called RE4 Tweaks for RE4: UHD, you now have even more options than what the dev's (QLOC and Capcom) intended. With even more graphical features & support - utilizing this on RE4: UHD is a great idea. Not only that, but it also gives the cut-scenes full-blown Subtitles support in English, which for some reason wasn't in any version of RE4 on PC. Having this mod is a must here, even if it's just for utilizing Subtitle-support here - but you can do a lot more w/ that than just that.

MR. KENNEDY...KENNEDY.
In this game, you play Leon S. Kennedy, the veteran cop who was in RE2. The U.S. President's daughter (Ashley) gets kidnapped...and Leon has to basically go down to a foreign country; investigate the village there; find Ashley & try to return her home. Of course, this isn't everything...as there's a mysterious cult causing all kinds of problems there & is up to no good too, as a virus outbreaking is happening there. Of course, some familiar faces from previous RE games return & all kinds of madness here is breaking loose, as Leon is here to save Ashley & the world here.

[snip]

MINI-REVIEW OF THE GAME.
Since this is going to be long-winded & I need to cut this review down to get it onto Steam, this is the RE that really redefined survival-horror genre & action, mixing both style of gameplay & action beautifully...and also utilizing a constant behind the character camera for your character. You have a really good & balanced mix of combat; action; puzzle-solving; item combining to solve some puzzles; story & plot development with some cut-scenes & environmental Lore & Items to find in-game; and even some QTE's (Quick Time Events) - none of this ever feels like it ever lingers too long, as it keeps everything fresh & balanced. While in some ways, RE4 is not the best technically as more modern games like RE2 Remake improved & refined minor things drastically with having a Quick-Inventory & Quick-Loot system similar to Fallout 4, where you can access the inventory on-the-fly & still remain in combat & gameplay...instead of going to a separate Inventory screen to access your equipment & items to pause the game. Also, you can buy and sell items & treasures and also upgrade your equipment, which also keeps the flow of the game & its equipment going too, as you can run into a Travelling Merchant at numerous points throughout the game. You cannot move your feet while aiming here in RE4 (future RE's would remedy that), so there is also tension here to pop, aim & fire quickly & smartly here; and this new camera-style & game-mechanic in RE4 felt fresh at that time & absolutely improved aiming & combat immensely. Back in the day, RE4 was a genre-defining game & the evolution of the horror-survival genre/action-adventure game, laying the blueprint down on how to make a modern & great RE title that many in this genre are still iterating on & refining to this very day.

OUTRO.
After almost 28 hours here (around 27h24m) or so w/ the Base-Game, RE4: UHD version was finished & added to the book. That certainly isn't the end of things, as there is an extra campaign here too (Ada's Campaign of Separate Ways - and yes, I will get to that at some point) & other modes (like Mercenaries) that you can unlock when you finish the Base-Game's Campaign. 

Regardless, RE4: UHD on Steam is a major improvement over the original RE4 Edition (2006). as this newer UHD Edition on Steam for the PC has improvements across the board w/ much better mouse-look controls for PC-style gameplay, better performance with also 60fps support, extra resolution support, more graphical bells & whistles, Steam Cloud Support, Steam Achievements, and improved support in other ways too. 

RE4's UHD Edition on Steam is the best version of the game found on PC currently & the best way to play my personal favorite RE game, which is often - for very good reason - regarded and on many lists of critics & gamers alike for The Best Games Ever Made. Throw the RE4 Tweaks Mod on top of this version for a few more improvements & features and here you have absolutely the best way here to play RE4 on the PC.

Simply put: RE4 is nothing short of a masterpiece here as a game & to experience it in its best form in this UHD Edition with also the RE4 Tweaks Mod equipped is nothing short of awesome & a joy to play. This UHD version is a must-play game & a must-play version of this survival-horror classic.

As of typing this review and having unlocked all the achievements of the game, played through Ada's campaign, as well as Mercenaries mode I have a good grasp of how well done the game is. To start off, as someone hyped to play the upcoming Resident Evil 4 Remake, I thought it best to try out how the original was. Suffice to say it was a fun, however irritating experience at times. The game has no doubt not aged the best. I don't doubt that it was revolutionary and amazing for its time and is still fun to play today; it certainly does not match up in any way to today's standards as far as game design goes. I am confident that the upcoming Re4 remake will iron out a lot of these issues, which I don't blame the game for having just to be clear. 

For one, Ashley's ai is very basic and this makes for some very annoying encounters. She can only follow you, duck when you aim her direction, and hide in garbage bins. This duck mechanic proves problematic during battle however because there would be times when you would be swarmed by enemies and she would simply duck as ganados surround her and either pick her up or attack her, putting you in an unnecessarily precarious position. Second, the horror aspect of the game is not very present, only really present for the Village section, which is no doubt the highlight of the game with it then falling from there. This is, rather than being a survival horror, an action game with horror elements. Third, the tank controls of the game also make shooting rather mind numbing to do at times as since you aren't able to move, you leave yourself wide open and vulnerable. This is a problem since certain enemies will use crossbows and in the Island section of the game there is an enemy that wields a minigun. Turrets are also an irritating experience to deal with as well as since there is no movement during aiming, you can't peek around a corner with your sniper and you are forced to either circle around the turret to shoot the gunner in the back or walk into the open and quickly snipe the gunner in the head. This is even more mind numbing to deal with in the Island section of the game when they make you deal with not one, not two, but three turret gunners that you have to pick off whilst fighting off hordes of roving ganados with shock batons and flails, all whilst having very minimal cover. I have no doubt that this will be fixed in the remake. 

With that said, I enjoyed playing through the campaign, albeit not being the biggest fan of the escort mission aspect of it. The Mercenaries mode was also fun to play although of course at times it can suffer from the tank controls aspect of the game I've listed. Ada's campaign was also fun but felt short and could've perhaps featured a few more missions, along with a wider variety of weapons to use. Overall, I would rate the game an 8/10 for its fun yet aged gameplay.

I want to make it clear upfront that this is not a positive review. I won't say that I don't recommend it because if you're playing through the series, you have to, right? If you're not playing it for that reason- you've likely played it before and you've already made up your mind as to how you feel about the game. 
I've spent enough time playing video games in my life that I know I'll have regrets at the end of my life and can see how it would have been a cool game when it released in 2005.
But this review doesn't end with "But it's all of it's ♥♥♥♥♥♥ shortcomings that really splashes me with a nostalgia that makes all of these things okay." I don't like this game. Not a single aspect was enjoyable. I didn't even love to hate it. 

[h1]I'm writing this because I want to ♥♥♥♥ on this game.[/h1]

So I'm gonna wax nostalgic for a minute and explain why I saw it through.
In 1998, I experienced Resident Evil 2 when my dad picked up a copy. My siblings and I would gather to watch him play through as Leon and we were suckers for every jump scare. I'd later play through RE2 as Claire, RE3 when it released, and some Code Veronica, but never finished either. Got some time in on Dino Crisis. 
I recently picked up most of the RE games and have been in the process of playing through the series. Thus far I've burned through Zero, 1, 2, and 3. So there's a sort of template, atmosphere, and feel in my mind that I associate with a Resident Evil game.

Resident Evil 4 doesn't feel like a RE game. It definitely wreaks of Capcom and sports Leon Kennedy and Ada Wong. But it feels as though it should have been an addition to the House of the Dead series. I could actually see it being a cool experience if it were a rail shooter.

[h1]And with that said: I ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ hate Resident Evil 4.[/h1] 
Not because it doesn't feel like a Resident Evil or because it suffers from old game syndrome. 
It's everything. 

-The camera is atrocious and is what I believe really killed the game for me. The field of view is almost permanently stuck in a state of infection. If there's any pseudo-difficulty to the game- it spawns from how intensely aggravating the lack of vision is. 
It wasn't a new trick to hide items in the game by placing them outside the default view provided by the camera's position/movement, but RE4 indulges in this frequently. You can't assume that the default camera position in the room you just entered is terrible because they're hiding something, though. It's just always ♥♥♥♥. 
This ties closely to how trash the aiming is.
(Note: The options will only allow you to invent part of the camera controls. As a child of Golden Eye- I need the inversion when using a controller. You can modify your controls through Steam.)

-The music is abusively loud and the game lacks audio adjustment of any sort. If there's an enemy around- the music is blaring and will only stop when everything that's aggressive to you is dead.

-The story sucks. You're supposed to be rescuing the President's daughter... in a RE game. Que? 
*In the waning hour of the game, Leon turns up the Bond and almost molds a redeeming moment in the story. This is just before Ashley offers up that booty and Leon shuts it down? There wasn't a single moment of Ashley's screen time that doesn't make you want to leave her behind- but it's the President's 20 year old daughter. You don't walk away from an opportunity to be able to call the President's daughter Smashley. 
He then proceeds to try and spit game at Hannigan by telling her that she's hotter without glasses.
It is a scientific fact that every woman is more attractive with glasses. If you disagree- you're probably fan of this game and I have nothing else to say to you.
Hannigan is of this same mindset and shuts Leon down. The credits roll with our protagonist sporting a case of blue balls. 

-Resident Evil 4 loves quick time events. These ensure that, if it's your first play through- you gonna die at least a couple times. Dying in a game is whatever, but quick time events are ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ in general. The more QTE utilized in a game, the more that game sucks.  
Playing Resident Evil 4 isn't the first time I've wanted to the know the address of the person who originally came up with the idea for QTE. 
Just want to talk.

A part of me wants to go more in depth and touch on more aspects of the game in an attempt to make the game suffer  the way I did, but I know it's a game and doesn't have feelings for me to hurt. 

If you feel compelled to play through Resident Evil 4 for the first time, I'd recommend waiting for the remake/remaster. The other remakes have been great but those were already great games.

[h1][b][i]A great influence back then, still a good game today![/i][/b][/h1]
Resident Evil 4 might be one of the most influential games ever made, atleast when it comes to third-person-shooters. It was an inspiration for games such as Dead Space, Last of Us and even the recent God of War, believe it or not. Even if it did not hold up today, it still undeniably would be one of he greatest games of all time. Thankfully it still is really good, though not perfect.
[b][u]Story[/u]:[/b]
The story overall is probably the weakest part of the game. Leon is back and this time has to save the daughter of the american president, all by himself for some reason, Upon arriving at his destination it becomes clear very fast that he won't be dealing with regular zombies anymore, but rather with parasite-infected spanish villagers and cultists. Certainly an interesting direction to take the series. After finding Ashley, the presidents daughter, the big bad shows himself and [spoiler]simply reveals his plan, thus instantly ruining his plan[/spoiler]. The objective at this point goes from finding Ashley to safely escorting her off the island. This pretty much sums up the first 2-3 hours of the game. I don't want to take away anymore, as there isn't that much left despite the game still continuing for another solid 10 hours. The story definitely is not the driving point of the game, that somewhat goes to the characters and gameplay.
[b][u]Characters[/u]:[/b]
The characters are my personal favourite part of the franchise and this game is not lacking in that department.
[i]Leon[/i] returns in what might be his best iteration to date. He is funny and sarcastic, but also skilled and badass and it's just a joy to witness his interactions with the other characters such as
[i]Ashley[/i], who is probably the most disliked aspect of the game in regards to the escort mechanics surrounding her. She is a cheerful girl... and thats pretty much it. I like her and her interactions with Leon are sweet but other than that there isn't much to her.
The same can be said about [i]Luis[/i], or [i]Lewis[/i] as Leon likes to call him. He has a grand total of 4 cutscenes and a few journal entries throughout the game and I'm not suprised some people forgot about him by the end of the game. Once again, I like him. He is charismatic and goes out of his way to help Leon and Ashley, which is nice and all but he simply does not have enough screen time to leave a lasting impression.
A lack of screen time also seems to be a characteristic of [i]Ada[/i], another returning character from RE2, though in her case it is intentional and helps adding to her mystique. Whether you like her or not greatly depends on how much you can endure her spouting cryptic messages and simply refusing to tell Leon what's going, which can be quite infuriating for some people. It is nice to see her actually care about Leon and [spoiler]disobeying Weskers orders to help him[/spoiler], really adds to her character and their interactions in RE2.
Other than that we have the first antagonist [i]big cheese Mendez[/i], who is just kinda there and then [spoiler]he dies[/spoiler].
Than we have [i]Ramon Salazar[/i], the second and honestly best antagonist of the game. He is a little 20 year old midget with his own castle in the middle of nowhere who has some iconic banter with Leon throughout the game, making him easily the most memorable of the villains. He is cowardly and yet also absolutely full of himself resulting in some extremely satisfying moments of Leon wrecking him up.
Next up is [i]Krauser[/i], who is sort of crammed into the last fourth of the game and serves as a sort of rival for Leon thanks to the past they shared, which isn't explored in the slightest in this game. He also ties this game to the overaching subplot of [spoiler]Weskers antics in the background[/spoiler] and that really seems to be Krausers single purpose in this game. Other than that he is fine, though if you want to actually know what happened between him and Leon I recommend playing "RE Darkside Chronicles", as it enhances their interactions greatly.
Last on the list is [i]Saddler[/i], the main antagonist of the game and probably the third best of the four. Despite being responsible for the majority of the game, he actually feels sort of like an afterthought. He shortly appears in the beginning and then has to step up in the last fourth after Leon has [spoiler]disposed of all his underlings[/spoiler]. He is sort of supposed to be a parody of cliché hollywood movie villains but it just doesn't add up. His final boss fight is pathetically easy and all of this just adds up to a forgettable character.
The last character I want to talk about is [i]Mike, [/i]a[i] [/i]talking helicopter that knows a good bar. Yeah that's it.
Most of the characters are just fine on their own but start to shine in interactions with each other.
[b][u]Gameplay[/u]:[/b]
This game is the grandfather of modern third-person-shooters and thus plays like those games, with a few things that got changed throughout the years. I think you have to acknowledge this to fully appreciate how well RE4 still plays to this day. One major difference to modern games are tank controls, which can throw people off but other than that still work perfectly fine. Instead of fixed camera angles the game is now in third-person, adding to the more action oriented approach this game takes. Enemies will recoil and react differently depending where you shoot them, which even to this day is not a given for whatever reason (looking at you Bethesda). Shooting enemies in the head or below the kneecaps will allow you to either kick or even suplex them, rewarding the player for precise aiming and thus preserving ammo. Sometimes shooting an enemies head off will result in the parasite inside of them to take full control, which seems to be decided by RNG for all enemies safe for a few near the end. This in turn makes every encounter different when replaying and makes you wary of even the weakest enemies. Another aspect of the gameplay is escorting Ashley, which honestly is nowhere near as bad as people make it out to be. She can follow or stay put on command, ducks when you shoot in her direction and cheers you on as you slowly commit mass genocide. The escort mission only takes up about 1/3 of the game and that's pretty much it. It adds another dynamic to the game that I think is needed considering it's length. As is traditon this game also features a bunch of bosses. Now, I think that bosses always are one of the weaker points of these games but RE4 definitely attempts to mix things up a bit, resulting in mostly decent bosses, each with their own gimmick and interesting design (definitely the best bosses up to this point in the series).
Here's a rundown of [b][u]a few other aspects of the game[/u][/b]:
[list]
[*]The music is pretty good with a few standout tracks throughout the game (The Drive, Serenity, Infiltration and the Save Room theme to name a few).
[*]Throughout the game you will visit a rural spanish area, a huge and contrived castle and a military island. It's nice that the game mixes up its setting but by the time you get to the island I think that the game mostly lost its steam and as a whole drags on for 2-3 hours too long.
[*]It still looks pretty good to this day and even better with the HD Project by Albert Marin and Cris Morales ([url=https://steamcommunity.com/sharedfiles/filedetails/?id=2739656707]Steam Community :: Guide :: Resident Evil 4 HD Project[/url]).
[/list]
[h1]Tl;Dr[/h1]
RE4 still holds up to this day. It features enjoyable but often underused characters, has good music and fun gameplay mixed with early 2000 charme. While it does drag on for a bit too long, it still remains one of the better games in the series and the praise it gets is fully deserved. Of course, all of this games' shortcomings can be fixed by the upcoming remake, which hopefully is atleast as good as its original.

[h1] Resident Evil 4 [/h1]

Resident Evil 4 is an iconic survival horror game from an iconic series known and beloved by most. The game is set in Spain where you take the role of Leon Kennedy, A US agent responsible for rescuing the president's daughter who has been kidnapped however when you get there things go wrong very quickly.

[h1] From The Perspective Of A New Player  [/h1]

Unlike most Resident Evil 4 players, I have never played Resident Evil 4 or any of the games from the series until recently. I was completely new to Resident Evil 4. As soon as I started the game I was caught off guard by the camera system and aiming system that the game utilizes as I have never seen or experienced anything quite like it. It felt clunky, slow, and difficult to use. This made the game feel harder than it already is, the game is already not the easiest out there. On the plus side, I felt as though the game's visuals are rather decent considering the game first came out in 2005. 

[h1] Getting Into It [/h1]

After some time of playing Resident Evil 4 I had gotten used to the camera and aim, it immediately felt more natural to me and I enjoyed it. I felt engaged in the absurd and unique story because of its unique characters and setting. The game's difficulty felt rewarding and as I got better at the game the more rewarding it felt.

[h1] The Characters [/h1]

Resident Evil 4 has some of the most memorable characters I think I will ever come across in a game. Ranging from the protagonists to the antagonists. Leon's one-liners will never cease to amuse, Ashley's clunkiness and constant screaming while being annoying is memorable and is part of what makes Resident Evil 4 feel like, well Resident Evil 4 and the oh-so-loveable merchant with his unique voice and voice lines that you are bound to never forget and always recognize. Even the basic enemies, the ganados are memorable and I will personally never forget them screaming out in Spanish or mumbling in Spanish,

[h1] Finishing The Game [/h1]

After having beat the game I felt satisfied having played such a fun and memorable game and would happily replay it over and over again, if replaying the story isn't your thing the game offers you an extras option with extra game modes that you can play and challenge yourself with to scratch that Resident Evil 4 itch.

[h1] Final Words [/h1]

Resident Evil 4 is a fantastic game even that can be enjoyed far after its release, whether you are a new player or just revisiting the game it is incredibly fun and memorable. The game is far from perfect as it does have some moments where it isn't fun or not as fun as it can be but I found these moments few and far in between.

[h1] Rating [/h1]

[b] 9/10 [/b]

I highly recommend the game to everyone and is worth its price tag and even more if it is on sale.
