It took me much longer than it should've (several months, literally) to finish this game, but now that I have..well, I have a few things to say regarding this game. Overall, I'd say I definitely enjoyed this game, I think it's aged well considering it's nearing 2 decades in age, but there are definitely certain areas of the game where you can feel its dated design, or limitations thanks previous games in the franchise setting a precedent for it. Without further interruption, let's get into it.

As always, my reviews will try to be spoiler free but do be warned that spoilers might still be unavoidable.

[h1]Story:[/h1]
Resident Evil 4's story, to someone who has not played the previous games, is best summed up as "generic" from my perspective. Is that a bad thing? Not necessarily. Even for a 2005 game, I don't think this game's story was anything really revolutionary, though the way it is presented and written here is admittedly entertaining, if flawed.

The premise of "you go in to investigate one thing but end up involved in all this other business" is executed well and I think the game does a phenomenal job building stakes. Right from the get-go in Chapter 1, you get your first taste of it in a cutscene showing what happens to the police officers leading you to your destination. Or later on where the game shows you what sort of demonic abominations your enemies are capable of becoming. It helps build tension and the way the game introduces scarier creatures as you go is genuinely great - some of the monsters, particularly in chapters 3 and 4, made my skin crawl as to how utterly creepy they were.

What does get me though about this game is the fact that the structure of the story is predictable. Once you finish chapter 1 or 2, you can easily pick up on its structure and it doesn't really do anything to deviate from it. While not a bad thing, it does end up being a bit repetitive and, admittedly, has put me off of wanting to continue the game sometimes.

[h1]Gameplay:[/h1]
Can I just say how much I hate tank controls? I get that this is what the early Resident Evil experience is like, but god do I hate tank controls. The one thing I did not enjoy while playing RE4 was fiddling with the controls, as I thought they served to break up the action way more often than I would have liked. Of course, this is purely a habit, but I do not find it all that fun to be in a scenario where I have a group of enemies chasing me and all I can really feasibly do about it is run back a rather long way, choose my gun, wait for the game to literally lock me into place so I can go into aiming mode and only then fight back against any potential threats. I can hear the RE veterans chuckling at me for this complaint and I realize that that's the whole point, but that still doesn't make it any more fun to play as a new player, at least from my perspective. To its credit, once you do get used to the controls they're fine, but there are so many little quality of life changes that could be made here that I hope its modern remake will address. At the very least - move while shooting, or be able to hip-fire the Rifle.

Regarding the game's difficulty, I enjoyed the challenge this game provided. It wasn't exactly an "easy" game by any stretch of the word - I found the game to be sufficiently challenging and that really helped set the mood and provide the player with a sense of danger. That whatever you're after isn't exactly harmless. That's partly because most of your guns are actually rather weak - you need to take your time and be very meticulous with your shots, because one missed shot can mean the difference between life and death. And some of these enemies take an ungodly amount of bullets to kill, it can become maddening at times to kill some of them. Also, the enemies that regenerate that also look like walking body bags - actually made my skin crawl, they were just that creepy.

Though some of the bosses...I feel as though some of them had more thought put into them than others. There's a particular boss at the end of the game that gave me a lot of trouble because he dodges very often and moves insanely fast, leaving very little room to attack. I ended up wasting all of my ammo on him, barely had any health to spare and was about to call in the towel - let him kill me to reset the fight. Except he never did. So I ended up storming at him, knife in hand and just slashed away. The stupid part? It worked. I beat him. Did I mention the encounter also has a 3 minute timer? Yeah, I finished with about 15 seconds to spare, got a cutscene and for some reason the timer DOES NOT PAUSE IN THE CUTSCENES, so I ended up failing mid-cutscene and had to start the entire fight over. It just felt sloppily designed.

As for level design, I really enjoyed the sense of exploration. While the level design is very linear, there are enough secrets sprinkled throughout and clever design that rewards exploration that it made traversing the world fun, though that didn't stop me from finishing certain sections with next to no ammo anyway.

[h1]Visuals, Sound & Optimization:[/h1]
The game's visuals, I'm sorry to say, aged poorly. Even with this "touched up" PC port, the game really looks bleak, dull and ugly at times. Actually, calling it "bleak and dull" is a compliment because that's exactly what this game was going for, but "ugly" in the sense that you can...notice a lot of "of its time" things in the visual design. On a CRT in 2005 it would've been totally fine, however blown up into 16:9 with upscaled textures? Yeesh.

Sound design was absolutely excellent. The soundtrack, while sparse, is very very good and I genuinely enjoyed most of the songs. Enemy noises, gun sounds, various sound effects that play when you score a satisfying headshot - great dopamine rush. The voice acting, though...well, it's not really amateur but it is pretty entertaining for all of the absolutely wrong reasons. If anything, the stiff delivery made it more entertaining than I thought.

For optimization, I have several complaints. First of all - poor controller support. Did not expect this - a console-to-PC port having abysmal controller support? How? This game was MADE for the GameCube, then ported to the PS2, which has a standard controller layout! Unfortunately, I had to play with keyboard and mouse this time. But poor controller support aside, I frequently noticed lots of micro-stutters, several instances of the game crashing on me, particularly in chapter 5-4, and the fact that I could not, for the life of me, get this game to run in native full screen on my 144hz monitor, so I had to run it in 1600x900 windowed just to play the game. Yeah, this port is rather shoddy without using any community-made patches to fix these.

[h1]Conclusion:[/h1]
Overall I enjoyed my time with Resident Evil 4, regardless of how tiring this game was to play between sessions. The game had its charm with the goofy voice acting and presentation but the engagingly difficult gameplay had me coming back and eventually finishing the game.

If you can stomach its flaws, like the control scheme, dated visuals and at times - poor boss design, I think you can have some genuine fun with this game, even without the remake.

Honestly, if a zoomer like me was able to enjoy this game regardless of its quirks, I think you could enjoy this game as well. Play Resident Evil 4, it's worth it.

First time in a long time I've been really blown away by a game like this. It's astounding how literally everything just [i]works[/i]. Of the many things [i]Resident Evil 4[/i] takes a stab at, there are few it doesn't excel in executing. The gameplay is fun and tense, the setpieces are a joy, the horror hits really hard when it's meant to, and every villain is just tons of fun to take down a peg. The villains are particularly fun because they're written like complete idiots, like everyone else in this game. The little phone calls between them and Leon are genuinely hilarious because it's like a competition between two losers trying to come up with the best insult (Leon always wins because his are the dumbest). And that just serves to make eventually taking them down all the more enjoyable, because you've really put a face to the baddie. It helps too that all the boss fights are generally great, even if do sometimes boil down to "get some distance then unload some strong ammo into them," which is why Krauser's bossfight is a real standout to me. He really puts to use everything you've learned up to that point, shooting certain points on enemies to stagger them, knowing how to take advantage of an enemy trying to protect themselves, even those corny as hell quicktime sequences. I just loved every second of that boss fight, even when I was ripping out my hair over the fact some weirdo goober decided to make "x" and "c" quicktime buttons when porting this. 

The story really is great fun, in part because of the aforementioned villains, but also because RE4 has some of the best pacing I've ever seen in a video game. You never linger anywhere too long, and once the game gets you used to navigating an area and its enemy types, it usually throws you a curveball by making you then spend the last bit of it escorting Ashley through it, adding another layer of gameplay to pay attention to along with everything you've learned. And on Ashley, I really love her inclusion in this. Her and Leon have the same kind of dog-brained conversations this game is full of, but they're pretty fun and cute since the two are really on the same side instead of trying to kill each other, and Ashley is just the right amount of whiney where it's funny and not annoying as hell. Even when I DID get annoyed at her screaming "LEON, HELP!!!!" while I was trying to solve a puzzle to get to her, I was never that mad because it felt like this time [i]I[/i] was the butt of the joke, there's no way they didn't make her screaming THAT grating on purpose. Her getting kidnapped consistently at the end of every chapter is great fun that really adds to that feeling of playing some schlocky action movie while also making it so Ashley isn't being annoying as hell while you try to work out the new enemies of each area. And the enemies are just great. Dodging, falling, just smacking the hell out of you, there's so much variety from the very start. Some have weapons they can either throw or just hit you with, some have chainsaws that can just instantly cut your head off, RE4 instantly teaches you to stay on your toes and always be ready for some dumb ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ that just comes out of nowhere and instakills you. If something looks like it'll immediately take all your health, it probably will, and you'd best keep your distance. 

Anyway, this review is already getting way too long for something absolutely no one will read so great game, probably my favorite ever.

It is almost miraculous how the mind manages to convince itself of its own logical infallibility, that it produces no wrong, that its product is the absolute objective truth.

I say this because the mind, in fact, is a powerful tool, a massively powerful tool, yet as amazing and profound as it is, it is also a dangerous trap, a lethal pitfall, inescapable for those ignorant of its unreliability, its flaws, its shortcomings, its innate fallacious nature.

The mind by itself cannot be relied upon, its products should be -until proven otherwise- treated as if they carry no logical weight. Why so?

Psychologically speaking, the mind is mostly working in favor of its owner, yet the problem lies in this: what the mind defines as “favor” may not align well with the pursuit of actual truth independent of bias. In other words, what the mind produces is subjective until proven to be objective by other sources or methods. 

The mind, again, is a powerful tool to its owner, yet when trying to use it to acquire truth, it is a dangerous trap because its owner is its priority, that is, protecting its owner’s psyche, their ego, their entity, all that takes precedence over what else exists.

This is where the hard-wired failsafe psychological defense mechanisms come into play. When the mind encounters a situation wherein not enough information is collected regarding the stimuli in question, or not enough experience is present to reach a sound and logical conclusion, it seeks to “fill the gap.” 

This is the crux of the issue, the mind observes the external world, which is rooted in objectivity, it processes these observations using what information it collected -what sensory stimuli it received-, it tries to “rationalize” what it observed using what experiences exist, and then it gives its conclusion. It cannot -most of the time- reach a pleasing conclusion, it cannot derive the truth, it cannot “see” the phenomena as they truthfully are. These “rationalizations” hold it back, they introduce bias, making the conclusion reached have some trace -however minor- of subjectivity, its reliability is put into question and further steps must be taken.

To reach truth, we can simply repeat, meaning we observe again, and again, we observe, and we let others observe, we collect, we compare, a more satisfying conclusion is reached, closer to the truth.

EXAMPLE: Water boils when put over a fire, Water boils when it’s hot, water boils when it reaches 100c, water boils when it reaches its boiling point (the temperature at which its vapor pressure is equal to the pressure of the gas above it.). Different levels of “truth.” The latter of which is the truest, which was reached by repeated experimentation, repeated observations, different perspectives.

This is the process of triangulation, when you approach an issue from perspectives other than your own, it lends to the credibility and reliability of your findings. It is not a method to be used in scientific settings alone, it can also be employed in all aspects of being.

All this above is a quick introduction to my resident evil 4 review, which will be brief and concise.

[h1] I Hate Elayne [/h1]

I played this game convinced it’s an action horror game, and rated it based on my experience with resident evil 2, an excellent action horror game I played previously. Comparing the two, one can reach a certain conclusion: RE4 indubitably has more action than RE2, yet it lacks in the horror department when contrasted with RE2.

And that was the basis of my evaluation of the game, more action, less horror. However, in doing so, I failed to use the methods I discussed in the intro -namely triangulation-, these methods I try to use as much as I can in everyday life. So how would approaching the rating from a different perspective change my opinion, I shall elaborate.

It is not action nor horror that I actually value the most in games, evident from the fact that most my favorite games are turn based RPGs that are old, sometimes very old, older than me personally.

What I favor in games is gameplay first and foremost, how the game controls, how tactical the game can get, how the game presents me problems and allows me to tackle them with a choice of which solution I deem best to use, which also lends to its replayability. 

The gameplay in RE4, while dated, one can see its influence on basically most 3rd person shooters nowadays. Granted, the vanilla controls had to be modded out for me to be able to play the game at all, but the big picture still stands. As for replayablity, I would say it has some potential, more than many a game, less than many others, even in its own franchise and genre. I think it sits in the middle, I’d replay it, but it certainly isn’t my first choice of game to replay.

Next criterion, player agency, that is how the game interacts with the decisions the player makes throughout the game. And here I must admit, it would be unfair to criticize the game for its lack of player agency since agency is associated mostly with the RPG genre which this game surely isn’t, and I won’t be evaluating it based on that fallacious assumption. In brief, I will ignore player agency and it will affect the final rating NOT at all.

Next on the list is the fun factor, and least important to me, the story. these factors come into play here so they will be discussed together. 

It cannot be denied that the story is lackluster, no character development, no engaging plot, nothing in the narrative itself stands out. A simple rescue mission. A generic special ops agent -who is on the Asperger’s spectrum-. A creepy locale. Basically, very rudimentary. But as I said, a story matters the least to me in a game, and here the other aspect to be discussed compensates for the shortcomings of the story.

As for the fun factor, it isn’t that much of a surprise to mention that this game barely takes itself seriously, especially when you dive deeper into this single character, Salazar. What serious tones and themes the game may have had is all thrown out the window the moment you encounter Salazar in his castle, who also has a giant statue of himself, which animates when you try to move away from and tries kill you. 

Herein lies the connection I want to make; the game sacrificed its ability to tell a compelling story in favor of a more comedic (satiric?) plot increasing the fun factor and originality, and again as I stated above, the story is the thing I would sacrifice first if it meant improving the other aspects

These criteria when used to evaluate RE4, paint a different picture, now the game is a fun, unique experience with good gameplay mechanics (revolutionary, at its time). This new conclusion is reached by simply shifting one’s perspective, looking at it from a different angle, appreciating details you never thought to consider at first glance. That is why critical thinking is a critical skill (hehe) to have.

And as a final word, this game I played and enjoyed, I don’t regret my time spent, and I would recommend it to all, it stands the test of time, a classic, mod it, the HD project is genuinely amazing. HOWEVER, Even with all the praise I gave this game, MUSHASHI كثير نفخها.

Resident Evil 4 is nine years old, and still the best action game I've ever played. It's still thrilling when I nail four Ganados with a single shotgun blast, still tense when I face down a relentless Iron Maiden before it impales me with deadly spikes. I'm on edge even when I know I'm safe, still creeped out by the foreboding pressure Resident Evil 4 constantly exerts through its thumping industrial soundtrack and grim environments.

Most of the time, this updated HD version of Resident Evil 4 is the best version of the game I've played, and I beat it on both the GameCube and the Wii. I wish it were perfect, but it's not quite there—occasional moments of slowdown and a few interface issues are minor flaws in an otherwise fantastic port.

If you've dodged RE4 in anticipation of a port like this, know that the story is cheesy and melodramatic in classic Resident Evil fashion. Curtain-haired hero Leon S. Kennedy lands in Spain to rescue the president's daughter from Los Ganados, infected villagers who stand in for zombies. What starts as ambiguously scary becomes increasingly insane as melodramatic figures like knife-wielding maniac Jack Krauser and tiny Napoleon man Ramon Salazar step into the frame.

Despite its age, Resident Evil 4 doesn't feels dated. Its best combat sequences are open-ended in a way we still rarely see in shooters, and I love the freedom of choosing how to approach that first house in the village, the cabin showdown with Luis, and the castle's grandest rooms.

Playing on the PC only makes the game better. I thought that the aiming precision of the mouse might make headshots too easy, leaving Leon's attache case brimming with unused rounds. But on normal difficulty, RE4 still feels remarkably balanced. Headshots are easier, yes, but tougher enemies can soak up the bullets, and swarms can still overwhelm me and cause me to miss plenty of headshots. That tuned-to-perfection over-the-shoulder camera angle keeps Leon vulnerable when I take aim. I jumped with surprise a couple times when Ganados snuck up on me from outside my field of view.

Capcom didn't build an FOV slider into this PC port, but even a small change to that field of view could ruin the fine line of empowerment and danger RE4's combat dances on. Capcom did include some basic PC options for adjusting key bindings and display resolution, though the game runs letterboxed on 16:10 monitors and doesn't let you customize each key in the options. And while mouse support works great for shooting, it hasn't been fully integrated with the the rest of the in-game interface. You can't use the mouse to move items around in the briefcase, and instead have to use a clunky combination of Backspace and the Page Up/Down buttons to pick up and rotate items around.

Those keys can't be remapped, which is annoying. Another quibble: two of the buttons used for quicktime events, X and C, are hard to press quickly when your fingers are poised over WASD. Thankfully, more important keys can be remapped, and I liked having the run button tied to my mouse for quick getaways. The Xbox 360 controller is also fully supported, including new in-game graphics for all of its buttons.

The most significant additions Capcom made to this version of Resident Evil 4—higher definition textures and a locked 60 fps framerate—are both adjustable in the graphics options settings. The game defaults to the new HD textures and 60 frames per second, but also includes the original textures and a 30 fps option.

I played the game at both 1920x1200 and 2560x1440 on two PCs, thanks to Steam Cloud support, and thought the character models and lighting held up well. They haven't been dramatically altered—higher resolution textures mean the characters and environments look sharp even at 1440p—but the models are still limited to their original polygon counts. Some environmental textures are mottled and ugly, others surprisingly detailed. And after playing at 60 fps, the original framerate feels comically sluggish.

There's a problem with that locked 60 fps, though—if anything causes the game to dip below 60, which happened to me multiple times in my playthrough, it starts moving in slow motion. Audio and video desynchronize. This typically happened to me when graphical effects like the heat waves around a torch appeared on screen, or when a ton of enemies crowded into my field of view. But I also sat through a pair of cutscenes at 40-50 fps, causing video to lag four or five seconds behind the audio. Another cutscene wasn't quite lip-synced properly, either, even though FRAPS said I was maintaining a solid 60 fps.

Most of this slowdown happened on an older Radeon 5970, but I experienced it once or twice on newer Radeon 7870 and R9 290X cards, too, with 2x anti-aliasing and motion blur enabled in the options. It shouldn't be this hard for a nine-year-old game to hold a solid 60 frames per second, and even the 5970 is a far more powerful GPU than what the GameCube had in 2005.

Even with intermittent slowdown issues on older hardware, I'd call this the definitive version of Resident Evil 4. It's clean and sharp at 1440p, mouse aiming feels fantastic without being game-breaking, and 60 fps feels as smooth as it should. And Resident Evil 4 itself feels as impeccably designed as ever, a high point against which other third-person shooters should be judged. If Capcom Frankensteins some 8K textures into it in another 10 years, I'll probably buy that version, too.

Well, come on, I don't need to explain anything about this game — it's RE4, a legendary title from the whole Resident Evil saga. Since Capcom released the new trailer for the remake, I have been playing it and giving it another try, and it was totally worth it. I have played both modes, the normal mode and professional. I took almost 30 hours to complete both, since the game on professional gets really difficult with boss fights and ammo is scarce.

If you don't know about this game, let me explain a little bit about it. You start as the main character, Leon S. Kennedy, a former police officer and survivor of the Raccoon City incident, now working as a special government agent after surviving all the disasters in Raccoon City and being one of the bravest police officers.

Years after the incident, Leon starts working for the government and gets involved in new top-secret missions. The one we deal with in this game is rescuing the President’s daughter, Ashley Graham, who was kidnapped by an unknown group in a rural town in Spain. While traveling there, we start searching for witnesses who can give us information about the location of our rescue target. When we try to talk to one of the villagers and show him a picture of the girl we are looking for, we notice strange behavior. He tells us to leave and suddenly reacts in a hostile way, attacking us, forcing us to neutralize him.

After this confrontation, we contact our mission partner, Ingrid Hunnigan, to report that something strange is happening in the village. As we finish the radio call, we hear noises outside, screams, and the car that brought us there being smashed against something. The two Spanish officers who helped us reach the village are gone, alerting us that this situation will not be handled easily. We have no clue what is going on with the villagers, but we have a mission to accomplish at any cost.

Since the game is cheap during the Steam Winter Sale, you should give it a try if you have never played RE4. I’m pretty sure you will have a great time experiencing the puzzles and getting jump-scared while running away from spooky bosses and enemies that can appear right behind you.

Pros:

Good puzzle minigames.

Amazing environments.

Intense enemy and boss fights.

The difficulty is really balanced whether you play on Normal or Professional.

They added great minigames and extras, so after finishing the game you still have more fun things to do.

Cons:

Dude, I know almost everyone says this, but Ashley… Ashley is a pain in the ass. She is always body-blocking you and not letting you shoot during action scenes. She also dies easily, and you have to move with her everywhere, which is really uncomfortable because you have to worry about both yourself and Ashley.

Some bugs with textures and screen settings, but this isn’t very important; it only happened to me once or twice.

I hope you guys liked my review!

Legendary. The controls are a bit wonky these days but once you get them down it's the same ole Resident Evil 4. Which is to say, it continues to be one of the greatest games of all time. Is it because of the story? Hell no, RE4 has quite literally the most forgettable story not only out of Resident Evil but fiction in general. I've been playing it since release and this has remained true to this day. Guess what? Honestly doesn't change much; RE4 is one of the greatest games by virtue of gameplay alone. It may not be as revolutionary anymore but it's still extremely fun and engaging. It has excellent gunplay, a wide variety of semi-intelligent enemies, cool bosses, awesome weapons, and massive replayability. It's one of those games that I can just pick up and play. Plenty of extra modes and Mercenaries, but I've only ever really cared about the main campaign. 

RE4 has made an indeliable mark on the gaming landscape much like GTA and Skyrim etc. It's DNA is everywhere, in many games....but if you haven't played the original then I highly recommend you check out one of the common ancestors of modern gaming.

A TERRIFYING PIECE OF HISTORY IN GAMING

You play as Leon Kennedy, a special agent sent by the President of America himself to save the president's kidnapped daughter from a rural place unknown to man. There you will encounter enemies from normal looking villagers to mutated creatures and monsters that are both scary and dangerous to fight. Its is up to you as Leon, to save to president's daughter from the horde that kept her.

I love this game. This is one of the games that pulled me from start to finish. While some games that I love had a slow start like Yakuza 0 and even Monster Hunter, Resident Evil 4 kept me hook from the moment I pushed the analog stick. This game is almost 20 years old and still holds up till this day. Really says alot on how much craft, effort, and passion is put in this game.

Resident Evil 4 takes a more action approach to the survival horror genre. You are now able to execute flashy moves on stunned enemies, and do more gunning down them than running away. Being a piece of gaming history, this is the first game to have an over-the-shoulder perspective in the third person shooter genre. Unlike the fixed perspectives from past RE games, you have more freedom here to look around and shoot enemies. Future games especially third person shooters start taking the perspective RE4 had, which is a good innovation.

Although you will gun down enemies alot, they are really scary and will have some events that will scare you alot. The place you venture really feels claustrophobic and dark. Plus, some events are quick-timed ones, or require you to engage in certain mechanics. This is a refreshing take on the genre, innovating the horror parts of the genre. Although scary, it never felt repulsive. I want to venture deeper in the village, although I know tough creatures are probably waiting to maul me.

Other than venturing deeper in the village, you will also encounter many puzzles to unlock more stuff. Either a new area or a new item. A staple of the Resident Evil series are the puzzles. Other than doinc puzzles, once you reach to the presidents daughter, she will be an NPC for you to always keep an eye out. A good way to not be always on the offensive when fighting. You have to make sure she's always safe. For a 2004 game, the AI for her is great. She reacts appropriately in all of your actions. And sometimes have funny interactions. I've heard some complaints about her being a burden throughout the gameplay, but I never felt that way about her. If she keeps dying, just order her to wait while you fight the enemies. Her death will result in a failure by the way, since that is the main goal of the entire game which is to "save the princess".

The story is just that, saving the daughter. Throughout the journey there will be reveals about the dark element of the game.  Also, many cheesey and charming moments sprinkled throughout the game. The voice acting is very 2004. I love the story not because of how deep or intricate the plot it, but how fun and entertaining it is in a horror genre.

I just really love this game. The remake announcement kinda made me worry since there are lot of parts of this game are already perfect. But seeing RE2R and its success, I'm hoping for the best. I recommend newcomers to take the game on easy, since that is my initial playthrough. Currently doing normal mode. But if you can handle and master its mechanics, Normal is always the way.

Overall, fear is good entertainment.

Resident Evil 4, originally released in 2005 by Capcom, revolutionized the survival horror genre and left an indelible mark on the gaming industry. This critically acclaimed entry propelled the Resident Evil franchise into new territory, delivering a heart-pounding, intense experience that remains unmatched to this day.

Resident Evil 4 follows the story of Leon S. Kennedy, a former Raccoon City police officer, as he embarks on a rescue mission to save the President's daughter from a mysterious cult in a remote European village. The narrative brilliantly blends horror, action, and suspense, immersing players in a twisted tale filled with unexpected twists and revelations. The atmospheric storytelling and the sinister ambiance of the game keep players on the edge of their seats from start to finish.

Resident Evil 4 introduced a groundbreaking gameplay formula that redefined the survival horror genre. Adopting an over-the-shoulder perspective, it offered an unprecedented level of control and immersion. The game's intuitive controls and fluid mechanics allowed for precise aiming and strategic combat, creating a heightened sense of tension and vulnerability. The intense encounters with grotesque creatures known as Los Ganados provided thrilling and adrenaline-pumping gameplay moments.

The inventory management system, weapon upgrades, and resource scarcity added a strategic layer to gameplay, forcing players to make difficult choices and adapt to ever-changing circumstances. Puzzles and environmental interactions seamlessly integrated with the gameplay, enhancing the overall immersion and keeping players constantly engaged.

Resident Evil 4 showcased impressive visuals for its time, with detailed character models, atmospheric lighting, and meticulously designed environments. From eerie villages and sprawling castles to underground laboratories, each location exudes a sense of dread and foreboding. The haunting sound design, coupled with the atmospheric soundtrack, heightens the tension and contributes to an immersive horror experience.

Boss battles in Resident Evil 4 are iconic, presenting memorable encounters against towering and grotesque creatures that push players to their limits. The game expertly balances moments of horror, action, and exploration, creating an unforgettable atmosphere that has become synonymous with the Resident Evil franchise.

Resident Evil 4's impact on the gaming industry cannot be overstated. Its innovative gameplay mechanics, cinematic presentation, and masterful storytelling set a new standard for the survival horror genre. It influenced numerous subsequent titles and inspired a wave of over-the-shoulder action games. Even today, its legacy can be seen in modern games that strive to replicate its intensity and fear-inducing gameplay.

Resident Evil 4 stands as a timeless masterpiece, delivering an unparalleled horror experience that transcends its era. Its gripping narrative, revolutionary gameplay mechanics, and atmospheric world-building cement its status as a landmark title in gaming history. Whether you are a longtime fan of the Resident Evil series or a newcomer to the franchise, Resident Evil 4 is an absolute must-play, showcasing the very best of what survival horror has to offer. Prepare to be enthralled, terrified, and captivated by the relentless horrors that await you in this iconic game.

After the fixed cameras and jank of Code Veronica, I was longing to return to the polished and over-the-shoulder gameplay of the RE 2 & 3 Remakes. Well, along comes RE 4 to scratch that itch(mostly).

First, the negatives. The original aiming system was incredibly floaty and unreliable, resulting in less stress and more frustration(thankfully, the remaster fixed this issue with an updated system). Also, the amount of QTE's was just stupid. In an interactive movie style of game, I feel that they are warranted, as there isn't much else in the form of gameplay for your Walking Deads and Detroit: Become Humans. But in a game that has aged so well on many other fronts, the simple amount of QTE's is a blemish on an otherwise extremely modern experience. Also, as tired of an argument as this is, the amount of screaming from Ashley is so annoying. Lastly, I personally feel that once you reach The Island, both the quality and the scares seriously decline(aside from one short area). It isn't bad by any means, but by the last hour, it's an RE game in name only, and symptomatic of the series' temporary decline.

But aside from those nitpicks, it is quite apparent why it rocked the gaming industry like it did. The gameplay is incredibly smooth, while still using tank controls to instill a sense of tension and fear through the vulnerability they create. The story is wonderfully simple, allowing for more focus on the flamboyant characters and scary thrills. The intensity of facing the Ganados and all sorts of abominations, humanoid or no, results in a experience that, up until it's last act, deftly mixes horror, suspense, and heart-pounding action. And graphically, while not as impressive as RE 0 or REmake, it is still incredible how well it's aged(may I also recommend downloading the RE 4 HD Project, it restores so much fidelity to the textures in this game). If it weren't for REmake and RE2make, and it's third act slouch, this would be my favorite game in the series so far.

This isn't the game you remember.

Washed out, muddy art style, incredibly clunky controls, adaptive difficulty that punishes you for doing well, endlessly spawning enemies, awkward inventory management....

I was always in a minority of people who thought Resident Evil 4 was just okay, even when I played it in 2005. The original PS1 games were scarier. They featured beautiful, unique environments instead of brown shacks and grey stone. Inventory management served a purpose, forcing you to plan your routes and loadouts carefully. Even with tank controls, combat and movement felt snappier. Puzzles were more involved.

Resident Evil 4 pioneered over-the-shoulder aiming, and I think it's a big part of why it felt so revolutionary to everyone at the time. But for as important as it was to video games, it plays like a prototype of something other developers would figure out in the years that followed. The Resident Evil remake of 2002 looks and feels better. Resident Evils 5 and 6 look and feel better. This game has been left behind.

I've heard from a few media sources that RE4 doesn't need a remake, but trust me, those people are looking through rose-colored glasses. Maybe the Wii and VR versions hold up better, but this PC iteration doesn't do any justice to Resident Evil 4's reputation.

I'm not rose-tinted or nostalgia-blinded, I've never played this game to completion until now, but even I can state with confidence that Resident Evil 4 is a triumph among this entire medium, and a shining example of superb game design.

A hallmark of creative enemy encounters, fluid combat, rollercoaster design and perfect pacing, this game stands the test of time and more than earns its place among the list of 'best games ever made.'

[h1]Third Person at its Finest[/h1]
Combat in RE4 is glorious, and restricting the player's movement while giving them just enough freedom to maneuver effectively makes for a unique gameplay experience - one that punctuates the 'survival' aspect in survival horror. This isn't Gears of War. Leon moves slowly, can't move while he's aiming, and there's no crosshair. But, these aren't negatives. RE4's controls reward careful positioning and intelligent play. There's no get-out-of-jail free card here, if you're too close to the enemy, you're going to get hurt. Being effective in this game means thinking constantly, repositioning properly and being pinpoint accurate. If you're new to RE4's controls, use a keyboard & mouse and be patient. It will take some time to learn. After a couple hours when you're finally competent, however... it feels fantastic. There is a reason why people play and replay this game over and over - it feels so good, and unlike any other.

As for the combat - this again, is different from Gears of War and most other TPS you're probably used to. The weapon types are highly specialized and where you aim on the enemy's body matters just as much as hitting them in the first place.  Headshots to stun, repeated headshots for a clean kill. Too many enemies? Shoot one in the leg, run up to them and do a roundhouse kick for a crowd control move. This works especially well for ammo conservation, with the third step being to knife 'em while they're grounded. If the enemies are throwing axes at you, Leon can shoot them straight outta the air. Surrounded? The shotgun doesn't just hit all the enemies in front of you, it forcibly blows them off their feet, stunning all of them for a quick getaway. Rifles are perfect for long range headshots and make for effective boss-killers. And, oh my, there's a lot of weapons to pick from. There is a ton of depth to combat that'll keep you entertained for multiple playthroughs, and a quick look at someone playing Mercenaries mode on YouTube will demonstrate how high the skill ceiling really is.

[h1]Aesthetic[/h1]
RE4 oozes style. Going from a dark forested Spanish village, to the cold, gray halls of a castle, and finishing off in an industrial concrete-bunker of an island, the world is so immersive, so effective at making you feel alone in a strange place. I can guarantee you these settings feel unique. The music accompanying these places is both haunting & groovy in its own way. Tying it all together with a parasite-infested-occultist theme is pretty neat while keeps things consistent. Staying rooted in horror with its visuals and audio is one of the many successes here, and the lack of it is dearly missed in the two sequels after this one. Coming away from the game, I have a very clear image in my head when I think of the words 'Resident Evil 4' and that can't be said for the majority of media.

[h1]Pacing[/h1]
First, I'd like to state what I mean by this. Pacing - what is it, really? To me, it's the flow of a piece of media. The combination and timing of different events and surprises. We've all been there when we thought a movie spent too much time on slow dialogue, or when the action was so fast, we blinked and couldn't even see it. Pacing is the rhythm of a work. RE4 is one of the best examples of pacing done perfectly in a game. 

The game doesn't rudely interrupt your fun like many cinematic games in recent memory. Keeping the focus on gameplay, studded with unique combat encounters & exhilarating set pieces offset by sweet cutscenes, entertaining dialogue and cool snippets of codec calls, everything is kept fresh up until the finish line. RE4 never focuses too much one one particular piece, and when you're having a great time, it decides keeps its hands idle, never interrupting your streak. The well balanced pacing makes for a clean symphony of play. Too many games now hold your hand and take the controller away when you're enjoying yourself, and it's a shame when this game clearly set the bar so long ago.

[h1]Conclusion[/h1]
The quintessential example of a game done right - it's no surprise it inspired a generation of creators and spawned imitators down the line, which some of them got it, while others (even Capcom's own sequels) were poor attempts to recreate what made this one special. My final thoughts? Sony Interactive Entertainment needs to take a look back at this one and remind themselves of what makes a game *fun*. Screw Naughty Dog and The Last of Us for screwing everything up and making creators forget the lessons Resident Evil 4 taught us. Gameplay is king, not walking around slowly listening to exposition. That is all.

I have a complicated history with Resident Evil 4. For a lot of people it was an instant hit, for me it was a frustrating experience. I didn’t “get” the appeal of the game for several years and only after several attempts, and because of the fact that the game influenced so many others, which gave me necessary experience to understand what it as going for, I started enjoying it. I still have plenty of criticism towards it, mind you, but nowadays replaying RE4 is an enjoyable experience for me. And I’ve replayed it many times over many different platforms, including this 2014 “Ultimate HD Edition”, which remains the best version of the game to play.

In fact, the main reason for my revisit this time was the fact that the version got even better due to fan work – I wanted to finally experience out the fantastic RE4HD mod, that more than lived up to my expectations. And in addition to that, wanted to have some fun with the recently released randomizer mod that adds some fun chaos to the overall experience. As I was about to play, the RE4 Remake got officially announced as well, so I decided that it might be the best time to revisit the original. And even in 2022 it’s still an extremely fun game… that really hates you.

Today you might have trouble comprehending just how important RE4 was, not just for the Resident Evil series, but action games in general. It didn’t just invent a new type of horror fueled third person shooter that Capcom dubbed “survival action”, it redefined what a third person action can be. It wasn’t alone, of course, nor were all of its ideas truly revolutionary – a lot of its gameplay was built on the concepts explored by other games (including previous RE titles). And yet, it’s one of those games which still influence the games of today.

Luckily, not via its QTEs… Those were praised when the game was new, by the way. As a thing that makes you “keep your guard” even during cutscenes, but if all else, what I’d love to see in a modern update to RE4 is the option to remove them or turn them into a single button press. They don’t work correctly without the mods on higher framerates too, by the way, requiring some insane mashing speed to count, but even when fixed they are a chore.

Also, the fix does not change the fact that the “dodge” QTEs are utter garbage, as the game often doesn’t let you hit/shoot/stagger the enemy of the attack you’re supposed to dodge when the prompt is up – the game will just ignore your input. It’s another frustrating leftover from the era, even if the idea of dodges is fantastic. It’s just that it got implemented much better in later RE titles, like the RE3 2020 or the Revelations sub-series. Fun fact, though – as Hideki Kamiya revealed a long time ago in his Bayonetta playthrough, Shinji Mikami wanted this dodge mechanic in the very first Resident Evil as a defense against Hunters. They just couldn’t figure out how to do it in 96, but eventually did it in 2005.

I really wanted to bring these up just because they might be the few elements that even the die-hardest fans of the game might dislike. Because the rest of RE4 clearly knows what it wants to be and how it wants to play. And the result is mad fun. Often “not fair”, but really fun. The concept of “fairness” in games is complicated in general, but thing about RE4 is that it loves to cheat to get a hit on the player. It was the game that introduced the “Difficulty Adjustment” concept (a few other games tried this too at the time, like SiN Episodes: Emergence) and it was willing to do it in either direction – to bias the gameplay for the player, or (if it considered you to play too good) towards the enemies. As a result, even apart from the poor dodge mechanic implementation, you could get absolutely stupid hits – through walls, from across the room, from a different height level entirely, – even without being aware of the danger. Tense, fun and unpredictable for an adequately prepared player who’s playing casually. But a potential failure loop for anyone not prepared for this, or someone who’s trying to play on the hardest difficulty or doing a challenge run.

Yet, people still do challenge runs. Still play on Professional. Still enjoy the mods like the aforementioned randomizer that can start you with an egg, while all of the crows around you are chainsaw ladies that can kill you with one hit. Because the core of RE4 is incredibly tight even in how it’s intentionally rude towards the players. The mods, like the fantastic RE4HD mod, just make the rest of the game shine better and look less outdated. Speaking of – a lot of locations with that HD mod look stunning even by modern standards. Even though the title was utilizing rendering tricks that are outdated today, the results are fantastic. Shame, it’s not an official part of the game. Or part of a NightDive or Pixel Remaster style remaster, with an engine port and quality of life improvements for the modern age, but the rest of the game left as is. Apart from QTEs, screw those.

Resident Evil 4 is still incredibly fun today and the PC Ultimate HD Edition is the best version there is. It’s not perfect, neither are the mods – there can be potential crashes and glitches related to them. And the controls (either keyboard and mouse, or the gamepad) do feel off, no matter how much you tweak them or mod them. And if you’ve never played RE4 before – it will beat you up a few times, that’s part of the experience. That’s just how the game is. It has a steep learning curve, steeper than I’d argue it should’ve been. But it’s worth it, even in 2022.

Resident Evil 4 is one of the most influential video games of modern gaming, and one of the greatest games of all time. Released in 2005, it included features such as "over the shoulder" aiming, weapon upgrades and quick time events- all new to the Resident Evil series and still fresh in gaming (there were upgrades for guns in the earlier RE games, but not to the level of customization in RE4.) It wasn't the first game to utilize these features, but it was the first to make them good and become synonymous with the Resident Evil series- along with other games. I first played RE4 back in 2006- I initially was not impressed by the commercials. I was used to the fixed camera, "tank" controls of the original games, and this looked like an action movie. "This isn't Resident Evil" I said. Well, thanks to my good friends Mark and David, who rented it on their GameCube- I started playing and was immediately hooked. This was something special, and I knew it.

Since then, I have completed the game many many times over- unlocking every single thing, on every platform. I have the platinum trophy on PSN, and about to finish it for Steam. Even to this day I still find new things- did you know that the ganados can kill the merchant on the Island? I killed one with a lit stick of dynamite, and it exploded and killed the merchant. I've upgraded every gun and done playthroughs with them- I have attempted "pacifist runs" (only killing the bare necessity of enemies.) Speed runs. All five stars on Mercenaries. Oh I forgot to mention- this also comes with all the bonus content from the PS2 release. This includes "Separate Ways," which is Ada Wong's side of the story, "Assignment: Ada" which is a non-canonical mini-game, and "The Mercenaries" coming back from RE3 and one of the best unlockable games ever. You get a lot of bang for your buck with this collection- I see it on sale for $5 frequently, and it will provide you with many hours of entertainment.

This game has been praised countless times over and is considered one of the greatest, so I am not going into great detail about the story or gameplay. What I will say, is that this game single handedly saved the Resident Evil series, which was quickly becoming irrelevant and losing interest by the gaming community. It adds an action flair that is welcomed- while still retaining the horror and creep elements of the earlier games. There are still plenty of jump scares and graphic sights- but you feel much more in control in this game. Almost like Ash Williams in Army of Darkness- he's already experienced all of this horrible stuff, but now your armed to the teeth and ready to take it on.

The big question is- has this game aged well? It is now almost 18 years old and what I will say is...yes, absolutely, it has aged well. There are components of it that are not great, admittedly. While the quick time events were interesting back in 2005, they are now annoying and at times even frustrating- slowing down the game and using the same two patterns. For younger gamers, the controls may seem stiff and in a way, tank-like as you cannot strafe or move while shooting. This can cause issues for combat- but this has been remedied in later games in the series. Luckily too- the developers programmed the game so that the enemies are not too fast and you can't react in time. Also...the escort parts with Ashley are irritating at best and infuriating at worst. Another vestige of old gaming, which has all but died out today.

Resident Evil 4 is my personal favorite video game of all time, and I highly recommend purchasing it (especially with the upcoming remake.) It has been ported to so many formats that you can probably play it somewhere, even on your own cell phone. I love to see how it continues to inspire and influence later games, and I will always cherish the memories it gave me.

as for the overall game i'll review it without spoilers. 
[b]Controls:[/b]
it's originally an old console port, so I wouldn't suggest playing it with a mouse and keyboard at least when you don't need to aim perfectly in a given amount of time, get yourself a Controller even a cheap one will do, at first it might be confusing but you will eventually get used to it, in the other hand you won't be able to move while aiming in that game which could be confusing to some of today's players and without forgetting, you will be dealing with QTE at times but nevertheless it would still be an acceptable journey for most people. 
[b]Gameplay and difficulty:[/b]
RE4 was the evolution of the third person gameplay and opened the door for many great titles we have witnessed over the years, and it's a great mix between horror and action.
the game also has a fun inventory system and many upgradable weapons, I had a great time buying from merchant and customizing them.
as a side advice your knife is your friend against common enemies or when you have a chance relay on it alongside with the kicks and that can save you ammo for the hardest fights.
the game can be frustrating at times for starters but it will be a sweet walk once you master it.

[b]Soundtrack and sound design:[/b]

Resident Evil 4 is one of my favorite games. I seem to say that a lot, but honestly I think about the game nearly everyday. It isn't a huge exaggeration either. It might not be everyday, but it is damn near most. Playing the game on the Wii with my brother are some of my most precious memories. Us sitting in the living room with the surround sound boosting the voices of the Los Illuminados.

Now I may love this game, but it does have many problems. I enjoy the story, the movement, music / sound design, etc. But nearly everything I just mentioned has either not aged well or wasn't amazing to start with.

The story has some weird plot holes, like how Leon survives Raccoon city and then six years later his first job for the president happens to be an Umbrella type mission. When it never seemed to be proposed as one. All of Assignment Ada doesn't really tie in super well. Luis's story was cut short by making you have to read his important points. Lastly he dialog is really cheesy, yes it is funny and part of what makes RE4 so good, but it just doesn't fit the universe very well. With that said, without this type of dialogue it wouldn't be as good as it was.

The tank controls feel good. I hate tank controls normally but not have a fixed camera angle helps out a ton. Aiming on a controller sucks but it is kind of intended to be that way. With a mouse it is so much easier, but movement then is really bad. For me that is. Luckily I was able to switch freely between the two. Movement with controller and aiming with mouse when I felt it was needed. Did make the game a lot easier tho.

The music and sound design show classic Resident Evil feels. The save room / type writter themes make you feels so comfortable after just watching Leon get decapitated multiple times by Dr. Salvador. The Island does have some problems tho, the music can be a bit too much and the Ganados are incredibly bass boosted. I know that they have a parasite in them, doesn't mean they need to break the microphones to get the voicelines.

The levels are all pretty linear which is perfectly fine. It is a linear game. Even with that, occasional backtracking isn't annoying because they put new enemies in those areas making it feel less empty.

Overall there are many things I love about this game and the series. But I have to mention its flaws. They did make some sexist lines in this title, but the did remove them in the VR version which is pretty cool. Hopefully the remake does the game justice and keeps the same quirky fun feeling of RE4.

Resident Evil 4 is one of these titles that sits among the top 10 best video games ever made and released to this day. It essentially inspired countless games released years after it and pretty much brought change to a franchise that had difficulty innovating at the time.

You play as Leon S. Kennedy, 6 years after the catastrophic events of Raccoon City that led to its destruction by the US Government in order to stop the T-Virus from spreading across the country. The former rookie cop is now an agent working directly for the President, whom sent him to save his daughter from her kidnappers, in a remote village somewhere in rural Spain.

This game is filled with action, intense moments as well as a very disturbing and eerie vibe at times. The levels are extremely varied, from a village to a castle, or even a mine or a military island complex. The story and humour is a bit over the place but I personally enjoyed it. As much as the controls can seem clunky at times, you very easily and rapidly get used to it and it turns into a very fun game.

Not only does the game comes with a pretty sizeable campaign, but you also get to experience another set of campaign where you can play as Ada Wong, as well as the famous Mercenaries game mode where you can play a few interesting characters with their own abilities and loadouts.

It's a must-have and you must play it, especially if you are planning on going through the Resident Evil franchise like I did. There are many people who consider it to be the best RE game, and even many who don't necessarily agree still consider it to be a masterpiece.

One of the best Resident Evil games, if not the best. I've yet to play the other 3, the classics, at the time of me writing this. I'd say you should buy this game over the remake. Why? It's cheaper, and the difference between the two are small, unless you're a total nerd like I am. This game has so much charm that comes from the era it was made in. I feel like the remake just doesn't capture any of that charm. I also don't entirely understand why this game needed a remake; same logic applies to the dead space remake as well. It didn't need one, as both games aged gracefully, albeit for some relatively small hiccups here and there, which could be patched out or fixed, but as we all probably know, patches don't sell as well as entire remakes do. Do whatever you want with your money. I don't really care. 

Anyways, back to this game. It's just the gift that keeps on giving! It's got so much to offer besides the main campaign, such as:


-Mercenaries mode, where you can play as a select few but unique characters across 4 maps from the main campaign. In this gamemode you have to rake up as many bodies as you can before the timer runs out. If you do this VERY well, you get to unlock a new character!

-Seperate Ways which serves as an expansion to the main campaign, one in which you get to play as Ada and see the way the story plays out in her perspective.

-Assignment Ada isn't anything special but it's still pretty fun to go through. It doesn't have a merchant either, but I'd argue it's still worth playing if you want a decent challenge. In this gamemode, you have to collect 5 Las Plagas samples and contact your rescue chopper. It's slightly more challenging than the other modes, except for maybe mercenaries, but it's still fun nonetheless.


I would also recommend playing RE4 2005 with the HD Project mod, as the default upscaled textures just aren't very good. It's faithful to the game's original artstyle and it also provides an excellent visual overhaul for those who might want it.

Inventory management, solid. Ammo is sparse, health is sparse, grenades are few and far between. Limiting the ammo makes you try out a lot of the weapons that you normally wouldn't.

Combat is solid. Just shoot them in the head until they die. You can stun them and kick them to get more easy shots off, or you can shoot their knees to suplex them.

Graphics are solid. Plays like a charm on the Steam Deck. Works a lot better than most newer games. The default settings are perfect. The animations of the cutscenes are lifelike, including subtle realistic keyframes such as in the car ride at the start of the game.

The collectables are solid. Treasures can be combined with other treasures for more reward, or can be sold separately for quick cash. They are out of the way, but give you a lot of money that can be used to upgrade your guns. Speaking of which,

The upgrades system is solid. The game's upgrade path, be it literally upgrading your weapons or buying new ones, scales well with the pace of the game. No enemies feel like they are too tough to beat as you can always pull out grenades or a rocket launcher. Defeating enemies is more of a choice of how much you want to spend on the supplies.

That's basically what the game is. It's a solid game. But this game is solid like how a jawbreaker is solid. Yes, a jawbreaker might take 24 hours to chew, and the whole time it tastes good, but the whole game is just... candy. The metaphor for a jawbreaker is that it's sweet and long, but the main downside is it's just so solid and unenjoyable. Let's get to the downsides of all of those solid bits.

Inventory management is solid, but it's a huge waste of time. You'll cycle through a full inventory of items every chapter, so in the end it just seems like a waste of time. Of the 24 hours, I have spent at least 4 hours in the inventory, just moving things around. That seems like a complement to the mesmerizing inventory system, and it is, but it just goes to show that I'd rather move perishable items into a nice neat row than continue playing the game.

Combat is solid. Just shoot them in the head until they die, but do it while having the absolute worst aiming system I have ever seen in any game. This game has tank controls that are worse than tank controls. On controller, the movement and the aiming is done with the left stick while peeking is done with the right. You'd think it would be better on mouse and keyboard, but it's worse. The mouse is so bad that the main menu is plain unusable because they apply some sort of mouse acceleration to it. Same thing applies to in game aiming. I turned off the mouse acceleration in the config, and it's a little better (the acceleration is still there for some reason), but there is still ~100ms input lag for the mouse. If this game had raw mouse input, and gotten rid of its tank controls, then maybe it would be an 8/10. Max Payne 3 has a mostly over the shoulder style gameplay, except with common sense controls. That one is an 8/10 with a more linear core gameplay and worse in some places than RE4.

Graphics are solid. I'd like for there to be ultra wide support, or higher frame rate support. Yes it's a game from 2005 and I'm talking about fairly new standards, but in a port made in 2014, I feel I can expect much more. With a little customizing, 1440p, 8x MSAA and 16x anisotropic filtering can make it look like it was made in 2010.

The collectables are solid, but after you realized that you missed some treasure and can never go back to it for the fourth time, you start to not care about them anymore. What's 30000 extra pasetas when I have 5000000? In the jawbreaker analogy, it's like if the jawbreaker had optional Kinder Surprises that required an extra 5 minutes to assemble, and the reward for assembling it is 5 minutes of struggling taken off of the jawbreaker. The complementing nature of collectables and the upgrades to form the difficulty curve is interesting, but that's like saying that having to grind in Final Fantasy an absurd amount of time interesting, or that the knife game has an interesting difficulty curve because as the song speeds up it gets progressively harder. All of that may technically true, but interesting does not equal fun.

The upgrades system is solid, but is it really fun to be a able to throw 3 grenades at a boss' feet and insta kill it? Is there ever any challenge if you can just wish it away at any time? Grenades are super OP, like they should be to be honest. They are also sparse, which is also good. I said that it's good because you get a choice at how to spend your supplies, but sometimes there isn't really a choice. No way am I going to throw a grenade at a straggler, so there is no other point to use them. So I'm forced to one shot the bosses, but I can't get past a lot of the slow paced combat. I'd complain about all of the different weapons and upgrades, but to be honest, I did earn them. It's not too OP when I did go through the work of selling hard stolen treasure. Plus switching between different weapons, using their unique strong suits to kill enemies is basically what DOOM is famous for and it works well. The only way to get multiple good unique weapons with powerful upgrades is to treasure hunt for hours.

That gameplay balance gives the game a 5/10 by itself. Pretty standard solid gameplay loop of get treasure, shoot guys, do fun bosses. 
-2 for terrible controls
+1 for good graphics
+1 for good performance
+1 for the excellent inventory system.

Not much I can say about about RE4 that most of you don't already know. RE4 is a 3rd person survival horror game that made it's debut back in 2005. I first played this game on my friends Nintendo Gamecube and begged my parents for a Playstation 2 copy for Christmas that same year. I later obtained the first PC port of the game for the potential MOD support and higher resolution. I have probably completed the main story a half a dozen times and 100% mercenaries mode twice. I'll be honest that when they announced the HD version of this game I wasn't to invested in it. I can appreciate the effort that Capcom was putting in to upscale the textures and try to make the game more modern but I just wasn't that impressed to go out and buy the game for a 3rd time, especially since the older PC port still runs fine and can have it's resolution manipulated by editing the config file. All of that changed when I stumbled onto the "Re4HD" project and saw the love and dedication that Albert and Cris the mods creators put into it. This whopping 37+GB MOD breaths new life into the game and doesn't just use upscaled textures but photorealistic pictures taken from the vary sources and locations that where used. So if your not already sold by playing the game that flipped the franchise on it's head and set something of a standard for Resident Evil games in the future, then I would at least invest in this iteration to check out the MOD that was 8 years in the making and definitely gives it more than a fresh coat of paint.

[h1] Review[/h1] 
I really liked the original Resident evil games. The unique adventure type gameplay with some action. The resource management and some puzzle solving is a really rewarding gameplay loop. I played this one a couple of times but never had the time to finish it. As the franchise didn’t die and kept being reinvented making it fresh all the time, I felt obliged to play this one too.

[u]Gameplay[/u]
Its interesting that the game initially started with a fixed camera angle development that changed into what It is now. I’m all for spicing things up all the time while keeping the initial vision of the game intact, not like the stuff the fallout series did. 

Here you have tank controls in third person mode, with a heavy focus on action. This is even in cutscenes the case, where you are always on the edge never knowing when a QTE prompt comes up that might kill you if you put your controller away, or keyboard how I preferred this game.

I really like the keyboard controls more, mouse aiming is just way much more fun, albeit QTE have weird buttons. Mouse prompts are fine, but the other two buttons often used are x and c for some reason.  Odd choice, you get used to it. Or don’t and use a controller. I didn’t mind it that much.

The game improved on the resource aspect, making you not only manage your items but also your inventory space in a grid system over your suitcase, which can grow in size if you upgrade it from the trader. Which is a neat choice, puzzles and exploring mostly reward you with additional loot via money, treasures or items that you can sell. Upgrading your weapons is fun adding a rewarding gameplay loop ontop of the existing one.

Combat is now more action focused, you can actually really see where you’re aiming but it’s still not too easy to fight enemies due to the restrictive camera and movement. Generally, an improvement albeit i miss that we probably never going to get a fixed camera angle resident evil anymore. 

There are really neat bossfights that are ruined by  adding  a one hit kill rocket launcher into the game. You find one and can buy one at anytime (albeit the price is too good/cheap for what it offers, basically skipping a bossfight completely). 

Saving is done after chapters or at typewrites, you can save infinite number of times, no cartridges needed.  Balancing wise its totally fine but is more on the easier side. Except the rocket launcher issue I mentioned I liked it overall.

There is also the issue that the game is basically a huge escort quest. About 4/10 of the game you need to take care of Ashley. Some absolutely don’t like that but I didn’t mind as they programmed her in a way that she is rather a gameplay aspect than an annoyance. She can die and need to heal, during combat she sticks to you and you can hide her aswell. If you aim at her she will jump to the ground so you wont hit her(and you can if you want a quick game over). Its quite unique and I liked that aspect.

My biggest negative aspect would be the liniarity and lack of interconnectivity of the map which i really liked in re 1-2.

[u]Story[/u]
I really like the initial plot of the game, saving the presidents daughter in some rural Spanish village where a parasitic virus turned the people into zombie like creatures with a certain degree of consciousness. The game turns into something really, really weird. I mean you meet Ada Wong at some point, wearing pumps and a red dress that acts as some sort of kung fu spyess that destroys the suspension of disbelief to a great point. Additionally, you meet Salazar, a midget who owns a huge castle and acts as some sort of comical relief. I completely lost it when I had to press X continuously in a QTE event to run away from a giant statue of him. 

This is quite sad as I really liked the initial atmosphere of the game and it never felt like a game that needed to be quirky and dumb just out of spire. The game plays and feels a lot in that regard to metal gear 3, which the games theme absolutely doesn’t fit. Its not a dealbreaker for me but something I just personally kind of dislike. 

[u]Sound[/u]
Most of the OST is more ambient, more horror focused. Even the combat theme if regular villagers attack you is a weird abstract piece of music, giving me the chills each time I hear it. Enemies also shout nasty things at you.

[u]Graphics[/u]
The whole game is saturated in such a way that the colours in the whole game are completely washed out. A very bold choice, as usually this is completely hated by me it solely works so far in this game. If you absolutely don’t like it there are some colour filters you can activate but they don’t look that good to me. I do dislike the movie grain tough, as its quite apparent and for me a bit too much.

As a gamer, I rarely revisit titles I've already played. With hundreds of titles still to play and new games released daily, why waste time re-experiencing something you've already done? With that context, let it be known as a testament to the quality of [i]Resident Evil 4[/i] that I have owned and beaten this game on four separate platforms (GameCube, Wii, Switch, and Steam), and am just as likely to dip back into this version yet again.

[i]Resident Evil 4[/i] is an action-based survival horror game, a mainline entry in Capcom's iconic [i]Resident Evil[/i] series. You play as Leon S. Kennedy, a special agent a few years off his stint as a rookie cop in [i]Resident Evil 2[/i]. Leon is tasked with investigating a report that Ashley Graham, the missing daughter of the U.S. President, was spotted in rural Spain. Upon arrival, you find that things are amiss in the Spanish countryside...and as the game's events progress, increasingly powerful and horrific entities confront Leon as he tries to foil an insidious plot and yet another zombie-like outbreak.

[i]RE4[/i] underwent an infamously troubled development cycle, taking years to materialize and gaining some distance from the mechanics, styles, and plots that defined its predecessors. Gone are fixed camera angles, 64-bit graphics, and zombies - this entry introduces an over-the-shoulder view, sleek polygon-free character models and settings, and a semi-intelligent people known as the Ganados for enemies. Each of these changes proved successful enough to pave the way for the series' future: [i]RE4[/i] as a third-person shooter feels as intense as ever, the graphics convey all the doom and gloom of the gross enemies and their dreary homes, and the Ganados' reactivity and mob mentality hit the perfect sweet spot between 'challenging' and 'satisfying to dispatch en masse.'

There's something for everyone to love in this game. The combat is intense and rewarding, hitting the genre balance of survival horror's resource management and action's wide array of weapons and ammo. Progression spans a deep upgrade tree for weapons, inventory space, and health, while collectible documents  shed light on the backstory to the game's events. The story is cheesy in [i]Resident Evil[/i] tradition, with voiced performances capturing the feel of '80s action film schlock. Yet the game still manages some geniune terror from the threats and situations Leon faces. Even the escort mechanics, a much-derided trope of gaming, aren't a drag as Ashley is intelligent enough to duck and cover or signal for help when appropriate.

This version of [i]RE4[/i] comes packaged with all the special features of prior releases, including The Mercenaries score attack mode, the special game-adjacent missions of Assignment Ada, and a host of galleries and collectibles like digital figurines. The Mercenaries was good enough to be spun off into its own game, and it retains that quality here: a variety of playable characters, including some series favorites not present elsewhere in [i]RE4[/i], each with their own loadouts makes for worthwhile repeat play for score attacking. Assignment Ada admirably fleshes out the story of a major player from the main campaign, with some unique looks at areas from the main game.

Be it the unforgettable first encounter in the village or the memetastic lines of the Merchant, [i]RE4[/i] is a genre classic that deserves a play. Barely showing its age after a decade and a half, this version includes all the extras and features that more than justify the purchase price. Do yourself a favor and check this one out - if you're ready to face your fears and blow off some heads. [i]Resident Evil 4[/i] gets an A+.

[h1]This game doesn’t need a remake[/h1]

[u]What I liked about the game[/u]
[list] 
[*]	I like the locations they picked for the game, like a spooky village and old castle. The locations can be quite creepy. 

[*]	I like that Leon can comment on things in his environment. 

[*]	Cheesy dialogue and one-liners. (“where’s everyone going?  Bingo?”) 

[*]	Likable protagonists like Leon and Ada. The game also has some awesome antagonists like Krauser, Saddler, and Mendez.

[*]	Awesome enemies like chainsaw man, regenerators, and the Armadura. The game also has some really good boss fights.   

[*]	Awesome soundtrack, especially the one when you’re in the same area as the merchant.

[*]	 Loads of cool hidden treasure, like rubies, emeralds, antique pipes, and a crown. I like the idea that you can find missing pieces of treasure like jewels and combine them with other treasure. 

[*]	I really like the over-the-shoulder combat. It is a nice change from fixed camera angles and tank controls. I like how sometimes when you shoot an enemy his head explodes and all these tentacles start to come out.  

[*]	Loads of weapons to use. I like that you can buy attachments and upgrade the stats of your weapons. 

[*]	I like the idea that you can unlock new content like costumes and new weapons once you’ve completed the game. It gives the game more replayability. 

[*]	Extra content, like assignment Ada, Mercenaries, and separate ways.  

[*]	Cut-scenes are very well done. 

[u]What I disliked or was disappointed with[/u]
 
[*]	I wasn’t keen on the quick-time events. 

[*]	Ashley can be a bit annoying. 

[*]	I wish the puzzles were a bit more challenging.  

[*]	Wish the game was scarier. 

[*]	Needed more steam achievements. 

[*]	Last boss fight is a bit too easy.
[/list]

[u]Conclusion[/u] 

This is one of my all-time favorite games. It is up there with Half-life 2, Bioshock, and Portal. It is the game that got me into the resident evil series. As a long time fan of Resident Evil since the first game's release in 1996, Resident Evil 4 is an odd entry in the series. It is undeniably a fantastic game, well designed and extremely fun to play, as well as highly innovative for 3d action shooters. But at the same time, it completely changed the series forever, shifting away from survival horror and more towards mainstream action.

I'm a bigger fan of survival horror than I am of 3rd person shooters, but RE4 is a great game and despite it's action oriented design, still manages to retain some of it's previous identity. The game's atmosphere and environments fit nicely with the classic horror influences of the series.

RE4 sadly was the last great Resident Evil for a LONG time, as many mediocre titles would follow for a decade until RE7 came out and found a great middle ground between run-n-gun and survival horror. 

I can safely recommend this game to fans of both survival horror and 3rd person action shooters as it does a great job blending the two into a really fun and unique package that hasn't been done nearly as well by any imitators since. 

Great value for the price as well as there is a lot of extra modes and unlockable content, as well as the main campaign being fairly long for the series. I also highly recommend playing this with the fan made HD texture project released in 2022. It looks amazing and is one of the best HD texture projects in modding history, it is extremely well done, beyond professional, makes most "remasters" look amateur by comparison.
