Resident Evil 4 is getting on in the years now, with the 20th year anniversary coming up. This game takes me BACK. Review is going to be short since the game has been talked to death for years now (almost 20 come 2024). You play as Leon Kennedy, a bit older, a bit wiser, and a bit more flexible with how he backflips and supplexes people all over the place. He’s on a mission for president himself, to locate his daughter, Ashley Graham, who was kidnapped after spending her break in Europe.

 She was last seen in a remote village in Spain (Where they speak Mexican Spanish apparently). Leon pursues the lead, and the lead pursues back, with all of it’s mates in a rather forward and aggressive manner. Turns out the remote village is under the control of a man known as Osmund Saddler and each of the villagers are bound to his will, which includes killing everyone NOT under his control. 

This game is one of the progenitors of third person shooters. Some remnants of the previous games are still there, there is tank controls and a higher emphasis on puzzles compared to the newer entries, but survival horror this honestly is not. That doesn’t mean there aren’t a few scares to be had however. The game has a variety of guns to choose from, from different kinds of pistols, shotguns, sniper rifles, Machine Guns, and Magnums to defend against the onslaught of enemies. It’s kind of insane the amount of variety the game has while still looking as good as it does. Of course it’s aged but if you compare it to games released back then it might as well be a next gen title.

My criticism is that the story isn’t anything worth writing home about, but it’s very memorable due to the campy dialog the characters say. It’s fun seeing Leon banter back and forth with the villains. It’s one of the reasons why this game is still beloved today, since in many ways although it’s gameplay holds up (Well, there are some crow’s feet, but this game would be applying for colleges if it was a person) it’s variety of enemies and gameplay set pieces make it very easy to replay. I’ve seen pistol, and even knife only runs. It’s fair to say that people will be playing this game in 2034 while we’re at it (And Capcom will certainly indulge them)

Port runs great. No performance drops or crashes. It’s pretty cheap nowadays so whether you want to go on an nostalgia spree, or try it for the first time I’d definitely recommend it.

[] Plot surprisingly good. Older RE games focused on two things, survive and escape. While RE4 doesn't mess with that formula, it does change it up some. Leon being tasked with rescuing the President's daughter, is on a hunt to find her in rural Europe, then find a way out once that task is completed. The main / side characters I found to be interesting, while a couple others do get annoying as the game goes on.

[] Atmosphere holds true to the RE games, and really brings in something new of its own from the very beginning. From woods, to villages, to castles, to an island, they all give off the same creepy vibe of something not being right. You'll encounter scary enemies, fight tough bosses, solve puzzles, and fight to stay alive. Keeping true to the series.

[] Sound is standard in this game. The guns sound good, enemies sound scary, and music is average. But the save room music in this game, like all RE games is so...mystic and mesmerizing. It’s hard to describe and really stands out that much to me, giving me an eerily safe feeling before heading back out into that dangerous unknown.

[] AI is good. While Ashley's character is generally seen as an annoyance, she does well to stick close by you and never stray far when danger is close. That doesn't make her any less annoying, but, there's at least no unnecessary frustration. Enemies are actually pretty smart too. They'll move out of the way to avoid getting shot, and will dodge, leap, and climb to get to you.

[] Puzzles got dumbed down this time around. This was intentional I believe, since the game was going more run and gun, rather than stop and think. There are quite a few puzzles in the game, but only two I found to be challenging. The rest involved simply finding an item or pushing a button to open whatever door / path that blocked the way.

Being a huge RE fan since the 90s, I recall playing the 4th entry upon its initial GameCube release. While there is no denying the impact it's left on the gaming industry, over the years, I've grown to resent RE4 more and more. This is the first entry responsible for why there's a divide within the fanbase. A divide between those who desire action-horror versus those who enjoy traditional survival horror; those who prefer over the shoulder opposed to those who want fixed camera angles. That divides continues to this day with RE7 having introduced first-person into the main series (previously optional in Code Veronica and side games like Survivor).

Every game beforehand felt it was setting up a showdown between the series' heroes and the big bad Umbrella. RE4 does away with Umbrella in its first cutscene, which felt like Capcom flipping the middle finger at fans who were hoping for a proper resolution. It isn't until 2007's Umbrella Chronicles and 2009's RE5 where fans got the resolution we deserved. With RE4 having little to do with previous entries, it's hard to invest myself in the story. I don't care about protecting Ashley, nor finding out more about Los Illuminados if subplots are carelessly dropped as with Umbrella. 

With rumors of a remake on the way, I decided to give the original RE4 a second chance. Well, even the gameplay has aged like milk. While in the newer over the shoulder entries you can run and shoot, in RE4 you are rooted to the ground whenever you take aim. There isn't an option to adjust the aim speed. If there's an enemy on your left and another on your right it takes forever to aim from side to side. Restrictive movement isn't necessarily the issue here, as you also can't run and shoot in previous entries, and neither later in RE5, yet its combat feels perfect in comparison. RE4 would benefit from better aim and camera distance. The camera is too close to Leon's back and you don't have full control of it to keep track of your surroundings. Not to mention Leon has awful hand tremors where the laser pointer flies all over the place. This again isn't much of an issue in 5.

By far the worst thing in RE4 are the quick time events, where most of your deaths will stem from. Capcom didn't think to readjust button prompts in this edition so they're less bothersome to execute, as they did with re-releases of RE5/6. There's even an entire cutscene filled with QTEs where a villain shows up out of nowhere to dump exposition. This is where I segue into the villains. The antagonists in RE4 are unbearably boring, the only exception being Albert Wesker, who while being downgraded to a background character, is fun to use in Mercenaries. Richard Waugh gives another outstanding performance. On the other hand, Krauser is by far the worst villain featured in RE4. His boss fight feels misplaced, as if it belongs in a Metal Gear game and only exists to extend the length of the game. His history with Leon isn't explored until 2009's Darkside Chronicles, where even then his hatred towards him makes little sense.

All in all, RE4 feels like a chore to get through each time. If you only care about the overall narrative/lore of RE, 4 is an entry you can skip without missing much. It's a dated experience which requires patience to get through. If you're looking for fluid OTS, action-horror gameplay, you might want to try the more refined RE5, RE2/3 remakes and The Evil Within series. While I doubt RE4's remake will leave as big of an impact as its classic counterpart did, I do hope it fixes all of the original's shortcomings, and turns out fun enough to satisfy either side of this divisive fanbase.

This is not a good game. If you want to play a game that does what RE4 wants to do, but does it well, do yourself a favor and pick up Dead Space and Dead Space 2. These are games that were directly inspired by RE4. There are video clips of Glen Schofield (creator of Dead Space) talking about this. For this reason we should be thankful that RE4 was created and tested the gameplay style that Dead Space would go on to perfect. We should not, however, under any circumstances, think that RE4 is a good game. Because it isn't. It is at best a somewhat okay game. And at it's worst it can be very infuriating.

Many people heap praise on this game. Many people are redditors. 

The laundry list of awful things that this game has:
- QTE's. And lots of them. Sometimes without warning, in cutscenes. For especially fun bonus points, there are QTE's at the ends of fairly long segments which, should you fail them, will bring you back to the start of said long segment.
- Tank controls. Yes, this clunky movement system can be used to good effect. No, it doesn't work to the game's advantage here. I hope you also like having only two turning speeds.
- Horrific camera position and camera control. This game was created for the gamecube's c-stick, and it certainly feels like it. There is no possibility of rotating the camera a full 360 degrees around the player character, which means that sometimes if you want to look right, you will have to play a balancing act with the tank controls when the right stick doesn't cut it. 
- Horrific FOV. I thought things were about to improve after meeting Luis & the merchant for the first time, as the camera momentarily zoomed out from the player character. I should have known better. I wish I could tell you what this game looks like, but the FOV makes playing this game akin to being stuck in the Allegory of the Cave.
- Music loops. Good lord. The music is nothing to write home about. But what really twists the screws for this is that the loops are very very short. And they will play over and over and over again, until you have cleared an area of hostiles. This would be fine if either the loops were longer, or if they were good. But I kid you not, some of these are... 3 seconds long? Yeah.

I think the only thing this game can really hold up as being interesting is the use of stationary camera, moving crosshair aiming mechanics. I have only ever seen this before in early Bond games, like Goldeneye or Nightfire. But those games also had the ability to move while shooting. Then again, this game uses a laser sight that collides with hitboxes to give it a nice 3D feel. Then again, so does Dead Space, except your lasers stay centered in the camera while the camera moves. I think ultimately this is the most interesting mechanic, and Dead Space still does it better.

The other positive is that the writing for this game is so cheesy that it starts to drift into the territory of being good again. But a lot of the writing also falls very limp. From some point in Chapter 3 thru Chapter 4 you will begin to feel that there is barely a scrap of writing that is moving you between areas of the map. It feels very uninspired, as do the environments that you are forced to go through. Everything looks poop-flavored.

Look, some people will say that the inclusion of tank controls and the inability to move while aiming helps heighten the tension. And they are wrong. There is nothing tense about any of the gameplay here. When enemies get too close, you simply quick turn and run to get some breathing room. This is goofy, when you think about it for more than 5 seconds, and the ability to simply back up—like you can in all video games—would have made things far better (and not goofy). There was the possibility for the developers to increase the level of movement control, but either for stylistic or monetary reasons, chose not to. But it's not good. It's bad. When looking at things of interest or trying to run around a corner becomes difficult, you know something has gone very wrong.

I think I could expand on a few more topics, but to sum things up: don't play this game. Play Dead Space 1 & Dead Space 2. Or Resident Evil 2 Remake. All three of those are excellent games! Resident Evil 2 Remake is like a hybrid between the more slow, methodical gameplay of RE1/RE2 and RE4, while the Dead Space games are more fast paced and you fight far more enemies, more akin to RE4. But don't play this game. There are better ones out there.

I’ve been a fan of the Resident Evil series since I was a kid. I was hooked the moment my friend showed me the first Resident Evil on PlayStation. When Resident Evil 2 released, I was so eager to play it I secretly unwrapped the present the night before my birthday and played it quietly at night for hours, before wrapping it back up again to hide my indiscretion. 

Life took over and I skipped Resident Evil 3, but whilst studying at university a friend on my course was horrified I hadn’t played Resident Evil 4. He immediately sent me away with a copy of the game and his GameCube on loan. I ripped through the entire game in days, and was amazed by how it blended horror and action. I’ll never forget the opening chapters in the village. The fear and adrenaline of barricading yourself inside, away from the pitchfork wielding mob, and then you hear that chainsaw fire up and think, “Oh ♥♥♥♥!”.

That wasn’t the last time I played Resident Evil 4 - far from it. I borrowed a PlayStation 2 a few months later and ripped through it again. And then when it came to PS3 I took another trip back in time to the village and that “Oh ♥♥♥♥!” moment. 

Flash forward to the present day, and I’ve owned Resident Evil 4 on PC for years, but like most games I own, it’s sat unplayed in my Steam backlog. But buying it was all part of the plan.

A handful of talented fans have dedicated eight years to remastering every single texture in the game, as well as patching bugs and adding other niceties you’d expect from a PC game in 2022. The RE4HD project released last week, and now I’m playing Resident Evil 4 for a fourth time, in glorious 1440p and HD at 60FPS, with a keyboard and mouse. This is the way this game was meant to be played.

This is a pretty decent port, but there are a few things you should know before you buy:

- This "Ultimate HD Edition" actually only upgrades a handful of textures, whereas the rest are either untouched or just the originals with a filter applied.

- If you're looking for an actual HD experience, you'll want to download the HD Project mod. It's a free fan-made remaster of the game that upgrades every texture and model and even restores visual effects that were lost since the original GameCube release.

- The HD Project also comes with re4 tweaks, another mod that includes a ton of fixes and new features such as an FOV slider, borderless windowed mode, adjustable controller sensitivity, and more. The mouse turning and remapped quick time event keys in particular made the game feel SO much nicer to play for me.

- If you're not interested in either of these mods and you want to play at 60 FPS, you're gonna run into this problem where the button-mashing quick time events will be practically impossible to complete. This is because the QTEs require twice the amount of button presses than they do at 30 FPS, so to fix this issue, just switch to 30 FPS mode, make a macro, or download re4 tweaks.

Overall, I really enjoyed playing this game for the first time last year and it has definitely solidified its place in my top 3 Resident Evil games. Highly recommend!

Let me ask you something: how do you define your FAVORITE game? What does a game have to do, or be like, for it to go that high? I think what makes a game truly that special to someone is if they can replay it endlessly, over and over, and never get bored. The highs never go down on subsequent playthroughs, it never gets worse with age, and it's got a high skill ceiling. You truly feel as if you could be stuck on an island forced to play only this one game the rest of your life, and you would not mind.

I can't say for certain if Resident Evil 4 is truly my favorite game of all time, but it definitely ticks all those boxes. RE4 is one of the best games ever made, period. It's from that glorious era of late sixth-gen when singleplayer games were being pushed to their limit in terms of quality, without having to add hundreds of hours of content, DLC, or online multiplayer modes. And it's so influential that games are STILL copying its design philosophies over 15 years later.

RE4 has the best pacing in video games, hands down. Every room you go into has you doing something noticeably different. The plot and gameplay ramp up with each other. It starts off on such a lowkey note and the atmosphere is genuinely spooky at points, but then it turns into [spoiler]a hilarious campfest that subverts the player's expectations[/spoiler], and then by the end it's [spoiler]balls-out action like the end of an 80s Stallone movie[/spoiler]. This goes for the gameplay too: the player starts out being scarce on ammo and deals with enemies that can kill them instantly 15 minutes in, but by the end you're not playing slow anymore, you're unloading your entire arsenal that you've built up on every enemy the game could throw at you. Just when you think the game is starting to have too much action, it slows down. Just when you think the game is too silly, it gets creepy again. This continues all the way through to even after the credits have finished. It hooks you so well that I can't even start playing this game to test mods without wanting to play the entire way through all over again.

Admittedly, it does seem like it's running out of ideas in its final act, but the combat is strong enough that it almost doesn't matter. Even without the main campaign, I could play The Mercenaries for hours. That's how good the combat is. It's that transitional period between older, clunkier controls and newer, more sensible but boring controls. The controls are just restrictive enough to raise the tension without making the player feel frustrated at things like not being able to move and aim at the same time, or moving like a tank. And because the AI is built around this, you can learn to manipulate enemies in all sorts of ways, which only adds to the skill ceiling. With that, plus Separate Ways, plus Assignment Ada, there is a HUGE amount of content and value in this game. You even get two sets of alternate costumes, one of which is significant in gameplay. And it's all included at the base price. It just goes to show how this game is from a different era, because such things would be paid DLC today. You can even customize your laser sight color. How cool is that?

So I highly recommend it, along with the HD Project mod. RE7 and RE8 might be perfectly good games in their own right, but RE will never again be as great as RE4 was. Well, maybe the RE2 remake. But please god Capcom, don't remake this game. Please. It doesn't need one, and you're going to ruin some aspect of it, I just know it.

As for the port itself, some people note problems with 60fps. I personally do not know what they're talking about. I have played this, unmodded, on professional, at 60fps, and I got through QTEs just fine. The QTEs WERE almost impossible in previous versions of the port, but they have since been addressed in patches long ago. They might be a tiny bit more difficult, but unless you have some kind of disability keeping you from mashing buttons fast, it's not "almost impossible" like people say. There is only one QTE now that is admittedly impossible at 60fps, but it's only during the final boss and it won't kill you (unless you never upgraded your health, in which case, uh...maybe 30fps isn't a bad idea then).

That is literally the only "real" issue with 60fps. The AI is not altered, as some people claim. The only other things that are different are some things like fire still animating at 30 and some animations like water are sped up, but that's hardly any reason to give up a smoother gameplay experience. There were legitimate problems with 60fps when the port first released, but they have since been addressed in patches.

I also recommend playing with a mouse&keyboard. That's my preferred way to play, and it plays really well. It's a compromise between the overly easy aiming of the Wii version, and the more difficult aiming with a controller. Just be sure to set it to "Modern" and tweak the sensitivity. Your aim will improve to the point where you won't even need a stock, or a scope.

One thing I WILL slam this port for is a crash that consistently occurs during Chapter 5-4. That really should've been addressed in a patch that sadly will never come.

The bonus Ada chapter was a bit of letdown since it doesn't handle the power progression as well given the much shorter runtime. She gets a few new levels but nothing near the quality of Leon's adventure.

Title: "A Genre-Defining Masterpiece - Resident Evil 4"

Resident Evil 4 is a game that not only redefined the survival horror genre but left an indelible mark on the entire gaming landscape. Capcom's magnum opus, released in 2005, remains a timeless classic cherished by both old and new generations of gamers.

From the moment you step into the shoes of Leon S. Kennedy, the game engulfs you in a gripping and immersive experience. The story follows Leon as he embarks on a rescue mission to save the President's daughter, Ashley Graham, from a mysterious cult in a remote European village. Little does he know that the horrors he will encounter will go beyond anything he could have imagined.

The game's atmosphere is dripping with tension and dread, expertly crafted through stunning visuals, haunting audio, and masterful pacing. From eerie villages to sinister castles, each location is intricately designed to evoke a sense of unease, keeping you on edge throughout the journey.

What sets Resident Evil 4 apart is its groundbreaking gameplay mechanics. It departed from the franchise's traditional fixed-camera perspectives and introduced an over-the-shoulder view, revolutionizing third-person action games. The controls felt intuitive and responsive, making combat a visceral and thrilling experience.

One of the game's hallmarks is its ingenious enemy AI. The menacing villagers, known as Los Ganados, are relentless in their pursuit of Leon. They intelligently adapt to your tactics, showing a level of aggression rarely seen in games of that era. Each encounter becomes a desperate fight for survival, leading to heart-pounding moments that stay with you long after you've put down the controller.

Resident Evil 4's inventory management system added another layer of strategy to the gameplay. Players had to carefully manage their resources, choosing between weapons, health items, and ammunition, all while being pursued by relentless foes. This created a sense of vulnerability and forced players to think strategically, amplifying the sense of survival horror.

The boss battles were nothing short of epic, each one uniquely designed and requiring different tactics to conquer. These encounters were pulse-pounding experiences that tested your skills and wits, providing a rewarding sense of accomplishment upon victory.

Beyond its intense gameplay, Resident Evil 4 also featured memorable characters. From the enigmatic merchant to the fearsome Ada Wong, each individual added depth and intrigue to the storyline, further immersing players in the game's world.

More than a decade after its initial release, Resident Evil 4 continues to receive praise for its influence on the gaming industry. Countless games have drawn inspiration from its mechanics, storytelling, and immersive gameplay. It's a testament to its enduring impact that it has been re-released and remastered on multiple platforms, making it accessible to new generations of players.

In conclusion, Resident Evil 4 is an absolute masterpiece that set the bar for action-horror games. Its brilliant blend of horror, action, and intelligent design established a new standard for the genre. It remains an essential experience for any gaming enthusiast, providing an unforgettable journey into a world of fear, tension, and survival. Whether you're a long-time fan of the franchise or a newcomer, Resident Evil 4 is a must-play that stands tall as one of the greatest games of all time.

Resident Evil 4 is one of the best resident evil games that I've played, and also one of the worst.

It takes a leap from the previous titles and dives head first from survival-horror into a more action focused survival-horror experience. For the most part, this is a great change - however, there are problems with this game specifically that hold it back. For starters, while I enjoy the ability to free-aim (enabling me to knock weapons out of enemies hands, or trip them over), the controls are a little hard to adjust to. I played on an Xbox Series controller with problems arising at certain areas of the game. More specifically, the worst issue I encountered had me tearing my hair out because it was simply impossible to complete with a controller. I had to switch to keyboard and mouse because despite me flicking the left stick left and right, literally faster than the speed of light, it would not ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ register how much I flicked it. This resulted in an approximation of a trillion deaths and enough rage to bend a frying pan. Thankfully, the controls are the only major problem I had with this game.

Moving on to something I actually thoroughly enjoyed, the characters in the game are super interesting. While I constantly wished for more notes to be scattered throughout (which made some potentially series-best characters a little less interesting), the story managed to keep me interested the whole 18 hours.

The combat is really fun, and often surprisingly tense. The gamecube's technical limitation meant free-aiming and moving was impossible and therefore, you are constantly required to either sacrifice your ability to move for your ability to defend yourself, or vice-versa. This really makes the entire game super tense, and without it I'm not sure I would have enjoyed it as much. The sounds guns make are chunky and impressive, and the way enemies react to being hit is all super fun, mixing together to make an overall pretty fun experience.

The enemy variety also helps to keep gameplay fresh. As this is a spoiler-free review, I won't go to deep into it however, there are some enemy types that are just poorly executed (including some bosses). While I understand the need to make things tense, some bosses have too much health, do too much damage, and last too long. Similarly, some enemies are just unfair with some just insta-killing you (i'm looking at you chainsaw dudes). This is either lazy game design, or bad game design that wasn't fixed in this remastered version.

The graphics hold up surprisingly well for a game that's nearly 2 decades old, even if they aren't the most beautiful that I've seen. The colours, textures, fog, and lighting all come together brilliantly to create an overall spooky atmosphere. Disappointingly, the game still didn't scare me (at all). I can't pin point why, but I imagine it probably has to do with the sheer amount of enemies you face (I had killed 898 enemies by completion), and just a sheer lack of horror elements. This wasn't an issue though, and I still think the graphics complemented the story and gameplay even if they weren't actually scary.

During the beginning chapter I was confused by the decision to play intense, fast music when I was shooting up an entire village. This decision actually made me laugh originally, and after that feeling had passed I was jamming out to instead. By the time I reached the castle, the music changed and when this happened I didn't even notice. When I did though, I really appreciated it as it allowed for a much creepier tone to be established that I ironically enjoyed a lot more than before. The music in the first chapter still puzzles me - it just totally contrasts the spooky vibe of the village that they otherwise did a brilliant job of. Other than that, the soundtrack is gorgeous.

I did finish the story, and I actually really enjoyed the game. However, by the final 2 chapters  I was just begging for it to end. All good things must come to an end, and this one really took it's time. Perhaps it was the frustration caused by some game-breaking bugs, or maybe it was just the length of the game making me numb to all the mayhem going on around me. Either way, the game could have done with being just a few hours shorter.

All in all, I actually really liked Resident Evil 4. While I don't think this is as good as the Resident Evil 2 Remake or my personal favourite, Resident Evil Village, I do think it still stands a chance to become the best with an equally good remake. It's a solid game, and one that I can certainly recommend to anybody despite it's shortcomings.

Absolute classic and still probably my favorite game ever made. RE4 changed gaming forever and was a major turning point for how third person action games handled. It's a bit clunky and its innovations have since been replicated better by every game under the sun (most notably Dead Space), but RE4 continues to stand as one of the best video games in existence.The steam port is in HD and offers 60fps that unfortunately can cause overclocking issues on certain late-game QTEs. As a speedrunner I know plenty of glitches to bypass them but would recommend switching to keyboard to perform certain ones if you're a controller player. They are considerably more difficult to execute on pro difficulty so I would recommend just sticking to normal unless you're an achievement hunter or immune to carpal tunnel.10/10 for ballistics alone, this game's gunplay is surprisingly deep and you'd be hardpressed not to commit yourself to challenge runs or at least spend several playthroughs trying out every weapon. Action is dynamic and the game features an incredibly exploitable internal difficulty slider that constantly adjusts itself to your skill level. The writing is Grade A cheese and this game somehow takes itself less seriously than every RE both before and after it (and the main villain is Ralof from Skyrim, you'll never unhear it).4 also offers a ton of content; the main campaign alone can run you 12 hours if you take your time, Separate Ways is an entire campaign of its own that while short is still a worthy addition, and the Mercenaries minigame is highly addictive and will keep you coming back to beat your old records.All in all, this is a game I revisit at least once a year to keep my reflexes in check and bask in nostalgia. I would recommend RE4 to literally anyone, for a shooter rooted in survival horror this game is highly accessible and a blast to play anytime.

Usually I have the displeasure of writing negative reviews from retro pixel amateur games and asset flips, but today I get to write a negative review for what was, at least on consoles, a AAA game (at least back last decade when it was released).  So what has gone wrong here?

Yes, on consoles this was a AAA game, no doubt.  This remaster should be on the same level.  Visually, you have 4K support and some graphics tweaks like FSAA... pretty good, and right on par for most AAA PC games.  Voice acting, decent graphics, some kind of story, not too complex of course because it was written for console peasants and as you know they don't understand words with more than two syllables.  Of course a shooter game is always best presented in first person, but console peasants require third person because if they can't see their avatar on the screen, they become confused, angry and afraid. 

Even these console peasant limitations can be looked over, after all, despite the console heritage, GTA:V is a great game... but this is because the developers also priortised PC gameplay as a major design element.  With the case of Resident Evil 4, well... no. 

The controls in this game are an abhorrent crapfest disaster.  It's literally unplayable with KB+M as you pivot around stupidly.  Frankly I don't know how console peasants get past the first level with even worse controls than this console peasant dumpster fire offers.  You simply cannot aim or move around properly using KB+M.  The console port of the controls is so hamfistedly bad the game is unplayable on PC. 

It's a weird place to be after having done over 6,000 reviews on Steam, mostly terrible amateur retro pixel games, to see what was a AAA game for some and to say it's unplayable garbage for PC gamers, but believe me, the control scheme here is an unplayable joke. Ok, but for real this is an amazing game that you should play if you haven't already. The combat is so much fun, there's a large variety of weapons for you to use and upgrade, there are tones of unlockables, it's paced almost entirely perfectly, the story and dialogue is goofy but is massively enjoyable, the bosses are great, the horror element is still good (for the most part), the adaptive difficulty is perfect, and Leon is hot; what more can be said about this stellar experience?

People will complain about the controls, but they're just not good at games tbh. Movement uses tank controls, but the game is from a third person perspective so it's WAY easier to get a grasp on. Plus, the game is entirely designed around this movement so there really is no leeway for people to complain outside of a lack of skill. Tank controls were always fine when they were with a fixed camera, so this more simplified perspective still works great. It will take a little getting used to if this is you're first time experiencing them, but you'll get a grasp on them really quickly. 

That being said, I do have two minor complaints about the game myself that don't make it unplayable or majorly detract from the experience, but I'd figure I'd still mention them.

1) There are no subtitle options. Unless if you're using a different language other than English on Steam, the game will not allow you to enable them. Given how I almost always have subtitles enabled for games this is annoying, but thankfully the plot and dialogue isn't anything super deep or all that important to pay attention to.
2) The last third segment of the game drags on way too long; past a certain point it starts to feel boring and a little "been here done that". It becomes entirely an action movie in what was an already pretty action based game, but not really in a fun way. I wish they had stuck more to the horror element still and maybe moved the final location to somewhere less "American Action Movie". 

Other than those two complaints, there's nothing bad about this game, you should play it now. Like right now, stop reading this review and buy it already.

Resident Evil 4 is one of the greatest survival horror game I have every played, as well as one of the genre's most defining titles. To give full disclosure, RE4 was the first Resident Evil games I ever played, back when it released for the Nintendo Gamecube, so I may have a somewhat biased opinion. None the less, RE4 has an incredible mix of action and horror which remains fun after multiple play-throughs and years later. The style and atmosphere of the game are wonderful, whether its in frantic moments with horrors closing in from all around, lonely and foreboding periods as you creep through the world, or contemplative moments where you observe the detail of each location while you investigate.

If you are a fan of the Resident Evil series, or survival horror generally, you'll find something very much worth your while. Step into the shoes of returning hero Leon, from RE2, as he investigates a kidnapping in a rural European area which quickly turns into a horrific mystery. Prepare for great action, horror movie camp, and some very real terror as you once again enter the survival horror of Resident Evil.

Longer Review (Some Spoilers Ahead):
Resident Evil 4 is an incredible game, but also became on of the most influential games for not only the Resident Evil series, but also the entire survival horror genre. Unlike the previous 3 Resident Evil games, RE4 uses a third person view point. The controls are still tanky and you need to stop to shoot, but this is, in fact, important for RE4 to build its intense and satisfying combat. This control scheme was expertly married to RE4's exploration, item management, and pressing horror segments.

Another key difference between RE4 and previous titles is that their is far less back tracking. In RE1 and RE2 especially, players spent large amounts of time in a singular location, the mansion in RE1 and the police station in RE2. RE4, in contrast favors a far more linear path. The caveat to this is that some rooms or areas in RE4 are expansive, allowing the player to move freely around them, dealing with enemies from multiple angles and rewarding exploration and observation. When RE4 does have players return to an area, it is usually changed in some way, and the loops tend to be larger overall.

As previously mentioned, you'll play as returning hero Leon Kennedy on a mission to save the president's daughter, Ashley Graham. You'll begin with little more than a pistol and some first aid spray, wandering through the misty valley of a rural European community. Each area/room is beautiful, with obvious care given to small details and items. Likewise Leon will often give commentary on specific objects and locations if you search. This, along with secret items, helps to reward exploration and vastly improve the player's experience.

The atmosphere changes between quiet and frantic. In the quiet lonely moments you can have a pensive experience investigating the area or be on alert for enemies lying in wait. These moments match well with many of the run down environments, and the overall haunted feeling of world. The next moment you can have frantic combat, enemies surging towards you from all directions, with the player having to quickly determine how best to move and dispatch enemies or take advantage of terrain.

Along the way you'll investigate multiple locations. The grim and haunting village is a personal favourite, with its run down cabins and farms and the foreboding woods and valley. Next you'll visit the Castle, whose aesthetics are wonderful both when medieval and barroque. Occult rituals and royal oppulence are married, though you'll need to suspend you feelings of disbelief at the sheer ridiculouness of the castle. Still, at this point your more than invested as a player, and have great fun uncovering the next elaborate death trap.

The final area is the island. It is the shortest, and weakest of the areas, but still fun and unique. Here we shift from the more spooky atmospheres of the village and castle into a more grungy industrial terror. At this point you'll likely be heavy with weapons and upgrades, but the game still manages to make itself challenging.

Speaking of weapons and enemies, RE4 has plenty of both. Some weapons you'll find, like the the 12 Gauge Shotgun or the Magnum Revolver. Most, however you'll buy from the enigmatic merchant. As you explore you'll find precious items to sell. Some can even be combined to improve their value. This incentivizes exploration and investigation further. In exchange you can buy new weapons, items, and upgrades. You'll not often find you have enough for everything, especially on harder difficulties.

As for enemies, most of the time you'll fight regular humanoid enemies. Instead of the T-Virus, the villagers have been infested with a terrible parasite, making them little more than brainwashed cattle, slavishly loyal to their cult leader. Each area has its own version of these zombie 'ganados'. The village has its townfolk, as well as chainsaw wielding lunatics, redolent of the Texas chainsaw massacre, with bandages or sack cloth executioner hoods. In the castle, they where occult robes, and the hatchets and pitchforks, has been changed for crossbows, sythes, and flails. They also mutter in rythmic chants, which are both evocative and unsettling. On the island, the its a rag-tag army of dregs dressed in surplus military gear.

Combat occurs not only in tight hallways, but also large sprawling rooms the player can tackle from many different angles. These rooms give the player freedom, but also serve as locations where it is easy to be ambushed or surrounded if you aren't careful. The most nerve wracking areas are the horde locations.

Like with previous titles, your weapons and ammo take up space, and RE4's grid system is the best inventory in a Resident Evil game that I have experienced. Each Item has a fixed size but can be rotated and placed in your attache case. Each combat drains you supplies, but enemies can drop ammunition for your weapons. Notably, ammunition cannot be directly purchased from the merchant, making it even more precious.

Apart from the phenomenal mechanics of RE4, it would be a disservice not to talk about the story. I've often expressed how much I enjoy some of Resident Evil's campy dialogue and plot, and much of that is here. There are quippy one liners and snappy dialogue and some horror movie cheese. However, RE4 also has some wonderful characters and great voice acting. Salazar is easy to despise, with his obvious sadism, but his enthusiasm for drama and tormenting you is compelling. Saddler has a softer more charismatic way of speaking with, and often seems to appreciate Leon's jabs and wit. He's highly believable as the cult's leader, while also being a powerful and enigmatic force throughout the entire game.

Leon's ex-comrade Krauser give a bright but brief performance, and helps illustrate and alternate view to Leon. Where Leon's efforts are driven by his ideals, Krauser is driven by his need for strength and ability. Luis Sera, a mysterious but friendly companion to Leon manages to be funny, charming, and just a bit of a cad.

Ashley and Leon are last two major characters, and I feel that both are excellent. Leon has grown from the rookie cop from RE2, into his own action hero persona. He's sharp witted, delivers some great one liners, but also cares for Ashley and Luis. Ashley, by virtue of being the often captured, and sometimes escorted victim of the game, can sometimes seem burdensome to the player. However, she actively resists capture when she can, and displays that while she is not a big action hero like Leon and prone to being captured, she isn't simply waiting for saving. She struggles, she screams, she helps Leon when she can. In game, she can be captured by enemies or hit by attacks to cause a game over, but canny players will quickly learn that she sticks close to Leon and ducks out the way of fire.

Resident Evil 4 is a must-have game, that I somehow missed in the last 10 years or more. Playing this masterpiece after completing RE 2 - Remake, 3 - Remake, 5, 6, 7 and Village (PS5), I've made my ultimatum. But before that, I'd like to summarize what I felt during the time I played this game. From the beggining I felt this RE:8 vibe, walking into a strange *European* village, meeting friendly spanish locals and finding a secret cult, which was quite welcoming and heartwarming. I'd like to point out that RE:4 has this unique gameplay, very genuine for a 2005 game, I must say I'm impressed with Capcom's ability to make games and impress us with their evolution each year. The important thing about this game is the characters. I'm that kind of player that hooks his attention to how these personas were made and how they interact in different scenarios. I was excited to see familiar faces like Leon and [spoiler]Ada[/spoiler], which was surprisingly good to see this continuation of RE:2 arc. Another important detail are your weapons and your legs, combat is fine, guns are good but having an upgrade menu for these guns, for a 2005 game, excuse me but this is smart, after upgrading a weapon I felt OP. As a final point, I'd like to mention the fact that bosses that we encounter during gameplay are challenging (on higher difficulties), each one of them is unique and has a background story, we know what they try to achieve and why we need to stop them. To end this review on a positive note, I'll give a solid 10/10 for relieving my childhood memories when I used to watch my cousin play this awesome game and now being my turn to enjoy moments in RE:4.

Pros: 
- Tight shooting and gunplay that not only holds up to this day but is way more fun than most modern games nowadays
- Incredibly entertaining story and cutscenes that alone will make one of the best horror/action B movies of all time
- Insane amount of replay value - collectibles, extra guns that are unlocked once you beat the main gam, outfits, tryign out different loadouts, etc
- Once you beat the game you get not only some extra goodies but also 2 new campaigns - one is granted less than an hour long, but the other can be an extra 4 hours of playtime! You also get access to Mercenaries which is basically 3rd person action arcade goodness.
- Best Leon and Ada model in the whole series. Though I do wish Leon's jacket could have stayed a little longer
- Despite their age, the graphics still hold up amazingly well today, especially with the HD mod (though they still look good without it)
- Even though it's more of an action than a horror game, it still has some good scares. Like the first sequence in the village, the chainsaw boi and the... regenerators. Seriously, when the regenerators showed up, it felt like I was playing classic RE, with the tight corridors, eerie anxiety-inducing music and the slowly-walking seemingly invincible monsters (they're easy once you get the thermal scope but still)
- Boss battles are incredibly memorable and some of the best in any game ever (though the final boss felt a little too easy once you realise what you have to do)

Cons:
- It makes other games look like crap in comparison and you know you are unlikely to play another 3rd person game like it
- Some issues with the PC version that can be taken care of with mods

Awesome game, well worth it, but I do think it has been a tiny bit overhyped. Having said that, I only started playing Resident Evil games with the RE2 Remake, and subsequently played the RE3 Remake, RE7, and Village prior to touching RE4 at all. And in my personal opinion the bar for quality is the RE2 Remake, and this game doesn't quite reach that level for me.

It's got really excellent pacing, and the combat is actually pretty fun once you get over the game's tank controls. It also has wonderful diversity in it's gameplay, frequently throwing new mechanics at you and making sure you're paying attention during cutscenes with QTE's. Where it falls somewhat short of RE2 for me is mostly driven by a relative lack of scary moments, interesting puzzles, and replayability. There are some intense moments, but there's not much horror to be found most of the time, and the few puzzles that exist are really simple. It's also pretty linear in most parts of the game, with very clever map design but often only one way to actually proceed, often looping back to that same area later on.

None of this makes it a bad game at all, it's phenomenal for a game from 2004 and was well worth the 15 hours. Do yourself a favour and download the HD pack though!

RE4 is an important game in the series, IIRC it's the first one that went for more of a third person shooter style.
This is evident by how many new features there are in the game and how the developer experimented with them.
That all being said, I personally don't like it all that much.

Graphically the game is rather bland.
There are like three male enemy models for most of the game and two occasional female enemy models.
And everything is smeared with a brown tinted filter.
They're all decent for the time, just so meh.

The audio is.. fine I guess.
Nothing really stands out, but the guns go bang and all that.
That's just the audio itself though.
The audio mixing is friggin' awful. The BGM is VERY loud, but the voice acting during cutscenes is very low.
And since there are NO AUDIO OPTIONS, this is extremely annoying.

The gameplay is the biggest negative for me.
Because it's an old game the controls are fairly awful.
They're this sort of awful combination of tank controls and TPS, which makes doing anything in the game more annoying than it should be.
There are also too many annoying QTEs, again a symptom of its age.
The level design follows the classic RE formula of being mostly corridors, which isn't necessarily a bad thing but in this case it annoys me since a lot of the game takes place outdoors.
And lastly partway through the game it turns into what amounts to one long escort mission.
I hate escort missions.
Also, I don't really like the Cthulhu-ness they're going for with this game and the enemies.

So to sum it all up, it's a clunky outdated game and this is a terrible bare bones port of it.
It might be historically (for the series) be an important game, but I think it's one of the weakest entries in the series.

So no, I don't recommend it.
Especially not when they're working on a remake, although I seriously doubt I'd recommend that one either since I dislike a lot of the core of the game.
And really, they probably should've remade Codename: Veronica first.

After finishing this game, I firmly put it in my top 10 games of all time. As a horror-survival game it nails everything perfectly, the atmosphere is top-notch, the scares are great, there's nothing more I can ask for. What about the "weird" combat? I love it. It does have a different way of being a third-person shooter but it's still good, I got used to it really quickly! Other than that, there is some getting use to the camera angles and controls but everything else is fine, so bear that in mind.
What about the story? The story and the writing is amazing, there wasn't a single point while playing this game where I got bored, everything was very interesting and it kept like that throughout the whole entire game. The character progression on Leon was satisfying and cool (going from a badass to even a more of a badass). The different antagonists in this game were awesome and they all had their own "atmospheres" and "areas".
SPOILER ALERT FROM HERE! The escort parts of the game are perfect examples of what good escort mechanics are when you escort Ashley around the game and the variety of things you can make her do and all the little details based on what you do (for example when you kill enemies, she sometimes makes a little "hooray" hand gesture). What about QTE (Quick-Time-Events)? I didn't mind them :) The QTE when you meet and fight Krauser are a really nice dynamic to the game because when Leon talks to him, Krauser sometimes attempts to stab him when the player is most vulnerable (when you expect nothing but dialogues when two characters are talking).
SPOILER ALERT OVER/GONE! In conclusion, I give this game a rating of 11/10 for being a masterpiece.

Excellent game! One of the best entries in the RE series and universe. I've had this game on multiple consoles now, PS2, Xbox 360, PS4, Xbox One and now PC. The fact that I keep spending money on the same game should tell you that this game has immense replay value, it never really gets old - simply a masterpiece! 

It's paced brilliantly and keeps the gameplay varied enough that it never seems to get stale. There's some good puzzles to break up the action and the boss fights are awesome throughout. 

I would say the only issue I have with this PC version is that it gave me crazy motion sickness to begin with, which had never been a problem on TV with consoles. I realised the FOV hasn't been optimised for monitor and it was obviously primarily made to be played viewing a television screen. You however install a program called "Flawless Widescreen" which has a fix for this game and makes it totally playable on PC and removes the motion sickness. Would also recommend turning off motion blur in the game options. Annoying that Capcom didn't see this as an issue for PC players, but they must have not thought it through. 


Overall though 10/10 and it's super fun to play with mouse and keyboard - you can aim so much faster, but the enemies still prove a challenge when they're in large groups surrounding you.

Edit: After an additional 21 hours, I've completed a play-through on Professional, Assignment Ada, Separate Ways, and cleared every stage of Mercenaries with a 5 star rating with each character, unlocking every costume and extra weapon. 

Resident Evil 4 is just as fantastic today as it was in 2005. 

For those more used to modern third person controls, it might take some time getting used to RE4's over-the-shoulder tank controls, and while the story itself is mostly understandable and doesn't contradict itself too much (one issue I have is how the game seems to flip flop on if the ganados have higher level brain functions or if they're nearly mindless slaves), the characters often act in ridiculous over the top ways. A good example of this is a villain holding a character at gun point to monologue about their plans, something that is obviously only meant to be for the player's benefit. Additionally, leaving notes scattered around the village and castle levels about how Leon needs to be taken care of is a very clumsy way to get across that he is being targeted and to tell the player not to let their guard down.

While fighting hordes of ganados can feel frustrating due to the controls (particularly the speed at which you are able to aim and move), the combat shines in 1v1 encounters against boss enemies, particularly those encountered later in the game. The upgrade system, while basic, does exactly what it needs to do in allowing you the ability to customize your equipment to your liking. The characters are charming, the gameplay consistently challenging and enjoyable, and there are several additional modes you can engage in after completing the game for the first time.

This review was left after completing the game on the PC version 1 time, and having spent time previously playing the game on Playstation 2 to 100% completion.

[h3] Completely personal and subjective review ahead [/h3]
I could yap and write about this game for hours but at this point, everyone who played it already talked about it and I agree with the pros and with the cons (which the game has a LOT). I played this when I was a little kid who got his first PS2 with many games, I remember to be TERRIFIED especially when Dr. Salvador appeared for the first time in my screen and holy crap we won't talk about Mendez fight or first Garrador.
I was never able to complete the game until I bought it 5 years ago on steam and 100% it and now, in 2026 I'm giving it a review for the first time ever, and how could I not since it's one of the few games that has been with me since I was a kid.
Despite being the "Ultimate HD edition", it doesn't look great, you can tell this remaster is already outdated especially with the textures, I totally recommend to download the HD Project mod because it makes the game look amazing and every single texture was changed and remaked by the mod creators.
Mechanics? quite the same as the previous og RE games, tank controls, you can't shoot, reload and move at the same time and old camera angles were removed so we can have a shoulder camera which I personally like. You can upgrade your inventory space and weapons to make your game experience a bit better or worse in some cases.
It has a lot of replayability especially after completing it for the first time, because it unlocks three new game modes: Separate Ways, Assignment Ada, Mercenaries and lots of new special weapons to experiment in your next playthroughs. 
Personally I think I won't ever get bored of coming back to this game, because it's one of those special cases where (from my perspective ofc) the game it's so well made and it's so fun to play that I just can't let it go easily.
Do you want to try it before playing the remake? Go ahead, you will have fun, if you never played a survival horror game this is a great choice to start with, it has humor, memorable characters and fun mechanics to get into the survival horror genre, despite this game being more an "action" oriented one.

If you're having technical issues with the game, try searching the community guides and discussions. Someone should be able to help you solve your issues relatively painlessly. I initially was suffering from low FPS, and followed a couple of guides which totally fixed the issues. That said, I would recommend this game for people who like myself have played it before, and those who haven't but may enjoy similar games (such as The Evil Within). You're not fighting zombies, but parasite-infected enemies, some of which feel like they would be at home in a The Thing game. The tone is a good mix of serious and comical, the story is fairly solid, and the big bad could very well have been a model for Handsome Jack's personality. You love to hate Saddler, but he's also got that weird air of charisma that many big bads lack. The banter and interactions between Leon and Saddler, Krauser, and Salazar very much feel like something out of a good action movie. Some may think that the new game plus can make you a bit game-breakingly powerful with boss-killer level weapons with infinite ammo. But, for a casual gamer like myself, it's very cathartic to be able to replay the game in "butt-kicker mode", so to speak. Is it perfect? No. Is it fun? Absolutely. And that's the real reason to play games. To have fun.

Resident Evil 4 is a classic title that has been ported to every system known to God and man since its release on the GameCube, and unsurprisingly, it still holds up today. It's easy to forget that this game revolutionized gaming as a whole, for better or for worse. It feels good to ready your weapons, and the laser sight helps heaps when mowing through groups of enemies. The updated controls that allow for keyboard and mouse help out a treat for moments in-game when finesse is required (read: Swapping to that control scheme during the shooting gallery almost feels like cheating). 

Ashley's AI is really well-implemented; she stops when you tell her to wait and will follow diligently behind you when you call her, but I feel the escort mission portion of the game (which is a good chunk of it) would have been less of a slog if she at least made an attempt to fight back or resist getting picked up rather than just going along with it. 

The briefcase inventory system was unique and intuitive for it's time, and I'm a little disappointed that of all the things that future games carried on from this, it wasn't the inventory system, but Quick Time Events (however, given that there's pretty much only four configurations for QTEs in this game, it can be forgiven).

The game still holds up remarkably well to this day, and with the polish applied to graphics in this remaster, it looks very pretty, almost like it could have been a new title released sometime in the last five years. I love revisiting this game every now and again, and I can still find moments that will make me flinch. A true masterpiece, through and through.

I first played Resident Evil 4 back in 2007 on the Wii, and it quickly became one of my favorite games. I cleared the story and side modes at least half a dozen times, and it remains a near-perfect blend of horror, action, and adventure genres. I was eager to give the HD version a go since parting ways with my original physical copy, and I’m glad to say the game holds up great. Keyboard and mouse controls are terrific for movement and aiming, and the clarity on the visuals is a gamechanger: I don’t think I’ve ever managed to get hit the Ganado driving the truck on my first try until now. Environments and backdrops look great, and it is much easier to make out details on complex character designs, such as Novistadors, U3, and Leon himself. 

That said, there are a few minor drawbacks to this version, though most are purely cosmetic. The developers seemed to have missed a blurry cutscene or two in the upgrade. The HD visuals make some of graphical shortcuts less convincing, such as wriggling maggots which are clearly 2D images and flickering light effects looking like TV static “snow”. Also, reloading animations for the bolt-action rifle play in a low frame rate for some reason. These hiccoughs clash with how good the rest of the game looks, but fortunately do not impact gameplay.

On a more significant note, you cannot easily change keybindings in-game, which means using X and C for certain quick-time events. I got used to it after a while, but it is still awkward when you keep your left hand on WASD.

These gripes aside, I’ll still call this a fun and nearly flawless game which I highly recommend to veterans and newcomers alike. It’s one I love to break out around Halloween every year!

it is a deeply broken and flawed masterpiece painted in expensive sauces on a window pane fading with age and rot. the development cycle was started with the castle version, then "dream" version that was basically a ghost story. critical time and resources were wasted and with each iteration it shows more and more. 

the original gamecube version the graphics were slightly sacrificed with letterboxing even if it was highly detailed and clairity was maxed out. the quick time sequences were live and responsive. it was for the most part groundbreaking and perfect if you have a TV that does overscan zooming. I only recently got to try it on original gamecube hardware. that's why I must make this painful review update. 

the PS2 port was outright cursed, the quick time events were video with a popup prompt pasted over it out of step by a few critical microseconds, the AI went to crap, the droprate was terrible and graphics went hazey. the muddy controls and lack of interactivity made it hell with shorter time to react and less visible feeback. the chaos and boss fights towards the end really show as being crowbarred in and the design and writing team rushing and out of ideas. it broke the immersion as you might get a good enough rhythm going and its 5 to 15 minutes before being ambushed by a quicktime event that might take you 25 tries if you aren't at your absolute best. the krauser sequence is a standout for this problem you have to watch a cutscene play out over and over with multiple instant death events redoing it until you get most of it right to get to a continue point. at that point it would be less obtrusive to just run it as a normal cutscene. am I pressing too fast? is it the right timing? am I pressing too slow? is it even registering my key presses at all? who knows! I sure don't. then you have AI tripping over itself with bad pathfinding making comically bad self/team kill stacks when some shambler with explosives holds up a single file line of them. missing water and shadows...

the cursed PS2 port was then re-ported to xbox and the xbox port was re-re-ported to PC where it got a lot of hate as it was hard on PCs of the day but that soon died back as updates, hardware improvements and an HD remaster making it feel much more worthwhile however IT STILL SOMEHOW USED THE SAME CURSED PS2 PORT AS THE BASE. the PS3 port brought back the live rendering... for the main game not the expansion. here is the incomprehensible part: on PC they recreated the QTE problems because they left the QTE timing tied to the framerate for the HD remaster. (a rookie hour mistake) the AI was still broken and the droprate still esentially borked.

then came the remake... everything is so much better and worse at the same time. the gameplay is perfect, the graphics astounding. level design fantastic, didn't really need the WKUK yellow mustard paint. AI superb... but they destroyed the atmosphere with the lack of soundscaping, microtransactions and removing critical set pieces that added tension. 

is this the best way to play it? unfortunately yes. until a second HD remaster comes along (of which there absolutely is huge demand for as a lot of folks will never accept the remake) but I need to be honest with myself and realistic: there is no such thing as a definitive version and this is basically RE4's Half-Life source edition. the remake ain't no Black Mesa. the best playing version is still the gamecube but the graphics are severely lacking now. Resident evil 4. One of my favorite games of all time. When it first came out, I watched my dad play it until I was finally able to play it myself. Once I did for my first time on the game cube. Tank controls are awkward and forced mouse acceleration is annoying. Once I got the hang of it however, I was very much enjoying the combat. Aiming, movement and spacing all became pretty natural, the control scheme is really just another layer of difficulty to overcome and mouse acceleration is not that big of a deal when everything comes at you in a straight line. All the guns feel great, the shotgun especially feels very powerful. Upgrading them is also done well. Quicktime events feel a bit out of place but they're challenging enough to not be completely pointless I suppose.
I was a bit disappointed by the bossfights because most of them would be over quite quickly. Every time I would blast through it by unloading on them with special ammo, which I can't imagine is very difficult since the game is pretty generous when it comes to ammunition. I would sometimes force myself to use the pistol just to see their moveset. I'd much rather overcome a challenge than stunlock Krauser with grenades and revolver shots.
Something else I was disappointed by was how they handled the regenerators. The first encounter is great because you're forced into this small space with this big hulking monster that you can't kill, you have to find a way around it by either maneuvering around the room or shooting it's legs. It's a great way to break up the flow but it happens only once or twice. Most of the encounters after that happen down long hallways where you really don't have much trouble just casually disposing of them by stunlocking them with rifle shots. Just seems like wasted potential to me.

Overall I'd say it's a good game with plenty of bonus content, definitely not perfect though.

Overall:
A classic in every sense of the word, a game that set the rules for 3rd person shooters in modern gaming, revived its series from a creative slump, and led it to new heights. A fun, campy action packed horror game with tense gameplay that's still satisfying to this day.

8.5/10

The good:

This game has fantastic combat that always challenges you to take care of enemies in interesting ways. That's because ammo is limited, so you need to use everything in your arsenal in smart ways to survive. Some may find the control scheme a bit limiting compared to modern titles, but that's a strength of this game, as it adds tension and rewards playing in a tactical manner. After completion there are plenty of unlockables, including the super addictive Mercenaries mode, which I could sink hours into. The script of the game has some very funny, and meme-worthy lines, which entertained me during cutscenes, and the overall silly tone was very enjoyable. The voice acting is much better than previous titles in the series, and the sound design is also very good (especially the [spoiler]Regenerators[/spoiler]

The bad:
Not much really. The main thing that I found a little disappointing was how low-res the textures were in this "Ultra HD" version. That's a given, since this is a game from 2005, but I expected the visuals to look a little cleaner. Thankfully there's an excellent HD texture mod you can install if that really bothers you. Sometimes I tried to launch the game and it got stuck on a black screen, so I had to reboot my computer to get it working.

The meh:
The game's plot is very straight-forward and not very interesting compared to other titles in the series. It felt like we were going to get some major revelation that never came. I found that the game's pace suffered a lot during [spoiler]the castle section[/spoiler], and overall the game could have been about 3 hours shorter without losing much of anything. These things may not bother many people, as the main draw is admittedly the gameplay. There are also tons of contextual button prompts and QTE's (one of the worse things that this game popularized in modern gaming). I didn't really mind them, but some people really despise them, so be warned.

A visionary game that has become a classic. Playing it now it looks and feels a bit rough around the edges and a little clunky but the B movie charm, moments of real tension and solid gameplay are worthwhile. The series hit a high point here and set the tone for the entire 3rd person action genre. It's far from perfect, but its a fun way to spend some time and a big piece of modern games history. If you haven't played it, you should.

Conclusion:
Despite minor frustrations and less-than-perfect controls, Resident Evil 4 is, for me, the best part of the series. After WAY too many years I finally got to play Resident Evil 4 and I’m very happy that I did! To this day RE4 still holds up as a Survival Horror Game with great Gunplay and a fantastic Atmosphere.   
     
[u][b]Story[/b][/u]     
You’re Leon S. Kennedy and send on a Mission to rescue the Presidents Daughter from a Cult. After your first encounter with one of the Villagers it’s certain that there is far more to it than it seemed at first.   
              
[u][b]Gameplay[/b][/u]         
You control Leon like in most 3rd person shooters from a behind the back camera perspective. A difference to modern games is, that he can only shoot while standing still, which feels weird at first but works out great after you got used to it. Beside that Resident Evil 4 plays like most games in the series, you scout the locations for Ammunition, Herbs and Money, to stay alive and upgrade your Weapons at a mysterious Merchant. The Boss fights all provide a different challenge to overcome and play out entirely different.      
       
[u][b]Graphic and Audio[/b][/u]     
For such an old game the graphic still holds up but of course shows it age compared to more modern games. Still, Resident Evil 4 is far away from being a bad looking game. On the other hand the audio and sound design can absolutely still hold up in every situation.    
       
[u][b]Pros & Cons[/b][/u]     
+Still amazing Game- and Gunplay
+Well implemented and fair Weapon Upgrade System
+Many different Boss fights
+Fantastic tense Atmosphere 
+Fair checkpoint system
+Enemy design and variety 
+Well designed locations 
     
-Ashley    
-For 2 QuickTime Events I had to quit the game, and lower the fps to 30 since the game didn’t register my key presses on 60fps, neither on Controller or Keyboard
       
[u][b]Final Thoughts[/b][/u]       
If you haven’t played this masterpiece of gaming history you absolutely should give it a go. Resident Evil 4 had a big influence on the genre at whole and still holds up to this day. It’s an experience everyone who is even remotely interested in 3rd person shooters and survival horror games should make.

Resident Evil 4 is a great, terrible game. Great because it varies up the classic RE formula with a new perspective and actionised focus, meaning the player will be spending more time fighting zombies and monsters rather than solving puzzles, all without losing the charm and fright factor of the prior entries (it was going to be pure survival horror, but technical limitations meant the game's director and team couldn't get their original plans across). The game design is perfect, and the tension is well-executed to such a degree that it demands a standing ovation. In short, it's tied with 2 as the most fondly remembered of the franchise for a reason.

It is terrible because of what it did to the series and almost did to horror gaming in general.
It's nice to take influence from RE, but 4 ended up being the final game in the franchise's golden age, as barring the Revelations spin-off, most Resident Evil games became victims of Capcom's doomed "westernisation" policy; and wound up as mediocre action games with zombies in them, learning all the wrong lessons from 4 and proceeding to jump the shark so many times that the older fanbase was alienated. In fact, other horror franchises would join the bandwagon and lose all of their fear factor.

Thankfully, this game came out the same year as Penumbra: Overture, an independently developed affair  which laid the groundwork for a renaissance of independent, weaponless horror. Capcom themselves would eventually learn their lessons fully with Resident Evil VII: Biohazard, which introduced another new perspective and returned to oldschool survival horror, creating a blend of old and new which took the world by storm. Again.
So in all honesty, with the series back to a better place and the horror genre becoming an underground phenomenon, there's never been a better time to revisit Resident Evil 4.

Legendary game. Better than overhyped remake. Unfortunately, no matter how I love it - had to uninstall it as well. Since Capcom started to infest older games with Enigma malware, I simply can't let it stay on my PC.

[strike] Without slightest doubt - great product of it's time. Within gaming industry in general and within RE franchise in particular. Great enough to come back after so many years and spend few dozens of hours. But can we say that everything aged well? Well, yes and no. It depends what aspects we are talking about.

As to the gameplay, for it's time it was innovative. Today? - rather outdated. Some gameplay mechanics are especially archaic. And camera... oh man, this camera - infamous console legacy, which infested lot's of good games. But overall, I can't say that gameplay is that bad either. Will it require some time to get used to it? - definitely. Will it ruin your experience - doubtful.

Story. In Resident Evil franchise it never was as serious, dramatic and full of symbolism as, let's say, in Silent Hill serie. It was always more like a porn-parody of horror movies. And rather good one, should I say. Secret agents, kidnapped U.S. president's daughter, spanish [strike] inquisition [/strike] cultists, evil organizations, inhuman experiments - all clowns in one place.

Atmosphere. Oh, this is where everything gets serious and where the game really shines. RE4 abounds with details, which create gloomy and disturbing atmosphere. It includes a lot of stuff: eerie music, great sound design (including monsters' voices/sounds), fascinating art design of monsters and locations (both exterior and interior), different weather conditions, and daytime, etc, etc. And level design is quite good as well. We visit many different and nice (in it's twisted way) looking locations, so you never get bored. 

Visuals worth special mentioning here. Of course by today's standards they are rather old, but still beautiful. A lot of efforts were indeed put into decoration of locations. Visiting the inner chambers of the castle, with rich furnitire, serving tables, grim paintings, while listening something as creepy as Infiltration composition, creates true atmosphere of coming horror, which totally consumes you.

Overall - yes, yes and yes. After so many years, even with some outdated mecanics RE4 is still in good shape. By the way, no technical problems or perfomance issues. If you are a fan of classic horrors - RE4 is something you are not allowed to miss.

P.S. If Capcom is planning to make RE4 Remake, they'd better give us an option to leave Ashley behind and fly away with Ada instead. [/strike]

Like most people I've seen pretty much almost of the RE movies (incl animated one), it only once I noticed that it was on special I told myself heck why not. I purposely choose RE4 because of rumours of its 2022 remake being announced: I needed to experience the original before trying the several remakes. Not quite sure if I will play RE1 & RE Zero due to the unfamiliar controls.

[u] Controls [/u]

The "tank" controls are a nightmare for me especially for someone like myself who's not really a casual gamer (keyboard & mouse). It only after two hours I suck it up and just "dealt with it", if it was not for the overall story & plot I would probably have quit. Hence why I might not play the other RE classics only remakes from this point forward.

[u] Graphics [/u]

Wow it feels like I'm in 2005, in a good way

[u] Character/Environment design [/u]

From the fairly wide open area of the Romanesque castle, with some Gothic characteristics & 18th century interior, to the claustrophobic underground mine & eerie lab the developers of the game constructed an environment that not only supplements the RE Universe but leaves you feeling that the villagers or mutated bio-weapons can be lurking in any corner. This is obviously the testimony of the Level design.

Leon always strike me as a character that belongs in early to mid 2000s, I cant help but cringe a bit at his hairstyle. Who can pull of that hair but egotistical/douchy Jarrod Leto, in this day & age yet for some reason it has not been updated to contemporary times however it a video game lol. Not surprising that the character design follows the same principal in most video game character designs: "perfect looking human beings"

[u] Level Design [/u]
 It became apparent around chapter 2 that the player will follow these patterns through out the game:  Door inaccessible /locked ===> explore other areas to search for an access key or insignia which really is disguised as an access key ===> fight boss or mini-boss or gang of cultist/henchman ===>Once obstacle or nuisance  is eradicated you can get hold of the access key ===> inaccessible door is now accessible. The process repeats in every chapter this became an annoying pattern by the fourth chapter, I found myself having to "push through" for the sack of the story. Yes I know that formula exist in many modern games however the anticipation of jumpscares and eerie atmosphere masked that flaw but by Chapter 5 (the last leg of the game) I was pretty confidence in my ability to not die no matter what bio-weapon was thrown at me thus the mask was removed once again. 

[u] Story [/u]

Great story and plot structure is great , this what drew me to RE animated movies. There stand-alone stories can hold there own.

[u] Overall Summary [/u]
I can see why some people recommend this  game it obvious that it invokes nostalgic memories however for me who's new to the RE games and only jumped on the gaming subculture recently the controls are annoying and the perspective of the viewer's FOV will sometimes trigger pure frustration and possibly rage quit. If you can get over that The game overall is not bad , if not above average . Great story, terrible controls  mediocre gameplay.
