I enjoyed everything that didn’t include playing the game. For its age, the textures, models and attention to detail is very good. The atmosphere and set design is done well too and I loved the variety and uniqueness of all the monsters. The plot itself is average, the characters are pretty good and memorable for the most part. At times the dialogue can get noticeably clique or just bad mostly because the voice acting is unbearably boring and uninspired. Leon says everything in a hard tone even when telling a joke, being the main character it definitely makes the game seem stale. One of the main antagonists, Salazar, is easily the worst and most pathetic villain in any game, movie, form of media I’ve consumed. As for playing the game, I almost gave up within the first thirty minutes because the controls are god awful and somehow worse than the first game. It's comparable to playing with a laptop touchpad and your keyboard is in alphabetical order. The aiming makes no sense because your mouse does not turn your character and you can only aim stationary. Good luck trying to find a fix for the mouse issue because I lost my patience trying to find one, so I just dealt with it and turned the difficulty down because I wanted to get through the game in a reasonable amount of time. You can get used to the controls but it's so insulting that one employee at the studio couldn’t spend an hour fixing the glaring issues. There are issues with certain actions where your character just can’t move when you want them too or they are just so incredibly slow you take unnecessary damage if you could turn and run properly. Likely because it’s a port, the majority of quick time events are not possible on the first try unless you’re on adderall which defeats the purpose since they’re supposed to be easy. Most of the game is straightforward and fighting the human enemies gets really old after you really get far in the game. A few boss battles at least don't put you to sleep like the rest of the combat and puzzles. The whole game is nearly entirely linear, which is fine, except all you do is first grade logic puzzles and bullet sponge combat and then have no freedom. I really wanted to like this since I played it for the lore but it took so much effort dealing with the bad port issues and boring segments that I just wanted it to be over as fast as possible. Luckily after some time I realized I could just run past enemies to get to the next area. Wrapping up, I tried to love this game, it is just not worth the effort.

I picked this up on sale a week or so ago for the first time in my life. I missed out on this game when it came out on the Gamecube because Resident Evil was a scary game series, and I was a scared child. Now I'm a mildly perturbed adult, so I decided to give what has always been heralded as the grandfather of third-person shooters a shot, and boy! Am I glad I did! To say this game still shines with passion, care, and love is a total understatement. The biggest complaint I had was the lack of something like a combat roll to quickly escape situations, but even that was quickly forgotten once I had figured out the lethal combination of quickturning and strategic retreats (turning around and running away as fast as possible.) 

Something that may turn potential buyers off is the fact that a big chunk of the game is an escort mission involving the president's daughter, Ashley. Ashley is not annoying and does not get in the way. In fact, I found her to be more fun than anything! When you ready a weapon she'll quickly duck behind Leon, and excitedly fist pump when you land a shot. The interactions between Leon and Ashley are another big piece in making her not an annoying prop to guide, but someone you actively want to keep around and healthy. Leon himself is a magnificent presence as well. He's completely serious, but still manages to keep things light with a smartass comment or wry observation. The word gets thrown around to the point of complete irrelevance, but he is a textbook example of a total badass. 

The story is a lot of fun and takes you through vaguely European settings like a village, castle, and sewer system to name a few. The villains that drive the plot forward are hammy and quite goofy at times, but remain threatening and individuals not to be taken lightly the whole time. Playing on normal difficulty I never found myself wanting for supplies, and doing a generally thorough sweep of every new area I was flushed with more than enough gold to upgrade my weapons and gear at a pace where I never felt like I was going into an encounter unprepared. This may be a turn off for those that are looking for a more "survival" survival horror, though a harder difficulty is unlocked once the game is beaten. 

I can't recommend RE4 enough. A solid game through and through that completely deserves the undying praise it has enjoyed for over 15 years. Check it out!

Whatever one may think about Resident Evil 4, its impact on gaming as a whole cannot be understated. For one, it proved that shooting in third person can be done real well on an analog stick (as not many titles had that down at that point in time). Unfortunately it was also the title that helped popularize Quick Time Events alongside God of War, but what can you do (at least they are done quite well here).

Nevertheless, it was so successful that it sold millions of copies and released on almost every platform that is able to run it at this point (and I own on a fair number of those copies too).
 
This game was monumental for Resident Evil fans. Gone were the “tank controls” and static camera angles from previous entries. You could now so precisely aim at a chosen body part or even shoot a flying projectile out of the air! And the knife! Gone were the “stabby-stabby” days of yore. Now, you could watch that sharpened piece of metal do wonders as the blade gracefully slid through the air (and probably someone’s face and/or torso later).

True, some lamented the departure from the slower paced previous installments and the fact that the game seemingly abandoned many of the horror elements. 
However, I would argue that the thing that lies at the core of the series is still truly present here, and it is realized better than ever before. 

You see, Resident Evil (a survival horror game) always was to me about the “survival” aspect with horror undertones. Sure, some horror elements (extraordinary enemies, spooky locales etc.) are necessary for the formula to work, but ultimately those games do not leave you wanting to cower before the obstacles before you. Even in the first game (which probably resembles a classic horror experience the most) while you may even feel hounded by your enemies at times, you ultimately have to embrace your fight or flight instincts.
You either run from (or past) your enemies, or fight through them, but ultimately you have to consider your options, manage your limited resources and then push forward and somehow persevere. 
You have to keep taking action to pull yourself from a bad situation – that is the soul of Resident Evil. And it is truly present in this game here.

You can play this title casually to get the feeling of pushing through an overwhelming force of enemies. Or you can choose to get really good at it, learn its various intricacies and feel truly empowered when you dispatch enemy after enemy, mixing calculated actions with a bit of improvisation when things go awry. This game really invites you to push your limits and keep getting better at it with its addictive gameplay. 

Either way, even though the game may feel a bit dated or quirky to a newcomer today, its overall formula is likely to quickly suck every player right in. You’d probably be doing yourself a disservice by not experiencing one of the most iconic games of all time, so go ahead and buy it.

While a fun game for people who like action, Resident Evil 4 to a fan of the original Raccoon trilogy (1-3) just doesn't feel like a part of the same series. The only thing making it a "Resident Evil Game" is the branding and (maybe) Leon. RE4 feels much more like a shooter with slightly scary visuals than a challenging survival horror game like RE 1-3. 

In addition, the game has little to nothing to do with the preceding and succeeding games. The only plot relevancy there is is in a small opening cutscene mentioning that after the [spoiler]destruction of Raccoon City in RE3[/spoiler], Umbrella Corporation's stock plummeted, leading them to go out of business. For those who aren't familiar with Umbrella, it's a pharmaceutical giant [spoiler]secretly involved in the creation of bioweapons to fund eugenics experiments,[/spoiler] and it's the overarching antagonist of 2-3 and the secondary antagonist in 1. The plot design of 1-3 is such that it gets you worked up and excited to take Umbrella down, only for 4 to give players a big "♥♥♥♥ You" and give them a ♥♥♥♥♥♥ cinematic instead of a clean and climactic end to the Umbrella saga. 

The fact that RE4 is a giant non-sequitur to the rest of the Resident Evil series aside, the plot is still awful. RE4 goes like this: Leon Kennedy, once a rookie cop in RE2 (and extremely out of character, but I'll get to that later), is now a secret agent working for the President of the United States, sent to investigate the kidnapping of the President's daughter in a rural village in Spain, where the villagers there are infected with a parasite called Las Plagas that makes them susceptible to mind control. You (as Leon) find Ashley (the daughter) pretty early on, and the rest of the game is basically a glorified escort mission instead of a survival horror classic. There are virtually no suspenseful moments or plot twists involved like the infamous [spoiler]Wesker betrayal in RE1[/spoiler], or the slow, suspenseful transition of Spencer Mansion into a [spoiler] bioweapons laboratory[/spoiler].

As I mentioned earlier, RE4's characters feel very bland, one-dimensional, and not true to their original counterparts. Leon in RE2 was a rookie cop wanting to right wrongs done to Raccoon City and save as many lives as he can. He didn't seem super overconfident, especially in his interactions with Ada where he was a bit gullible. Capcom in RE4 decided to change this (for whatever reason) and change him from a sweet little rookie cop wanting to do the right thing to... a macho, womanizer secret agent spitting pickup lines to his superiors and not showing an ounce of fear even in front of giant bioweapons? It's like two completely different characters. Ashley, even as a secondary character, is very one dimensional in her role as a dimwitted useless bimbo.

The last negative point for RE4 is its gameplay. A key component of the preceding games (and, ya know.. survival horror... the genre RE is supposed to be.....) is the conservation of resources and choosing your battles. As RE4 enemies drop loot (ammo, herbs), there's never a time when you will be like "oh ♥♥♥♥, I need ammo" and have to avoid a fight because of it. The fights just aren't threatening because of this. The "Merchant" character also exacerbates this. Instead of finding cool new weapons in the environment by exploring, you just show up to him (he is marked on the map) and pay him a easy-to-get amount of money for OP weapons that make fights even less of a challenge. 

The final few things I will say are the positives of the game. I don't have any specific ones in mind, even the graphics because they just aren't anything new, but a lot of the negatives can be viewed as positives by fans of different genres. If you've never played a Resident Evil game before and you really like shoot-em-up action games with maybe a little bit of a scary ambiance, I would highly recommend RE4. It checks all those boxes. However, if you're a fan of the preceding games and the RE franchise in general, I really wouldn't recommend this game. It may have been good as a side game, but as a main installment in the franchise it's sorely disappointing. It doesn't "feel" RE.  If you enjoyed RE for its gameplay and ambiance, I suggest you replay the first game, as its the most exemplary in the series. If you enjoy RE for the plot so far... just skip 4. It's a giant disappointment. Play RE5- it suffers from some of the same gameplay problems as 4 but is faithful to the original RE story and has some insane graphics.

I believe it's a function of a super low FOV (i.e. everything seems way zoomed in), the default camera angle and the way the inputs work for character movement.   All character movement happens with the left thumbstick, without a strafe.  You simply push it in the direction you want the character to turn and move. M&K is similar, where all movement happens with WASD, while the mouse is nothing more than a free-look.  This may have been similar input scheme to prior RE titles, but the zoomed in behind the shoulder camera angle which resembles your average FPS, combined with an input system that doesn't match that same FPS, causes the screen to move dramatically quick in a way that doesn't connect with how my brain has been wired to expect.  The screen movement difference is like comparing between driving on a highway at looking at distant houses you slowly pass by, versus the road signs which whip by you.  Couple it with a completely different movement input scheme, and now my brain isn't connecting with what it thinks should be happening, causing me to feel nauseous.  It's too bad because I've heard this is one of the best RE's in the series.  It's just going to have to be a pass for me unfortunately.

Resident Evil 4 took a big risk when it was being made. The previous games were all using as little items as possible as you walked around spooky locations with static camera angles. And then Resident Evil 4 came out and took all of the series principals out back before shooting them with a rocket launcher. You now have compete control of the camera, you are rewarded for shooting and killing enemies, and instead of being scared Leon just keeps saying one-liners. (insert small time clip here). And all of these changes led to one of my favorite video games of all time. Your constantly thrown into situations that have baddies coming in from all angles, and its up to you to figure out how you want to get past them. You could shoot one in the knee then kick him into the rest, use the shotgun to knock them all down then run past, or just chuck a grenade and kill em all. The locations where these fights take place all vary drastically. Sometimes your fighting off hoards of guys while cooped up in a tiny house, or maybe your fighting invisible bugs in a sewer. And sometimes your just fighting off guys in a mine shaft when you hear a chainsaw start up. And then it is time to run. The game also has a lot of boss fights and every one of those is fun as well. There just intense menacing creatures with super unique patterns and arenas that make them fun to fight. Everything about this game is fun and I cant think of a single thing I did not enjoy. 10/10.

From a guy with no nostalgia blindness for this game, I have to say I am very disappointed with this game.  I had played RE2 Remake, RE7, and RE8 (Village) and loved all of them.  They were fun, had a good story, and most important of all, the gameplay was stellar, even in RE2 Remake.  I loved, and still love, RE Village, but I had seen many videos of people saying that Village is just RE4, but worse.  I've been seeing people put this game on a pedestal for being a "masterpiece."  While I had seen people say the same thing about RE Village, I had come to believe that RE4 is just as good, if not better.  I was led astray in such a way, that I wish I didn't even spend $5 on this thing.  It doesn't even scratch the surface when it comes to how good RE Village is. 
 I can appreciate where many functions in RE Village came from, such as the Merchant (but I still strongly prefer the Duke).  The first few hours are the finest no doubt.  Full of mystery and uneasiness that I had come to expect from a Survival-Horror game. But very, VERY soon, it all came crashing down.  One of the worst offenders is the stupid, absolutely horrible QTE's.  I was not a big fan of them to begin with, but the way they are handled in this game legitimately make me wonder if Capcom even playtested these!  They are horrible.  I wish I could say that was the worst of it, but it isn't.  The outdated tank controls really don't serve this game well.  I think this game would benefit from a Remake, with modern third-person over-the-shoulder mechanics, and, dare I say, with parts cut out.  This leads to my biggest gripe with this game:  It draaaaaaaaaaaaaaggggggggssssss.  I had already lost some of my interest within the first 5 hours or so, but the story just kept on getting more and more outrageous!  At around 11 hours in I was waiting for this game to end.  "Ugh, when am I finally going to be finished with this game," I'd think, only to find out that I have half of the game left to go.  What a joke.  Even for $5 I am extremely disappointed.  There are so many people blinded by nostalgia, and I am convinced that is one of the reasons why the game is sitting at a "very positive" rating, besides the people who genuinely liked it without bias.  Masterpiece?  Far from it.  This game is at most a 6/10, though I am tempted to bring it down to a 5 or 4.

Resident Evil 4 is untouchable.

From its masterful pace of gameplay, enemy design, weapon management, and its absolutely beyond-bonkers big boss battles that are  littered throughout... Resident Evil 4 was a marvel in the video game industry upon its release in 2005, and it still holds up quite well years later. I consider it dumb luck that we even have this game, given how many times Capcom had restarted RE4's production. It does everything you could want in a game. It still provides some really tense moments with its music, atmosphere, and gameplay overall. I don't think I have ever called this game "scary" when it came out, but this game is balanced oh so well, that whether you are a Resident Evil fan or a survival-horror fan in general, this game was meant for you. 

RE4 is one of those games that is surely aging, as most games tend to do, yet the experiences I have had with this game are untouchable. RE4 did it all first. No, it's no longer the best graphics-wise, but that occurred in the late 2000s as the next gen PS3/Xbox 360 really changed video game landscape. The only thing that bothers me sometimes in the game itself is the dark, muddy pallet of colors that the developers chose to use, especially in the Village area. I guess that's what the developers wanted, and/or that's what they were limited to at the time, and/or of course Shinji Mikami, the director and creator of RE, may have wanted the game to look like it does. I want Capcom to brighten up that area for the inevitable REmake of 4. I probably have simply been too spoiled by modern video games since RE4's release, with HDR, etc. And, okay okay...sometimes Ashley gets on my nerves a bit too...! But, I actually look forward to seeing her in the game now after many replays since RE4's release.

I bought RE4 the day it was ported to the PS2 in 2005 with probably half a dozen or more playthroughs within the first couple years. I only wish I had a GameCube console and all its goodies so I can then play this game as it was originally released. I had the Wii version for a while which was good, like others say, but the experience for me wasn't the same with the Wii controller.

This "Ultimate HD Edition" released for Windows really is top notch. I don't have any complaints with this version if I ever feel like slaying some Ganados! Using an Xbox One controller feels pretty good with this game. I am tempted to get either a PS4 or PS5 controller, since I am used to PS2's layout the most, but the Xbox One controller works well enough. The keyboard & mouse combo on this game works well too. The mouse allows for reeeeaaaallly precise movement a weapon, which I appreciate, since I am still used to using analog sticks for aiming. Yet, using the keyboard for this game isn't my favorite, but I enjoy the challenge. This game was clearly meant for use with a dedicated controller in my opinion.

I can't wait for the RE4 REmake to make its debut so we can all compare/contrast it to the original for whatever Capcom ultimately decides to create for its REmake version. It should be fun! See you all on the internet then!

That aside, I think that this game has a great art style, and has an inventory management that I adore. If you are willing to chug through some dated controls and Ashley, I would say that this was overall enjoyable experience, but I would recommend pacing yourself so you don't get bored by the end like I did.

2nd Thoughts (April 9th, 2026): Reading my old review, I was unreasonably harsh on the controls and the pacing. And I HADNT played the original RE 1-3. Since then, I've gotten a lot more of a perspective on this franchise, with only 2 mainline entries incomplete in my library, and in general I have played a lot more games out of the 5th and 6th generation of consoles. Frankly, I've also just gotten better at games in general. With that, I felt the need to refresh my take on this game. 

That being said, I absolutely love this game. 

This time around I used the RE4 HD Project Mod which really pulled out the beauty of the textures made for this game, as well as solved a lot of the refresh rate jank of this port. I love the remake, but there is just a classic "creepy" vibe to this version that draws me back to it. Out of all of the RE games I've played, this is easily my favorite setting. The shift from the village, into the castle, to the underground labyrinth, mines, and military compounds made for really diverse environments to explore.

I played on Professional, which really pulled out my combat chops for the game, and really got me to learn the smart ways of dealing with certain encounters that had a trick to beating them. I thought the challenge would maybe frustrate me, but it actually made the game feel a lot more entertaining. I think maybe an initial issue I had was that due to the adaptive difficulty, its hard to feel challenged when the game starts to pull its punches the minute you slip up. Without that safety net, it was such a blast. Did I cheese it a little? Maybe...... but c'mon, it is WAY too hilarious to kill Salazar in half a microsecond with the rocket launcher.

This time around, I also didn't really have any issues with the pacing, in fact I actually really enjoyed the constant scenery changes and momentum forward that this game exhibits throughout each chapter. For how much I complained before, honestly playing through it again, there is almost no fat on this game. Aside from the brief Ashley section which is way too short to complain about, the rest of this game just gives you full control of Leon. Also, Ashley is honestly not a big concern even in the parts where you have to babysit her if you just actually remember to tell her to "wait" and deal with the enemies BEFORE you try and bring her through.

The controls for this game are so unique, so much so that there really isn't another game that scratches the same itch for the playstyle this game offers (aside from RE5, but I have my gripes with that game. I'll save that for another time). The ebbs and flows of trying to time when you should stop and stand to mow down the crowds of Ganado adds an interesting back-and-forth to the timing of combat, and it is really satisfying to get a full grasp on this relationship and just start whaling on literally anything with minimal expenditure of ammo. 

Overall, I felt way more positive about this experience, and I am really glad I decided to revisit it. With time, I am sure I will be revisiting this game time and time again because of how replayable it is. I'm thinking of adding it to my annual Halloween roster of games, right next to Luigi's Mansion and Silent Hill 2. In my honest opinion this is the best Resident Evil game made. Now I know there's quite a few people who would disagree with me, especially those who believe the original three were the best as they were geared towards survival horror and less towards blockbuster action. Resident Evil 4 is a mix of survival horror and plenty of action taking on tropes from action movies. There's a lot of going on at one time, you can shoot weapons out of peoples hands, shoot them in the mid air when they throw them at you, you run outrun boulders and even fight extremely gigantic bosses. With that out of the way let's get on with the review of this amazing game. 

-----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
Part 1: The Story (Early Game Spoilers):
The rough idea for the story is you play as Leon Scott Kennedy. You're one of the lucky survivors of Raccoon City. The game takes place 6 years after the events of the nuclear destruction of Raccoon City, Leon went from being a rookie cop having a bad day to becoming a federal agent and having much better training. You were sent by the president of the united states to rescue his daughter who was kidnapped, Leon goes to Spain to look for her and eventually stumbles upon a village where everything goes to ♥♥♥♥. Your main goal is finding and rescuing Ashley but after a series of unfortunate events your goals end up going from rescuing Ashley to figuring out how to stop the cult Los Illuminatos from taking over the world using a parasite known as the Las Plagas. Goodluck.
-----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
Part 2: The Gameplay:
The gameplay is very dated but also pretty damn good for what it's worth. You move like a tank and with tank controls essentially. It's really weird and hard to explain. It's very clunky yet very precise at the same time. It's a odd mashup you wouldn't expect yet it's still much better than the older games with their devil may cry view angles. The guns feel really impactful and shooting enemies in different areas other than the head can wield different results.For example if you shoot a non special enemy in the foot or leg, they wills tumble opening them up to a context option which is a "Kick" where you kick them backwards with a roundhouse kick. It's pretty awesome and in the early game it's usually a one shot on your first playthrough (on Normal) more or less it gives you i frames and can be a great crowd control maneuver if the enemy lands into other enemies which will knock them back.You can also shoot weapons out of their hands, shoot enemies explosives in their hands to blow them up and even shoot weapons that are being thrown at you MIDAIR to stop it from hitting you. This game was way ahead of its time. The gameplay is awesome once you get used to it.
-----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
Part 3: The Content:
This game comes packed with loads of content. You get the main game which is known by the community to be Leon's Campaign. Once you beat the game you unlock a new campaign following a different character and seeing the events of the main game through their eyes. Which is just awesome and it's canon! You also unlock a additional campaign mission that isn't canon but it quite the challenge to play through and you unlock The Mercenaries which is a side mini-gamemode where you play as various characters throughout the game, both antagonists and protagonists. You can get special abilities through them and it's a horde mode style, with a time limit. Killing enemies in combos will extend the time limit and rack you a larger score. Your goal is to get the best high score possible and reach a specific amount of "Stars" which unlocks more maps, more characters to play as and is overall the ranking system to unlock content within the mode. It's highly replayable, in-fact the entire game is. Once you beat the campaigns on professional and do other various tasks you can unlock infinite ammo weapons and other cool bonuses but be warned they can cost up to 1 million in-game currency. Luckily it's easy as pie to get to that much currency once you enter New Game +. 
-----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
The End:
All in all it's a more action packed game with some survival horror elements. I recommend it to anyone who's a fan, especially if you enjoyed Resident Evil Village.Which that game takes major inspiration from this one in terms of architecture of certain areas, how you backtrack,etc. It's worth your time if you can get used to the controls. It's also only $20 USD but typically goes on sale for about $9.99 USD every Winter, Summer and Lunar sale, every Capcom sale and periodically for weekend sales. If it isn't worth $20 to you, it might be worth $10. I highly recommend you at least try it.

And you can't rebind the QTE bindings without [url=https://steamcommunity.com/app/254700/discussions/0/3108018050534635927/]fiddling and downloading a dll,[/url] and even that isn't perfect (the game can still throw every once in a while a sudden "C" prompt making you fail when you don't expect it).

I like the smooth RE2Make controls better, I like the things Dead Space thought to add on top of RE4 (able to move while aiming, melee not aiming, aiming shooting, two fire modes, stomp, even later the dodge roll)
But I still don't want to see RE4 changed, here you still feel great popping a kneecap and then running up to do a kick and then quickly knifing a downed enemy before they get up, changing weapons mid combat by entering the inventory still feels good because it gives you as long a pause as you need to think about what you need to do next in the heat of the moment.

Graphically it has held up really well, the personality in the UI back when AAA didn't just converge on the lifeless functionally minimalistic designs that are paradoxically harder to navigate, the moody lighting, atmospheric fog, environmental details and particles, fire effects, the tasteful use of shaders, character models, animations, combat feedback, the excellent soundscape - All are really satisfying. 

Sure, some environmental textures are a lot lower quality, but I think this is a case where film grain actually helps to compensate, add some roughness, a bit like the crunchy unfiltered textures of past. 
And most low quality environmental texture work is in larger open rocky environments, stuff like the industrial areas, areas inside buildings where they can keep the loaded parts smaller to have more detail between loading screen doors, that's where they cram a lot of neat details into the environments.
There is a popular HD mod, but I don't know, screenshots make it look like they went a bit overboard, when I think a proper HD mod should stay faithful not only to the style but also to the times. A HD texture mod that only improved it to the level of some other games from 2004 that managed better quality textures would have been more appropriate, like bringing it up to HL2 textures or something.

I did download a "shaders fix" though, since I just assume those could be broken as that was an option, with that mod it looks great and I can't see any issues or glaringly jarring unfitting shader effects.

Towards the end as I in a stress-induced state started to hammer all the keys as I didn't know which one it would change to, I discovered to my relief that the game didn't punish me for it, so in quicktime events, sure I needed to hammer that X button to sprint, but then whenever it changed I just hit all the Xes and Cs and M1 and M2 at the same time and it worked.

Resident Evil 4 was released in 2005 for GameCube and was later released on other platforms. It looks like Capcom wanted to significantly improve its visuals for the second PC port as the first PC port was released in 2007. The graphics are sharper than ever and the gameplay is very good, although a few small problems exist.

This game has been enhanced for 1080p resolution at 60FPS. There is keyboard and mouse support with the ability to customize the keys. Resident Evil 4 HD comes with the Separate Ways campaign to increase replay value. The keyboard and mouse work very well together, but sometimes the laser targeting is not perfect and that can lead to problems when there are multiple enemies near you or when a large boss monster is approaching.

The plot of the game begins with the kidnapping of Ashley Graham, the daughter of the president of the United States. Leon Kennedy, the well-known protagonist of the series, has been sent to a village in Spain to rescue Ashley. What happens in the Spanish village is that there is a religious cult that has released an ancient parasite called Las Plagas on to the countryside. The religious cult does not consist of zombies like other Resident Evil games. You begin fighting ganados, a group of foes who carry pitchforks and are both males and females. Later, you will meet darker and tougher foes known as cultists, religious zealots who wear red or black robes.

As Leon progresses through the story, there will be memos explaining the plan of the cult known as the Illuminados. These memos keep you well informed of the plot and it seems to get darker and darker. The environments are appropriately creepy as Leon looks for Ashely. Resident Evil 4 retains the series’ history of creepy and dark locales. There are misty forests, decrepit houses, moldy caverns, a large castle, and military facilities. The locales display diversity so that there is no monotony. Leon is joined by other characters like Luis Sera and the Ada Wong. Luis Sera is a local citizen who is willing to help Leon. Leon engages in a long shooting with the ganados while Mr. Sera helps out in this long battle. Ada Wong is a familiar figure to Resident Evil fans and has had a long relationship with Leon. There are bits and pieces of the script that indicate past romances and rivalries. However, the plot keeps you at the edge of your seat at all times, which is the way it should be for a Resident Evil game.

The graphical enhancements of the diverse locales are what make this game feel like it is not so old. The details of Leon, his allies, and enemies are impressively sharp and well defined. The walls of the castle look extremely realistic. You can see the dust falling from the ceiling of caverns that make the caverns both realistic and creepy. The textures look amazing in high resolution, but in some cases they look a little bit archaic and out of place. However, the details of the textures are sharp enough to outweigh any archaic look you may find. Military facilities make you feel like that there is a nasty experiment going on while it also feels abandoned.

The bosses are diverse and require you to figure out their main weaknesses in order to defeat them. One issue that pops up in boss battles and in other parts of the game is the quick time events. Sometimes you have to press two buttons at once very quickly to avoid key attacks or avoid deadly traps. It can feel awkward trying to press the X + C keys or the two mouse buttons while using the WASD keys in tense circumstances. While it is appropriate to have tense circumstances in a Resident Evil game, it can get frustrating trying to press two keys at once but dying in the process because of you are not able to press the buttons in time. Another issue that comes up is the laser targeting of the firearms. There are times when the laser targeting takes time to be accurate while one or more enemies are quickly approaching you. Also, the laser can twitch in the spur of the moment, leading to more difficult encounters with the various types of enemies and possible waste of ammo. Ammo is always at a premium in the game, so twitching is a bad thing in a game like this.

All firearms can be upgraded by visiting the various merchants that stand around waiting for you. Upgrading your weapons will make your shots noticeably more powerful. You can upgrade your weapons to the max so that you can be an “exclusive” weapon that will be far more powerful than the weapon you fully upgraded. The challenge is to find the pesetas scattered throughout the locales and dropped by the enemies. You will have to quite a bit of searching for pesetas and treasures with lots of value if you want to upgrade any of your firearms to the max.

There is some randomness when it comes to shooting enemies, especially in the head. Some ganados and cultists will simply fall to their deaths with a headshot. Other enemies will show their Plagas, spider-like figures that emerge from their necks, and continue to try to attack you. You can either fire a shotgun at their Plagas or use a flash grenade to finally finish them off. There are encounters that require crowd control, so you can use different types of grenades to bring some relief to these tense encounters.

Other enemies that are interesting and horrific include garradores, colmillos, and regenerators. The garradores do not attack unless they hear your sound and are blind. Their only weakness is the Plagas shown on their backs. Colmillos are terrifying dogs that can jump on top of you by surprise. Regenerators are special monstrosities in that you can only use a sniper rifle with an infrared scope to locate and shoot their Plagas on their torso.

Resident Evil 4 is worth playing for its diverse locations, creepy atmosphere, and tense encounters. The nail biting gameplay lives up to what Resident Evil fans expect from a Resident Evil game. The high resolution graphics make the PC version the definitive version to play.

Resident Evil 4 is the first RE game, and one of the first games, to popularize the over-the-shoulder third-person POV. Like many others in the franchise, RE4 is a survival horror game, where you play as Agent Leon S. Kennedy who travels to rural Europe to find the President's daughter, who was kidnapped by a cult. I actually played this game on my PS2 almost a decade ago, but never finished it due to difficulty, time, and creepiness. And I bought this game 2 years ago, but refunded it (more on that later) but after enjoying the RE2 Remake I decided to give the franchise another try.

Unlike RE2, which is short and consists of open areas where you need to solve a puzzle to progress, RE4 is much longer and also more linear. Some areas still require solving a puzzle to progress, but none of those areas are as open or as complex as the ones in RE2. This game is also more action-packed, with more enemies and bosses. The overall atmosphere is creepy and depressing, especially in the anachronistic village and castle areas. I play the game on Easy, but the sad thing is that on Easy difficulty, some areas are cut or skipped. It would be better if the Easy mode still retains those areas, but lower the number of enemies or the damage they do. If you want the full experience, play on Normal.

Once you finish the game on any difficulty, you will unlock the Extras menu. There are 3 new game modes, and 2 cutscene viewers. The Mercenaries mode is a score attack game, where you must fight waves of enemies within a time limit. There are 4 areas, and reaching 4 stars in an area unlocks a new playable character. Another game mode is Assignment: Ada, a non-canon, hour-long game where you play as Ada Wong, and the mission is to collect 5 Plaga samples. There are no manual saves for this mode, although there are still checkpoint saves, so you must finish this game mode in a single session.

The longest extra game mode is called Separate Ways, and you play as Ada Wong again, but this time the story is canon and takes place between Ada's appearances in the main game. This mode features many similar levels to the main game, but there are some unique areas. SW is pretty long, about 1/3rd or 1/4th the length of the main game. There are manual saves, and some unique weapons as well. It's a good thing, because if you were to exit the game, you cannot load checkpoint saves, only manual saves.

The biggest problem with RE4 and the reason I refunded it back in 2019 is the horrible controls. RE4 was designed with consoles in mind, so playing with keyboard and mouse is kinda difficult. The movement feels so clunky, and instead of moving a character it feels like moving a slow vehicle, and you cannot move while aiming a weapon. Luckily, there's a quick turn button (Q) and you can use the aim for quicker turning. Some quicktime events also become harder and surprising because the buttons required are not the usual buttons we keep our hands on. The FOV is also very narrow and nauseating, and requires another program to fix. Steps to that are available here: https://steamcommunity.com/app/254700/discussions/0/558749824940806269/

RE4 is a good game, and many people consider it the best Resident Evil game. While I do prefer the atmosphere and setting of RE2, I enjoy playing this game as I feel like continuing Leon's story, who was also the protagonist in RE2 but not in RE3. If you enjoy playing the RE2 remake, or a fan of horror shooters like Evil Within, you'll most likely enjoy RE4. It's playable with keyboard and mouse, but if you have a controller that would be better.

[h1]Ah, the audacity of youth...[/h1]
Going into [i]Resident Evil 4[/i] in 2021, having never played it before, the weight of expectation sat heavy on me. I was aware of its legacy; how it changed every third-person action game from its original release, right up until the present day. It was also responsible for nailing the final few nails into the coffin of one of my favourite genres, (if not my favourite), old-style survival horror. The detached camera angles, vulnerable protagonists and a sense of isolation often made those original survival horror titles masterworks, among other things. But, of course, time moves on. Things change. If anything had to change survival horror, I am glad it was [i]Resident Evil 4[/i]. 

It's amazing how well it holds up today. I've heard a lot of demand for a REmake of this game, but personally I don't think it needs it. The most common complaints I saw were about the tank controls, and how it doesn't make sense that Leon can't move or strafe while shooting. I can see why people would complain, but the point of that is to make every single decision pivotal. You have to be constantly assessing everything in this game, from the amount of ammo you have left, to the amount of money you have to buy new weapons (or upgrades), to the number of enemies, the layout of the level, the danger level of the enemies, and it goes on. It's action horror at its absolute best; just enough moments of downtime to make the rest of the relentless onslaught of enemies bearable. Each new setpiece and room is marvelously designed, forcing you to test your skills in a new, interesting way. It is a game about thinking on your feet, and it is all the better for it. 

What surprised me most about [i]Resident Evil 4[/i] was its capability to be tense and stressful, which is a great and important quality from these games. It wouldn't be so if you could strafe around enemies, but with every time you stand to fight you have to hold a single point, the onslaught often becomes stressful. There were few points in the game where I thought it was scary, but I found the eerie chanting of the castle cultists to be wonderfully harrowing, and the Regenerators are, as many others have said, awesome enemies. 

The story is simple enough to keep you motivated, and self-aware enough to not just be merely silly. It's certainly camp, which often prevents it from being as frightening as it could be, but that's not what [i]Resi 4[/i] is trying to do. It's an action game at heart, but an action game built to be as tense and frightening as possible, while still tossing puzzles and a huge variety of enemy types at you so you are never bored. 

Functionally speaking, the only flaw I can find in the game's design are the Quick Time Events, which often require you to mash at phenomenal speeds, and make playing with a keyboard and a mouse annoying, as some of the inputs come up in an annoying spot on the keyboard. However, that's a fairly small complaint, as most of the time, QTEs aren't required. 

Part of me still kind of wants to hate [i]Resident Evil 4[/i] for the impact it had on horror games, and the shift away from psychological horror to action horror, but I simply cannot deny that everyone should play this game. It doesn't really need a REmake at all - the only things it could improve are the graphics and the QTEs, which are such minor complaints it doesn't warrant spending the millions of dollars it would require to remake it. The only two groups of people I can't recommend this game to are people who loathe horror, and people who loathe action games. For the rest of you, play this damn game. I think everyone needs to play it, or at least try it. I can recommend the original [i]Resident Evil[/i] and [i]Resident Evil 7[/i] above this, but it's still amazing. It's a masterclass in level and shooter design with a great horror aesthetic, not to mention some fun dialogue. Highly recommended.

I can run the game on max everything just fine and it only uses 80% of my GPU power. The funny thing is, in some areas, the game starts to chug with high AA on. 

While watching the metrics readout, I noticed something odd. When the game starts to chug, it uses LESS of my GPU power and my temps DROP. But the core clock and everything else stays where it ought to be so it's not my hardware.

60FPS support for this game is a joke, and it just doesn't work in some cases. 30fps works fine, the game does not run properly with 60. Most places 60 is fine, then some places the engine just gives up.

Resident Evil 4 was released in 2005 for the Nintendo Gamecube and later ported to almost every new platform ever since. Marking a big shift in it's gameplay, RE4 is a controversial game, that is either revered as the best Resident Evil game, or a travesty that ruined great series. Love it or hate it, you can not deny it's impact on the industry. Ever since the release of RE4 a lot of the games in 6th an 7th generations followed the blueprint of the RE4 with it's over-the-shoulder camera and combat elements. For it's time RE4 is a revolutionary action game, that inspired a lot of games to come. And it's very good.

The story of RE4 follows Leon S. Kennedy, who after the destruction of Raccoon City became the part of the President's personal special service, and is heavily trained to be a perfect soldier. For his first mission Leon is tasked with saving presidents daughter Ashley, who was kidnapped by the cult of Los Illuminados and brought into Spain. Turns out, Los Illuminados are controlled by the parasitic virus, known as Las Plagas, and intend to use it to control the whole world.. Leon will travel to the village, where the Ashley is supposdely held. On top of that, he will need to stop cult's plan of the world domination and stop it's leader Osmund Saddler.
The story of the game and it's tone is much lighter than the previous games. The cutscenes are over the top, the characters are so overblown, bordering on parody, and the dialog is so bad, that it becomes so funny you can't help but love it. Every time Leon attempts to make a joke you don't know to laugh or cringe at how bad it is. But it still has it's own merits and manages to be entertaining. It really sells the feeling of a cheesy action movie.

The graphics of the game are dated. The game was made for Gamecube and PS2 and uses relatively early 3D technology, that for it's time could be considered decent, but here on PC we already had sych powerhouses like Doom 3 and Half-Life 2, so comparing them feels like a joke. The textures look low-res and muddy, and this port doesn't help it, trying to mask it behind absolutely horrible motion blur. Still, the character models actually look pretty nice. Leon and Ashley have a some nice details on their costumes, enemies, while being constantly copied and pasted from same 5 models are also pretty good. The graphics are dated, so if it's a deal-breaker to you, then probably wait for the upcoming remake, that will probably screw-up 90% of things that made this game good. Otherwise, yeah it looks old, but that doesn't really matter.

But still none of the above really matters, since RE4 is a supreme example of what an incredible action game with survival elements should be. Let's get this out of the way, this game is not really scary, at least not in the same way that classic RE games or their remakes try to be. However, what it lost in it's transition to the new genre, it gained a lot more. Just let's look at the history of the Capcom after Resident Evil, it tried to turn every game into it and released basically REsident Evil in ancient japan with Onimusha and Resident Evil with dinosaurs with Dino Crisis, also apparently action RE with supernatural elements that became Devil May Cry, but was no longer RE because it was "too action"(ironic). But still, things needed to change and one of the 
main Capcom franchises was at risk of being stagnant or losing it's identity amongs miriad of copycats. So the game was reworked like nine billion times to be next great thing. After showing to public several demos that emulated classic RE formula, Capcom made this. 
Now, a lot of fans of classic RE are not a fan of this onw, but if we speaking not from the point of a blinded by nostalgia fanboy, this is probably one of the greatest games ever made. 
Everything comes down to the great combat system. See, the ganados, the main enemies of RE4, are not as tanky as zombies of classic RE, and they give clear feed back when hit in different parts of their body, but unlike classic RE games, where enemies mostly few, the number of enemies that RE4 gives you at one time is massive. Leon is a great shooter and can be equipped to the teeth with different weapons, but due to the limited controls, which are basically classic RE tank controls with third-person camera, can be easily overwhelmed. The crowd control can be very difficult if you are in a bad position. thankfully, almost every arena with enemies here is a sandbox that allows you multiple ways of dealing with a crowd. The first battle in the village is a perfect example of that, where you have so much room to experiment and try out different tactics. Returning back to the feedback of enemies when shot, connecting hits on enemies feels MEATY. Even the weakest pistols actually feels useful because you can see that it does actual damage to the enemy. on top of that, you can stagger an enemy if you shoot them in the face or a leg, ehich allows you to perform a powerful melee attack that will knockdown an enemy, and any nearby enemy caught by the attack. This combat is so good, there is an entire mode dedicated just to fighting enemies with the time-limit, which would be impossible in older RE titles. Add to that amazing inventory system that allow you to hold a lot of items, but is still limited enough for you to manage all of the resources you have. Seriously, the attache case is the most satisfying inventory system in the RE series (https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=t8xz5Lcyn94). 
Of course we lost puzzles, since most of the puzzles in RE4 require you just shoot something to go further, but most combat engagements actually feel like puzzles with how much you have to manage. You can just shoot your way out of the problems, you actually have to think about what you do next in any situation. And this what makes RE4 so beloved. Also this game is full of content, not only you get the main campaign that goes for 10-12 hours, you also get additional mercenaries mode and two alternative scenarios as Ada Wong. So you really get a lot of value out of this game.

Resident Evil 4 may not be the horror game of your dreams, but in what it does it succeeds so well you just can't deny it's qualities. And action was always in RE's DNA, I mean, it's the same series where protagonists kill final boss witha rocket launcher and then fly away from an explosion in a helicopter. RE4 is a pinnacle of an action RE, just like REmake is a pinnacle of horror RE. And maybe we will never achieve the perfect balance of those two sides of this series, we still have two perfect games in their own right.

After all these years, this is a game I truly can never get enough of. It has a particular charm that just makes you want to come back. 

Even with the game's age showing in certain aspects, the base the game was built on works with these "flaws" so that it really compliments the game. For example, the tank controls would really work against most titles, but Resident Evil 4 was designed with this in mind. So it really creates all the tension and excitement you get from every engagement without it feeling forced. Not to mention, the attache case design for the inventory is one of my favorite things in any video game ever.

Furthermore, Leon S. Kennedy in this title is the most perfect nonchalant bad ass protagonist I've ever encountered. Paired with the game's incredible ability to not take itself too seriously, you get a perfect balance of everything in a action/horror genre title. The incredibly cringe yet memorable one-liners really elevate the game in such a rare but special way.

I understand the story of this Resident Evil title isn't particularly strong from a "realistic standpoint" but damn if it isn't fun. It captures the fun gun play, puzzles (while these are admittedly on the weak side) and exciting environments you could really want in a Resident Evil game. Even Ashley Graham, everyone's least favorite whining AI companion really isn't that bad. While annoying yes, she operates better and listens perfectly fine, even better than most modern day AI's. 

My only real complaint I personally have with this title is the final boss is probably one of the most lackluster one's I've encountered in my time. Almost all the other boss battles in the game are more interesting, even if their characters aren't. 

Without a doubt, one of my favorite games ever made, and I still find myself playing or wanting to play it at least once a year. I'm not one to go the Skyrim route and buy a single game across multiple platforms, but with Resident Evil 4 I have. There's a reason this game is still gushed over almost 20 years later. If for whatever reason you haven't played this game yet, please give it a try.

Trust me when I say that you've gotta persevere in this game. Now I can't speak to the smoothness of the controls on the playstation when this game was first released, but the controls have not aged well. For the first 2-3 hours it is a very clunky experience. Turning is a very tedious task that leaves you frustrated and VERY unexcited to continue to begin with. But once you get over that curve, this game is a joy brought from the heavens by god himself- without a doubt the best Resident Evil game to date.

While the newer games such as Resident Evil 7 have a very tightly packed map (which is certainly intricate and should be appreciated), this game contrasts that with a vast map from small rural villages to rooms filled with lava and fire traps. The range of settings perfectly shows the developers capability of designing an enjoyable and unique area for each chapter of the story. The writing also mirrors this difference: when compared to the small scale story of RE7, Resident Evil 4 is loud, dramatic and unwaveringly silly in the best ways. 

This game, more than any other Resident Evil, has the most memorable bosses my a long shot. I can name every boss in the game off of the top of my head simply because they are all so full of life and compliment the gameplay style so well. My favourite boss throughout the whole game is Jack Krauser because it is a complete departure from any other fight in the game: there is no huge beast to fire rockets at. Instead you just fight a blonde dude with a knife and yet it is still the most entertaining part of the game. The fight keeps you on edge as you tip toe around the ruins and makes you think on your feet whenever Krauser pops out to fight you. It transitions from a perfect cat and mouse style chase in the first phase to a ruthless brawl in the second phase and never fails to capture your undivided attention.

Item management is essential to a Resident Evil game so the devs have to put a lot of effort into making it just right. It is such a delicate mechanic so that, if resources are too common, then the game loses its sense of survival which RE games should be striving for. But if resources are too hard to find, then you are bound to be unbelievably frustrated throughout your playthrough. RE4 hit the Goldilocks position though- the item management is just right so that you still feel like a badass while also feeling vulnerable when the games wants you to.

To sum things up this game will be branded into my mind for many years to come and for all the right reasons: it has likeable characters, a simple yet engaging story and the best ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ combat system out of any game I've ever played.

Resident Evil 4 is Capcom's Skyrim...

It has been constantly remastered for every generation since its Gamecube debut. And there's a reason for that.

Even after 16 years, Resident Evil 4 still holds up as one of the greatest games of all time. And I didn't even play it on the Gamecube. I first experienced this masterpiece on the Xbox 360 9 years ago, I played through it at least three times on that console. Later on, I got it on the Playstation 4 and played through it a few times there.

Some might argue that the controls and gameplay mechanics are outdated. But I beg to differ. I truly believe that the gameplay not only holds up, but offers something very unique even on todays standards. The "tank" controls crank up the tension to 11 and make the game 1000x more enjoyable. The enemies are very evasive and smart.

Sure the story might be cheesy, but you must understand it's intentionally cheesy. Capcom knew exactly what they were doing. The dialogue and plot points are without a doubt influenced by cheesy western action horror movies (Evil Dead immediately comes to mind). 

Leon is one of my favorite protagonists of all time. Ashley is extremely good at holding her own, and even though this is an escort mission she causes absobulety no problems for the player in terms of gameplay and progression. The AI in this game was very ahead of it's time. 

Replaying this work of art on PC made me realize how innovative this game is. Without it, we wouldn't have Gears Of War. We wouldn't have The Last Of Us. 

Please, if you've never experienced Resident Evil 4, go ahead and try it. It's worth every penny. I will continue to play through this game over and over again until the day I die. It is gaming's Mona Lisa. It's my 3rd favorite game ever (behind Metroid Prime and Persona 5).

This is probably the best action-horror third person shooter ever made. It's cheesy, it's campy, it's goofy, and it's genuinely terrifying in places. Music sets the mood, graphics do their job (it doesn't look ugly but it looks like a game that's literally old enough to drive a car in America, luckily it's easy to mod higher resolution textures into the game), voice acting is... well it WOULD be god-tier if not for Ashley's shrill screaming for help. Sound design is impeccable. Animations are fantastic (the first time you reload the bolt action rifle or the revolver magnum, you will nut). Level design is, well... it's pretty good for a linear experience.

Now the bad. The controls are a little clunky- okay, a lot clunky. Tank movement and you can't move while aiming your gun so anyone who's never played Goldeneye 007, Metroid Prime, any OG survival horror game, etc, will definitely struggle with movement at first. The story is silly and full of holes and has some weird random sudden tonal shifts but come on this isn't The Thing or Alien we're talking about here, this is more like Die Hard meets Evil Dead 2, and you don't play Resident Evil games for the PLOT. The plot just delivers monsters for you to fight. The aforementioned monsters are hit or miss and most of them are mediocre. It is painfully easy to cheese glitch savescum and exploit your way through. And the difficulty is incredibly cheap in places (for the most part it's pretty fair even on Hard [Professional] but there are spikes EVERYWHERE and unsuspecting players will end up having a chainsaw rip through their face within ten minutes of press start).

But even despite the flaws, in fact maybe because of some of them, this game holds a special place in my heart as well as that of millions of others. I have beaten this game upwards of 80 times on Gamecube, Xbox, and PS2, and yes, I have purchased this game on four different consoles and if I had a Wii I would buy it again. To put it in perspective, my [other] favorite video games of all time, Tales of Symphonia and Dead Space 2, I received for free on Gamecube/Xbox360 and bought on Steam for $5 on sales. Not only is RE4 a piece of gaming history and one of the most influential titles on the market, you have two main campaigns, an extra mission, and the mercenaries mode which offers four stages, five characters, and nearly infinite replayability. This hearkens back to a time when games were about both substance and value. You'd be a fool NOT to take advantage of a sale and play if you haven't yet. Even if it's not on sale, this game will make for a fun weekend.

This game is almost a "greatest of all time," but is brought down for some key reasons for me. The level design is fantastic, with every combat area having multiple paths that allow for creativity while navigating and defeating opponents. The enemy design is great, having multiple varieties of humanoid enemies that truly feel unique due to different behaviors and weapons, and monster enemies that are a good change of pace occasionally throughout the story. The writing is corny in a way that isn't seen today, with a self-aware earnestness rather than being stupidity hidden behind 12 layers of irony. My biggest issues are the QTE's and bosses. I can give grace on the bosses, as the rocket launcher will allow you to "skip" most of them. They aren't necessarily poorly designed, I simply find them to be the least engaging form of gunplay and movement in this game. The QTE's, on the other hand, almost ruin the game for me, especially on my most recent professional playthrough. Having X and C be the bound keys, switching prompts for mashing when a miss-click can lead to severe damage or death, and requiring mashing so fast that it requires me to abandon the mouse with my right hand to mash are all incredibly frustrating and instantly bring me out of the game. However, when thinking about it more objectively, this game is very well made overall, with some shortcomings here and there.

By the time that this port had made to PC, they failed to include not just an auto/quick saving system, but also had some playability issues pertaining to quick time events that would require the player to switch from 30 to 60 frames per second. That was an option you could only do by going to a main menu if you hadn't recently saved. This was something I had to do twice (as well as lower the anti-aliasing), and killed it for me were it not for the kindness of strangers who found a workaround that the devs refused to correct. Also, don't include a merchant who often stands in front of and behind an abundance of ammunition only to never sell you a single bullet. The adaptive system of the game predicting you needing ammo by dropping some from whoever you killed sucks. Who would expect a small bug to be hiding 30 TMP bullets in their prison wallet? It's as believable as the cringe-inducing dialogue throughout the game, but the level design alone is worth going through for. Masterful stuff, really. 

People largely read these reviews to stoke their own egos about what was a pivotal game to them or their childhood. And, make no mistake about it, this was a unique bestseller for Gamecube for a good reason - level design, art style, over-the-top combat and a cheesy script make this a blockbuster that has influenced many other classics. If you played The Last of Us or the Dark Souls franchise, you'll find similarities in the ambience. 

The game absolutely crushes it in terms of:

- Appropriate length (10+ casual playthrough guarantee on Normal difficulty);
- A diverse enemy and boss pool that will kill you in many frustrating ways.
- Surprisingly satisfying shooting mechanics without a reticle or much/any aim assist
- A cohesive plot in detail-rich apocalyptic environments/levels
- Competent voice acting 

However, I think with the onset of stellar remasters going on in this series that this is worth holding off on playing in its current state. It is not a bad game, and I was able to go through it for all of the listed reasons. I just think that the controls killed it for me. If you want a retro game binge or take another dip into the infinity pool of nostalgia, then fine. For nostalgics, just understand that you have undergone a great deal of self-deception if you think that it played as fine or as smooth as your younger self thought it did. You're better off waiting, or at least do a cheeky playthrough on an emulator where you can tap a quick save feature when you get clapped.

Resident Evil 4 is one of those games that I wanted to play for the longest time, and after almost 10 years of wanting to do so, I finally did it. The game is as good as everybody else says, that is undeniable. Even though it's over 15 years old, the game still holds up.

The game has a good story, very engaging gameplay (that may take the more modern players a while to get used to) and pretty good exploration. The stiff movement makes battles much more dangerous, specially when most enemies do quite a bit of damage and healing items aren't very common at the start of the game. The adventure overall is, in my opinion, where Resident Evil 4 shines: The athmosphere of the game is constantly changing, you go from a spanic village to a medieval castle, then you explore underground ruins, etc. This constant change of enviroment makes it so the game never fells too samey and repetitive, specially when new types of enemies are constantly being introduced.

Speaking of enemies, though, that's where my main criticism of the game comes in: Enemies sometimes feel too spongy. Some of them feel like they are invincible until you spend half your Rifle ammo and suddenly they drop dead. Killing the strongest enemies in this game isn't very fun, with few exceptions like the regenerators, which have a clear weakspot and "visible health" [spoiler]and by that I mean the amount of parasites hanging onto their body[/spoiler]. Ironically enough, the solution to those sponge enemies/bosses, which is the RPG, is also another thing I don't like, they are too cheap, specially in late game, and one shot all enemies and almost all bosses.

These small criticisms aside, I really enjoyed Resident Evil 4. It aged really well since it was released, and people who never played it before should definitely give it a try.

Time and memory go hand-in-hand, which might be why I wasn't able to remember much about Resident Evil 4 after finishing Resident Evil Village, 15 years later. All I could recall was buying the game four times, the game's intro, the merchant, and Ashely being annoying, which actually might have been for the best. It felt as if I was playing for the first time all over again, allowing nostalgia to be a nonfactor while I trudged through this heck of a game.

[b]Here are the Nifty things I liked, and the Lame things I didn't.[/b]

[h1]The Nifty[/h1]
✪ Though you can't help but feel its age while you play, there are a lot of features that were so far ahead of their time that they ended up serving as the most impressive bits in Resident Evil Village; a game that released 16 years later. Semi-open world exploration, key items no longer taking up inventory space, treasures being combinable for more money, an expandable briefcase opposed to universal storage boxes and a merchant allowing you to not only buy but also upgrade gear are just a few.

✪ Even when setting aside the clunky controls, Resident Evil 4 remains the most challenging Resident Evil game to date. In most cases you'll be dealing with far more enemies than most "survival horror" games allow, and you often won't be able to choose between standing your ground or fleeing the scene. These enemies become much more difficult to deal with as the game progresses, and with no way to block or dodge, clever inventory management and preparation for future encounters will be absolutely necessary to reach the end.

✪ Every time I started to feel as if the game was getting stale, it managed to change things up in ways that kept it engaging. This is nothing new for the franchise, but unlike games prior to Resident Evil 4, this wasn't just done up by introducing new enemy types or making some changes to previously visited areas. New locales with impressive amounts of detail for their time made Resident Evil more than musty old buildings and long corridors. Wide, open areas somehow felt claustrophobic, and as enemies became more persistent, Leon's struggle genuinely felt as if it was intensifying.

✪ Its enemy designs have me wondering how future titles were able to get away with so little. In Resident Evil 4 the biggest and most common threats simply appear to be dull, angry people holding various weapons. However, their ability to attack in unison and wield more effective weapons as the game progresses can occasionally make them frightening. That is especially the case once popping their heads starts sending out angry parasites that become deadlier as you get further in the game. Combine them with the handful of other enemies you have to deal with, and you've got yourself a pretty impressive roster. 

✪ There's still more to do after RE4's main campaign than there is to do in most other single-player games, all without needing to spend more money. To start, Professional difficulty unlocks alongside New Game+, allowing you to choose between starting anew on a more punishing difficulty, or going through the game again on a difficulty you already completed with the money and gear you've already collected. Popular survival mode, The Mercenaries, also becomes available, letting you to test your skills against hordes of enemies. Finally, Ada Wong gets two modes of her own; one being a 2 to 3 hour campaign that shows what was going on beyond Leon's perspective, and the other being a roughly 30 to 45 minute mini-game.

[h1]The Lame[/h1]
✘ Tank controls with third-person perspective, not being able to reload without aiming, not being able to move while you aim and several other little gameplay gripes ended up making me truly appreciate how far we've come. I genuinely cannot remember the last time I struggled to play a game, and since the playstyle is a borderline insufferable mess compared to modern standards, getting used to it took a bit more time than I thought it would. This *was* the first time I ever played the game with a keyboard and mouse though, so I'll sprinkle some sugar on this negative point.

✘ This game reminded me of literally every reason I had to be glad about Quick Time Events (QTEs) slowly disappearing from most games, and completely being absent from the series in Resident Evil 7 onward at the time of writing. Just about every moment requiring them feels unnecessary, the speed in which buttons need to be pressed is unpleasant using KBM and the conditions for failure are often deaths that can send you back to the beginning of this game's most frustrating segments. 

✘ Ashley. Escort missions are always a major gripe of mine, especially when you're escorting a defenseless being with their own health bar, but Ashley turns an already dreadful game mechanic into a chore. Not only do you have to make sure she stays safe from enemies who can harm and attempt to kidnap her, but you can accidentally injure or even kill Ashley yourself if she fails to get out of the way in time. She's also incapable of descending ladders and has to be caught after jumping down instead. In addition to all that, you also have to use your own health items to heal her when she's on the verge of death, make sure she's following you, tell her to hide when there are too many enemies around and be careful not to let her get one-shot by environmental hazards for an entire half of the game. It's not all bad though. Her one and only redeeming quality is the fact that she'll occasionally do a cute little cheering gesture when you kill things.

[h1]Overall[/h1]
Resident Evil 4 was a great game for its time and has a lot of outstanding features that were far ahead of it. However, saying it didn't age well is an understatement, and because of that, I have to recommend it with extreme caution. Its pros outweigh the cons from a numeral perspective, but the weight of those cons and how often you have to deal with them are sure to rub newcomers the wrong way. Nostalgia has been carrying this gem for 16 years and will likely continue to do so until the REmake releases. Unless you carry even a little of that nostalgia, immense amounts of patience will be required to truly enjoy this game.

Resident Evil 4 is one of those games everyone seems to worship, and somehow I’m just sitting here wondering what I’m missing. I fully understand and respect what it did for the series — the over-the-shoulder aiming, the pacing shift, the influence on modern action games — but none of that makes it enjoyable for me.

The tone is where it loses me first. Instead of tense survival horror, the game leans heavily into action, quick-time events, and exaggerated enemy encounters. Gone is the dread and fear the older games built so well — replaced by loud set pieces, waves of enemies, and constant combat. It feels more like an arcade shooter than Resident Evil.

Then there’s the pacing. The game bombards you with fights, sections that drag on too long, and encounters that feel more exhausting than fun. The escort sections, and some boss fights all added to my frustration instead of excitement. It never clicked the way other entries did, and I constantly found myself forcing progress rather than wanting it.

I know the industry sees RE4 as a masterpiece, and clearly most players love it. But personally? It’s the one Resident Evil I’ve never truly enjoyed, no matter how many times I tried to give it another chance.

It may be iconic — just not for me.

After recently getting all the achievements for this game, I figured it was time to write a review on it. This was the second Resident Evil game I ever played, and easily one of my favourites, within my top three.

Pros:
- Excellent gameplay loop that involves unique enemies and bosses, as well as a perfect blend of survival horror and action that requires you to consider your spacing and navigation through different environments as you deal with the hoards of enemies
- A good OST that contains some real memorable tunes (The Save Room theme in particular is noice)
- A story that is over the top and ridiculous, but in a good way. Cheesy as hell and likely to make you smile as you experience Leon S. Kennedy's epic one liners and play through holly wood style set pieces
- Retains most of the horror elements from the classic games, with certain enemies having perfect introductions and designs to creep you out
- A good amount of replayability due to multiple weapon and costume unlocks, as well as three bonus modes in 'Separate Ways', 'Assignment Ada', and 'The Mercenaries'
- Tons of quotable lines ("No Thanks, Bro!" and "Ah! I'll buy it at a high price!")

Cons:
- While not the worst graphically, some textures have aged significantly, but this can be remedied via mods
- While by far from the worst escort companion, Ashley's screams of "LEEEEEEEEEEEEEEEEEEEEEEEEEEEEEEEEEEEEEEEEEEEEEEEEEEEEEEEEEEEEEEEEEOOOOOOOOOOOOOOOOOOOOOOOOOOOOOOOOOOOOOOOOOOOOOON HEEEEEEEEEEEEEEEEEEEEEEEEEEEEEEEEEEEEEEEEEEEEEEEEEEEEEEELLLLLLLLLLLLLLLLLLLLLLLLLLLLLLLP" may drive you insane
- Many QTEs within the game. Not as bad as other games as they are integrated into the gameplay, but I can see it being annoying for some
- Boring and bland main villain compared to the silliness of the rest of the game and the other antagonists
- Tank controls can be difficult to grasp at first, stick with it, trust me
- A few bosses can be annoying due to the over reliance on QTEs and/or gimmicks
- Final act of the game gets a little too spammy and actiony for my liking

Conclusion:
Overall, this is a fantastic action/horror game that absolutely deserves its status as a classic. I know a few RE fans dislike this title due to the direction it took the series, and while I can agree to some extent with the subsequent entries, RE4 itself is still easily one of the best games in the series. If you're into survival horror and are interested in the series, RE4 is an excellent place to start along with REmake 2. And if you're already an RE fan, then idk how you haven't played this already lol.

Final Verdict:
Highly Recommended (Worth it for Full Price)
