This might turn into a long review, but it'll be honest and detailed. Spoilers are kept to a minimum and I do not review to anger fans or look like a fan, I say what I think and I'm not looking for approval of any kind. I try to be as unbiased as possible, I also do not compare to previous or later entries (I might provide some insight into what I've played or where I come from), I also always review each game title as a standalone title, regardless of remakes or re-imaginings.

This review will be structured as such; 
- I will start with giving a little "background" into why and how I've come to play this game, for the sake of perspective.
- I will comment on this game from the perspective of it being a PC port. I never played the original console version.
- I will discuss what I feel are pros and cons and finally give my verdict in a score on 10 (1=garbage, 5=average, 10=perfect).

So let's get on with it!


[U][B]BACKGROUND[/B][/U]
My first experience with Resident Evil, if we don't count the first live-action movie I went to see in theatres and don't count any kind of demos I may have played in my young age... would be the Resident Evil 2 Remake.

I loved that game so much, it pushed me to want to explore the entire RE franchise, but mostly on PC, as I was never a console player (not because I have anything against them, I just did not grow up around them, and my interest has always been in computer components and building my own). So after playing RE2Remake, I decided to backtrack to play games in release order; RE2R, then RE1HD, RE3R, RE0 and finally RE4.

I would also like to make it clear, I am NOT a lore hunter; as long as there seems to be some form of connection between characters and the ideas behind a virus and genetic modifications, I'm okay with it. So, I will not comment on lore accuracy, canon or lore issues.


[U][B]PC PORTS COMMENTS[/B][/U]
With a PC port, or any PC game released anytime after the year 1998, you have a certain level of expectations in 3rd and first person games.. that comes in terms of camera field of view, controls, movement, graphics, sound, etc... after all, what is the point of a PC release if the game cannot make use of the extra potential of a PC hardware?

After having played Resident Evil 1 and Zero in a short time apart, I was looking forward to a modern control scheme (and let's not hide it; for 3rd person games, it's hard to even compete with the RE2/3 Remakes in terms of controls and movement polish).. and unfortunately, here, I was really disappointed. To be honest, I would have preferred a fixed camera with old-school controls over those of this game. Movement, turning, field of view, etc.. all feel like they we're kept EXACTLY as if I had to play it with a controller on a TV (using A & D to turn, instead of the mouse, not having any way to sidestep or strafe feels really weird for a game release after the mid-90's). The only advantage of this port is the higher resolution and "HD" rework.. 

Thing is, these are technical issues that we can often put behind when a story is tense, immersive and powerful....

so, is it?


[U][B]PROS & CONS[/B][/U]
Let's start by a few things I did like.
+ I did like that there was a good amount of choice in firearms and customisation. This provided a kind of tactic or choice to the style of play you decide to go after. You can go for weaker weapons that put down more bullets, or stronger weapons that require way more precise aiming. It was one of the rare times during the game that I actually thought of anything at all...
+ A couple interesting boss fights.
+ Music is "okay".

+/- Not a very hard game, easy bosses.

This is where the "good" stops unfortunately. 

- I've rarely encountered such sloppy and poor writing in a video game. Even if I know Resident Evil isn't the "deepest" or most "thought-provoking" franchise... this level of writing and dialog is some of the weakest I've ever played in my history of video games (since the VERY early 90's)..
- The type of dialog you can expect to hear is in the vein of: "I'm coming for you!" "oh we will see" "muhahaha" "I defeated your traps" "oh I have more" "I'm coming!!!!" "we will see, you are welcome to die".... this is the level of writing and dialog in this game. It's pathetic. This makes FMV's in Red Alert and C&C look like they hired experts.
- Level design of the worst kind; in a horror franchise that was built on some form of puzzle solving and some minor to major backtracking... expect NONE of that here. No puzzles, no choices, just follow the path forward. It's linear like most extremely linear games.
- Linear can be okay when the story, setting and atmosphere make up for it, linear can made to look open of full of choices with the choice of environment and layout, lighting effects, etc.. But there is none here. For a "horror"-themed franchise, there is little to no horror to be found here. I realise, tech was limited on the Gamecube, so I cannot expect any good lighting or atmospheric effects.
- It's a cookie-cutter formula, you enter a new location, as soon as you cross a certain "trigger", enemies will spawn somewhere and the battle music ramps up... hey!! some tension you think!! NOPE, none of that, let's make enemies spawn far away in front or behind and give you PLENTY of time to see them come!! When you've defeated the last enemy, battle music stops.
- The "battle" system I just explained leads to a game that has no tension, no buildup in suspense. 
- A few quicktime events...
- This game feels like a mix of arcade shooter and House of the Dead style "on-rails shooter" you found in arcades (when those were still around)
- One of the worst levels is the one with the castle. You've got a castle with catapults shooting flaming "bombs" at you... on the castle.. so a castle shooting at itself.. Then there is a level later near the end of the castle where these is a huge mechanized statue of Salazar that runs after you, pretty much destroying itself, the ground and part of the castle.. makes so much sense. Building an entire huge section and statue so we can trap one guy. Sure. At that point though, I was already anxious to get this game over with. This was beyond what we call "cheesy".
- I don't want to spoil it too much, but minor spoiler here: the girl you save ends up having a "crush" on you. That's okay, I mean, you play a tough hunky dude and there is a early adult girl who finds you cute. Why didn't they build it up by having banter between the two? I mean, Leon isn't interested, but they could have put in some banter from her, she might always be asking him questions, just trying to talk to him.. but no.. the vast majority of the game, she is following you like a mute person. It's kind of sad and a missed opportunity to actually maybe make you "feel" something for the characters. the game was already "cheesy" to an unbelievable level.. 


[U][B]FINAL VERDICT[/B][/U]
I went in with a good outlook; looking forward to some good tension, atmosphere and "horror" but was left completely unsatisfied, mostly feeling like I played a game written by children, for children.

To me, this is among the worst games I've ever played, period.

[h1][b]Introduction[/b][/h1]
Admittedly, I got into the [b]Resident Evil[/b] series with the latest titles, namely [b]Resident Evil VII[/b] and the remake of [b]Resident Evil 2[/b]. I thoroughly enjoyed both titles, and as I do not mind playing older games, I was naturally interested in the rest of the series. So, the acclaimed fourth game was supposed to be the right choice for me. Unfortunately, I was wrong. While I cannot deny [b]Resident Evil 4’s[/b] influence on its genre, it would be a blatant lie to claim that I enjoyed playing it.
[h3][b]Story[/b][/h3]
The U.S. President’s daughter, [b]Ashley[/b], was kidnapped by a mysterious Spanish cult, so the government decided to send their agent, whom players of the series already know well, [b]Leon Kennedy[/b]. He ventures into Spain and begins with the search in an old, abandoned village. At least it looked like it at first glance. Leon quickly finds himself surrounded by a group of hostile villagers, who seem to be under the cult’s control. However, as the clocks are ticking, [b]Leon[/b] has to find and save [b]Ashley[/b] before something happens to her and destroy the cult, if possible.

Unfortunately, the whole story is just a mess full of cheesy lines and unhumorous jokes about everything by [b]Leon[/b]. It becomes tiresome pretty quickly, as they are overused. Another issue is that the plot gets prolonged numerously by the constant kidnapping of [b]Ashley[/b]. To be honest, I expected the same or at least a similar theme as the remake of [b]Resident Evil 2[/b] had. Meaning, a decent horror with a few cheesy and ridiculous situations at best. Instead, I got a tedious, uninteresting plot with over usage of unfunny jokes, without any proper horror elements at all. And if this story intends to be a parody of the horror genre, then it fails tremendously.
https://steamcommunity.com/sharedfiles/filedetails/?id=2271717301
[h3][b]Gameplay[/b][/h3]
Something that annoys me right from the start is when the game locks harder difficulty setting and requires you to finish it on the lower ones first, which is even worse when it is already utterly easy to play. Nevertheless, the campaign took me around fourteen hours to finish, and I spent a few more hours with the game’s additional content.

To my unpleasant surprise, [b]Resident Evil 4[/b] is a more linear experience than the abovementioned titles, as there is not much to explore. Most of the items, such as ammo or healing materials, are handed to you way too often, which takes away the fear of having scarce resources, making the game easier than necessary. Another issue is that puzzles are primitive, mostly requiring you to move an item from place A into place B. The only thing I liked about this simplistic exploration is that collectables are useful, as you can sell them for money at the trader.

Speaking of trader, you buy weapons and upgrades from him. There is not a storage box anymore, so you have to either sell or discard superfluous items, as your inventory is limited. I am not a fan of this because it restricts me a bit, as I cannot change weapons that often anymore, which is more annoying as they are upgradable. It is also a shame because there is a decent weapon variety, as there are several types of handguns, shotguns, rifles, and such. So, some weapons might be more precise, while others offer a decent penetration through enemies. There are also grenades, which are quite fun to use.
https://steamcommunity.com/sharedfiles/filedetails/?id=2271717921
What I grew to like was the gameplay implementation of your companion, [b]Ashley[/b]. She has her own health bar, so you have to protect her. It adds a bit more challenge to it, as she is basically defenseless. She also occasionally points out some loot. So, overall, I prefer this approach, as it is more immersive rather than having a companion invisible to enemies. The problem with her is that her English voice is absolutely annoying, and I can hear her in my head even now.

As for the enemies, they are pretty varied. Especially boss fights are interesting, as each requires a bit different strategy. There are also a few unique enemies that occasionally make combat with the hoards of regular enemies more interesting. Most of the common enemies, like villagers, can wield weapons, such as axes, crossbows, shields, and others. And you can actually shoot weapons out of their hands or even immobilize them by shooting them in the legs! Gameplay details like these are something I definitely appreciate.

My main problem with the combat is that there are way too many regular enemies, like villagers. It is boring to fight them, as there is no challenge in it, and those fights are not memorable. What I enjoyed about the abovementioned [b]Resident Evil[/b] titles was that most of the encounters were a bit unique and presented a bit of challenge due to having scarce resources. You just brainlessly shoot dozens of enemies, move onto the next location, and do it again, without caring about the resources, as you know that you will get tons of them. That is just the exact opposite of the other titles, as this is rather an action game than survival horror.

Regular enemies you fight most of the time also tend to sprint towards you once they spot you, but they will stop running like two meters in front of you, as they will start walking super slowly. This design decision throws any tension out of the window because you know that you will always be safe and have a lot of time to kill them.
https://steamcommunity.com/sharedfiles/filedetails/?id=2271716239
I am also not a fan of these horrible controls. I ended up using a controller, which still was not the best option, but at least it was manageable. I do not remember another shooter, made by a bigger studio, in which I would have so many problems with controlling the character. During the whole game, I had the feeling that I fight with the game’s controls than with the enemies. [b]Steam’s Guides[/b], unfortunately, did not help me.
[h3][b]Additional Content[/b][/h3]
New game modes unlock after finishing the campaign. The most interesting one is [b]Separate Ways[/b], where you witness [b]Ada’s[/b] actions during the campaign. You should play this one if you enjoyed the base game, as it expands upon its story a bit. It took me around three hours to finish it. Another one, [b]Assignment: Ada[/b] is rather a minigame, where you collect some samples, and I would not bother with it. The last one, [b]The Mercenaries[/b], is about killing waves of enemies. It is intended for people who enjoy the game’s combat, so I did not bother replaying it. Nevertheless, it is a nice addition.
[h3][b]Audiovisuals & Performance[/b][/h3]
Although visuals are pretty dated, I still love the game’s distinctive locations. You will visit a foggy village, castle, caves, labs, and more. It manages to provide a decent variety to keep you interested. I especially liked the castle chapters due to its design. The appearance of various monsters should receive a fair share of praise too. Unfortunately, I cannot say the same about the soundtrack, as it is pretty forgettable, and some of the English voice actors deliver a questionable quality.

The game was tested with an [b]i5 8300H, GTX 1060 6GB, and 16GB RAM[/b], running at the highest settings, at [b]30-60 frames per second[/b], at [b]1920x1080 resolution[/b]. However, if the framerate does not run constantly on 30 or 60 frames, the game tends to run in some weird slow-motion mode.

[h1][b]Conclusion[/b][/h1]
Sweet gameplay details, weapons and location’s variety, as well as good-looking monsters cannot save this game for me. Mediocre port, terrible controls, uninteresting story, no horror elements at all, and tiresome combat is all I have in mind when thinking about this game. Maybe the possible upcoming remake will make it better?

Every so often you get an entry in a long running series that is so good it's worth checking out even for people with little investment in the franchise. Silent Hill 2, Persona 4 and Breath of the Wild are examples that jump to mind, as does, of course, Resident Evil 4. Resident Evil 4 isn't just a great Resident Evil game, but a great game period. It's just so good and so much fun that even if you bounced hard off of the tank controls, bad acting and BOWs of classic Resident Evils, RE4 is a standalone all time classic definitely worth playing.

I wasn't always a big fan, actually. A lot of my friends were completely obsessed with Resident Evil 4, one in particular beating it thirty odd times on the Gamecube and then beating it some more on the Wii. But I had left behind my [url=https://steamcommunity.com/id/crateboxer/recommended/304240/]weird Resident Evil idolation[/url] by the time it came out and that first chainsaw man was just too much for me to deal with.

Now older and more [strike]dead inside[/strike] mature, I finally appreciate why people were so obsessed with this game. It's amazingly fun. Resident Evil 4 effortlessly swings between scary and tense, like the siege on the cabin or village opening, to goofy and campy, like whenever Leon suplexes a dude or throws out a ridiculous Bond one-liner ("Where's everyone going? [i]Bingo?[/i]"). There's tons of truly memorable set pieces and inspired enemy design, to the point that I still vividly remember every single awesome moment even after my one run two years back.

It did on the fly difficulty adjustments before anyone else. For better or worse, it certainly popularized QTEs. Indeed, it basically invented the modern third person shooter. Resident Evil 4 is probably the most influential game of the 2000s and games today would look wildly different without it.

So Resident Evil 4 is well worth playing, both from the historical importance perspective and the fact that, again, it's really damn fun.  This version is basically definitive with all extra content and some cleaned up textures, though there are alternate HD mods if they take your fancy. But do play it! Even if it did start a big shift away from my kind of Resident Evil (look forward to those reviews!), it's still one of the greatest video games ever made.

RE4 just makes me happy, there's not a boring moment in the campaign, sure, the gameplay is a bit dated but it's satisfying and hella tense, and it's drenched in carefully crafted atmosphere, in my opinion and many others, one of the best games of all time.

I had the original version of this game when it came out for the PC in the early 2000's. Decided to re-install it from the DVD and was disappointed with the 30 fps that was locked into that version which apparently was just a port from the PS2 version. Also, the resolution was awful (no 1920x1080 support directly if I remember unless you wanted to stretch it out) and visually, just ugly. Jagged graphics, fuzzy textures, and not the best controller support.

A friend of mine had the HD version so I tried it out and was hooked with the smooth 60-fps so I purchased it. It's been probably 10+ years since I last played this game and having come off from RE2 and RE3 remakes, as well has the HD versions of RE0 and RE, this definitely was a different take from what I remember from the first time. But even after playing the HD remakes of RE0 and RE, I can see how even with this HD "upgrade" (it's not a remake like RE, RE2 and RE3), it's still dated in how it renders everything. Lower polygonal count so things look jagged in the character models during close ups, hand models are blocky, etc. HD seems to apply to how they've smoothed out the FPS and some of the character models and the backgrounds. Still, textures are fuzzy and backgrounds are still blurry, just not as bad as in the original.

There is the Resident Evil 4 HD Project which aims to fix a lot of the texture issues and it does. They've even worked on the cut-scenes to make the backgrounds more sharp and detail as well as the in-game backgrounds. But this could also detract at times as it shows the age of the game. Compared to the HD remakes of RE0 and RE, this still looks dated. 

But what matters is the game play. If you want to use a controller, it gives the correct buttons to press based on your controller whereas in the original, it just gave button numbers which was difficult to remember which button was 0, 1, 2, etc.

The game-play itself hasn't changed, nor the story so this is [i]not[/i] a remake. It's just a visual overhaul, including an increase to 60 fps. 

Is it worth getting if you already own the original? Only if you want the smooth 60 fps and some updated visuals as well as playing at higher resolutions, or your a completionist and need all versions of the RE games. But if 30 fps is fine, then it's probably not worth getting. But, if you want to use the RE4 HD Project, then you must get the HD version of RE4 because that's what it's based on and it does help with textures.

Still, not disappointed with my purchase. It's still a fun game and I forgot how funny it was at times too.

This was my first time playing through Resident Evil 4. Despite its age, I really loved this game. The controls are still pretty tanky and a little clunky in comparison to modern over the shoulder 3rd-person shooters.

I played through with the [url=https://www.re4hd.com/?page_id=6064]Resident Evil 4 HD Project mod[/url], which really smooths out some of the rougher textures in the game, but it’s unfortunately not complete yet and hasn’t seen a public update since July 2018. The developers of the mod are still working on it though and recently showed off a [url=https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=GF2rr-0Sjko]preview of chapter 5-3, which looks fantastic[/url]. 

[h1]Story[/h1]
Resident Evil 4’s story is pretty great. Leon Kennedy’s mission is to rescue the US President’s daughter in a rural village in Spain. Where, you guessed it, another outbreak has occurred. There are several different unique environments that you’ll travel between, which helps to keep the gameplay from becoming overly stale and “samey.”

[h1]Gameplay[/h1]
The combat can be pretty tanky, but once you get used to the quick-turn button, it’s honestly super playable and holds up really well. After getting accustomed to the controls and overall janky controls, I honestly loved the gameplay. Killing those infected with Las Plagas was endlessly satisfying.

There’s also plenty of puzzles throughout the game. Most of them are pretty simple and don’t require a lot of effort. However, some of them are super lazy, [spoiler]like moving the statue during Leon’s fight with Krauser[/spoiler], and some of them were actually pretty confusing, [spoiler]like the family insignia puzzle in Chapter 1-3’s cemetery.[/spoiler] 

There are several really cool sequences in this game that stood out to me, and one that I really hated. I loved the knife fight sequence between [spoiler]Krauser and Leon[/spoiler] in Chapter 5-3. It’s got some fantastic animation work, and was just really fun to watch, especially for a 15 year-old game. It really impressed me. However, the helicopter section in 5-4 was such a drag. I hated every minute of it. I also got to the end of it, walked through the door, and then the game crashed on me. So, I had to endure it a second time, which probably has a lot to do with my feelings about it. 

[h1]Relics[/h1]
Despite loving this game, there’s still several relics that scream “old game.” To name a few:
[list]
[*] Tank-like controls: Yeah, I know I just said it was “super playable,” but that doesn’t mean I wouldn’t prefer playing this fantastic game with a bit more mobility. 
[*] No weapon hot swapping: Each time you want to change weapons, you have to pause the game, open up your inventory, scroll over to the weapon, equip it, and then unpause. Being able to bind weapons to hotkeys, or even a weapon wheel would be much better, in my opinion.
[*] Framerate: The game runs at 60fps, but not all of the animations translated well. There’s still several animations that are stuck at 30fps (meaning that at 60fps, the animation only updates every other frame). There’s also issues with the QTEs running at twice the speed at 60fps, meaning that you have the spam the absolute ♥♥♥♥ out of the button to not fail a QTE.
[*] Clipping: There’s several textures that clip through one another. For example, when Leon’s carrying the Red9 with a stock equipped, the stock commonly clips through Leon’s forearm when moving around or climbing up ladders. 
[*] Egregiously reused character models: I think there’s like 4 human enemy types. There’s unique character bosses and some odd creatures here and there, but pretty much every human shares the exact same model, which can be pretty distracting. I played the first Witcher game earlier this year, which struggled with the same issue. It’s distracting, but not a dealbreaker by any means. 
[*] Dialogue: I hope I’m wrong about this, but I feel like some of the dialogue in this game won’t make it into the inevitable Resident Evil 4 Remake. There were several comments about Ashley’s butt, which I found weird, because Ashley looks like she’s 14 in this game, but [url=https://residentevil.fandom.com/wiki/Info_on_Ashley]according to the wiki, she’s 20[/url], so maybe a lot less weird than I initially thought.
[/list]

[h1]Ultrawide Support[/h1]
As an ultrawide user, I’m no stranger to using community fixes to mod in ultrawide support, especially for older games. For the life of me, I could not get ultrawide support to work properly in this game. It’s no problem getting Hor+ to work with Flawless Widescreen, but I found it impossible to get the HUD to work properly. Even with Hor+ FOV, the HUD was still Vert-. Ultimately, I opted to play the game at 2560x1440 with Flawless Widescreen used to increase the FOV by 27, which was the maximum value that didn’t produce the Fisheye effect, in my opinion.


[h1]Separate Ways[/h1]
Separate Ways is a short “Side B” campaign featuring Ada that takes place in tandem with the main RE4 story, casting some light on Ada’s mission in RE4. However, I honestly can’t say that I was a fan of this. With the exception of Chapter 4, every level was just a retread of an existing RE4 level. All of the cutscenes in this campaign were very low resolution FMVs, even though the FMVs were 99% the same as the main RE4’s in-engine, native resolution cutscenes.

Ada also doesn’t have any upgrades available, so the combat felt like a slog after spending so much time and money upgrading Leon’s guns. It was nice to see things from Ada’s perspective, but I don’t think I learned all that much, and it felt more or less like a chore. 


[h1]Conclusion[/h1]
I loved Resident Evil 4. For years, I’ve read comments on reddit and watched videos on YouTube praising it as one of the best games ever made. And now, after finally having finished it, I can see why. It’s fantastic. I think I would have loved it even more had I played it closer to its release, as it came out during my peak “nostalgia building years.” 

So, [b]does it hold up in late 2020?[/b] If you can look past a little bit of clunkiness, then [b]absolutely yes[/b]. I’d absolutely recommend anyone that’s a fan of survival horror (or the non-survival horror Resident Evil 5 and 6 games).

Ah… RE4.

The game Capcom has the audacity to port silly on every gaming device and the nerve to think we’re stupid enough to buy it again and again…

Well they’re damn right, because it’s Resident f#*@!ng  Evil  4, boys!

Let’s do this.

[h1]INSIGHT[/h1]

Resident Evil 4 is a game you’re probably more than familiar with and own several copies to say the least, but if some chance you are unfamiliar with it; then here’s the brief introduction:

Resident Evil is a zombie horror/action series that follows a series of characters dealing with Umbrella’s (The OG main baddies) shenanigans of BOW’s, zombies and other crap that wants to kill the utter 7 shades of ♥♥♥♥♥ out of you; usually ending with you blowing up some behemoth with a rocket launcher, getting the girl and flying away in a helicopter off into the sunset leaving the carnage behind for the under-paid sods who do the clean-up and maintenance. 

Resident Evil 4 continues on with one of the main characters, Leon Scott Kennedy; who gives you some backstory anyway on how much of a Bellend Umbrella was whilst he’s travels down a Spanish country rode with two Spaniard cops consuming narcotics whilst on the drive to a location where a missing girl, the El Presidente’s own daughter, Ashley Graham was reported to be seen.
However, upon Leon’s arrival, things begin to take a turn for the worst as what sinister motivations were conducted in this rural part of Spain begin to surface. From this point on, it’s Bingo, Sonny Jim!

[h1]VISUALS[/h1]

Even with its nice HD remaster, the game is still visually quite dated, although for myself, it stands with a nice does of nostalgia and a reminder there’s a lot worse. Although being on PC, there are mods out there for ‘true’ HD remasters or ‘Ultra’ HD to spice it right up.

[h1]GAMEPLAY[/h1]

Upon its conception, RE4 was a game changer. Although it went through some development hell; our boy Shinji Mikami did it again. Ditching the old-school fixed camera angles, this title went with its revolutionary over-the-shoulder camera that has since been widely adopted. Orientated with more action and shooting focus, RE4 drops its puzzles and horror a bit in more favour of action, humour and all the aggro Ashley will give you along the way.

This one has more focus on QTE’s (quick time events), fast-past action, guns and explosions. However, despite all this, the puzzles still remain to a small degree – but the horror is far from dead.

The first section of the village has more than a fair share of ominous ambience, music, environment design and enemy encounters. This continues to the game’s mid-section (the castle) and even to the heavy-action end-game island level (stares uneasily into the distance with thoughts of U3 and the regenerators in mind).

So, if you’re looking for a balance of puzzles, action, horror and some humour, you’ve come to the right place. Looking at it, Re4 is in a way, an amalgamation of different video game genres blurred into one.

I mean, even the inventory system management itself screams Tetris.

And let’s not forget the whack-a-mole with the crane on the island section.

[h1]STORY[/h1]

This story for this title is pretty simple and generic as always for Resident evil; and this one is no exception and is just as cheesy as ever. For me, this has Leon’s best incarnation for his character – Ada’s too.

Simply, Leon’s a government agent sent off to rescue the US President’s daughter from a parasite-fuelled cult organization injecting people with narcotics without their consent.

Don’t worry; it’s not the same narcotics the Spaniards were jacking up on.

But by kidnapping Ashley, they use her as a device to further their means of by infecting her, from which they can take power from their within the US and altar the socio-political world that they see fit.

In other words, Leon’s got some nutters to sort out. And sort out he bloody will.
[h1]AUDIO[/h1]

Audio wise, the game is completely fine in regards to the action and other sounds going on around you. The voice-acting is damn solid from all parties involved and has shown how far the series has come since the days of the ‘Jill sandwich’ ‘Chris’s blood’ and ‘WESKEEERR’.

The music though for me, is damn solid. Despite the heavy action focus, there’s many ominous and creepy tracks sprinkled throughout the OST, and the typewriter save music is sweet whilst the actual save room music is mesmerising and unforgettable; as expected from this franchise.

[h1]PERFORMANCE[/h1]

Re4 performs well, although whilst I’ve not played it in a bit on steam and primarily played it on PS4; I do recall having some issues of the frame-rate dropping to 30fps and everything going slow-motion like you’re in the 2012 film ‘Dredd’ and you just took the slo-mo for some karl Urban pounding. Dropping the peak for my frame settings resolved this, however.

[h1]REPLAYABILITY[/h1]

RE4, as probably still shown by the abundance of videos on YouTube and its continued popularity and remake; is a timeless classic and a game that some at least, to be regarded as one of the greatest games of all time.

This is no doubt helped by the several costumes you can choose to equip, the general strength of the story, gameplay and pacing itself, the characters and level design, Ada’s separate campaign, the unlockables, the challenges, Ada’s other game mode and the Mercenaries in which you can also play as Krouser, Hunk and even wesker to rack up high scores and unlock something special for main-game play.

This game always has something to offer and there’s usually something you learn years later despite playing it a hundred times. Resident evil 4 is just one of those damn games, and I wouldn’t be surprised if it remained so, even long after the remake.

[h1]CONCLUSION[/h1]

[i]+ Insane replaybility[/i]
[i]+ Original title that never gets old[/i]
[i]+ Powerful atmosphere and good sound design[/i]
[i]+ Good level and game design[/i]
[i]+ Much enemy variety, with some iconic monsters amongst its ranks[/i]
[i]+ Has good old Mercenaries[/i]
[i]+ Given this one is PC as well, there’s plenty of modding opportunity there[/i]
[i]+ All-round fun game to play and slaughter both time and Ganados[/i]
[i]+/- Game does utilise tank controls[/i]
[i]- Could have dodgy optimisation issues you get these days with ports[/i]
[i]- Game may be aged slightly. [/i]

This game is a classic and I have zero qualms with it being ranked amongst the best of the best of gaming. This game offers so much and has done even more for our video gaming industry and the influence it’s had and continues to have even now: and with mods, that fun is amplified limitlessly further. 

Even though a remake is on the horizon; with that remake is good or bad, the courage, struggle, innovation and the difficulties this game went through and presented moulded the piece of magic you’re reading about now, will never fade as long Capcom don’t do a Konami P.T. and remove it. Because until then, you’ll keep seeing people leaving reviews for this, people still talking about it, modding it, buying it and making YouTube challenges videos about it.

So go and do yourself a favour, mate; buy this game and add it to your list. No one will judge you, and if by some twatty chance they do; then introduce them to the handcannon.

But until then…

An otherwise excellent classic is marred by a horrifyingly awful control scheme based on severely outdated tank controls. There's no excuse in the modern age, especially for a third person over-the-shoulder shooter of this kind.  This isn't classic Resident Evil with fixed camera angles. [h1] STEAM REVIEW TLDR [/h1]

[b] PROS [/b]

+ Great combat and gunplay
+ Great variety of guns all of which can be upgraded.
+ Memorable boss fights
+ The environment and the ambiance that comes with it.
+ Great mix of action and horror
+ Rewards the player for exploration
+ Tons of optional content

[b] CONS [/b]

- Anything and everything that involves Ashley, 
- Plenty of QTE's which can lead to some cheap deaths.

Final Score - 9 / 10

[h1] INTRO [/h1]

Resident Evil 4 has been released countless times. Now of days with the PC rerelease the game runs at 60 FPS and is way more smooth than I am used too. The question we are asking here is how is Resident Evil 4? Is it a great Resident Evil game or was it the point where the series began to feel bland? 

[h1] STORY [/h1]

The story of Resident Evil 4 is a pretty average plot overall. You're Leon Scott Kennedy, one of the survivors of the Raccoon City incident who went from being your average cop to a US government special agent. Leon has been sent to Spain, his mission, to rescue the presidents daughter Ashley Graham who has been kidnapped. Once Leon arrives at the village he discovers something is horribly wrong with the locals. He will have to fight through crazy chainsaw wielding maniacs, villagers and etc, Some of which can mutate with the disgusting virus, Plaga. You will also have to fight giant monsters. This would not be Resident Evil without some creepy mutations and monsters.

[h1] LENGTH [/h1]

The length of the game feels just right. If you are one of those people who enjoys doing everything the game offers you. You should usually get 30+ hours out of the game, This includes replaying it plus optional extras and side stuff. A first playthrough could take anywhere around 10+ hours depending on your play style.

[h1] DIFFICULTY [/h1]

One of my first great memories for this game was finally reaching the village and having to survive against countless angry villagers, only to be greeted by a man with a chainsaw who promptly lobbed off my head and killed me quite a few times. Once they are finally defeated you are treated with the games logo. I remember yelling "That's the start? That's the tutorial?" The game set itself up to be pretty rough and tough, which overall yes it's a pretty difficult game. However I feel like the difficulty is perfect, just the right amount of frustration and happiness if that makes sense. It helps that the game plays fantastically. You will be running out of ammo, fighting hordes of angry enemies even plenty of annoying super enemies that aren't even bosses. The bosses themselves are pretty fun and fair overall.

[h1] CONTROLS [/h1]

This game has some pretty fun and tight controls. Aiming even with a controller feels nice and smooth. Quick turning is a life saver. Knifing things to get items and even knife kills are even pretty easy to do. The game was made for controls even though the PC rerelease plays great with a keyboard and mouse.

[h1] GAMEPLAY [/h1]

Resident Evil 4's gameplay is fantastic. The gunplay feels fun, shooting and killing the infested enemies feels fluid and fun. Shooting enemies in the head or knees then running up and giving them a nice roundhouse kick is great for solo enemies or even knocking down a group of enemies to get back. You will be collecting tons of treasure as you proceed through the game which you can then sell to the weapons merchant to buy plenty of guns and etc. No ammo though sadly. The only major complaint I have about the gameplay is Ashley. I'm not a fan of escort quests, even though this game for the most part becomes one big escort quest. Now I can admit that Ashley is somewhat smart and does not normally get in your way while shooting however she can die very easily with her low health early game. Sometimes while she is being carried away you can simply and accidentally kill her in one shot. However the least fun bits with Ashley come from when you are controlling her yourself for her puzzle sections, made even worst with some almost instant kill QTE's that are very fast. This game does use QTE's but overall I am fine with the use of them. The only time you are forced into a heavy QTE will be late in the game when Leon comes face to face with Krauser.

[h1] MUSIC [/h1]

Before we talk about the characters I have to ask how is the music? Overall the music is very fitting. Mostly creeping ambiance to fit the atmosphere. Some eerie music to let you know when you have been spotted. The music is more fitting for use in the game than listening to out of the game. For what it's worth i think the music is great

[h1] CHARACTERS [/h1]

Throughout the game you will meet plenty of interesting characters. Our boy Leon Scott Kennedy who we have already talked about. Ashley Gram the daughter of the president who tends to be more annoying than helpful. The mysterious man Luis Sera, the merchant, friend or foe who tends to be everywhere you are, Ada Wong the sexy agent who has a crush on Leon but is always working towards her own goals. Chief Bitores Mendez the giant brick wall in Leon's path, Krauser a man from Leon's past, Ramon Salazar the head of the castle not too far from the village itself. A tiny little man who is more dangerous than he looks and has some scary looking body guards. Osmund Saddler the leader of the cult known as the Los Illuminados and someone who is very good with parasites. I like the characters in this story quite a'bit, this includes the enemies as well from the default villagers all the way to the terrifying regenerator's. I feel like this game has the right amount of spook to it's characters.

[h1] SECRETS / UNLOCKABLES / REPLAYABILITY [/h1]

This game has quite a nice amount of unlockables and extras. Outside of the main game and it's new game + carry overs we have other game modes, We have The Mercenaries in which you are trying to survive while racking up a high score while killing as skillfully and as many as you can, which leads to you unlocking more playable characters. Separate Ways in which we play through Ada Wong's campaign. Seeing what she was doing while Leon was busy saving Ashley. She even has some unique boss fights of her own. Assignment Ada, a small game mode that has Ada running around the Island collecting Plaga samples. Unlockables for the main campaign such as the infinite rocket launcher, the overpowered Chicago Typewriter, the terrifying P.R.L. 412 and etc and of course even alternate costumes for Leon and Ashley. During the story there is also an optional shooting range that's pretty fun and challenging and has you gaining collectables. So overall this game has a ton of extras and a very high amount of replayability.

[h1] FINAL VERDICT [/h1]

I love Resident Evil 4. I have since it's original release and even with the PC Rerelease. I have played it on many different consoles and each time I have enjoyed it more and more. There are not many flaws with the game itself. I find it to have a very nice variety of action and horror, Sure it's not as scary as the previous resident evil games but it still has its moments, especially with the regenerators and iron maidens. My only real large complaint with Resident Evil 4 is honestly having to hold Ashley by her hand, escorting here everywhere. Plus the playable Ashley segments are just not fun. So overall I would give this game a [b] 9/10 [/b] I highly recommend this game to anyone that has not played it and loves action games, Even more so if you like some horror in your actions games.

Those who finished RE:3 now find themselves here, and are probably wondering if it's worth continuing with the Resident Evil saga. The answer is an absolute YES.

RE4 goes back to it's creepy roots with a slightly off-kilter story in the Spanish countryside. Leon Kennedy - survivor of RE:2 - is now tasked with rescuing the US president's daughter singehandedly from some unknown fanatics. Pretty soon things take a turn for the weird and Leon is going down a parasite infested rabbit-hole. What follows is a massacre of village Amish folk, and a visit to the "Eyes Wide Shut" castle with a dash of "Tomb Raider". The following events seem like they have some connection to Umbrella and the events in Raccoon City... but what is the connection? And what the hell is going on?

The tank controls from the old Resident Evil games are long gone, only to be replaced with over-the-shoulder display. With wobbly gun aim and the inability to turn around quickly, it's still a bit tank-like and not totally easy. We may have lost our Hitchcock-inspired creepy camera angles, but we gain the shooting gameplay you have seen in the RE:2 and 3 remakes... and it's very satisfying and a lot of fun. I think this instalment of the series concentrated more on combat as there is ammo everywhere - which I think is a detriment to the survival horror gameplay where you are usually tasked with conserving ammo as much as possible. 

The puzzle elements that Resident Evil is renowned for are here, but they aren't too tricky, and the castle itself is unfortunately a bit too linear - unlike the Resident Evil mansion in the first game where you could unlock and revisit earlier sections to find secrets. It would be hard to argue that this entry in the Resident Evil saga didn't inspire Dark Souls in some way - particularly with it's creepy castle level design which is also strongly reminiscent of the RE series' first outing. I enjoyed it all the same, even though the castle room design looks as if it wasn't designed for anyone to actually live in!

Unfortunately the story gets a bit silly and cheesy in some places - with one villain in particular being more comic relief than anything else - but it is enjoyable all the same.  Additionally, after so many Resident Evil games having confident and capable female leads - this one finally introduces a female character who is a completely useless ninny and constantly in need of rescue. Then there is a merchant  - complete with ridiculous voice acting - who buys the hidden treasures you find in the game. He magically seems to show up again on the path ahead of you just after you defeated some hideous boss blocking your path. How does he do it? 

It's a long, yet engaging campaign of at least 30 hours or more on your first unseen normal playthrough. Definitely worth it from a game length point of view, although it starts to drag on a bit at about the 20 hour mark. If that wasn't enough there are DLC missions made available after completing the campaign, so you really are getting your money's worth.

It would be funny to see a remake of this game though. It would be doable, but in an attempt to keep a serious tone with previous remakes, all the quirky plotpoints would have to be lost - possibly resulting in a cut-down game.... but maybe a remake will never happen!

Resident Evil 4 (2005) – A Revolutionary Masterpiece in Survival Horror

Resident Evil 4 is a landmark title that redefined the survival horror genre and remains a shining example of game design excellence. Released in 2005, this installment took bold risks and innovative steps that not only revitalized the Resident Evil franchise but also set new standards for action-adventure games as a whole.

At the heart of Resident Evil 4 is its gripping narrative, which follows protagonist Leon S. Kennedy on a mission to rescue the President's daughter, Ashley Graham, from a mysterious cult in a rural village in Spain. The story is engaging and filled with unexpected twists that keep players invested throughout. The blend of horror, action, and intrigue is masterfully balanced, making every encounter feel significant and charged with tension.

The gameplay mechanics in Resident Evil 4 are revolutionary. The introduction of the over-the-shoulder camera perspective allows for a more immersive experience, enhancing both exploration and combat. This shift brought a level of control and precision that was a game changer for the series, enabling players to engage in intense firefights while maintaining the suspenseful atmosphere that defines survival horror.

Combat in Resident Evil 4 is both thrilling and strategic. Players must manage resources carefully, balancing ammunition and healing items while facing a variety of enemies, from deranged villagers to terrifying bosses. The diverse enemy types and clever AI create challenging encounters that require players to think on their feet, enhancing the overall tension and excitement.

The game's visuals were groundbreaking for its time, featuring detailed environments and character models that brought the world to life. From the atmospheric village to the eerie castle, each setting is richly designed, contributing to an immersive and chilling experience. The sound design further enhances this atmosphere, with haunting audio cues and an evocative score that heightens the tension during key moments.

Resident Evil 4 also introduced memorable characters and iconic set pieces, such as the infamous chainsaw-wielding enemies and the thrilling encounters with the enigmatic Ada Wong. These moments have become legendary within gaming culture, further solidifying the game's place in the hearts of fans.

Additionally, the game offers a wealth of replayability, with unlockable content, multiple difficulty settings, and the inclusion of the Mercenaries mode, which adds an exhilarating competitive edge. This commitment to providing varied gameplay experiences ensures that players continue to find joy in revisiting the title.

In summary, Resident Evil 4 is a monumental achievement that expertly blends storytelling, innovative gameplay, and unforgettable design. Its influence on the survival horror genre and the gaming industry as a whole cannot be overstated. Whether you’re a longtime fan or new to the series, Resident Evil 4 is an essential experience that delivers thrilling moments and haunting memories. Prepare to embark on a journey that will leave a lasting impact, solidifying its status as a true masterpiece in gaming history!

It's nice to play an old game without glasses of nostalgia on and to still understand and appreciate why It's considered a masterpiece by the people who played It back in the Gamecube era. The story is intriguing enough to keep you playing and the graphics are still bearable and add to the well done body horror which makes every enemy at least intimidating. In my opinion the atmosphere might not be able to go against the first Remastered Resident Evil game (the other only RE game I played) but the deafening scary soundtrack mixed with the limited camera still concludes in a daunting experience.

The controls might hinder a lot of new players to even continue trough the first hour, which is why a gamepad is definitely needed and just after 2 hours one mastered this clumsy old control scheme. Another negative point is that there are at least two quick time events that aren't possible (or just really hard) when you play on 60FPS. Other than that I didn't run into any issues or glitches.

There are also some nice little extras which include a short campaign with Ada Wong where the player basically goes trough the story again with a different perspective, another Mission (“Assignment Ada”) and the “Mercenaries Mode” which is a fun little survival game. Nothing wrong with adding these extras but the “Separate Ways” campaign could haven been more than what It is.

TL:DR Resident Evil 4 is a great game which deserves It big praises and additionally redefined the TPS-genre with the chosen camera perspective.

This is my second review of RE4. Previously, I gave it a bad review after playing for 1.8 hours, giving up due to the extremely poor control mechanics. Many months later I decided to give it another chance, and having completed the main game once I feel ready to give a more unbiased opinion about the game. I consider myself an RE fan, but not one who will gush over it fanboy-style.

In general, I think this is a very well designed game in terms of its levels and "story". It features the same ridiculous storytelling and illogical architectures, true to the spirit of its predecessors. But as genius as it may be, I hated the game more than I enjoyed it. Here's why:

1) The tank controls. Really, this is the major culprit. I understand that this game was designed for game consoles back in the day, and tank controls were perhaps the only way to go then. I didn't grow up playing games with a controller, so I admit I am not very skilled with it. However, I have played a few recent third-person action games with a controller before and they weren't very hard to control, simply because they didn't have tank controls. I died so many times in RE4 because I couldn't turn or move away fast enough. I guess some people might attribute this as a positive thing as it makes the game "harder", but really this is more of a limitation than anything else.

2) The game's absurd difficulty. I don't think this game is more difficult than say RE2 Remake or even RE7 in a general way, but because of its wonky controls, the game is exponentially harder. That's not the worst part. Some enemies are truly unfair and you only have a fraction of a second to react before you are dead by a single hit, and even if you react fast enough, you might not be able to move fast enough to avoid death anyway because...wait for it...TANK CONTROLS. This makes the game a truly frustrating experience. Many times it almost seems like the developers knew the limitations of the controls and deliberately created enemies/scenarios to make it even more sufferable for the players. While I think a game should definitely be challenging, it definitely should not be due to the controls. 

Otherwise, I really have nothing else to say. Its shortcomings are pretty consistent with some of the more recent RE games, so I'm not gonna mention them. Even though I said I hated the game more than enjoyed it, why do I still give it a thumbs up? That's because I think this game is really amazing and it would have been extremely kickass if not for the controls. Like its predecessors, I do think this game is way ahead of its time and the technology then could not keep up. I can only hope the remake comes true and if that follows the spirit and energy of this game, it would be truly godsent.

The game looks like it does on the PS2, Gamecube, and other early systems that Resident Evil 4 has been on. The "HD" graphics in the options are what would be HD to someone only accustomed to the Nintendo 64. They don't look like anything that is HD nowadays. The models are passable, but the textures do not look good close-up.

The game plays as well as it did on the launch consoles, if you use a controller. Even then the camera controls are bad, but you get used to them. Anything is better than the PC controls. Managing the inventory is better, moving and aiming is better, and QTE's actually use buttons that you use all the time in game.

All of this is to be expected, as it is a direct port of the enhanced version of the PS2 game. What makes me not recommend the game, despite thinking it is one of the best PS2 games on the system, is that this is the PC version. As a result of it being on PC, there is an option for 60 FPS. "Well what's wrong with that? 60 FPS anything is great!" you might think, and yes you are correct. 60 FPS Resident Evil 4 is amazing to play, until you cannot proceed any further in the game while running it at 60 FPS. Every other quick-time event is easily doable on the PC in 60 FPS. The only two that are not doable are the ones in Chapter 4-3, and Chapter 4-4. [spoiler]The ones with the minecarts and the statue.[/spoiler] 

Those two QTE's are impossible to do if you want to play at 60 FPS on PC. You have to know about this issue before playing, and adjust your FPS option when you are in those chapters, or you must quit the game (losing progress because there are no typewriters just before the minecart section) and adjust the option in the main menu, because you are unable to adjust it elsewhere.

It is for this reason that I cannot recommend the PC version. You simply can't beat the game if you play in 60 FPS. So much for the supposed "ultimate" edition.

Resident Evil 4 is one of those games that feels illegal to have experienced firsthand when it actually came out. 

Like, imagine just casually being alive at the exact moment Capcom decided to reinvent third-person shooters, speedrun the genre into the future, and also make you babysit the loudest blonde on Earth for 15 hours. Historical blessing and a curse in one disc.

Gameplay-wise, it’s absurd how tight it still feels. The pacing is insane: village, lake, castle, island—every area has at least one sequence that permanently carved itself into gaming culture. The opening village fight alone feels like a final exam you get in the first 10 minutes. Limited movement, yes, but the tension, enemy design, and encounter layout are so good that you don’t care. It’s the perfect balance of action, resource management, and “oh God, I have three bullets and a dream.”

And then there’s Leon S. Kennedy, peak himbo government agent. This man is drowning in trauma, surrounded by cultists and parasites, and his first instinct is to throw one-liners like he’s auditioning for 2000s action movies. He’s sassy, mildly done with everyone’s ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥, and has the emotional range of “cool guy under pressure” and “slightly more annoyed cool guy under pressure.” Every time he opens his mouth it’s either something iconic, stupid, or both. He’s the kind of protagonist who suplexes a ganado and then flirts with danger and every woman within a 10-meter radius.

Which brings us to Ashley. Babysitting simulator: the game. Capcom really woke up and said: “What if we made you protect someone who screams your name every five seconds and stands exactly where the enemy is aiming?” And somehow, it works. She’s annoying by design, but that’s what gives the game its tension and identity. You’re not just surviving—you’re responsible. You’re planning routes, making space, yelling “wait” and “follow me” like a tired parent at the mall while villagers with pitchforks try to end your bloodline. When you actually pull off a clean section with her, you feel like a tactical genius.

The tone is this perfect mix of horror and unhinged nonsense: cult leaders with dramatic speeches, a tiny psychopath in a fancy coat, giant monsters, QTEs that want to break your fingers, and a plot that feels like it was written by someone who watched three different action movies and said “yes” to everything. It shouldn’t work, but it does. It’s campy and ridiculous without ever losing its edge as a survival horror game.

Resident Evil 4 isn’t just “a good game.” It’s one of those rare titles that completely reshaped how shooters feel, how cameras work, how pacing in action-horror is done, and then had the audacity to be stupidly fun on top of that.

On his way through a remote village in Europe, Kennedy discovers a new danger far away from the traditional zombie-infected opponents from previous series parts. Ammunition tends to be in short supply, but it all depends on the level of difficulty, as this varies. Later you will be happy about every available shot in your pocket.

+ Moments of shock

+ very detailed graphics
+ scary, beautiful sound

+ Achievements and Trading cards

Between my mid-teens to early adulthood I was convinced that in order for a game to be truly good it required a strong narrative, a complex cast of characters, and mature themes. I held to this conviction in spite of being surrounded by a bunch of titles I loved that did no such thing.

It’s no coincidence this period coincided with my attempts to marry a burgeoning interest in telling stories to game design. I’d get together with my writing partner, pen a story, and then set about trying to recruit other people to make it a reality by doing the gameplay bits.

I met with failure every time.

I didn’t even really know what I wanted from the stories I was telling, let alone how they applied to interactivity - or rather didn't. I just knew I wanted to [i]tell[/i] them, and games were my then medium of choice. The best games possessed a strong narrative, I reasoned, and those were the kinds of games I wanted to make.

Bad reasoning, boyo. The video game does not require a strong narrative, at least not in the traditional sense. Sure, if they’re trying to tell a complex, twisting tale with believable characters then yes, that which makes a good [i]story[/i] in other mediums is equally applicable here. It is an amazing space in which to tell stories tales rooted in empathy, emotion and all that good stuff. There are many terrific examples of the narrative-driven game. Better yet, some tell them in such a way that only the video game is capable of doing – a true testament to the medium’s artistic merits.

But games aren’t engines of narrative in the way we consider, say, films to be. And that’s for a really simple, obvious reason: they’re [i]games[/i], and they’re meant to be [i]played[/i]. The game can tell emergent stories – stories that are realised in the interaction between player and gameplay. These stories are unique to individual players, because games are systems we interact with; systems that predominantly emphasise [i]choice[/i].

And unlike narrative-focused mediums, the game can survive just fine without a good narrative. It can even survive when saddled with badly written trash, which is just as well because it often is.

See the [i]Resident Evil[/i] series, which is most certainly badly written trash (I love it dearly).

More specifically, see [i]Resident Evil 4[/i], again badly written trash, but nonetheless a near perfect game and arguably one of the best ever made.

[i]Resi 4[/i] was released in 2005, about the time I was starting to apply a real adolescent smugness to things I loved. My parents bought me a GameCube for the sole purpose of playing this one game. I adored [i]Resi 4[/i] then and I adore it now – with one difference.

In 2005, I thought it would’ve been better if it had characters who didn’t speak in cliches even the worst of action movies wouldn’t countenance, or at least had those characters feel like real human beings. That it called for better story than the dumb, juvenile occult nonsense it served up without shame.

Bad reasoning, yet again. [i]Resi 4[/i] would not be improved if it had been penned by someone who could write. It’s not even an argument about how it’s ‘so bad it's good’, which I don’t really believe in anyway…

...I just don’t think it [i]matters[/i].

Watch the cutscenes or skip the cutscenes, it doesn’t make a blind bit of difference. [i]Resi 4[/i] makes plenty fun of itself and is sufficiently self-aware to know what it’s doing – or not doing – but it’s still not necessary to engage with the story.

And that’s because [i]Resi 4[/i] succeeds at capturing the [i]elemental spirit of action[/i] in the substantive sequences that occur between them. As a game it’s raw, white-knuckle poetry; almost as rhythmically rewarding and gratifying as watching a superlative piece of choreography.

The first set-piece is a sublime example of this artistry in action, and to this day it’s a bona fide masterpiece of an introduction to [i]Resi 4's[/i] core gameplay, then a major reimagining of the series from survival horror to essentially action.

On the hunt for the US President’s kidnapped daughter (lol) in rural Spain, you arrive at a village. You’ve already been attacked by grumbling, crazed locals – wryly noting they aren’t the zombies of old – and your two guides have gone missing, so it’s fair to say the mission isn’t going well so far.

It’s about to get worse.

Approaching the village, you see a pyre in the centre, around which are several barns, a few grotty cottages, and a bell tower. In the distance, a church. The cluck of hens and a succession of deep moos from stable cows create a thick, heavy atmosphere – you can almost smell the fetid mix of manure and ash.

What are they burning? One of the guides. He’s hanging from a meat hook above the pyre. More of those villagers are lurking about, too; crazed, yes, but apparently compos mentis enough to push hay around and sprinkle the ground with seeds. Y’know, farm stuff. It’s jarring, unsettling.

And here we are, standing on the threshold. ‘Go on,’ the game seems to goad. ‘There’s no turning back now.’ 

Almost as soon as you cross that threshold a villager spots you, points, and cries out. And then it begins. A madcap dash to relative safety takes us into one of the cottages, where a brief cutscene demonstrates the ability to push furniture in front of windows. Taking the hint you quickly set about sealing the house, hoping to create an impenetrable fortress.

The revving of a chainsaw cuts through the cacophony. Well, this escalated quickly.

A window shatters upstairs: a ladder was just slammed against it. Bang. Bang. They’re hammering at the door. You dash upstairs. A shotgun – thank God. But it’s slowed you down: they’re already clambering through the broken window. There’s a second window on the landing. You need to get out, but they’re on the adjacent rooftop.

Aim the shotgun through the window, pull the trigger. Glass shatters and enemies scatter. Some straight off the roof. It won’t be long before they’re back up: more ladders are being raised even as you try for a 360 degree turn to properly assess just how ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ ♥♥♥♥♥♥ you are.

What then ensues is a frantic, brutal confrontation with an angry mob that seems only to swell in number. Your goal is simply to survive, which takes you in and out of buildings, finding new ways to slow the mob down, be it knocking away ladders, kicking flinching enemies, or lobbing your only grenade into the biggest congregation of them you can find and praying it’s enough to stem the tide.

Eventually an ominous bell tolls, sending your attackers into a trance. They drop their weapons and shuffle away one by one. It’s over.

From there [i]Resi 4[/i] only escalates further, constantly refreshing its set-pieces and turning them into something new and exciting, whilst at the same time redeploying that core premise: white-knuckle action. It’s something we’ve seen attempted many times since, but few succeeded. Even Capcom failed, offering the lacklustre [i]Resident Evil 5[/i] as a follow-up.

In raw narrative terms [i]Resi 4's[/i] closest cinematic equivalent is [i]Indiana Jones and The Temple of Doom[/i]. And by ‘raw narrative’, I mean the bits you [i]play[/i]. That’s not just because there’s mine cart chases and goofy traps; it's that they’re both essentially roller-coasters that take you from set-piece to set-piece without ever letting up. They both trade in macabre horror, but there’s a genuine sense of [i]joy[/i] to their respective adventures.

RE4 may be an old game by now, but its illustrious reputatation is well-deserved. 15 years after its initial release it remains the gold standard for Resident Evil games, and one of the finest games ever made.

The switch to over the shoulder camera was a bold one, taking the series away from creeping, fixed camera, claustrophobic horror and into a kind of gothic action-horror with the emphasis on shooting the monsters rather than hiding or running. But the game does everything right - being atmospheric and creepy one minute, tongue-in-cheek the next. The three sections of a pretty big game - village, castle and island - all have their own character, and the pacing, upgrading of weapons, tense setpieces, level designs and boss fights have never been equalled.

Although there have been successes since, such as RE7 - and the RE2 Remake is highly regarded by many, though I feel it to be overrated personally - this higher-octane reinvention of the series was an amazing achievement by Mikami & his team. Rumours are it'll be remade soon, but I hope not - it will be difficult to match the genius of this game.

I loved this game as a kid, it had top tier graphics that scared the ♥♥♥♥ out of me nearly as much as the original RE2 did while still holding up to this day and it also offered innovative, never-before-seen combat that allowed for unique interactions which no other game did with the exception of MGS3 but even that game didn't have the same level of on-action mechanics that RE4 had as it focused more on stealth.  RE4 is a grand achievement in gaming history as a game that forever changed the Survival Horror genre and sparked the rise of the 3rd person shooters that were so plentiful during the late 2000s.

Me playing this now, 15 years later, nostalgia glasses off and a different view on games is a completely different story however.  My main issue with the game is it's loss of identity as a Survival Horror; the genre prior to RE4 offered very little resources to kill your opponents and killing just one took a lot, this meant you had to make the choice whether to kill or run past the enemy with either choice giving you nothing but despair as killing the enemy meant losing a lot of resources while running past the enemy meant having to encounter them again in the future as the usually brilliant level design made you return to certain areas multiple times.  RE1 remake is an example of a game that did this to near perfection in which it's combination of level design, lack of resources and added punishment to killing enemies created this beautiful coalescence of survival and horror to create the genre we know as 'Survival Horror'.  

RE4 however, doesn't follow this formula; in normal difficulty you are given enough ammo in the game to kill every single enemy 10 times over, enemies also drop ammo and since it only takes 1-2 shots with a pistol or tmp to kill an enemy, there's a chance you can leave every encounter gaining ammo rather than a loss and there's no reason not to kill them as they drop ammo or money unless you're not finding the combat fun.  As opposed to older games where areas only had 4 enemies at most with each enemy forcing you to weigh the opportunity costs of killing or avoiding them, each area in RE4 is filled with 15+ enemies which you simply treat as interactable loot boxes that have a chance of killing you.  Professional difficulty remedies this a little by reducing the amount of resources available but even then the gameplay still consists of blazing through 100s of enemies.  Gone is the coalescence of survival and horror and you're left with a horror game with bare-bones minimum 'survival' mechanics which basically just involves switching to a different gun when you feel like you're getting low on ammo.  Now, while I commend Shinji Mikami for trying something new, it was at the cost of losing the genre's identity as RE4's success forever changed the Survival Horror games that came after it.

Now the game's main merits are it's action which as I stated earlier was innovative and never-before-seen during it's time but it's been 15 years since then and games have taken inspiration and adapted to be better.  It was incredibly fun 15 years ago but in comparison to modern day games it is far from it.  The action loop involves shooting the enemies' legs once or twice, suplexing them and then knifing them while they're on the ground, there are a few cool interactions like shooting projectiles coming towards you like arrows and dynamite but this action loop remains consistent for the entire game.  The loop doesn't flow well, shooting an enemy's limbs and seeing them react to it is cool, it requires you to be fast and precise while facing multiple enemies and then suplexing them after while in my opinion shouldn't belong in the RE series is also a cool interaction that offers an additional reward to your skill; knifing them on the ground however breaks the flow as you move your camera away from the view of other potential enemies in front of you and behind you while you slowly chip away at some dude on the ground with 5+ knife slashes.  This weird flow gets boring and tedious really fast as you repeat it 100+ times.

Quick summarised points on the story, it's nothing to write home about but such is the case for every RE game.  Cringe dialogue as always as expected of a Japanese-made game that makes you question whether to take anything seriously as Leon's devil-may-care attitude and one liners are more fitting of an action game like DMC rather than RE.  Every villain is comical and feel like they should belong in Power Rangers with the exception of Mendez and the superhuman-like abilities of the human characters Leon, Ada and in some sense Krauser really kills the Horror aesthetic,

The game as a whole isn't Survival Horror, it's Action Horror.  Blazing through 100 enemies, suplexing them and flipping through lasers are there to fuel the player's power fantasy and power fantasies don't belong in Survival Horror.  An absolute masterpiece of it's time but don't let people blinded by nostalgia fool you, it hasn't aged well, a trash heap of a game in current times and a stain on the Survival Horror genre.

This is a hard one for me. I LOVE Resident Evil. I've played 1 and 2 more times than I can count. I know a lot of the 1's dialogue by heart. I've played the crap out of the remake and have gotten sub-2-hour speedruns on it multiple times. RE3 is also good, but I haven't played it nearly as much as the other two.

RE4 though? On one hand, I do like it. I played it as a kid around the time it came out on PS2, and I played it again now as an adult and got to see all the early 2000's jank from a fresh perspective, as well as cheese enemies in some hilarious ways and for once feel powerful with a knife. 

But on the other hand, there's a lot of stuff I [i]don't[/i] like. On many occasions the game just feels clunky or unfair. It makes no sense to me why Professional difficulty is easier than Normal difficulty. It's supposed to be harder, but the more predictable enemy AI makes it easy to cheese and exploit every enemy. Ironically, I found Normal mode to be the hardest mode just because enemies would often pull some cheap ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ and you'd randomly take damage for it. 

It makes no sense that it has what I guess you could call a third person shooter playstyle, while retaining the tank controls from its predecessors and ditching the very necessary static camera angles. 

It's annoying when you're trying to save ammo by using the knife on downed enemies only for their heads to explode and force you to either continue knifing for an extremely long time or waste a ton of ammo on them. 

It's annoying that the merchant never sells first aid spray if you have even a single healing item in your inventory. 

It's annoying that the merchant has piles and piles of ammo laying around every shop he sets up and yet he refuses to sell any of it to you, and the only way to get ammo from him is to exploit what must be a glitch or design oversight, by tuning up your ammo capacity so that the game will autofill the ammo on your weapon (I stopped running out of ammo when I had 4 half-upgraded guns on me).

But most annoying of all is that often times the game feels like a dumbed down action hero movie rather than a survival horror game. The QTEs especially brought my blood to a boil.

Again, I don't hate this game. I actually do like it. But when I recommended Onimusha Warlords, it was based on nostalgia, because I felt that most people who would be interested in it probably played it before. In the same sense, I have to ask myself if a resident evil fan with the same tastes as me would find RE4 worthwhile, and honestly? No. Someone who fell in love with RE by playing the first two games will find RE4 jarring, and, like me, they will continuously bang their head against a brick wall trying to save up money for potential future weapons, and play up to the water room without having upgraded a weapon even once, all the while trying to dodge enemies and save ammo wherever possible, just as one would in the original trilogy. And they will [i]suffer[/i] for that playstyle. I almost couldn't believe how much easier the game got once I finally dropped a bunch of cash on upgrading my TMP as far as the game would let me at that point. Suddenly, I was able to actually take out the novistadors without taking cheapshots and getting my health whittled down to nothing. Suddenly, I was able to fight the cultists without having to spend several minutes bottlenecking them in a room so I could shoot them in the legs and knife them for what felt like far too long. Suddenly, I was stockpiling grenades and healing items and actually running out of inventory space.

It's almost like RE4 shouldn't have been a [i]Resident Evil[/i] game, honestly.

Now on to the next part.
