All of these years later, [i]Resident Evil 4[/i] is something spectacular to behold; in one game, you can see the reinvention of third-person shooters, the return of a popular survival horror series to prosperity, a shift in paradigm for survival horror games, and all of the warning signs about what the future held for other [i]Resident Evil[/i] games.

In [i]RE4[/i], players assume the role of rookie-cop-turned-super-spy Leon Kennedy on a mission to retrieve the president's daughter, Ashley Graham, from a mysterious cult in a fictitious corner of darkest Spain. The set-up is campy to say the least, but while the game isn't afraid to lean into camp and humor (a la [i]Evil Dead 2[/i]), it'd be a mistake to assume that [i]RE4[/i] has abandoned its horror roots. The looming trees and menacing chanting of possessed townsfolk are deeply unnerving, and reading the various document hidden around begin to reveal an almost Lovecraftian plot unfolding around the characters. The balancing act between horror, comedy, and action is a delicate one, but [i]Resident Evil 4[/i] pulls it off in spades.

For the horror/action dichotomy, much is owed to the control scheme. Though the tank controls take a moment to get used to, it's no exaggeration to suggest that [i]RE4[/i] changed the way third-person action games play. Prior, it'd been common for the camera to have been placed in a high position that made it easier to survey the battlefield (a la [i]Max Payne[/i]), but [i]RE4[/i] glued the camera to Leon's shoulder, creating a tenser, more intimate experience. That, combined with many subtle details in the game that stemmed from environmental interactivity and consistency in the game's internal logic, proved to be a crucial ingredient to making the setting spring to life. (As an aside, [i]RE4[/i] controls and world feel [i]so[/i] intuitive that it actually ruined a handful of modern games for me that I'd been playing concurrently. These controls feel [i]tight[/i].)

But there's a grimmer side to [i]RE4[/i], one that rears its head in hindsight in a particularly nasty way. See, the game was revolutionary and absolutely holds up, but some of its design decisions, [i]bad[/i] design decisions, wormed their way into regular use at the game's success, like the parasitic Las Plagas of the game. Looking past the somewhat disjointed narrative (which is not in and of itself bad as much as underwhelming) and the egregious use of quick-time events (which both date the game [i]and[/i] make the game less accessible to players with physical disabilities), perhaps what stuck out to me was how the game descended into action machisimo by the end in a way which rather ruined the nice tension the previous two acts built up. Save for the appearance of the [spoiler]regenerator[/spoiler] in the third act, the game's finale feels a little [i]too[/i] over-the-top, and it's hard not see the design trends which would come to inundate [i]RE5[/i] and overwhelm [i]RE6[/i]. For as much as [i]RE4[/i] must be lauded, we should also hold it accountable for the wave of mediocre survival horror it brought with it.

[i]HOWEVER[/i], that is not to say that [i]Resident Evil 4[/i] is a bad game. Quite the contrary - because the game was so good, there were nearly ten years of games trying to mimic its success, even within its own series. [i]Resident Evil 4[/i] is one of the few games to not only revolutionize the its corner of the medium but to influence [i]adjacent[/i] genres of video games. It's clever, sharp, well-designed (mostly), and damn entertaining to boot.

Now, I want to preface this review with one thing - I am reviewing the Steam version of the game. Not the whole game. I want to make this clear.

Where to begin... Resident Evil 4 is one of my all time favorite video games. Played it for the first time when I was 14. Today, I'm 24, and writing this review. I first played it on the gamecube, and I can't even imagine the number of hours I poured into this game. Hundreds. Maybe something close to a thousand. I cleared the game on easy several times in a row, because I wanted to see the story over and over again, and I was a kid who wasn't super skilled with video games yet. Then I played it on normal, and higher difficults. Several times. MANY times. In all of my playthroughs, I took time for the minigames, made sure to collect all the bottle caps, get perfect scores, try to get the highest shooting accuracy per chapter as I could manage. I kid you not, I beat this time probably over 50 times, in different difficulties, on the gamecube alone. Let's not even talk about the Mercenaries part of it, or Ada's subplot, which I also spent many hours on.

I hope that this gives you a clear idea of how much I love, no, how much I ADORE this game. I know most of the lines by heart. I can speak them along with the characters with a perfect timing. Resident Evil 4 was a solace in my teenage years and my opening to horror games in general.

But why is my review negative then?

Because you shouldn't play this game on Steam, if you can help it.

The game is very poorly optimized for computers. You can't balance the audio or the video settings AT ALL. The FPS sometimes go all over the place. I've had some glitches happen that I hadn't ever seen in my hundreds of hours playing this game. It's just not made for computers. Even if you have a very good gaming PC, it's just. Not. Optimized. And I mean, that's the case for all Resident Evil games on Steam prior to RE5.

Resident Evil 4 is an EXCELLENT game and has aged perfectly, but your computer is NOT made to run it. Whether it is the gamecube or the Wii version, I strongly suggest playing those instead if you are able. You will experience a much better, more comfortable gameplay.

But if Steam is your only way to every play it? Then to hell with everything I've said. Be patient with the clunky PC port and give this game a go. It's a classic. You will experience true fear. You will be anxious. Some of the things you'll see will be nauseating. And, if you're like me, you'll be back for more once you've stomached all of it.

Don't expect the story to be anything more than a popcorn movie. It doesn't over stay its welcome and keeps the player engaged throughout the whole story. Leon Kennedy is a likable hero, and though he doesn't really have much inner conflict or difficulty, its still fun to see him persevere and take down the Los Illuminados. The other characters are fairly well voice acted and create a good supporting cast, though I would say that several of them do suffer from some pretty anime lines.

The gameplay is where this game really shines. The enemies are all balanced well, there is a good variety of them, and they give a decent enough challenge to keep you on your toes. The weapons that Leon has access to are just as balanced and fun to use. I found myself often swapping weapons throughout fights (although I tried to save ammo for the stronger guns by mostly using the pistol), depending on the situation. I actually found I was a bit too careful with my ammo supply as I had 30+ magnum bullets at the end of the game. I also spent a lot of time checking every crevice for extra money/gems/ammo. I guess that shows that with some careful thinking and not rushing yourself, you can get through the game smoothly. I found the tank controls to be a bit of a pain at first, but once I got the hang of them (probably after an hour or two) they were not a issue. They certainly make the game more of a challenge, though some might say that this is actually make the game more of a scarier. I don't agree with that idea, but again, it wasn't something that hindered the experience for me.

I am not a huge RE fan (though I did enjoy the RE2 Remake, which I played and finished before playing this game), but I can see why this game has been ported to so many different consoles and has such a huge following. It deserves to be be played and respected for the great game it is. I would say, in my opinion, the only thing that this game lacks is a more enthralling story. I give resident evil 4 a 4/5.

[h1] Resident Evil 4 Review[/h1]
[h1]TL;DR[/h1]
[b]Resident Evil 4[/b] is an interesting game that focuses on the atmosphere and options that present a lot of diversity in its gameplay. Boasting huge replayability while providing a great core experience, is a game that is sure to entertain you for a while and that is worth your time.

[TH][H3]Pros[/H3][/TH]
[TH][H3]Cons[/H3][/TH]
[/TR]
[TR]
[TD]
[list]
[*]Atmospheric from start to finish.
[*]Tons of replay value with new game +
[*]Includes mini-games and extras to explore.
[*]Diversity of choice in weapon acquisition. 
[*]Surprising number of bosses to overcome 
[/list]
[/TD]
[TD]
[list]
[*]Controls can be clunky at some points.

[h1]The Villa Will Drawn you In[/h1]
During my first few hours with [b]Resident Evil 4[/b]one of the things that impressed me the more is how atmospheric the surroundings were. Laboratories are dark and silent while a village is like a maze, with different buildings from churches to lakes or underground facilities. You can hear the sound of your footsteps or something making a sound in the distance, the deep silence makes you question if you are truly alone at any given time and the ominous music gives you a sense of tension rising.

https://steamcommunity.com/sharedfiles/filedetails/?id=2101588648

It took some time to get used to the controls, as I was not familiar with the scheme choices they presented to me, and at times, I would get confused and press the wrong buttons. I wish the default loyal would have been something more updated in the remaster but I got used to it after a couple of hours. Strafing, in particular, felt awkward to me as it was a bit forced, sort of like clunky and the camera movement while helping the immersion, also gave me less control of how I played the game. 

[h1]No Rest for The Wicked [/h1]
There is a lot of replay value built into the game, so after beating it there is a lot to explore or try out. Upon completion, I noticed that I unlocked a new difficulty to tackle the game on as I played on normal, which to me felt challenging enough. There were also rewards such as new weapons, outfits, and other caveats. It adds a lot of replayability and easily justifies giving the game another run, especially if you had a good time with and would like to keep on upgrading weapons and unlocking more rewards on higher difficulties.

https://steamcommunity.com/sharedfiles/filedetails/?id=2101592239

I didn't like that some of the dialogue tends to be too cheesy or that the plot itself was too simplistic, get in-save the girl while the bad guys were using the "dominate the world because we are evil" plot-line, it also didn't server too well that as we get introduced to new characters we don't spend a lot of time familiarizing with most of them (that is to say, they have little screen-time). I enjoyed some interactions such as [b]Leon[/b] talking to [b]Salazar[/b] but that's about it.

[h1]Got Some Rare Things on Sale, Stranger![/h1]

The game also includes a lot of mini-games during the core base of it in addition to new ones after beating it once. You can participate in ones such as shooting paperboard zombies on rails that awards figurines to complete your collection or the popular [b]The Mercenaries[/b] mode. I found the rail shooting to be an entertaining side diversion from time to time, a break from my main run that was something to attempt to get a perfect score on! As for the [b]The Mercenaries[/b] mode, I always love that in every entry it appears as it is fun and has tons of replayability.

https://steamcommunity.com/sharedfiles/filedetails/?id=2101591431

There were some crashes during the game, which were annoying to deal with and broke up the immersion at times. In my experience, I crashed on three different occasions while playing during the main course of the game and then every time I try to play any of the new modes unlocked after beating the story for a bit. The port itself is not perfect and shows some imperfections overall but ultimately it was a solid experience. Just keep in mind it has it crashes which can ruin the moment.

[h1] Strong and Weak Points[/h1]
The strong point that caught my eye the most was the amount of diversity that is given to the player in their gameplay choices. From which weapons they will upgrade over others and what will they prioritize as important. There is a lot of variety in sub-types of each weapon, for example, I preferred the [b]Riot Shotgun[/b] as while not as powerful as the [b]Striker[/b], can work from a distance to keep me safe from enemies. A player that favors close-quarters and damage might instead choose the [b]Striker.[/b]

At the same time, the weapon-switching in the game was terribly tedious, there is not an option to switch weapons on the fly which means anytime you want to use another you will have to press the menu button. It stops time and allows you to react to enemies but at the same time is annoying having to press the menu button so much during later parts of the game, breaking the fantastic flow of action with monotonous pauses of selecting a weapon.

[h1] Story[/h1]
The story of [b]Resident Evil 4[/b] is for the majority of the game simple and cheesy. You play as a special agent from the United States [b] Leon Kennedy[/b] who returns after his debut in [B]Resident Evil 2,[/b] he is tasked with the mission of rescuing the president daughter that has been kidnapped by members of a mysterious cult.

Interactions between some characters can be fun and entertaining because of how cheesy they are, which is something that I enjoyed a lot but at the same time, there was never a deeper plot and it lacked exposition in a meaningful way. It is like watching an action movie only that there is a lot of loose ends and it there could have been room for more material in it. 

[h1]X Notes[/h1]
Game crashes sometimes, particularly when aiming and it runs pretty well on a GTX 1060. Elements during it can be confusing because the game fails to communicate with the player, and you can have situations such as fending off a wave of enemies only to find out the main idea was to escape or activate a trap somewhere else. This waste those resources and make for missed opportunities, smart communication between the game and the player always helps.

[h1] What makes it Special[/h1]
What makes [b]Resident Evil 4[/b] special to me is that is a game that has is moments, from the tension I feel all the time when the music is playing if enemies are near, to the silent corners making me wonder if there is something monstrous in the next hallway. It is a very atmospheric game and I appreciate that. I had some good laughs with the dialogue and the few jump-scares got me pretty good because even when I was expecting some, the execution of them caught me off guard. 

I also love a lot that the game has a lot of bosses in it, I would imagine that they were running out of it at points during my run but they just kept coming and their designs range from interesting to downright creepy. They each have their own strength and weakness, making their challenge to be more enjoyable! From digging underground to shooting doors to escape and even more, each boss brought something new. 

[h1] Finally…[/h1]
[B]Resident Evil 4[/b] is a classic that is well-known to a lot of players and while this port might not be perfect, the soul of the game is intact and is worth delving into. A game that sought to re-invent the franchise and that introduces a lot of content for players to enjoy, I easily recommend this to [b]Resident Evil[/b] fans and those that want to play an amazing third-person shooter.

It's a simple plot, but it is well explained. The game doesn't look that bad for a game made in 2005. Even though this is a remaster, they didn't change much down at Capcom. They essentially made it run frames in a more stable way. Leon saves Ashley, Ada saves Leon. It just works. There are random jokes throughout the game that can give you a little chuckle and the second you meet the mysterious Merchant you just become friends with him for life. 
Gameplay Mechanics: You use guns to go BANG BANG and shoot the enemies in the game. The merchant allows you to sell items, upgrade weapons, and purchase weapons/items from his shop. You are able to unlock more stuff as the game goes on. One of the things to mention is the knife. You may not think about it at first, but the knife will become your best friend, especially if you start playing in professional mode. The knife is infinite, meaning it doesn't take up any of your ammo, and it doesn't break. The knife does a surprisingly high amount of damage too, an even higher amount for a very specific enemy, but I wouldn't want to spoil the surprise if you somehow still haven't played it. There is a neat mechanic in this game where you have to organize your inventory. Now you see a similar thing in games like Minecraft, Terraria, and even some of the earlier Resident Evils. You start out with a certain set of limited space. On your first couple of run-throughs you may wonder why you should even organize or upgrade your inventory space because you may be struggling during fights. However, after your second play-through or so, you will notice that it is getting harder and harder to find where to put stuff with all your items stashed up.
Controls: Yes, the controls are wonky, WHEN YOU START OUT. Yes, we've all been spoiled with the ability to shoot while moving and to be able to switch guns on the move, but the controls honestly aren't that bad. The game was originally meant for a controller, so the movement and stuff will be a little weird at first, but after at least an hour, you'll have all the controllers memorized and ready to go!
DLC: There is a few DLC modes that you can try. Those are "Separate Ways", "Assignment Ada", and "Mercenaries". You can actually earn some items for completing these modes. For 'Separate Ways' you can earn a secondary costume for Ada, Ashley, and Leon. This costume can be very helpful, because it gives Ashley a full suite of armor so she can't take damage. You can also earn the "Typewriter" from this mode. It is practically an overpowered Tommy-gun that once fully upgraded has infinite ammo. The item that you can unlock from 'Mercenaries' is way more difficult. There are several mercenaries that you can play as: Leon, Ada, Krauser, Hunk, and Wesker. You have to fully complete all the stars allowed with each character on each map. After doing this, you practically get bragging rights because you will have had successfully unlocked the most powerful gun in the game. And no, I'm not talking about an RPG, I'm talking about a revolver, an elephant killer. IT'S THE STRONGEST GUN IN THE GAME. Once fully upgraded it will have infinite ammo and its firepower will be 99.9 per hit . That is enough to practically one shot every boss. The downside to this however, is its firing speed. This gun can shoot through several enemies at once, you can take down an entire crowd with one bullet if you wanted to. BUT it takes approximately 1.5 seconds to shoot again. The gun shoots pretty slow, but it packs a punch.

This game is amazing, it's no surprise why people have enjoyed it and will enjoy it for years to come. I know there are plenty of skeptical people out there, but just give the game a try and have an open mind. You won't be disappointed!

[h1] Did you say "old game", Mr. Kennedy? It might come as a surprise, but I'm only 15 years old. [/h1] 

If you haven't played it yet, do it. Resident Evil 4 is a timeless classic unlike anything else you've seen before. You'll understand why Capcom kept porting it to anything than can possibly process 3d graphics.

The game has aged like fine wine, because it's been built with insane production value standards (we're talking about a game originally released on 2005), with all of the brilliant excess crammed in by Shinji Mikami. Just like many other 2000's games, it's weird, it's quirky and occasionally whacky. BUT it's still oddly convincing and definitely frightening, thanks to its great direction. Think of a b-movie, vintage horror,  a blockbuster, Silent-Hillesque visuals... served by Leon “Help” Kennedy who's now more jaded than ever after the Raccoon apocalypse and realizing that love is a lie in a red dress. All of this... in a highly baroque adventure involving non-stop bloodshed, aberrant horror, overkill, strong narration, hair-raising soundtrack & sound design, cheesy  post-9/11 scenario that's deeper and more clever than it seems,  no zombies, babysitting Paris Hilton, inevitable phallic symbolism, overkill again, bald Rasputin, Transilvania but actually Spain, adamantine xenomorphs with eyes, Ada, Looney Tunes-worthy traps, boulders without Chris Redfield, naked grey asthmatic john-malkovich-looking ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ regrowing their limbs, blind constipated Wolverines, smoking green herb like always, treasure hunts, and overkill too, ???, the mystery of the wiggly sack in the dumpster, flashing crows to death. I mean... with a flash grenade. Of course, Leon's endowment is undoubtedly spectacular, Capcom even named [i]El Gigante[/i] after it. But no, i hate to break it to you, you can't expose it to crows. There's a lot of other great activities if you want, like fishing at the lake with guns and grenades. Or visiting SalazarLand, there's a shooting range, a rollercoaster, and real-life Duck Hunt with monks. 

The graphics were impressive back then, and tbh it still is, thanks to a lot of pre-rendered stuff and constant loadings  (they rarely last more than 1 second anyway) . I used the HD texture mod, no idea how the game looks without it, it should be mandatory imo. It makes everything much sharper and more detailed without altering the fantastic art style at all. The results might seem uncanny at first glance, specially if you spent a lot of time on the old SD version on Gamecube like me, but it's definitely worth it. Those graphics would probably not hold up so well without some face-melting artistic direction tho. It's without any doubt one of the best looking games i've ever seen.

The outdated controls could require some period of adaptation, but it's nowhere near as bad as other games from that era. It just feel utterly wrong with keyboard/mouse so you might want to use a controller (dualshock 4 worked fine).  Being Leon can feel like driving a tank, he can't perform many basic moves. This said, the whole experience is a lot of fun nonetheless, the gameplay and combat have been carefully crafted. Those stiff controls are actually a nice  mechanic. The pew pew itself isn't the core of the gameplay. RE4 is still essentially a Resident Evil at its heart. Don't listen to people talking ♥♥♥♥ about it. As long as you play on Normal mode. Easy mode is too easy (yeah no ♥♥♥♥ sherlock) and it's for wimps.

I can't think of any notable downsides. Even the old school inventory isn't really a hassle. You eventually learn to like it and submit to the unknown pleasure of managing items. Manically. Constantly.
 
The port istself is good, no major issues. Had crashes in a bonus mode because i tried to examine weapons, but nothing to whine about. 

Anyway, you made it this far but the only thing you need to know is that RE4 is not only one of the most influential shooters ever, it's one of the best games ever made. That port is currently the best way to play it. So don't be a cheap ass. That's at least 20 hours of masterpiece for 5-20 bucks.

What I really like about this game is it gives a viable alternative to where 3rd person shooters could have gone. I know this was considered a stepping stone for much of modern gaming, but it does enough differently that it feels refreshing to play today. Although, with the way the camera moves it can honestly be quite headache-inducing. 

The knife combat is iffy, as gauging distance between your knife and an object is largely guesswork. However, I do love breaking those boxes, and it's not the worst backup weapon I've seen in games. 

The 'Survival Horror' is largely based around resource management, and strategic decision-making of what to spend money on, which weapons to upgrade, which herbs to mix and use for healing, and which weapon to drain of ammo in moment-to-moment encounters. It sometimes can feel quite improvisational, when you decide to use a precious grenade to clear a room rather than waste all your shotgun shells for example. 

The story is laughably bad but the pacing is great. Every character is a moron but their interactions are so cheesy it has a B-movie quality that makes each encounter at least entertaining. The game knows when to speed up and slow down, and is quite generous with its typewriter save spots, all things considered. 

There's arguably not a lot of variety in the scenery of the game. There are essentially three main environments you'll work your way through, but I started to feel a little sick of the spaces by the time I'd near the end of each one. That might be a personal thing. 

Enemies on the other hand are plentiful and each type is introduced in surprising and suitably SPOOKY ways, they each bring their own weaknesses and risks, and you'll find yourself needing to make quick decisions, prioritising who to disperse of first in a room and how, the designers found creative ways to make you change up how you kill different baddies.

Boss fights were tense but easily exploitable once you could see their pattern, which may be the intended experience, but felt a little cheap when I identified these solutions a little too quickly. Speaking about cheap, the 'puzzles' in this game were little more than brief obstacles, so short I couldn't even call them tedious, just surprisingly simple every time. 

One of the great things about this game is its atmosphere. I wouldn't describe the game as scary, but the game managed to make entering each new room or hallway a foreboding experience, with help from music cues and frequent use of ominous silence, and the game made backtracking feel unreliable at times too, so you never felt too safe turning a familiar corner. 

The slowness of the camera and the movement mean that each action you're going to take need an appropriate build up, and the rush and anxiety of hoping to reload on-time or interacting with a lever compound on the intensity of combat.

It's kind of perfect for what it wants to do, but I'm looking forward to seeing what they do with a remake, maybe they can make the camera stop giving me motion-sickness :)

The spunk thrown at this game by critics and fans alike is something I never fully understood. RE4 marks the series' downfall of old school survival horror and serves as the blueprint for the rise of mainstream over-the-shoulder immersion-breaking on-screen QTE-infested action rollercoasters that would follow after its release in the mid-2000s.

Revisiting it from time to time is interesting though, and it still manages to hold my attention as a relatively fun action shooter up until the point right before entering the castle (roughly four hours in), the journey up to and including that point is tense, atmospheric, and disturbing, with the barn sequence being quite possibly the highlight of the entire game.
Everything that follows afterwards such as the castle, sewers, mines, island etc. may look great in some parts artistically but is ultimately uninspiringly drab and only worth suffering through to experience the epic boss battles found within these segments. Not to mention babysitting Ashley makes the entire experience feel like Escort Mission: The Game.
At least Ashley can be temporarily disposed of by instructing her to hide in a ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ dumpster where she and her whiny "Omg, like, I can't even"-voice belongs. Maybe that's why RE4 received such high praise? Who knows.

There's a reason why Resident Evil went down the crapper and RE4 is it. It has aged poorly, especially in terms of controls -- Which by the way are still tank controls. Meaning that forward = forward, back = back, left = pivot left, right = pivot right. Try calling a spade a spade, people. The only thing that has changed is the camera perspective. The latter by default is positioned nauseatingly close to the main character, thus obscuring up to 45% of the entire screen (can be fixed with a Flawless Widescreen plugin, though this introduces new issues).
Other gripes I have with the PC version specifically include that the game was not designed to run at 60fps, making some QTE sequences impossible to complete without locking the framerate to 30fps (which can't be done on the fly and requires going back to the main menu, so farewell in-game progress).

The back of the box of the original European Gamecube release states "Forget everything you know about Resident Evil. Forget survival horror. This is the most epic, intense and horrific action game ever."(*) I agree with the first two sentences. Hurray for honest advertisement I guess, eh? Worth a playthrough to explore the Village and witness the excellent boss battles but nothing more.

Resident Evil 4 is considered one of the best, if not the best game in the franchise. This game has been pretty much ported to every modern platform. Yes, there is even a mobile version of this game. Why not? Capcom knows we love this game and want people to keep buying it. 

As for as for the game, it plays very different from other RE titles. The camera is now behind you, instead of in a fixed location. You will not feel like a tank moving around anymore. The gameplay is very satisfying and keeps you engaged for hours. I wish the story was better, but I did not mind it as much. There are several moments that make you scratch your head and say how is this possible? For instance, why would Leon be sent to rescue the U.S. president's daughter all by himself and with only a pistol? If you can look pass the goofy story, there is much fun to be had with this game. 

The gameplay is amazing, but the upgrade system is also just as good. You can gather money from defeated enemies and from crates throughout the game. With money, you can use it to upgrade your guns. It is quite satisfying to upgrade your guns and test them out on the hordes of enemies that stand in your way. This game is not quite as scary compared to the previous RE titles and that is okay with me. I would highly recommend this game for all RE fans and fans of action games.

I'm giving it a thumbs up even though I don't think it's particularly good. I enjoyed it, but there were many aspects I didn't like.

So the good:
+ It's entertaining. It's fun having an arsenal of weapons, or if you want to carry just like 2 weapons that's fine too, the upgrading mechanic with the merchant is honestly so memorable "WHAT ARE YOU BUYING"
+ I like that there can be so many enemies all at once coming towards Leon at parts, if you aren't good you might end up cornering yourself
+ Story, while a meme, has some funny parts, which I enjoyed

Now the bad:
- Those tank controls, man. While I got used to them pretty quickly, it's not that good. I've heard people defend them because when you shoot you can't move, or enemies can sneak up behind you. I mean yeah you can't move when you shoot, but it's not hard to just walk past enemies (because you do not really get punished for running into an enemy, they don't react fast enough to grab you). And about enemies sneaking up behind you, do people just play without their audio on? And you can literally press a button and your character will do a 180. Seriously an outdated mechanic that isn't as good as people remember it to be.
- Speaking of no audio, the "music" in this game. While I guess it does an okay job of giving a creepy vibe, other times it makes you wanna just get to the next section or kill all the enemies so the soundtrack will just stop. The enemies chanting and stuff is also just comically bad. I cringe every time (although I'll give that it's pretty memorable) 
- While the gunplay is pretty okay, the enemies are not. They're literally braindead (what can you expect from AI made in 2005). I also do not like the fact that they run towards you, but once they're within like 3 meters of you, they come to a screeching halt and just walk a snails pace towards you. There is no tension 99% of the time. There are some enemies that throw things at you, but they'll miss most of the time if you move away 1 inch.
- The boss fights are terrible, just like in every Resident Evil game. I liked the boss fight with Verdugo a lot, because that was pretty creative, but all the other ones were just so lame. Especially the ones where it's just shoot the weak points. For all these bosses it's even funnier because you can literally walk next to them and they won't react in time as you run away
- The story is honestly a joke. While comedic, that is not really what I want from a Resident Evil game. I want a horror game with corny elements, some downtime where there are jokes. This game is not horror, and it's not scary at all. It's just an action game, and you can see how RE went downhill with the start of this game, devolving into a joke of a series
- The characters are so godawful. Ashley is so annoying, and she has absolutely 0 personality. Any time she yells "HELP! LEON!!" makes me wanna shoot her in the face every time, and it happens a few times. There's no interesting dialog between her and Leon, or between Ada and Leon, or any of the other characters.

So why do I give this game a thumbs up instead of a thumbs down if I seem to have more negative things to mention? I just enjoyed the game regardless. I was entertained for several hours, not the entire game though, as the end was kinda boring. If you like older games you'd probably like this, otherwise it definitely takes some getting used to.

One of the best games ever made. Take no notice of the 3 hours play time as I've recently moved from 360 to PC and it is by far the game I have played the most times through completely. Not your typical Resident Evil game, but that is part of it's charm and for the most part you don't need to know much from the previous games. It's a campy survival/action(sort of?)/horror(maybe?) game that is self-aware because the humour in some parts is just so bad/cheesy. 

No forced stealth sections is a bonus, however, get ready for the longest escort mission in gaming history! If they get kidnapped/die, you die and it's game over. To be fair it's really not that hard to escort the useless jug-eared chimp, but the incessant shrillness of the protagonists name being shouted or repeated, over and over, is tedious at best and cause for character homicide at worst (I guarantee more than a few people have killed them just for the thrill of shutting them up). Also your AI 'companion' can climb up ladders, but not down, so you have to catch them, they will imply you're being inappropriate when you look up at them at the top of a ladder. The AI is definitely not that bright and will walk into traps, even if you have cleared a wide path for it. 

The AI companion can hide, but cannot fight, use a gun or even defend itself, if you are shooting at enemies and it is in the way, it will duck and hide it's face instead of running away, even for a few feet. I don't know why they didn't make it so that your AI would run behind you in these situations, because most of the time it's up your backside anyway, unless you make it wait, which always reminds me of Abe's Odyssey ha.

Camera and controls take a bit of getting used to, you can't run and aim or reload at the same time, but practice makes perfect. Inventory is limited but you can upgrade it and is the most generous of any Resident Evil game, be warned if you have OCD you will spend a lot of time managing your inventory. In RE5 an egg takes up one inventory slot, the same as a rocket launcher and so did your armour (in a pocket of your armour!), but the inventory in this game is a bit different. An egg takes up one square, whereas a grenade takes up two and a gun takes up 6+ depending on the type of gun (don't worry, you have a lot more space than that). 

Not too difficult of a game (although I don't like dying so I've never played on professional difficulty), and you won't really miss anything by choosing easy (my original difficulty, before I became more confident with the controls), some sections are cut out for easy. The comments above sound the complete opposite but it really is a good game, the graphics may be dated and the controls a bit wonky to start with, and the fact you can't reload/aim and run/walk at the same time, but one of my favourite games of all time, despite all of it's faults.

Such a great game. I have very little that I have to complain about this one. This is my first resident evil that I have completed. I want to get into the other ones but have been intimidated(?) by them, I havent really dwelved that much into survival horror. But this more arcadey, actioney take on the series fit like a glove for me, and I loved it. Im not sure if this game is all that scary, or if id even call what id imagine a survival horror to be like. But its this really strange mix of action and horror elements that surprisingly really works. There are so many off the wall moments that feel so dissonant from eachother, yet the game ties these moments together with perfect pacing and a perfect difficulty curve. The mechanics are amazing, fights with normal enemies were never boring, and I was always ready to get back into the next wave of enemies, because its just such a crunchy experience. I think what makes it so engaging is how dynamic the enemies feel. Pulling off headshots and making their heads disappear in a pool of blood, tripping them by shooting them on the foot. Bringing them to their knees and doing a number of really fun special aoe moves on them. The combat just feels so right, its so simple but somehow never gets boring. I love all the different guns and how you have to manage them, I felt like I was always making meaningful descisions about my loadout that changed the way I play. The game goes really off the walls, and I gotta be honest, it almost lost me at the end there, but the bulk of the game really leads into the more over the top stuff really well, like more of a natural progression from more traditional horror to uh...fighting a spanish napoleon dude, setting up traps for you as hes gleefully running away trying to foil you. Or when the game tries to be metal gear solid with krauser in the most over the top way possible. I was laughing the entire time. I didnt take the game seriously at all, but that wasnt a bad thing because of how fun and memorable those moments are. Uh, yeah, really solid game. if you want to get into the series, and you are more into action games, definitely start here.

I bought this on the gamecube when it came out in 2005. But it sat on my shelf and I never played it. Years later I re-bought it on Steam with a bunch of the resident evil games, and again for years I just kept playing other games. Never got around to it.

But a few weeks ago I decided to get it together and finally play this game, and I gotta say, it's pretty damn good. 

Obviously this came out way back when - during the Xbox, PS2, and Gamecube era of games - so some stuff does not hold up as well as it used to. 

The areas of the map are small, and divided up between multiple loading screens. Backtracking is common, probably to save on disk space but keep the game length long enough. The graphics even with an HD remaster look pretty simple and do show their age as well - and the story is silly, like REAL Silly (and yes I know it was meant to be, but this is really cheesy stuff we have here).

But having said that. There is something really satisfying about the gameplay loop in this game. Like the gunplay is really addicting. Having to stop and aim (at first felt really off) but over time it just feels so good. Add to that the way the enemies react to being shot and you have one of those "easy to do, hard to master" systems that really rewards players with movement and aiming to control the fights. Facing off against multiple villagers/cult members becomes a puzzle as you run and retreat and hold your ground in certain situations. 

It's hard to explain but seriously by a third through the game - the gun play starts to feel really good. You'll shoot enemies in the legs to drop them to the ground, you'll shoot them in the head to do extra damage/stun them. If you have not played this game, it hard to explain, but it's really awesome stuff.

PROS: This game still holds up quite well.  The gameplay essentially defined what an over the shoulder shooter would become, with the guns having a solid kick to each of them.  The controls are smooth and accurate, adding to the seeming power and fragility the player has.  The shift to a moire action style suits the game well, ramping up the tension in high firefights, providing the player with ammo when needed, and making the knife quick and easy to use.  Action commands make it even easier to take out targets, though requiring the player to target some weak points.  The set pieces come one after another, giving many areas unique sections that are quite memorable.  The visuals on the characters have some pop to them, and the soundtrack lets the player know when enemies are nearby, kicking the music up when in battle.  Some of the enemy noises are especially terrifying, such as the Regenerators.  The Mercenaries Mode and extra Ada campaigns can feel a bit like an afterthought, though they provide some extra challenge, as well as letting the player control some quite powerful commands thanks to the extra characters.  Finally, the completion rewards are a wonderful treat, the game showering the player with them after completing different ones to truly make the player feel like a badass while running through the game one more time, especially as this feels like one of the longer, meatier Resident Evil games out there.

CONS: Though the gameplay escorting Ashley around can be annoying to some, the use of hiding spots to clear out areas can be a huge help.  This doesn't change the fact that a fairly large chunk of the game is an escort mission.  The visuals on the backgrounds are fairly ugly, with the exception of small sections in the castle and base.  The camp of the story can turn a few people off, swerving around from serious moments to cheesy one liners, but some may see this as a shining positive that calls back to some of the original titles.  The quick time events can also really hurt the game's experience, popping up both during gameplay and in the middle of cutscenes, adding very little to any of the moments beyond asking the player if they were still paying attention.

ACHIEVEMENTS: This is a very basic list, most of which popping through story.  Most of the extra challenges aren't even tied to achievements, and though the Professional difficulty is a bit of a challenge, it adds very little compared to the original, and isn't that much harder.

FINAL: This was a genre definer for it's time, and it still holds up very well.  It's few problems can stand out a lot more now that it's been well over a decade since it's release, but it's still a fun, amazing romp to run through.  For a bit of a history lesson on the shift of the games market, the originator of the action horror that slipped over the shoulder, or the change from survival horror to action horror in a long running series, this is definitely a must play.

Resident evil 4 is commonly referred to as the best in series, as well as one of the best games of all time. It follows the protagonist, Leon, as he must try and find the presidents missing daughter. The story starts out relatively simple but has a ton of twists and turns, so much so that the first half and second half feel so distinctly different from each other that they are like two separate games. RE 4 starts in a rural village as you defeat crazy villagers trying to kill you, with the level design changing to a castle and then later a military like island. The change from the locations aren’t too jarring as they are built up to, however, the island does feel a bit rushed in. As mentioned, the plot gets truly insane, it starts relatively grounded but by the end you will be running from a mechanical statue of a midget and escaping an exploding island on a jet ski. This can lead to the game feeling somewhat confused and inconsistent, however that kind of adds to the charm of it. The writing is both the best and worst thing in the world, it is so cheesy that it, much like the story, adds charm to it. Similarly, the voice acting ranges from decent to awful, Leon and Sadler standing out as good ones. The best way I can sum up the narrative is a weird low budget horror movie from the 80-90s.

The graphics are still pretty decent today. The character models are detailed, and each character feels distinct from each other. The environments are good such as the castle and village areas, however, especially towards the latter half of the game, most conform to the sort of grey and brown colour scheme that plagued so many games back then, it just isn’t too appealing to look at.

That’s all well and good, but how well does the game play? It plays masterfully. Its no secret that RE 4 was the benchmark for third person shooters at the time and inspired many games for years to come. Its pretty simple on paper, you aim and shoot, but then you realise that you can kick enemies when you shoot them in the head, then you realise that this effects enemies near you, and when they add different varieties of enemies it leads to a lot of experimentation. The best aspect of this is the fact that the player will need to improvise and strategies on the spot. For example, what if you have a whole load of shielded enemies around you? Throw a grenade on the ground to quickly dispose of them and give you room to breathe. Its that style of gameplay that is so fun and makes the game tense in a handful of moments. Don’t get me wrong, this is not a “survival horror” game, it is fully an action game with some horror elements and a little less ammo than normal. I don’t truly understand people who say that RE 5 was where the franchise became action orientated as this is, whilst not as action heavy, still loaded with a ton of action set pieces. However, we need to talk about the screaming banshee in the room, Ashley. She is the most annoying part of this game, always finding some way to get snatched up in scripted and non-scripted segments as she begins yelling “LEOOOOOOOOOON”. Her inclusion in the game is obviously rather mandatory since the plot resolves around her but she just gets in the way. Then you have the tacked on and weird gameplay segment of her which feels completely out of the blue and destroys the pacing of the game, thankfully this doesn’t last too long. She is even annoying in the context of the story, she gets kidnapped around 5 times and then you need to go and rescue her again, she is the cliché damsel in distress. 

Resident evil 4 is still a superb and fun game that is worth trying in 2020, as long as you can forgive some of its short comings and not take it too seriously.

RE4 is a classic, it introduced the concept of 3rd person over the shoulder combat that the entire gaming industry holds so dear. Then there's the Separate Ways campaign, an entire second story where you play as a different character with unique weapons and move sets. But wait, there's more the mercenaries mode is fantastic, multi-tiered, timed challenge mode that unlocks even more outfits and weapons. This game, for the time was revolutionary and even to this day it stands the test of time. Easily one of the best games ever made. Story is daft I'll admit but the way that all the characters take it so seriously gives the whole thing a hilarious degree of B-Movie camp that only Capcom can provide. This game is a staple of all gaming, if you haven't played it, then buy the damn thing and playit.

What is Resident Evil 4 ?

Well, I was never been a fan of the resident evil series, to be honest I dont really care about it neither have the motivation to play either the old games or the new games, I cant stand franchises that have like 30 ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ sequels with no foreseable end, so I couldnt give a single ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ ♥♥♥♥ about a resident evil game at all, the exception is the fourth game, why ? I got it as a gift back in 2005 from my father when I was a kid and back then I had a PS2, I have some really good childhood memories from it, I played RE4 a lot and I always had fun with it back then and I found the game to be quite scary since I was a kid during those times, the imagination runs wild. I sold my PS2 4 years later and I never played it again, its been pretty much a decade and half since I have played it and I finally got it here on steam due to nostalgia and I went for a full playthrough nonstop for 2 days and now I am going to talk about it, lets go...

First of all, RE4 is a game like no other, its one of those types of games that just stands out and no matter how much time has passed it refuses to age or even lose respect or relevance, Imo, its one of the best games of all time, a masterpiece, it just works really well on every perspective, visuals-wise considering the time of its release, it was beautiful, well-detailed, had a good sense of atmosphere, the voice acting was good, soundtrack was full of presence and my god the gameplay is just incredible, its full of impact, I remember getting impressed by the enemies reactions, shooting their arms they would stop to put their hand on the wound or shooting their legs they would fall on the ground and I would use this advange to kill them melee so I could preserve ammo, the environments are great and diverse, I had a lot of fun exploring those here again, theyre pretty open and the puzzles here are fun without overstaying their welcome, the game keeps the pacing good by constinuously changing the locations you go, throwing at you new enemies with completely different fight styles, there are cool boss fights and nice setpieces scattered through the game, no one forgets their first time with the lake monster, its just an iconic game.

However since I only replayed it recently after all this time, on my pc, with a different mindset, I would say a more modern one, getting used to the controls at first It wasnt easy but once you get the hang of it, it becomes natural and its all worth because the gameplay is really good, the story I wouldnt call it great, it was good, had cool characters and a scary villain, the fact that the story is detached from the previous games made me like it enough without feeling I need to replay other resident evil games to understand it, It took me around 15-16 hours to finish which is Imo, a bit lengthy but I never fell bored because the game knew how to distribute its pacing well, although Im going to admit that the worst part is the one in the end in the island it just felt generic and weird and too action heavy with the stupid-looking military zombies, it felt like the game lost momentum in its third act compared to the first two. For fans of the series many agree that its one of the best, some think that its where the series lost its horror roots and I see why, theres tons of action in this game but there is some horror too, I never got scared during this new playthrough but again getting scared by a game as an adult is very hard but thanks to the great atmosphere I felt either frightened or tense in a few ocasiations because I felt weak compared to the enemy I was fighting, for people who never played resident evil before this is a good start and for players who just want some great survival experience this game holds up today extremely well, youre looking for around 16 hours of gameplay to finish it first time, its pretty replayable since it unlocks new stuff on your second playthrough like a NG+.

To close this review I'm going to say that there are some bonus modes for people who may want a little bit more, but that "more" doesnt mean its going to be good, the infamous mercenaries mode is very fun to me despite being pretty basic but Im not sure about the other two, Ada Assignment just felt boring and bland, like completely useless mode that recycled an existing level of the main game that I didnt like already and I just ignored it, Separate Ways on other hand started promising but once I hit the third chapter, It reminded me of those forced dlcs we see in many games today, it was just more of the same, same locations, same plot but playing as another character with its own perspective of the events which happened in the main game, nothing new or interesting to see here and the story in this side chapter is very forgettable, it doesnt have the same touch or even the likeness of the base game its just a really low-effort and boring side chapter that isnt fun to play and what proves my point further is how horrible looking its cutscenes are, it looks like its some pre-recorded 240p video, what a lame and lazy trash, despite being 3 hours long I was already bored to tears in the middle and just dropped it, either way, resident evil 4 is a masterpiece and you should definitely play it.

I want to start by saying that I have no nostalgic attachment to this game, and am experiencing it for the first time in 2019. That being said, the combat loop that originated from this particular game is one of my favorite types of shooters. If I'm not playing a high-octane game like Doom, I prefer to be scavenging and strategically using my resources over the typical cover shooting mechanics.

However, I would be lying if I said it didn't take me an hour or two to get used to the game being a bit dated. Things feel a little clunkier than say, the Resident 2 remake or Evil Within, but I do believe this is redeemed by its level design and and boss variety. The fact that you can only aim when you're standing still also makes the clunkiness a bit more forgivable, as the aiming itself works perfectly. 

I don't think there is much more I can add that wouldn't just be beating a dead horse. This game is beloved by most who play it for good reasons, and a remake from the ground up like they've done with 2 and soon 3 would be a solid 10/10 in my books.

Let's put it that way. If you are a die hard Resident Evil fan, you probably haven't skipped that one already and if you have, well you should reconsider getting it as it is an important title fr the whole franchise. 

If you are not a keen Resident Evil fan but have already played titles such as RE 5 or RE 6, you should know that the controls and in particular the moving mechanics of the playable characters are kind of weird in this day and age, it is one of the very pioneers of the over-shoulder third-person shooter so do not expect refined over-shoulder camera, it's not something that is as responsive or as smooth as some 7th and 8th generation titles such as RE Revelation or RE2 Remake. I recommend that you watch some videos on YouTube first to get a grasp of the controls. Maybe it would be a better experience for you guys and gals to try it with an XBOX 360 controller rather that using mouse and keyboard.

For non-Resident Evil avid followers, I'd say the story is entertaining as hell, but it's the "wacky" entertaining type, it is just fun and not necessarily a very thought provoking story. The lore is okay and the art direction is decent enough to keep you following the narrative line. The graphics production quality are from somewhere around 2005 but it has aged pretty well. Thought, that's not an optimized PC port and you might have some problems running the game on 60 FPS using its default setting.

But the game is full of playable content : A rather long 10-hour ish story line that is not half-assed or rushed, two completely different stories that are unlocked after beating the game on any difficulty one of which revolves around the adventures of a supporting character that takes place parallel to the main storyline and lasts about 5 short chapters (4 to 5 hours) and another story mission lead by the same supporting character that is a single long quest with the core games mechanics. Then you'll have another extra mode that is called The Mercenaries and lets you play as one of your favorite characters from the core game and it's basically some pure over-shoulder shooter fun in 4 different sceneries whit 5 playable characters with various skill sets.

Surely not the best RE game that there is in terms of loyalty to the franchise's spirit, but it's a hella of a fun time to play it. Honestly there is little to no flaws in this game.

Main story is fun. Ada's segments are fun. Mercs mode is fun if you are not going for full stars. The QTE are fun, even though RE4 set a bad example for Capcom and they decided to overdoit later on with RE5 and RE6.

The only thing I am a bit sore about is that it doesn't let you go into max difficulty at once and forces you to complete the game twice, which is a pain for completionists that don't like to replay the same thing over and over. Specially since there isn't really any major difficulty spikes in terms of items or enemies spawns (as far as I know), just the fact that ganados take more damage as well as bosses, but the latter is nullified by using RPGs that cost less than a Magnum upgrade. The unlockables you get are also blocked for your first Pro run, which means you don't have any reason to ever use them unless you get kicks out of blowing up the same enemies you already killed twice by now. 

As far as the port goes, mouse and keyboard are a bit unresponsive at times and some turns are simply not possible to execute as fast as I wish I could. You get use to it, tho. Not exactly gamebreaking.

Bottom line, I'd not recommend completing the game on Pro, just doing Leon's main story and Ada's is enough to fully appreciate it. Resident Evil 4 surprised me. I played it in the middle of my run through all the main-series Resident Evil games, which I started after falling in love with the RE 2 remake. RE4 feels dramatically different than the other games so far. In a lot of ways, that's great. In others... well, not so much.

First, the technical stuff: RE4 looks pretty darn good for its age on high settings at 1440p. It's definitely still old, but it's old in an endearing, smooth sort of way. I played it on a 2070 Super, 8700K at 4.7, and 16GB RAM. And because the game force-limits FPS to 60, my rig practically napped through the whole experience. 

The game looks good and runs well, but I'm not so sure the same is true about how it plays. I really enjoyed the heavier focus on action, the lighter inventory management, and the (relatively) bountiful access to ammunition and weapons/upgrades. But the clunky old-school tank controls were a frustration throughout. Even by the end of my playthrough, I still felt like I was trying to play an action game with my feet.

The controls are workable--maybe even fun--when you're fighting lumbering zombie-parasite-things. But the game also insists on periodically making you fight bosses or handle situations that demand a certain level of finesse. In these situations, I definitely hated them. 

Beyond that, the atmosphere of RE4 feels off for much of the game--at least compared to the first few games in the series. The opening chapter in the spooky village and a later area in some dingy, underground corridors came pretty close to replicating the stress of the older games. But a strangely whimsical castle in the middle of the game and a final chapter on a military island steered things into more cliched action game territory. I could have done without either of those areas.

As a matter of fact, I could have done without about a third of the game. Despite the fun I had early on, RE4 had outstayed its welcome with me by about eight hours in. By hour 13, as I raced through a poorly conceived quick-time sequence to finish the game, I couldn't wait for it to be over.

I don't mind longer games that are longer because they have more to say/do/show you. But RE4 seemed to drag itself out for the sake of dragging itself out. And as good as the gameplay is, it isn't good enough to support the extra hours--especially given the linearity of the game and the threadbare (and mostly nonsensical) plot.

All that said, though, I still had fun with RE4. It was well worth a playthrough, especially to see what I was missing after all the years of hype. But I wouldn't include it in any "greatest games ever made lists," and I doubt I'll come back to it again.

TL;DR: It's still the classic that redefined not just the RE series, but 3rd person shooters in general. However the port is just OK and elements of the gameplay don't hold up as well as you might remember.

It's still Resident Evil 4. In all of its cheesy, goofy, fun-as-hell glory. You'll be shooting Spaniard Semi-Zombies with Mexican accents and jumping out of windows as Leon "I had the worst First Day ever" Kennedy within minutes, and it's hard to put down once you start a run of the main campaign.

Coming back to it all these years later, it doesn't hold up as well as I remember. The controls truly are a bit awkward compared to the refinements the series adopted starting with RE5, and it's pretty obvious how thrown together the last act of the campaign is in retrospect. You can tell Mikami and Company kind of just threw everything they had left over together on that island - it's an oil refinery, now it's a bio lab, now it's an ancient tomb now it's an industrial zone, now it's a cave complex now it's a lab and then an industrial area again! And every thing Leon needs is so conveniently placed in just the next room!

But ultimately, it's still fun. And that's all that matters, really. Plus this game still has the best Mercenaries mode in the series as far as I'm concerned. You can honestly drop hours on just that mode, and it's a tiny little bonus game!

As a port there are some flaws. As I understand it, the devs didn't have access to all of the assets the game was made with, so the first big noticeable one is that any of the pre-rendered movies that play in the game are astonishingly low-res. It's not a huge problem at first, since most of the game's cutscenes are real-time, but it becomes an issue especially once you beat the game and do the Ada campaign. Also, the game hitches a here and there and I don't think it's a PC specs issue since this game is ancient in terms of requirements by today's standards. I think it has to do with them porting off of the PS2 version, because as I recall, that version always had this problem (it's also the version that came with all the bonus Ada stuff, so you win some, lose some). Oh, and there are basically no audio options, which is really weird to say the least. Who doesn't give you volume sliders on FX, Music, and VO these days??

CAPCOM, that's who!

Still, this game has you throwing a knife at an albino princeling dwarf who has the skin of an 80-year old but claims to be twenty on the radio he taunts you mercilessly on. It's really hard to not want to do that every once in while, Know what I mean?

Resident Evil 4 is a great game.

Even if it's your first RE game, it does well enough on its own to not need any backstory or prior knowledge of the series to enjoy and keep you interested. The variety of weapons and upgrades to choose and the different ways to handle enemies keeps the game interesting enough to replay many times. There is not a gigantic selection of enemies, but there are a lot, and the difficulty can vary wildly depending on how each  unit is modified by the story mechanics. The boss fights are fun, and many cutscenes require you to press specific buttons in time to avoid death while the scene plays out, which keeps you on your toes. But can be irritating at times if your reflexes aren't fast. The knife fight scene in the last quarter of the game is particularly irritating until you get the hang of the timing and possible button combinations that can show up.

This was the first RE game that I tried and enjoyed enough to finish. The previous games never really hooked me. The over-the-shoulder camera and combat style really worked out well. It feels awkward and slanted at first, but transitions to second nature surprisingly quickly. The hardest part of this game is within the first 20 minutes. You're given a tutorial handbook and stuck in a small village full of enemies and only a clip or two of ammo. Once you overcome this challenge, you should understand how important conserving ammo and using kicks whenever possible is, and be ready for whatever else is thrown at you.

There is also another campaign to play as Ada after you finish the game, which lets you see things from her perspective. The Mercenaries mode also opens up, which will let you challenge yourself with limited ammunition, a timer to race against, and loads of enemies. You also get to choose who to play as in this mode, from a roster of several interesting characters that will unlock as you hit benchmarks in that mode.

TL;DR: Very fun game. Worth buying. Is not terrifyingly scary. Great replay value. Will prepare you for the next entries in the series (same combat system). Extra content after the main game is completed.

And thus begins RE4, one of the most important milestones not only in the history of horror games, but also videogames in general, redefining two genres forever (or perhaps killing one entirely, depending on who you ask). Survival horror and third person shooters. For fans of classic survival horror, thsi was a pivotal moment. Gone are the limited ink ribbons and ammo preservation, the mazelike, puzzle-filled mansions and the undead slow zombies. However, despite taking some bold decisions, it is still not yet transformed to the mindless Michael Bay-action romp it would become in future installements as the game still respects its roots , with sustaining not only the dreaded atmosphere, horrible mutated mosters with usettling animations, atmospheric locations and creepy music, but also having -albeit in a lesser fashion - some kind of ammo and item management (at least on the early stages of the game where your inventory space is more limited)

However this again can al;so attributed to a very well thought-out design decision, some sort of refinement of the older style of tank controls. The missing link perhaps between the old and the new style of RE controls

Make no mistake, this game is still the "Sandwich-Maker" we all know and love, never taking itself extremely seriously, with Leon being not only an awesome hero but also spouting some amazing/cheesy one-liners as if he were some James Bond hero... not that you should be surprised, as the villains are equally bizzare and with their own 007 charm, with giant robot statues chasing you, mutant right hand men, a Rival,  booby traps and secret buttons, and let's not forget you really have two "Bond Girls" along for the ride, the archetypical cute girl-next-door one and the femme fatale.
This game is a blast to play and see the story unfold!

As for the port, capcom has made an amazing job overall, compared to the really old version, RE4 HD edition finally does justice to the game, with clean crisp graphics that despite their age still look very good. Voice actors deliver their lines with constistency and gusto and I didn'tencounter any bugs.

Once you finish the main campaign you can also unlock bonus game modes, like the always fun arcade shooter "Mercenaries", a lenghthy 5-chapter campaign where you revisit locations as Ada and see some major plot points from her point of view and asmaller mini-game where you need to retrive special samples. together with unlocking weapons and extra costumes, (all in-game without the need of paid DLC) the game offers amazing content for you to enjoy.

This game came out in 2005. As of writing it is 15 years old. To this day, it is still one of the greatest games ever made.

Things to know:
• The controls may seem a bit clunky. This was one of the earliest third-person shooters, and it was made for use with a Gamecube controller, which only had one control stick. Using mouse and keyboard can mitigate some of this, but either way, if you're having trouble give it time. Once you adjust you'll find the controls to be so smooth you don't even notice them, even when you're using a controller.

• This game has a difficulty curve. Most shooters these days are powertrips meant to make you feel like a badass. RE4 [i]does[/i] make you feel like a badass, but you have to earn it. Make each of your shots count, use your knife as much as possible, watch out for treasure in each level and don't forget to sell them when you get the chance.

This game is a blast. Without a doubt, it is a must play for anyone even a decade and a half later.

It's weird to come across a game like this. All jokes, memes and quotable lines aside (all a product of how memorable the game's writing is); This is one of the greatest and most important videogames ever made. It has some of the best sound design ever heard in the medium and Capcom's gamble on making a widescreen-only game back in 2005 paid off as it has managed to age beautifully in the visual department.
The game pioneered the over-the-shoulder camera present in every single AAA third person shooter that came after, something they did for good reason, as Resident Evil 4 is still just as fun to play as it was when it first came out.

But what's more amazing is that it is a game that manages to be great thanks to things that later on the series would start being criticized for, such as its lack of horror in exchange for action, a removal of some of the "metroidvania" elements that were heavily present in previous Resident Evil titles to be replaced by a more linear experience, and a protagonist that more closely resembles a wisecracking superhero than someone with no training who is fighting to survive in a desperate situation. All of these work in the game's favour, but didn't for any other game in the franchise. Resident Evil 4 also had a troubled development history, featuring a lot of scrapped content and concepts that never made it into the final game and several changes in direction all throughout.

Resident Evil 4 serves aspiring game designers as an example of a game being great in spite of having had so much going against it, and players as an unforgettable story with charming characters, tight gameplay that really makes you feel like it's your fault when you die, a beautiful artistic direction and right hands that come off. Resident Evil 5 and 6 were not able to recapture the magic of Resident Evil 4 and the series went back to being horror again with Resident Evil 7, and I think the reason the series was never able to do what Resident Evil 4 did again is because you just can't improve upon Resident Evil 4, it is lightning caught in a bottle.

There are a few armfuls of games that need no introduction, and Resident Evil 4 is definitely one of them. Despite its namesake, it's actually the 13th instalment of the famed survival-horror franchise; a whopping nine releases separate it and Nemesis. Originally released for Gamecube in 2005, this title has found itself ported to nearly every console that has released since, including the PlayStation 2, 3, and 4, Xbox 360 and One, Wii, iOS, Android, and most recently, the Nintendo Switch. While many of the later releases in the series divide fans considerably, the majority of the player base can agree on one thing; Resident Evil 4 is a masterpiece. With that said, is it still as impacting in 2020, and does this PC port stack up?

Let's cut to the chase; you've probably already played Resident Evil 4. If that's the case, and you're looking to play the game on PC, then this fairly solid port has you covered. You're able to switch from the updated HD textures to the original ones, and there's even some fine folks working on full-on brand new textures, which are available via mods. The gameplay is a smooth and buttery 60 FPS, and the overall functionality of the port is high. I will admit I did have a couple of random crashes, and there are some bug and crash reports in the forums, but it seems that these problems are few and far between. Along with nice keyboard and mouse support, Xbox 360 and Xbox One controllers work well; PS3 and PS4 controllers have a lot of problems in key areas, however, and ultimately their use should be avoided. Newer generations of gamers will more than likely find themselves struggling with the controls, which are the most aged aspect of this release. Though it's a step up from tank controls, Resident Evil 4 does feel clunky and cumbersome at times, especially in the heat of the moment. With that said, it's something that can be gotten used to, and it's by no means a deal breaker... it's simply a mechanic that isn't ageing well at all. 

If you're just getting into the virus-riddled world of Resident Evil, then this title is a good place to jump in. The game opens with a generous retelling of the main events thus far; it takes place six years after the events of Resident Evil 2, the last time (at the time of release) that we saw Leon S. Kennedy in a leading role. Having traded in his S.T.A.R.S badge for a career as a government agent, Leon has been sent on a mission to rescue the president's daughter, Ashley Graham, who has been kidnapped by a mysterious cult. After travelling to an unknown area in Spain, he discovers that entire villages have become infected with a new type of parasite known as the Las Plagas; a far cry from the zombifying G-Virus he previously dealt with. Along the way some familiar friends, foes, and new enemies make themselves known, and Leon has to not only prevent Las Plagas from becoming a worldwide epidemic, he also has a limited time to remove the parasite from both himself and Ashley.

Speaking strictly in the context of main games in the franchise, Resident Evil 4 presents a lot of firsts. It's the first to follow a more linear path in terms of puzzle solving and gameplay progression. Long gone are the item hunts from previous releases, instead being replaced with solutions that are rather easy to find. It's a welcomed change of pace for most, as the core gameplay from earlier in the series has been maintained, but in turn has been put on the backburner so that players can focus on the environments, atmosphere, and story more than worrying about backtracking for items. Though it's a hit-or-miss mechanic for everyone, this is also the first Resident Evil to sport QTEs (quick time events). Survival elements also take somewhat of a backseat, though they are present; inventory management is still a necessity, but items drops and placements are charitable, and living is made all the easier by being able to purchase ammunition, guns, and health items from an NPC.

Perhaps the biggest addition to this title is having a secondary player that you must be aware of at all times when she is present. Though she isn't a constant companion like Shiva in Resident Evil 5, nor is she a helpful sidekick like Cody/Rebecca in Resident Evil Zero, Ashley is a burdensome mechanic of a whole new nature. She cannot hold her own and must be taken care of like a little puppy, as she can get hurt and die easily, thus ending the game, and she can also get carried away by enemies... which also causes a game over. She can't even jump down a ladder by herself, and only in a few areas can you make her hide so that she is definitively safe. Let's also not forget her annoying, incessant screaming "LEEOOOON! HEEEELLLP!" when she does find herself in a dangerous situation. It's always a relief when the story leads to her being separated from Leon, as she only serves to cause undue stress on the player in a game that's already focused on survival; however less to an extent of previous entries that focus may be.

Despite Ashley arguably being the worst element of Resident Evil 4, there are many, many boons that keep players coming back to this game year after year; for dozens of playthroughs. There's an impenetrable atmosphere in this release, unlike in any other entry of the franchise that has come either before it, or after it. Everything from the gloomy, isolated setting, to the landscapes, to the thick fog and pounding rain effects, it all ends up melding perfectly into one of the most ambient masterpieces of survival horror history; second only, in my opinion, to that of the original Silent Hill. There's hardly a soundtrack to speak of, therefore forcing all of the atmospheric duty to be carried out nearly solely on visuals alone. The best modern comparison that can be made is the original Dark Souls, where there's hardly any sound at all, the world is blocky and hollow, but it boasts a massive wealth of incomparable visual ambience while also instilling a sense of dreaded loneliness.

If you're a fan of horror, especially survival horror, and you haven't yet played Resident Evil 4, there's no longer an excuse. It's a timeless classic that has earned its place in video game history, alongside greats such as Silent Hill and Eternal Darkness. It's still holding itself up firmly 15 years after its initial release, despite some of its annoying mechanics and ageing control system. If you have played Resident Evil 4 and you're looking for an excuse to pick it up on yet another platform, grabbing this port on sale is your best bet. This release does come with the extra campaigns that were present on the PlayStation 2 version; Separate Ways and Assignment Ada, along with the standard Mercenaries unlock. Some people find the restrictive aiming system frustrating, but not being able to move while you shoot makes the slow moving Las Plagas zombies all the more intimidating and limited ammo drops means at higher difficulties you frequently find running away to be the best option. New game+ provides replay value and also gives you some overpowered goodies to get your revenge on the more frustrating enemies. 

It also serves as a good introduction to the Resident Evil series. If you enjoy the action more then continue on to Resident Evil 5 and 6 where inventory management is less of an issue. If you enjoy the horror and survival aspects more then try out the original Resident Evil trilogy. If you want more games that hit the balance between the two of them I highly recommend the original Dead Space. If any of that sounds interesting it's worth it to give this game a shot.
