The gunplay is satisfying, I love shooting a guy in the leg and then running over to suplex his head off. Not being able to move while aiming seems weird at first since every modern shooter lets you move, but it adds a ton of tension to every fight where you're constantly worrying someone is going to sneak up behind you.

The story and characters are campy and silly but thankfully not childish. Yet at the same time the gameplay, enemy design, and art direction make the game legitimately scary quite often.

The game is structured like an escort quest, which is usually poison for a game, but works fine here since you can tell Ashley to hide in a dumpster.

The balance is perfect, you always feel like you have just as many resources as you need to get by.

But what really makes this game are the ideas. Every single chapter introduces something new or a curveball of some kind, be it a new enemy, a boss battle, evading explosives in a swamp, avoiding flaming catapults, navigating a hedge maze, riding a minecart, and on and on and on. And all of the ideas are polished and fun.

So yeah one of the best games ever made. Not sure how Capcom can up it with the remake.

Resident Evil 4 is the first action oriented game in the series, unlike the previous games with fixed cameras, this one is a third person shooter featuring tank controls. Unlike the following RE games in the series, you can't strafe left or right in this one. You can't rotate your character using mouse, you have to rotate him using left and right buttons. Your character won't move towards where you are looking with your mouse. While aiming and shooting, you will be stationary, you won't be able to move. So it might feel a little awkward and clumsy at first, but after playing like 15 minutes, you will easily master it and play accordingly. 

Combat the game offers is mainly tactical. You will have to use grenades or shotgun against tightly packed enemies, which will be encountered through the game pretty often. You will have to snipe some crossbow wielding enemies with your rifle. Some enemies will throw melee weapons at you and you will have to shoot those weapons before they hit you, but hitboxes for them are pretty big, so it isn't much of a trouble. Most enemies will die normally with enough bullets, but some of them with strong parasite in them will have their head exploded and a parasite will come out, so you will have to deal with them too. Most commonly used tactic in the game is to keep your distance, if you can't finish your enemies with your guns before they get close to you, all you have to do is turn around, run away and start shooting them from a distance again. It is pretty easy and repetitive.  You will breeze through the game, at least in normal mode. (I haven't played harder difficulties).

When you shoot an enemy in the head, they will be staggered and you will be able to kick them if you are close enough, just like in other RE games, however, when they are kicked they will fall down and you won't be able to stomp on them, so melee, unlike in RE 5-6 and Revelations, will often feel quite useless, considering the game gives you tons of ammunition, so you will find shooting them in the head repeatedly much more convenient. Melee in this game is pretty underdeveloped, but this feature was a quite brilliant idea when the game was released since it is a very old game, so it is forgiven and appreciated. 

Boss fights are pretty much the same, you use your highest damage weapons, keep your distance. However in boss fights, most of the attacks must be dodged using certain buttons. The game will display which buttons you need to press, if you are quick enough to press them, you will dodge those attacks and will be unharmed. But all boss fights are designed to have an easier way to do massive damage to them, such as shooting explosive barrels or freezing them using nitrogen tanks. However game provides you plenty of powerful ammunition so you aren't forced to use those tactics. When the game was over, I had 1 rocket launcher, over 20 magnum rounds, and more than 50 shotgun shells and 30 sniper rifles and never used those specific tactics. You won't have any trouble with ammunition in the game, as long as you are using low damage weapons on weaker enemies and saving powerful ones for bosses.

There is a merchant in the game and he sells you various powerful weapons and provides means to upgrade their speed, capacity and damage. In return, you give him money, which drops from containers and enemies, but mostly by selling treasures, which are found in various locations in the game. Merchant also sells you a map for a pretty cheap price that shows you where all the treasures are located, so don't worry, you won't have trouble finding them. 

In the game your mission is to save the daughter of American president, who is kidnapped by a cult called The Enlightened, so you will have to keep her with you and protect her while fighting enemies, however your ways with her will often be seperated thoughout the campaing and you will be alone on your own for like %80 of the game, so no worries, there won't be a lot of baby sitting. 

Game has a pretty dark and ominous atmosphere. You will often feel threatened by environment alone. Although regular enemies look like humans and there aren't any zombies; monsters, mini bosses and bosses look truly scary. Music is well done and story is pretty interesting. It takes a different turn for the better after first three Resident Evil games, it manages to be unique. I think it would be pretty boring if we fought zombies all the time. Plus, different variations of the virus did already exist in previous games, so this new setting feels welcome. Game is old so graphics are obviously dated but they are not hideous at all. You will get to like it. 

After beating the main campaign, three new games will be available. One of them is Mercenaries, in which you fight waves of enemies until a timer runs out. Other two are story campaigns that lets you play as Ada. However they are shorter than main campaign. They are pretty fun and have their own unique moments. 

I am Resident Evil fan and had so much fun playing this game and recommend it to other RE fans. But if you aren't crazy about RE series there might be better choices for you in the series.

Resident Evil 4 is without a doubt the quintessential survival horror experience. 

From the introduction of the over-the-shoulder camera angle that we now associate with games like Gears of War and Dead Space, to the pioneering of quick-time events now prevalent in Telltale games and the God of War franchise, this game is on par with Ocarina of Time with how it shaped many games within the horror and third person shooter genres. 

The game is good at what (the horror-based) Resident Evil titles are about: Stress. There are no jump-scares or moments of hide and seek, because there truly is nowhere to hide, only high-stress combat situations involving some of the most brilliantly crafted and truly horrifying enemies. As mentioned before, the quick-time events extend to cut scenes in the game as well. Failing them will result in an instant death, so the player must be on guard even when they might feel safe, adding to the stress of the experience. What makes the enemies so terrifying is how human they look and act. While there are enemies that kill the player characters via eating, most of the deaths the player will experience (or avoid, once they're skilled enough) are via conventional means, such as stabbing, slashing, bludgeoning, beheading, strangling, etc. The enemies also converse to each other and to the player, and (due to the game being set in Spain) knowing Spanish will give you clues on their locations as well as what they're saying. Boss battles are also a core feature of Resident Evil 4, and each area has inspired boss battles that range from theatrical to true challenges.

Of course, while the enemies are dangerous, so is the protagonist. Resident Evil 2 male protagonist and Secret Service agent Leon Scott Kennedy is the main character of this game. Leon is an expert with firearms, close quarters combat, explosives, and utilizing the environment around him to his advantage. These are all skills the player must master in order to succeed in Resident Evil 4, but the most important skill is split-second decision making, including knowing when to fight and when to run, as that is oftentimes the difference between life and death. 

Oftentimes, these split-second decisions won't happen in the heat of battle, but while managing the inventory. The player cannot carry every weapon in the game all at once, but must manage an attache case which carries weapons, ammunition, and recovery items. Larger cases are available for purchase from the mysterious merchant in various locations throughout the game, and the merchant also offers a bevy of new weapons, the ability to upgrade them, and the ability to sell anything the player comes across that has worth. The player would be wise to hold on to any treasures that have the ability to be combined with others until the full set is complete, and buying treasure maps from the merchant is the best investment any player could make.

Starting from Chapter 3-1, the player also has access to a shooting gallery which serves to act as a break from the high tension of the game, but also offers monetary reward for earning six prizes each time the player visits the shooting gallery in another location. There is no price to play in the shooting gallery nor any loss from under-performing in the gallery, so players should take full advantage of this. 

The story of the game is simple. It's been six years since Raccoon City, and Leon has since then become a Secret Service Agent. Ashley Graham, daughter of U.S. President Graham has been kidnapped. In order to avoid a political and international crisis, the president has dispatched Leon alone with the radio support of Ingrid Hunnigan to find Ashley and bring her back home. Her last known location was a remote village located somewhere in Spain, but as Leon begins investigating, he quickly learns that the village is a violent and dangerous place for anyone who dares to wander in. But they're not zombies, as they seem sentient, and they cooperate and communicate with each other. Leon must fight his way through the village and bring Ashley home, but like with all Resident Evil titles, nothing is as simple at it seems... 

Speaking of Ashley, she is the only true negative aspect of this experience from a game play perspective, because she is the character the player is meant to protect through large portions of the game, and cannot defend herself. She is a hassle to protect, and the game incurs two more game over conditions (the first and most obvious of which being Leon's death) with her around (her death and recapture, respectively, save for the times she's recaptured in cut scenes). That aside, the majority of the game will be spent figuring out and surviving through combat encounters that will test your stress, patience, and adaptability, and having Ashley along for these portions will add to the challenge.

Once the player has beaten Resident Evil 4 (for the first time), there is so much more the game has to offer via The Mercenaries mini-game, and the two side missions involving Ada Wong, Assignment Ada and Separate Ways, respectively. These mini-games and campaigns unlock bonuses that are available for the main game after a full play through is complete. New Game + is available for the main game and Separate Ways, where the player will receive bonuses by ways of alternate costumes for protagonists Leon, Ada, and Ashley, as well as bonus weapons available for purchase in both Leon's and Ada's respective campaigns. Professional difficulty is also unlocked after completing a play through of the main game and Separate Ways respectively on Normal difficulty, which offers more enemies that do more damage, and a special weapon available for purchase after completion. 

However, Separate Ways has a glaring issue when it comes to its cut scenes. Since this is an HD remake of Resident Evil 4, the cut scenes in the main game look crisp and new, even by today's lofty standards. However, the cut scenes in Separate Ways look like they've been taken straight from the PlayStation 2 port of the game and given no HD treatment. This is quite a pity, as Separate Ways helps to explain many of the events and strange occurrences of the main game. It is my hope that Capcom will patch these in the future, to make this game the best it could be.

Resident Evil 4 is also quite simple to mod. Those seeking further challenges should look up the "Welcome to Hell" and "No Escape" mods which greatly increase the difficulty of the game, and those seeking more humorous mods should look up ones where enemies and other NPCs are playable, thus extending the enjoyment of this game further for those who seek it out.

Resident Evil 4 is not for the faint of heart, as there are scenes of grotesque gore, intense violence, and truly terrifying enemies that will haunt the nightmares of the players who decide to face it. But for those that do take on this challenge, it will be a memorable gaming experience that will be carried with them for the rest of their lives.

[h2]One of the GOATs. A personal favorite![/h2]

[b][i]Minor gameplay spoilers ahead. Feel free to skip the following section, if you're an RE4 fan.[/i][/b]

[quote=]
[h3]Common criticisms:[/h3]
[b]"Great game, but not a Resident Evil game."[/b]
Suit yourself. To me, RE has always been about power fantasy, after surviving the horror by carefully managing your resources. Agree that the game focuses more on action, hands out adequate ammo to survive, and simplifies puzzles. However, we are choosing to ignore the classic RE attributes in RE4:
[list]
[*] Oppressive atmosphere with visual horror elements
[*] High-tension gameplay from start to finish
[*] Tank controls calling for proprioception
[*] Option to dodge all enemies, except for bosses
[*] Inventory management (with attache cases)
[*] Interconnected levels with some backtracking
[*] Masterful sound design, with divine save room theme(s).
[*] Bullet-spongey bosses (albeit competent) with/without weak points
[/list]
[b]"Ruined the stellar RE series."[/b]
Seriously? While I agree that RE1 is a masterpiece, RE2 is awesome, and RE3 is pretty damn good, RE: CV and RE:0 were just ok. With fives games prior to RE4 in the classic RE style, it had to change to be fresh.

RE4 shook the industry at the time, and I believe Capcom's higher management's misconception about RE is what ruined it. If you read the previous line item, you'll see that RE4 is still very much an RE game. RE3 and RE:CV were already pushing well into the action scene with ammo crafting, set pieces, dual wielding guns, sniper rifles, destructible barrels etc. Nonetheless, turning RE5 and RE6 into full-blown action games is where the series regressed.

[b]"Capcom, remake RE4!"[/b]
No! God! Please! No! Remake RE: CV, with better game design and boss fights. RE4 holds up exceptionally well today. Also, you ask for upgrades where?
[list]
[*] Visuals: The art design is still strong. If you're using RE4 HD project mod, why do you still complain?
[*] Controls: Yes, it takes some time to get used to. I hope you get that the game is tuned for tank controls with slow moving enemies. If you're able to move while shooting, the tension is reduced considerably.
[*] QTEs: Do you know why RE fans hate cerberus aka dogs, zombie monkeys and other fast moving enemies? They go against the slow movement from tank controls. QTEs make the controls work vs. the pesky Novistadors, and a couple bosses with quick attack patterns.
[*] Story: This is not Silent Hill...REs have silly and straightforward plots. How many understand the gut-wrenching part about how the peaceful village became hell with las plagas?
[/list]
Spend your money on the RE4 remake/reimagining otherwise, where you'll get 50-60% of the original's content at full price. Your money, your choice. I learned my lesson with the cash-grab that's the RE3 remake. With that said, if you hate RE4, a remake is unlikely to fix it.

[b]"Ashley is the worst!"[/b]
Having played hundreds of games, I can say there are five types of companion AI:
[list]
[*] The one that treats you like a child: Navi, or Fi from Zelda.
[*] The brain-dead: Natalya from Goldeneye, Sheva from RE5.
[*] The fragile, but tolerable: Maria from Silent Hill 2, Emma from MGS2.
[*] The "helpful"/"human" AI that everybody loves: Ellie from TLOU, Elizabeth from Bioshock, or Atreus from God of War. They exhibit aggravating human attitude, while being invincible, plus invisible to enemies. Ellie, in particular, runs laps around the enemies at tense situations.
[*] The Yoshi: Integral to system dynamics, adding to the overall experience. Ashley's here.
[/list]
Ashley is one of the best companion AIs I've seen. She ducks when you shoot, her pathfinding is neat, is not with you against boss fights/fast enemies requiring QTEs, and hell, she's there by your side for less than 1/3 of the game. I've played the game several times, and except for a bug, I caused her death every time. I killed her with my unstable TMP aimed at a zealot's leg, or simply with bad grenade throws.

In a nutshell, it's on you if:
[list]
[*] Your spatial awareness sucks. Not being aware of where you're being attacked from, unaware of bear traps et al.
[*] Your aim blows. Shooting her instead of the enemy's legs is not her problem.
[*] You leave her alone thinking the AI is not smart enough to go for her.
[*] You miss out on dumpsters you can ask her to hide in
[/list]
Sure, her high-pitched screams can be annoying. However, it's just a way for you to consider her a priority. Ashley isn't perfect, but let's not pretend the AIs mentioned above are.

[b]"RE4 is overrated/trash."[/b]
If you think a game that influenced so many other games, and executes everything extraordinarily well, while being a joy to play is overrated/trash, so be it. Understand that a well-designed video game such as this, requires intelligence and skill to play. Not for everyone, so move on. 

If you'd rather whine, please do, while enjoying your uncomplicated "edgy" interactive movies, battle royales, glorified slot machines, and cookie-cutter annual releases with grindy gameplay, or get lost in the boring open worlds riddled with filler content.

[b]"RE4 allows you to kill bosses with RL!"[/b]
Totally optional speedrun strat. 30K is a big amount for a single use, while taking a huge amount of inventory space. Just don't use it...the amount of b*tching over this, is laughable.
[/quote]

[h3]Positives[/h3]
+ Pitch-perfect pacing
[list]
[*] Knows when to crank the intensity up, slow down to creep out, get a boss fight in, and when to have a save room.
[*] Coupled with superb level design, this is how a spooky B-movie action-thriller should play out. Doesn't get any better than this!
[/list]
+ The best encounter design I've seen in a video game, with crazy enemy variety. If playing on Pro, any enemy can take you down in 2-4 hits. Along with unarmed and "special" variants that you get from headshots, there are:
[list]
[*] Ganados with knives, axes, torches etc.
[*] Zealots with flails, shields, crossbows etc.
[*] Four different types of mini-bosses, with fascinating variations.
[*] Including many many more enemy versions that I won't list here.
[/list]
+ The weapon upgrade system is simple, yet deep, and super-satisfying.
[list]
[*] Every gun sounds and feels different.
[*] The guns feel powerful, and have extremely satisfying hit feedback.
[*] Exclusive upgrades max out your favorite guns to encourage replayability.
[*] P.S. The Merchant is a legend.

+ Unprecedented level of detail

[*] The best hit-reactions I've ever seen, based on where you shoot enemies. Can you shoot or knife projectiles? Hell yeah!
[*] Get ready to be surprised by AI's brilliance all the time.
[*] Increased immersion - the enemies speak Spanish by default!
[*] Even the f'n reload and death animations are straight-up fire!
[/list]
+ Super-engaging tactical combat
[list]

Resident Evil 4 took a brave step to move the franchise from the fixed perspective camera of the first three games to a fully 3D environment and became the cornerstone for subsequent entries in the main series and the Revelations spin offs. 

It picks up the story 6 years after the events of Raccoon City and sees Leon Kennedy return as the protagonist with Ada Wong hot on his heels again. Key features from previous games such as puzzle solving and inventory management are retained and are supplemented with new ones such as upgrades to weapons. Quick time events are present in many cutscenes and although they are easily failed if you are not paying enough attention they can be replayed and do not overly punish the player.

The game starts in a bleak and remote township and creates a strong sense of menace with Leon quickly coming up against more intelligent enemies than the traditional zombies. As the game progresses however it trades creepy castles for more familiar surroundings such as secret laboratories and industrial areas and by the time it reaches its final act it also trades in its horror elements and ends up being an out and out shooter.

Although it does have its shortcomings it is a solid entry in the series that has aged well. It also has replayability through several additional modes that become available following the first playthrough and is well worth a look, especially if you can pick it up in a sale.

The only complaints I really have are puzzles are a little too overly simple, and the lack of all the infinite item box inventory management planning route stuff from previous and later games. A perfect example of "You don't have to endlessly repeat the same formula to make a good AAA title." 
This totally reverses or eliminates several hallmarks of the series (ammo is everywhere, enemies aren't really "zombies," no jump scares, in game merchants... and yet it always still feels like and RE game, and one of the best. Despite having really only Leon and the title to connect it with the series and being otherwise a totally different action-shooter, the game captures the frenetic feel and addictive qualities that all the best Biohazards offer. 

Some people complain about controls, well, here's your chance to play with M+K, but I found it trivialized most of the games and the gamepad controls become super intuitive after a while, even though EVERYONE hates them at first. The recent HD project upgrades mean this has never looked more beautiful, and even ironed out some of the "lazy port" bugs of the steam version. 

The one blemish is still the quick-time events... a dated and silly mechanic that can be frustratingly bugged at 60 fps (making them impossibly quick and requiring you to reset to 30 fps to complete). Thankfully, the game is huge and they're mostly just sprinkled here and there in boss fights etc. The game can at times feel too long, as well... and with the same 3 enemy skins for each area it can get repetitive, but I usually find in the good, meditative way that the best repetitive games keep you coming back for more. The familiarity breeds technique, and the skill required for a speedy professional run is just enough challenge for a non-Chad like me who doesn't go in for too many "INSANE" or "ULTRA-HARDCORE-NIGHTMARE" difficulty bumps.

The graphics are primitive. The game is HEAVILY consolized, to the point where it is pretty much impossible, and certainly an awful experience, to play on keyboard and mouse. The sound is passable I suppose. The voice acting is mediocre. The body of the main character takes up nearly half the screen, leaving precious little for what surrounds him. You.

HOWEVER, even with all these caveats, the game is fascinating. Mesmerizing. Enthralling. I am at this point unsure exactly what makes it so, but it truly is a prime example of how games don't need very flashy graphics, sounds, actors, to be good. I'm a demanding player and usually get bored very quickly of shooter single player games and this game didn't wear on me until 10 hours in. Let me explain.

This game is built on a "try again" basis. A bit like games used to be, way back before there wasn't enough CPU or RAM to make a game skill-based, be that reflex shooting, smarts, or whatever else. But no. At first, there is pretty much no "try again". You wing it and that's good enough. But after about 7-8 hours when you rescue someone important, things change.

From that point on, your save location is followed by running around, cutscenes, minor obstacles, more running around, likely another cutscene, and THEN you get to a "difficult" situation. It's not really difficult, you understand. You just have to KNOW WHAT TO DO. And in order to know what to do, you need to have died at least once or twice at that very point. So you start again from your save location, run a mile, endure cutscenes and THEN you get to try again that one second where you died before. 

You made it? Great! Now there's another event that WILL KILL YOU. 100% sure. So you go again. And again. And again. Until you can make it out of that sequence, meaning you might have played it 30 times. Sure, that makes for a "long" game, but it's still an abominable methodology for games.  -2 points for that. There is simply no excuse, we are not in the 1980s anymore.

I would give it an easy 8/10 without the FALSE 'difficulty' of the 'try again' style of gameplay, but frankly it's only a MEH 6/10. It could have been SO MUCH BETTER.

It’s not often that I play a video game, beloved by many and considered amongst the greatest of its genre and find it to be worthy of its high praise. Usually I play a game and find that it’s “good for it’s time” (read: bad, but nice graphics for 1997!) or just straight-up remembered more fondly than it deserves. [i]Resident Evil 4[/i] is the rare exception. I went in totally unfamiliar with the game and the series, with only a brief couple of attempts at emulating the original game’s PlayStation release for reference, but I do really think this is among the best single-player shooters [i]and[/i] the best horror games ever made.

Far from what anybody would call ‘psychological’ horror, [i]Resident Evil 4[/i] is essentially just about lots of horrible monsters that try to kill you and the cool guns you use to try and stop them. It’s a distinctly different type of scary to other horror titles like [i]Amnesia[/i] or [i]Alien: Isolation[/i] - you’re not hiding under tables from very powerful enemies that will kill you quickly, you’re barricading the doors and windows against hordes of possessed people with pitchforks, blasting away with your back to the wall and barely making it out of each encounter by the seat of your pants. And [i]then[/i] they bring out the very powerful enemies that kill you quickly and it’s your job to blast [i]them[/i] before you’re decapitated instantly by a chainsaw-wielding giant in a burlap sack.

I love this game. Every fight is as much about ammo management as precision accuracy, and failing to manage your surroundings, your weapons, and the impotent sidekick you’re forced to babysit will result in a quick game over. That’s not to say the game is overly difficult, it’s just balanced well enough that you never really feel like you’re assured an easy victory and that you’re compelled to hunt for goodies just so you can keep enough bullets on hand to survive a sudden ambush.

If [i]Resident Evil 4[/i] isn’t the perfect horror-shooter, it’s very, [i]very[/i] close. Balls-to-the-wall action, stupid haircuts, and the best gun animations in the world combine into an absolutely delightful experience and if you truly haven’t played it yet you’re doing yourself a disservice and need to remedy it immediately.

Still to this day I hear many people, my favourite twitch streamers included, say that RE4 is their all time favourite game and I finally understand why after many years of knowing about but never having played it before myself. Its quirky, cheesy and janky in its own perfect way and it bundles it all together into a great gaming experience.

In addition to all its other differences from its predecessors, they added pesetas as a form of exchangeable currency that could be traded with a merchant, dealing in things from weapons to attache (Inventory) spaces to hold more weapons, ammo and healing items. This made exploration have more meaning for me personally, beyond challenge or just to find a herb or useless collectable.

Resident Evil 4 is basically the last good entry in the RE series in my opinion (Except the recent RE2 Remake). I'm a bit biased towards the original RE 1, 2 and 3.

[b][h1]GAMEPLAY[/h1][/b]
Resident Evil 4 is quite interesting to me. It's like a prelude to the catastrophe that was about to hit the series, starting from Resident Evil 5. The camera changed, it was now a TPP game but it still managed to retain some atmosphere of its predecessors. It's by no means a horror game. First three Resident Evils were spooky at times, they were more tense, atmosphere was amazing. Fourth game still manages to capture some of that atmosphere while being focused more on action than survival. There are a lot of interesting enemy designs like famous Regenerators or my favourite Garradors, blind warriors with claws or the assassin Verdugo. There is even quite a variety when it comes to the most basic Ganado enemies, they are just reskins but that makes them fit the stage. There are also few boss encounters, and most of them are fun to fight against. Some of them feel like they could've been final bosses but no, the game continues after that. In short, there are plenty of filth for you to smear across the walls with your shotgun. I also advice you to hold on to as much ammo as you can, because there are moments in the game that will really narrow your supplies and they happen without warning. What I really like too is the perfect use of quick time events. You cannot relax in this game, at all. You have to be focused all the time, even in cutscenes, because you might think it's a good idea to put down the controller in cutscenes but I highly advice against that. One second of losing awareness of what's going on the screen might cost you your life, and the prompts themselves change too, even if you're doing the same qte, so keep that in mind. The biggest quality of RE4 is the amount of content it has. It's a VERY long game for RE standards. You could complete first three games in around 4 hours, more or less. Meanwhile RE4 main campaign lasts for around 17 hours. After you complete it, you unlock extra modes (Yes, you UNLOCK them like in good old times, you're not buying them as DLC's, costumes are unlockables too). Separate Ways mode is the most interesting by far, because it puts you in the shoes of Ada and it allows you to witness the story from a different perspective, there are also few different encounters, it puts a bit more perspective to what was happening in Leon storyline, and the best part, Separate Ways lasts for another 3-4 hours so basically it's like another game. There are also other modes, like classic Mercenaries and Assignment Ada but I found them to be the worst. They focus entirely on pure action without a hint of story to them. 

[b][h1]MUSIC[/h1][/b]
Soundtrack... hmm, could be better. It's nothing spectacular like in original RE2. I do like some tracks, like the one that plays in saverooms (Although it's speculated that RE4 ripped off Cube soundtrack by using a certain sample, but that's for you to decide). Most of the time it's good, but forgettable.

[b][h1]TL;DR[/h1][/b]
So, to summarize. If you enjoyed first three games, there is a high chance you will enjoy this game aswell. And even though you can definitely feel the change, how the overall "generic shooter" vibes starts to creep in through the cracks, it's still atmospheric enough to make you feel like it's still true to what Resident Evil should be; on top of good gameplay loop that's very extensive for a RE title (17-20hrs), that doesn't let you relax because of ammo management (especially in late game) and smart quick time events.

I originally played through the game on the Gamecube which was the first-ever system it was released on and considered by most to be the best version of the game. It was certainly one of the games that I enjoyed on that system along with many others and in a lot of ways it made it my favorite system. I know that I replayed it at least 5 times (typically with the Chicago Typewriter). Playing this again after so long makes me remember how great this game is. With an updated look the graphics still hold up well today. The gameplay which by today's standards seems sluggish is what made the game so enjoyable. It wasn't the dumb tank controls of the previous games while not turning into a ridiculous action first game (looking at you RE6) It's still hands down one of the best survival horror games to date and helped lead the way on rejuvenating the genre as games like Condemned, Dead Space and Alan Wake soon followed it.

By today's standards, it has aged a little but the game is nearly 15 years at the time of this review. It still has plenty of content and it's also a game where there are small side quests that can easily be ignored as well as easily be completed due to having treasure maps. Backtracking can happen but it luckily does not get repetitive. The only major flaw I can say this game has are the damn Quick Time Events. RE4 was not the first game to do this but due to its massive success and critical acclaim, it helped bring QTEs to the mainstream. I hate QTEs as they take away from storytelling and emotions during a cutscene. Additionally, RE4 has a couple of cutscenes that drag on and on (Krauser) and it's very easy to mess up and have to restart the entire thing over again. Quick Time Events are horrible and RE4 does not deserve a pass in that regard.

That being said it's still an amazing game that offers a lot of variety and challenge. And while it borders more on survival action horror it does an excellent job in keeping tension and frightening players. Without question, it's still hands down one of the best games ever made.

This is one of my favorite games of all time, not just in the series but overall. However the port quality was an issue (some have it real bad, I didn't).

[h1] Port Quality: [/h1]
The game ran okay for most of it, but some random points (not even when a lot was going on) cause the game to drop in FPS, making the character slower than molasses. KB+M controls are odd for someone who's never played an RE game on PC, but can be figured out (if I have to press page down to rotate a thing, I don't like that).

[h1] Game Quality: [/h1]
Let's be honest: this is the best RE game ever made. Some may say it's either RE2/RE2Make (like a close 2nd) or even CV (Steve ruins it), but this game has phenomenal story and gameplay, and there are no points where I get exhausted from the game. Enemies are really neat and unique, and some can provide good scares (Regenerators are spooky). Bosses (mini or not) are fun to battle, especially the Wolverine(?) dudes. [h1] OG RE4: A GOATED Product Of Its Time [/h1]
Yeah. That was "clickbait." GOTCHA! But in all seriousness, this whole internet drama bs between RE4 Remake and OG RE4 is getting seriously out of hand. Pretending like OG RE4 is a flawless masterpiece ignores all the things that are objectively wrong with it, and pretending like the game is timeless is also ignoring all the early 2000isms that are all over the game, dating it heavily. OG Re4 is just as much of a product of its time as RE4remake is a product of its time.

[h1] The Good [/h1]
The "stop n go" gameplay of OG Re4 is still really solid. Popping an enemy in the head for a roundhouse just doesn't seem to get old. Every killing blow to the head causes them to explode, and any melee kill causes this effect too. Its grossly satisfying, like popping a zit. Gunplay in general is simply satisfying.

OG Re4's story isn't great, but Leon's dumb one-liners keep him likeable, and make the game feel more like a campy, B-rate horror film with a badass 80s action hero protagonist. It's an integral part of OG Re4's charm. Adding to this, the game is riddled with the "edge" many of us gamers identify with the early 2000s, with crude jokes (that "modern audiences" might find "offensive"), accompanied by Matrix inspired action cut-scenes with unnecessarily long sequences that play out in slo-mo, and numerous references to concepts such as "terrorism." That last point being quite topical for the time the game released (though also topical because the RE franchise entire theme is bio-terrorism but that's an argument to be made for the series as a whole).

The best thing about OG Re4 is just how ridiculously replayable it is. The game is so well crafted that I play it every year, learn something new, or re-learn something I had forgotten, and enjoy it time and time again. Combine this with Mercenaries mode being quick, easily accessible combat just to have fun and engage with the mechanics adds to this even more so. I really do love this game. I've got it on 5 different consoles, like a hundred hours on each.

[h1] The Bad [/h1]
OG RE4 isn't perfect. Let's stop pretending like it is. Weapon balance is horrible, with some weapons being blatantly better than other options. Money is grossly over abundant, as you almost never are left wanting for money to upgrade weapons. You can have every ideal gun for every possible combat scenario in your inventory at the same time, with more than enough ammo to spare, even on Professional difficulty, of which, isn't as hard as people make it out to be. This game is actually pretty easy, and if you think it's hard, you definitely got a skill issue.

Del Lago is one of the worst bossfights in the franchise, with the obstacles and positioning of the boss being entirely RNG dependent from the moment you start your playthrough. Nevermind that it introduces gameplay mechanics that never return. Is it hard? No. Does it suck? Yes. It's not the only boss that's rather lackluster either, as there's a few, like U3, Mendez, even Ramon.

OG Re4's pacing worsens once you get to the island, being haphazardly slapped together for the final send off of the game, and was and still is a common low-point for many people, including OG re4 lovers like myself.

Separate Ways is a terribly short side-campaign where you play as Ada, retracing the same areas Leon goes through. She only has one original level, which is one of the worst parts of OGRe4 sadly, and she has one unique bossfight (which is actually okay but yeah, she only gets ONE).

The puzzles in this game are hardly even puzzles. Like they're so bad, so simple, the game would be better without them. I mean seriously, dumb spiked ceiling puzzle anybody? Really? With glowing, obvious red flashing parts the player's gonna shoot anyway, with it moving as slow as drying paint? Come on man.

I could go on and on, but I'd need a whole separate review box for this.

[h1] The Ugly [/h1]
Despite being a "deliberate" design choice, tank controls make the game feel older than it actually is. I grew up playing classic RE, and have played OG re4 so much I know all the little ins and outs about it's movement, but any "modern" gamer is going to find this kind of control scheme off-putting and archaic. It's not bad, you get used to it, but it's not like the game is any truly better because of it. I'd argue that it detracts from aspects from the game more than it adds, but that has less to do with it feeling clunky and more so because it's easily exploited, since the devs didn't consider the possibility of what might happen when players learn to abuse it. This means that enemies are slow and overly telegraphed, letting you easily avoid them, manipulate them, and it makes the game trivial as soon as you figure it out. This is part of what makes OG Re4 easier than most "casuals" might realize.

This port is rather poor. It's not a true HD remaster, and there are many things that should have been added to the remaster that aren't (like the ability to mix and match costumes, wear Leon's jacket, etc.) necessitating the need for mods like RE4 Tweaks and the HD project. Lame. It's one thing for the original console releases for this game not to have these features or improvements, but the HD remaster should have added these little "cherries on top," even back when this first released.

[h1] Conclusion [/h1]
OG Re4 is a goated game that's so well crafted replaying it over and over again seems to not get old. It's not as much of a masterpiece as people might glaze it out to be, but it has always managed to stand the test of time, even with the remake out now. Don't be fooled about my "the bad" section, as OG re4's lows hardly impede on it's highs, but pretending like they don't exist is intellectually dishonest, and does more damage to what makes this game good over-all. I personally may have had my opinion soured about it over the years, replaying it over and over again, and playing the remake at the same time, but that might be because I've "meta-gamed" it so much it's gotten a little stale.

Regardless, OG re4's a great game and it's goated for a reason. All you gotta do is play it and feel it first hand. Just know that it's equally a product of it's time as the remake is.

A Critical Examination of Resident Evil 4: A Paradigm Shift in Survival Horror

Abstract: Released in 2005, Capcom's Resident Evil 4 redefined the survival horror genre, utilizing innovative gameplay mechanics, a compelling narrative, and an atmospheric design that continues to resonate in contemporary video game culture. This review examines the multifaceted components that contributed to its critical acclaim and lasting impact, exploring its narrative structure, gameplay innovations, character development, and audiovisual aesthetics.

Introduction: In the landscape of video games, few titles have managed to achieve the cultural and artistic significance of Resident Evil 4. Developed by Shinji Mikami and released for the Nintendo GameCube – subsequently ported to numerous platforms – the game marks a pivotal moment in the evolution of survival horror. Through its strategic blend of action-oriented gameplay and traditional horror elements, Resident Evil 4 has garnered recognition not only for its influence on subsequent titles but also for its contribution to the broader discourse on video game narratives and player agency.

Narrative Structure: Resident Evil 4 centers around protagonist Leon S. Kennedy, tasked with rescuing the U.S. President's kidnapped daughter, Ashley Graham, from a mysterious cult in a rural Spanish village. The game’s narrative is expertly crafted, balancing suspense with moments of levity, as well as cleverly interweaving revelations about the cult and biological horror inherent within the narrative. The plot unfolds at a meticulously paced rhythm, allowing players to absorb environmental storytelling that enriches the game world. This layered narrative depth elevates the storyline beyond a mere vehicle for action, engaging players at both emotional and cerebral levels.

Gameplay Innovations: Resident Evil 4 is perhaps best known for its significant departure from the franchise's earlier fixed-camera perspectives, favoring an over-the-shoulder view that enhances player immersion. This shift not only allows for more fluid combat mechanics but also serves to amplify tension in confrontations with enemies – a hallmark of the survival horror genre. The introduction of context-sensitive actions, coupled with an inventory management system that challenges players' strategic thinking, facilitates deeper engagement. The game masterfully balances combat, puzzle-solving, and exploration, ensuring that players remain invested in their progress while navigating a richly realized world.

Character Development: Leon S. Kennedy emerges as a more nuanced character compared to his predecessors, embodying both a sense of duty and an undercurrent of vulnerability. His interactions with Ashley, the kidnapped protagonist, establish an emotional resonance that enhances the player’s investment in their fates. Moreover, the game's antagonists, particularly the charismatic but sinister Osmund Saddler, provide a compelling contrast that serves to elevate the stakes. The layered characterization throughout the game invites players to explore themes of sacrifice, loyalty, and the moral ambiguities present in survival scenarios. 

Audiovisual Aesthetics: The artistry of Resident Evil 4 is exemplified through its stunning visual design and atmospheric soundscapes. The use of lighting and shadow creates an oppressive ambiance, ensuring that every corner could potentially harbor threats. The environmental design reflects a meticulous attention to detail, from the rural landscapes to the claustrophobic interiors of the castle, evoking a sense of dread characterized by isolation. Coupled with a haunting soundtrack and effective sound design, players are continually immersed in an existential tension, enhancing the horror experience.

Cultural Impact and Legacy: The revolutionary mechanics and design philosophies introduced in Resident Evil 4 have become cornerstones for modern video game development. Its influence is evident in numerous titles across genres, prompting a reevaluation of the parameters defining horror and action games. The game has also incited critical discourse surrounding player agency, narrative engagement, and the construction of fear within interactive media. 

The voice acting in Resident Evil 4 significantly contributed to the game's immersive experience, particularly through the performances of its main characters: Leon S. Kennedy, Ashley Graham, and Ada Wong. Each voice actor brought a unique interpretation to their characters, enhancing the narrative depth and emotional engagement of the game.

Leon S. Kennedy (voiced by Paul Mercier)
In Resident Evil 4, Leon S. Kennedy is voiced by Paul Mercier, who provided a performance that perfectly encapsulates the character’s evolution from the rookie cop introduced in Resident Evil 2 to a seasoned agent in this installment. Mercier’s portrayal effectively balances Leon's confidence, determination, and occasional vulnerability, allowing players to connect with him on multiple levels. His delivery of Leon's lines often blends a calmness with an underlying urgency, reflecting the character's ability to maintain composure despite the chaos around him. Mercier's voice work also adds a layer of charm and charisma, particularly evident in Leon’s interactions with other characters, enhancing his role as a protagonist faced with both physical and moral challenges throughout the game.

Ashley Graham (voiced by Heidi Anderson)
Ashley Graham, the president’s daughter, is voiced by Heidi Anderson. Her performance is characterized by a blend of fearfulness, strength, and resilience. Anderson delivered Ashley’s lines with a genuine sense of anxiety and vulnerability that mirrored her precarious situation. However, she also infused the character with moments of agency, particularly as she navigated the dangers posed by her captors. Anderson’s voice acting plays a crucial role in establishing Ashley as more than just a damsel in distress; her cries for help, moments of bravery, and developing bond with Leon contribute to an emotional weight that heightens the stakes of the narrative. This portrayal emphasizes the growth within Ashley's character as she evolves from a scared young woman into a partner who can assist Leon, embodying a degree of empowerment.

Ada Wong (voiced by Hedy Burress)
Ada Wong is another standout character, brought to life by Hedy Burress. Although Ada plays a more enigmatic role in Resident Evil 4, Burress's voice work brilliantly conveys her complexity—portraying both allure and treachery. The sultry and confident tone used by Burress captures Ada’s multifaceted persona, making her a captivating character in the story. She expertly balances the character’s mystery with moments of warmth and vulnerability, especially in her interactions with Leon. Burress's delivery adds depth to Ada's motivations and ambitions, suggesting a deeper connection and unresolved tension between her and Leon. The nuanced quality of her performance allows players to question Ada's true intentions, enhancing the game’s intrigue and complicating the dynamics between the characters.

Conclusion: Resident Evil 4 stands as a seminal work within both the survival horror genre and the broader video game canon. Its narrative sophistication, innovative gameplay mechanics, rich character development, and atmospheric design coalesce to form an experience that transcends mere entertainment. As gaming continues to evolve, the foundational principles established by Resident Evil 4 will undoubtedly influence future generations of artists and designers, solidifying its status as a classic in the annals of video game history. The game not only redefined the survival horror genre but also proved that video games possess the capacity for profound narrative expression and artistic depth.

With the next generation of consoles like gamecube and playstation 2, Resident evil moved more and more away from the survival horror genre, and towards the survival action, mostly because the new perspective and gameplay changes that started to occur in Resident evil 4, continued in Resident evil 5 and ended in Resident evil 6. These 3 games have the most basic things in common, but they have a lot of differences as well. I will review and compare them.

The Plots

Good characters. 

RE4: We have Leon as the main "Hero". It has evolved since the Raccoon city events in RE2, I mean the old version, before it was an amateur anti-hero, now is a veteran anti-hero, the tragic one man army of this adventure. Which has a lot of cliches, as Saddler would say. The police men that accompany him at the start are just for bait. He will meet with Luis, which will be a really dumb sidekick replaced with Ada later, Ashley the damsel in distress that acts like a game over trigger and screams like a goat, Ingrid Hannigan is just for the game exposition untill she is replaced by the bad guys, Mike is another character that will only have a highlight in the entire game and then vanish. So, bottom line, in RE4 will be the bad guys that will steal the show and make it worth watching, despite Umbrella's moment is over. 3/10

Story.

RE4: The president's daughter has been kidnapped, and Leon has to rescue her. While the zombies, and Umbrella are gone forever, a new virus called las plagas can be injected into anyone and a few hours later his or her mind will be controlled by the leader of a "religious" group, called the Los Iluminados, which has the plan of controlling the world. Apart from them, other people will be interested in obtaining the virus for unknown reasons. 3/10

Bad Characters.

RE4: Bitores Mendez, also called the big cheese, Ramon Salazar, Krauser, Osmund Saddler. All them appear in order, one after another dies, to face Leon. They are very original and threatening, but also a bit funny when they jack the line, and they have also minor and major creatures under their control as well. All them will have to mutate themselves to give Leon a bad time, just like William did in RE2. Then we have Ada and Wesker in the shadows, what else can you ask? 10/10

Side stories:

RE4: Ada will have to retrieve the samples of the virus from Saddler, Leon and Krauser, while helping Leon at the same time, and send them to Wesker. These two minigames are shorter but harder. 6/10

The Action:

Gameplay

RE4: The one that started the change from survival horror to survival shooting. 1 player only, your partner can only wait and follow you. The game is over if: Leon or Ashley has 0 HP, suffers one deadly attack, fails certain QTEs, or Ashley is taken away by a ganado during regular gameplay, but you have infinite continues and door saving to make things easier. You can still use typewriters to save but without ribbons or memory cards now, and the game is now episodic to make it longer. Oh, and here you can start trusting on your knife to attack or break stuff. It can stun enemies, making you able to kick or suplex them, and thus conserve ammo for harder enemies later. If you get stuck or get good at the game, it will change its difficulty dinamically.  7/10

Surviving:

RE4: Apart from automatic death attacks or scenes, you can get the traditional red and green herbs, and mix them to recover more health. Blue herbs are removed from the game but a new yellow herb appears here which when combined with a green herb or a green+red one will make increase your maximum health points while recovering the health as usual, but with a limit. You can apply that to Ashley as well. There are first aid sprays that act as a full healing, and the merchant can sell those if you have almost no health herbs or sprays. And you can get food such as eggs and fishes, but the last ones occupy a lot in your inventory. 8/10

Weapons, items and currency:

RE4. Basicly perfect. You can unlock and buy new weapons as you progress the game and also buy updates to them and accesories from the merchant. You cannot buy ammo, herbs and grenades though, but the enemies drop a lot of that or currency or herbs as you need them. Also you get maps with treasures which you can get and sell and upgrade your case. Some of the treasure items can also be combined for a more expensive treasure to sell to the merchant 9/10

Replay factor:

Re4: 3 difficulty modes. Some extra weapons post game. 2 different extra costume sets for Leon and Ashley. And a few extra stuff that can be achieved within one playthrough or the short but tricky side stories by Ada, and the mercenaries with different characters and stages to get 5 stars in all them by all them for another reward. That's just something, but not good enough against RE5 and RE6, so the score is 3/10. Luckily there are a lot of versions of this game out there, without counting fan modifications to compensate that.

The main thing that makes this game so good is that it prioritises fun fast-paced over-the-top action and survival horror above anything else. The whole game feels like a cut to the chase. You are then thrown into a small village with about 30 enemies and a boss that will cut your head off instantly if it catches you. It doesn't slow down after that. The story is cohesive and easy to follow with short and genuinely entertaining cutscenes backed up by good voice acting and a nice deal of cheesy, campy humor. The combat is unique and satisfying and the bosses are cool and exciting to boot. In terms of enemies you'll mostly be fighting against humanoids but their AI is very good for a 2005 game and I still get outsmarted by them regularly, especially on the hardest difficulty where they pursue you brutally. Exploration is great and there's plenty of detours you can take across 3 maps to find loot or some of the game's many amazingly designed guns. The one complaint everyone gives it is that it is cut down from the previous survival horror games - that's partially true and the marketing campaign even said this, but the mechanics are still there. No health regen, limited ammo, limited carry capacity (through a very fun little minigame) and a focus on when to fight and when to avoid during combat. It's just one of those games where everything works as you'd expect and nothing frustrating gets in the way. Resident Evil 4 is my favourite game ever. Hopefully the remake holds up.

To cut a long story short: This portation of Resident Evil 4 disappointed me so much that I stopped playing after just a few minutes. While I did not experience the general compatibility problems that many other users had with just starting the game, the controls just made this game unplayable for me.

The fact that you cannot strafe with your character and that the mouse view is both sluggish and awkward at best makes you stumble around in this Zombie shooter like a complete fool. The only alternative that you have as opposed to the catastrophically bad keyboard + mouse layout is to switch to a gamepad to play the game (pretty much the same way as it was released for the consoles a few years back). 

If this works for you, then you may find that RE4 can be a good or even great game after all, but for me this certainly did not work. 

The control mechanics of its successor RE5 are flawless and of a specific console port to the PC I pretty much expect the devs to invest some work to make it playable on PC hardware. The de-facto standard for PC shooters / third person perspective games is a WASD control layout with strafing on A and D and this standard has been existing for decades now. Even if the Leon character in the original console version may not have been able to strafe, that is a very pathetic excuse for not adding this feature for the PC version and I cannot accept the argument that RE4 was “designed to keep the player on the run” and to "make the player fear the hordes of zombies". There are numerous better ways of creating anxiety and keeping the player under stress.

Taking that and adding the problems with even starting the game that many other users had, I can only arrive at one conclusion: I cannot recommend this game (as PC port). 

I find this really sad, because I heard so many positive recommendations about this game and I cannot give the actual game the credit it (most probably) deserves.

I can definitely recommend RE5, though, which I find to be one of the best coop-shooters (with some added horror flair) I ever played.

It's a lot like RE5, which I played first, as in, pretty much they took THIS game and then copy-pasted it into a new file and changed a few assets to get Resident Evil 5: Partners 4 Evar. The basic plot for this game is, Leon is a special forces agent who survived Raccoon City, and Is He a Bad Enough Dude to Kill All the Zombies and Rescue the President's Daughter? (He is.)

You start off in the most brown place in the world, Spain(?), and immediately you find some villagers who walk very slowly up to you so they can... bite you or hit you with their pathetic little hand scythes or whatever. And that's pretty much all you fight for the rest of the game. They vary it up on occasion, and the dynamic difficulty of the game will scale 'certain' enemies into the mix as a nasty surprise to keep you on your toes almost at random and more and more frequently if you haven't died in a while, but ultimately you just fight dudes. They're not really zombies, they can talk and have most of their motor skills, but they're cunning and obviously still mostly intelligent.

Shooting in this version of the game is miserable, I seriously wouldn't try it, just get the Wii version. Weirdly, unlike RE5 there's like four or five different handguns but only one automatic gun, the TMP. It's not really a problem but it sure is odd. It'd be nice to have 'more' but it's not really a problem. I was at least unsatisfied by a lack of unscoped rifles. All of the rifles have a scope and it's restricting. You can buy separate scopes for them anyway, so...?

There's some pretty good bosses in this game, not too many but a few. RE4 starts a bit weak with the boring old village, some chainsaw guy, nothing very interesting, but there's some great stuff lategame. The Mercenaries mode (time attack survival) is a ton of fun, and some of the characters you can (HUNK HUNK HUNK HUNK) play as are really really awesome. Like Hunk. He has nothing but a TMP and a surplus supply of grenades, and where Leon has a kick and a suplex to deal with staggered enemies, Hunk can just walk up and snap their necks, which is not only fast, it's a one-shot kill AND works on some minibosses. 

I don't really know what else to add. The story? It's mostly just nonsense, but there's a few nice grains in there. Ashley, the girl you rescue and who follows you around for a few chapters is charming enough and Leon and her build a nice enough rapport over the course of the game. The bad guy is just laughable. Actually, all of the bad guys are laughable, they make Skeletor look like a professional name-taking badass. Not only are they all worthless, they desperately try and make it look like every time you gun down one of their most useful and valuable henchmen, you're doing them a favour (you're not). They are so incompetent, when Ashley gets caught in a trap and taken away from you, the bad guys themselves go, "Oh, that wasn't us. But, uh, we'll find her soon! Muahahaha!" (they never find her)

Yeah. Really good game, I guess. Just don't buy the PC port.

When it came out, Resident Evil 4 was an iconic advancement for the survival horror genre, if not for third-person action games in general. Though like many other games that were innovative for their time it hasn't aged with much grace, its odd blend of action and horror is still quite fun.

[h1]The Gameplay[/h1]

RE4's core gameplay is pretty solid; It mixes the slow-paced combat and movement of classic RE with some modern shooter mechanics, forming a methodical and strategic tone to the combat that meshes well with the small map sizes and horror themes. Needing to stand still to aim/shoot makes dealing with enemies a tense experience, but your guns still have enough kick to them that you don't feel overly vulnerable from the restriction. Rather than the more common survival-horror tone of being in-over-your-head and barely scraping through each encounter, you feel like a professional thrust into an extra-challenging situation, and though it sometimes pushes it to the point that I barely felt like I was "surviving" the horrors inasmuch as I was just badassing my way through them, it was a neat change of pace compared to the rest of the genre.

However, it hits some significant hangups with its controls, which have aged like cheese left outdoors in the summer. Tank controls work okay until you're actually trying to use them in combat, at which point maneuvering around becomes a clunky, awkward mess due to how imprecise and sluggish your movements are. This is especially apparent if you're trying to dodge around enemies due to the lack of evasive actions beyond "try to move past them". Bosses often use attacks that trigger a QTE, but the window to input these is incredibly small, and they'll sometimes just outright fail to appear if your position isn't just right, leading to unavoidable damage. You need to pause and open your inventory to switch weapons, awkwardly breaking the otherwise intense pace of the combat, and your laser sight is significantly offset from the center of the camera, which makes aiming pretty awkward. To credit, the controls aren't -terrible-, but even after I'd had time to get used to all of their oddities I still found them rearing up to cause frustration semi-regularly.

[h1]The Enemy & Item Design[/h1]

By far its strongest point, the sheer number of fully fleshed-out enemy types you'll encounter across the game is just phenomenal. The regular infected humans sport an incredible variety of weapons and armors, gradually upping the stakes from villagers with pitchforks, dynamite, and throwing hatchets, to cultists with flails and crossbows, or soldiers with shock rods and bulletproof masks, all of whom have a chance for their heads to pop into a variety of deadly giant parasites, and there's a huge variety in combat encounters just from all the ways they can mix up groups of humans.

Monsters range from basic (albeit still creepy) infected dogs, to bestial giant bugs or the disturbingly humanoid Regenerators, bringing with them a host of unique mechanics such as camouflage or weak points only visible through an infrared scope. There's nearly a dozen unique bosses, most of whom are humans who've undergone grotesque mutations, and the reaches of creativity the devs reach with the body horror is nothing short of fantastically terrifying.

Nearly every enemy type has a number of unique reactions depending on where you shoot them, and both regular enemies and bosses have plenty of variety to their attacks, so everything feels like a genuine threat, and even the weakest of enemy types escape feeling like fodder. From the perspective of action shooters, this is a huge breath of fresh air compared to the genre's often one-track enemy designs.

Your own arsenal is likewise quite impressive. Most gun archetypes (e.g. pistol, shotgun) have 2-3 variants (even more, if you count NG+ unlocks), and rather than going for new guns being straight improvements, each new weapon is a sidegrade that brings new options to the table (such as a shotgun having tighter pellet spread). You're given frankly ridiculous amounts of inventory space, but this means you'll get the opportunity to try out plenty of weapon combinations to help keep combat interesting.

[h1]The Balance[/h1]

RE4 is much more actioney than survival-horrorey, and this is most apparent with how they balance the combat. The game quite literally throws over a thousand enemies at you over the course of the story, and you're given piles of ammo to deal with them, to the point that to actually run low you'd have to have some stupendously bad aim. For the most part it actually uses these large enemy counts quite effectively, using the enemy variety to constantly give you new and challenging encounters, often throwing in special environmental hazards (such as catapults, tripwire bombs, or bear traps) to further mix things up, and it manages to keep the pressure on without making you feel unfairly overwhelmed. It's a damn long game (my main save clocked 22 hours, but said time ignores time lost due to deaths), yet it never felt like it was dragging on due to the sheer amount of variation and solid challenge it had packed into it.

If I have some major complaints, there are a few areas where there's multiple waves of reinforcements that spawn, and such areas tend to slog on annoyingly, on top of the reinforcement spawning being so utterly wonky that -you can be inside of a room with only one entrance, facing the door, and enemies can phase into existence behind you-, but thankfully these encounters are few and far-between. Smaller encounters were sometimes blazingly easy due to human enemies being very simple to deal with if there's only 1-3 of them, and a number of the bosses have easy-to-discover cheeses (one basically can't hit you if you don't move from your starting position, and most of them can be instantly killed with an RPG), and even the ones that don't never reach particularly satisfying amounts of challenge.

Also Ashley is fine. Her pathfinding doesn't get stuck, enemies tend to pick her up to slowly walk towards exits rather than just kill her, and 9/10 times you can just have her stand in a corner or hide in a dumpster while you deal with enemies, plus she's not actually with you for much of the game. Overall I felt the need to change your strategies a bit to keep her safe actually helped add to the variety.

[h1]The Story[/h1]
 
It's like a cheesy B-movie, replete with silly one-liners and over-the-top acrobatics/explosions during the cutscenes, while still remaining just grounded enough that you can get invested in the cast. The plot is standard "stop the bad man from using virus for world domination" secret agent stuff, but having an original villain with their own ambitions who isn't involved with Umbrella is a welcome change.

[h1]The Graphics/Sound[/h1]

Though the color palette is pretty washed out, there's still an impressive variety of environments to explore, and the updated texture work of this version holds up nicely. Enemies have some fantastic modeling and animation, especially considering the game's age. Sound design isn't amazing, but neither is it bad by any means, and the soundtrack is pretty good, leaning more towards actioney orchestral tracks than spooky horror stuff.

[h1]In Closing[/h1]

At the end of the day, RE4 is far more an action shooter with survival-horror elements than the other way around. When I went in expecting the opposite I was disappointed, but once I started to play it for what it is it really grew on me. It was groundbreaking for its time, and this is still apparent in spite of the flaws age has made more apparent. If you're an RE fan it's an essential play, and still quite enjoyable if you want a change of pace compared to the modern conventions of either genre.

A very clever game - one that I was glad to overcome my aversion to horror games for.

RE4 builds well-balanced scenarios of suspense, action, and learning that tempt me to label it as a strategy game. Resource management and inventory organization get you more involved in shooting. Misses, reloads, and your immobility while aiming add a refreshing pressure to gunplay.

Combat encounters contain distinct points that reward player observation, foresight, and planning. A variety of weapons and upgrades ask you to make important decisions on how best to tackle the obstacles ahead.

Alongside this, there are plenty of unique set pieces that add flavor and memorable moments to each chapter. A few of these features can build off one another, but they never feel tiresomely recycled. This was a little stunning given that many games choose to get as much out of a segment as possible.

One serious pitfall for the game is its notorious placement of unexpected quick-time events during unassuming cutscenes. A few poorly placed QTE's can even totally kill you at the end of gameplay segments. You can learn to see them coming, but they do feel out of place.

Furthermore, RE4's tank controls, while integral to the game, can take some time to get used to. Despite movement initially feeling sluggish, RE4 can still be fast-paced with slower motions becoming obstacles to plan around.

The story balances a level of over-the-top action and cheesy voice acting with moments of intense and serious suspense. Overall, the narrative is part of what makes RE4 a treat to play through.

Even if horror games aren't your style, I'd urge you to play RE4. The game has visible traces of carefully designed elements and, as someone who spends too much time thinking about these things, it's great to see a game be so honest about how it operates.

[i]Side Note: There are plenty of different versions of RE4 out there. Given its accessibility, I stuck with the PC version although I am uncertain if it is considered the definitive edition. However, the chance to play the Wii version which operates quite differently.[/i]

Some games age like a fine wine, Resident Evil 4 has aged like milk, and the PC port in particular has turned to cottage cheese.

Resident Evil 4, considered both the savior and murderer of the survival horror genre. It injected fresh air into (at the time) a series that was still going strong yet was feeling somewhat formulaic in design by nearly completely changing how the game worked.

To really understand what is going on with RE4 you have to know its backstory in that it was remade several times in development, its early versions actually being repackaged and spawning other Capcom series like Devil May Cry and Haunting Ground. The problem from this isn't obvious but its clear those influences stayed in the final game, most prominently Devil May Cry's Campiness is all over RE4. 

The "cool" hero, sarcastically blowing away otherworldly horrors is deeply ingrained in the RE4 version of Leon, and frankly took away all horror from the game, why be afraid when my character isn't? Monsters that would ordinarily be horrifying end up being a joke, the only bosses that maintains any sense of horror are the ones that don't retain any human personality and thus Leon can't have a snarky retort with to take out the sense of danger, even if the danger is there.

The next major change that separates 4 from its brethren of the time was its full 3d transformation. Up until that point main entry REs were a 3d character over 2d environments, there were REs that went 3d before 4, but 4 was the first main entry. Because of this, I really attribute 4 to having "Final Fantasy 7" syndrome, graphically wowing people over at the time so people forgave its many flaws and mistakes. With the graphical changes also of course the gameplay would change to far more action orientated pace, gone was any fear of a single foe, it takes mobs to threaten Leon due to all the tools at leon's disposal, from grenades, many many guns, to the worst culprit of all, the counters. Melee countering is what makes Leon far too powerful to instill any fear in the game. When you can "counter waltz" from one enemy to the next to cross a map, you feel like a superhero, not a person fighting for their life.

The last major change/mistake is not necessarily the fault of game or Capcom, but rather a fad that was sweeping the industry at the time, the QTE or Quick Time Event. QTEs were a industry idea of trying to keep the player engaged even during cut scenes by putting in quick interactions that if you failed you died and had to retry. There's several things wrong with this thinking; "so you don't want me to watch the cutscene?" if you're always on edge waiting for a QTE you're not watching the cutscene in a normal manner that lets you absorb the story. Second problem is you die and retry, do you like seeing the first 30seconds of a cutscene over and over and over? Imagine if you were watching a movie and if you didn't press up on your remote when it said fast enough, you had to go through the opening credit crawl again again and again. Lastly, QTEs were used a lot for "press button for awesome" instead of the act of actually having to fight they would substitute QTEs for something that would be too hard to code into the game. So the character could QTE, do amazing action instead of you having to physically do the action, and the game looks "cool". There's a problem of feeling fake in this, you don't feel a genuine sense of victory.

So that's the major problems with RE4, now we get to the steam/PC version itself which is absolute garbage. "Port" describes this game perfect, barely any advanced options are present in the game, I was amazed mouse aim was even in even if its lacking. I had to edit config files to be able to turn with the mouse and thus make the game feel smooth and natural. There's also a very known issue that if you run the game at 60fps it makes some QTE actions essentially impossible cause it raises the threshold for how many button presses needed to an impossible to keep up with amount. You can fix this for dropping the frame rate down to 30 for these sections, which while this means you can reach the end of the game, its rather ♥♥♥♥♥♥.

Resident Evil 4 está ampliamente considerado como uno de los videojuegos de terror más impactantes y aclamados de todos los tiempos. Se lanzó por primera vez en 2005 para la consola Nintendo Gamecube, aunque desde entonces se ha reeditado y adaptado a diversas plataformas. 

Resident Evil 4 sigue al protagonista, el agente especial Leon S. Kennedy, en su misión de rescatar a la hija del presidente de los Estados Unidos, que ha sido secuestrada por una secta fanática. A medida que avanza el viaje, Leon se enfrenta a una serie de peligrosos y terrorificos enemigos. La trama está llena de giros inesperados, y el jugador estará enganchado hasta el final.

La jugabilidad de Resident Evil 4 es uno de sus puntos fuertes. El juego tiene un sistema de control en tercera persona que permite al usuario maniobrar y disparar con facilidad. Además, el juego introduce un mecanismo de puntería "inteligente" que permite al jugador apuntar a distintas secciones del cuerpo del enemigo para infligirle más daño. Esto añade cierto grado de estrategia a los combates y hace que el juego sea más interesante.

La ambientación y el diseño de niveles también son destacables. El juego se inspira en distintos lugares de Europa y Latinoamérica, y cada uno de ellos está repleto de características y escenarios que sumergen al jugador en la experiencia. Además, el diseño de los niveles es soberbio, con una gran variedad de escenarios que explorar.

Los gráficos siguen siendo excepcionales incluso después de más de 15 años desde su lanzamiento inicial. [b]Resident Evil 4[/b] is a survival horror game, though it replaces the survival part with action in the middle of the game. You play as Leon S. Kennedy, he got a new job as a special agent and his task is to find President's daughter. The intel says that she's being held by some strange cult in a god forgotten village in Spain, so you set out there and immediately get attacked by cultists, who behave a lot like zombies from the previous games. It's an engaging premise and the story has a lot of unexpected turns. It's more interesting than in the previous games, though this comes at price. 

The gameplay was changed in order to accomodate for a new story-based approach. So levels now are set in a linear order, no more exploring the same location and solving puzzles. Sometimes you comeback to the previously visited locations, but it doesn't feel like you're backtracking, because you are being led there by a game's story. Another big change from previous Resident Evil games, is that you have to actually aim your gun at the enemy. Shooting is done very well, enemies react to shots to different body parts and headshots feel statisfying. But this change also comes at a price, now there are a whole lot more zombies and most of the time you have to kill every single one of them. Then there's another controversial feature - QTE. Most of the cutscenes don't feature it, even though your character might fight someone in the cutscene, so most of the time you will put your controller aside while watching the movie, but there will be times when you have to press buttons in time or your character will die and you'll have to start over. It would have been better if they gave you warning before cutscene, that there will be QTEs or used it in every cutscene, so that you will always be waiting for it.

Switching from pre-rendered backgrounds to full 3d made the game look more modern, though most of the locations now feel the same. Copy-pasted houses and rooms can be seen with a naked eye. There aren't any memorable locations like in previous games, but that may be because of the graphics palette, everything looks gray and depressing. This makes for some dark creepy atmosphere. Voice acting is much better than in the previous games, but the dialogue feels badly written, though funny in way. 

[b]Pros:[/b]
+ Fun gunplay
+ Engaging story
+ Funny dialogue
+ Great action set pieces
+ Epic boss battles

[b]Cons:[/b]
- Unexpected and some unreasonably hard QTEs
- A lot of shooting, no way to run past enemies
